* 13 October: a global study of ~320,000 sleep-tracker users, published in the journal ''[[Sleep (journal)|Sleep]],'' found that high ambient temperatures (99th vs 50th percentile: 27.3 °C vs 12.2 °C) were associated with a mean sleep loss of approximately 15–17 minutes and a ~40 % increase in the probability of a short-sleep night.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lechat |first1=Bastien |last2=Toson |first2=Barbara |last3=Scott |first3=Hannah |last4=Nguyen |first4=Duc Phuc |last5=Kaambwa |first5=Billingsley |last6=Reynolds |first6=Amy C. |year=2025 |title=How do we sleep while our beds are burning? High ambient temperatures are associated with substantial sleep loss |journal=Sleep |volume=zsaf323 |issue=7 |article-number=zsaf323 |doi=10.1093/sleep/zsaf323|pmid=41081739 |doi-access=free |pmc=13357511 }}</ref>
* 16 October: the [[World Meteorological Organization]]'s ''Greenhouse Gas Bulletin'' reported that from 2023 to 2024, atmospheric carbon dioxide increased by 3.5 ppm, constituting the largest single-year increase since measurements began in 1957.<ref name=WMO_20251016>{{cite web |title=WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin |url=https://wmo.int/sites/default/files/2025-10/GHG-21_en.pdf |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251017023916/https://wmo.int/sites/default/files/2025-10/GHG-21_en.pdf |archive-date=17 October 2025 |date=16 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 28 October: ''[[The Lancet]]'' estimated that in 2022, 2.52 million deaths globally were attributable to ambient air pollution from burning fossil fuels.<ref name=Lancet_20251028>{{cite journal |last1=Romanello |first1=Marina |last2=Walawender |first2=Maria |last3=Hsu |first3=Shih-Che |last4=Moskeland |first4=Annalyse |last5=Palmeiro-Silva |first5=Yasna |display-authors=4 |title=The 2025 report of the ''Lancet'' Countdown on health and climate change  |journal=The Lancet |date=28 October 2025 |volume=406 |issue=10521 |pages=2804–2857 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(25)01919-1 |pmid=41175887 |url=https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/153624/1/The_2019_Report_of_the_Lancet_Countdown_revised.pdf }}</ref><!-- Must log in; could not archive -->
* 12 November: a report from [[Amnesty International]] said that at least 2 billion people, including 520 million children, live within {{convert|5|km|mi}} of fossil fuel infrastructure.<ref name=AmnestyIntl_20251012>{{cite web |title=Global: Fossil fuel infrastructure is putting rights of 2 billion people and critical ecosystems at risk |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2025/11/fossil-fuel-infrastructure-rights-critical-ecosystems-at-risk/ |publisher=Amnesty International |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115200022/https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2025/11/fossil-fuel-infrastructure-rights-critical-ecosystems-at-risk/ |archive-date=15 November 2025 |date=12 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 12 November: a report from the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) said that the remaining [[carbon budget]] to limit global warming to 1.5{{nbsp}}°C is "virtually exhausted"—equivalent to four years at 2025 emissions levels.<ref name=AAAS_20251112>{{cite web |title=Fossil fuel CO2 emissions hit record high in 2025 |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1104936 |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115205322/https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1104936 |archive-date=15 November 2025 |location=University of Exeter |date=12 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* May: an EIT Urban Mobility study of [[non-exhaust emissions]] published by the [[European Institute of Innovation and Technology]] said that because of [[regenerative braking]], electric vehicles produce ~83% less [[Disc_brake#Dust|brake dust]] than equivalent conventional vehicles, though their increased weight leads to 20% higher tire and road wear emissions.<ref name=EIT_202505>{{cite web |title=Study on Non-Exhaust Emissions in Road Transport |url=https://www.eiturbanmobility.eu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/41-EIT-Emissions-Report-5a-Digital-1.pdf |publisher=European Institute of Innovation and Technology |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250628031740/https://www.eiturbanmobility.eu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/41-EIT-Emissions-Report-5a-Digital-1.pdf |archive-date=28 June 2025 |pages=30, 49, 63 |date=May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 9 December: a report from the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network concluded that, from 1980 to 2024, Caribbean hard coral cover declined by 48%; and that, between 1985 and 2024, mean sea surface temperature over coral reef areas increased by +1.07{{nbsp}}°C.<ref name=GCRMN_20251209>{{cite web |last1=Acosta-Chaparro |first1=Andrés Felipe |last2=Agudo-Adriani |first2=Esteban |last3=Aguilera Pérez |first3=Gabriela |last4=Alegría |first4=Andrés B. |last5=Alemu i |first5=Jahson B. |last6=Allen |first6=Mary |last7=Alonso-Carvajal |first7=David Alejandro |last8=Alvarado Barrientos |first8=Juan José |last9=Alvarez-Filip |first9=Lorenzo |last10=Anderson |first10=Louise |last11=Anderson |first11=Robert |last12=Anseeuw |first12=Shamwari |last13=Aponte |first13=Maria G. |last14=Appeldoorn Sanders |first14=Eric |last15=Arbona Fernández |first15=Melissa |last16=Arias Isaza |first16=Francisco |last17=Arias-Gonzalez |first17=Jesus Ernesto |last18=Ascanio |first18=Alfredo |last19=Bak |first19=Rolf P.M. |last20=Balza |first20=Robert |last21=Beets |first21=James |last22=Berger |first22=Aude |last23=Bervoets |first23=Tadzio |last24=Bidenbach |first24=Hadrien |last25=Blanco-Pimentel |first25=Macarena |last26=Bodmer |first26=Max |last27=Bon |first27=Mélanie |last28=Bonnardel |first28=Clément |last29=Bordin |first29=Amandine |last30=Bouchon |first30=Claude |display-authors=1 |editor-first1=Jérémy |editor-first2=Laëtitia |editor-first3=Auriane |editor-first4=Andrea |editor-first5=Melanie |editor-last1=Wicquart |editor-last2=Mathon |editor-last3=Petit |editor-last4=Rivera-Sosa |editor-last5=McField |title=Status & Trends of Caribbean Coral Reefs: 1970-2024 |url=https://gcrmn.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/gcrmn_caribbean_2025_low-res.pdf |publisher=Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN), International Coral Reef Initiative (ICRI) |doi=10.59387/BDHF9180 |date=9 December 2025 |page=10 }}</ref>
* 9 January 2026: a report published in ''[[Advances in Atmospheric Sciences]]'' said that [[ocean heat content]] in 2025 had reached a new record for nine consecutive years.<ref name=AdvAtmosSci_20260109>Pan, Y., Cheng, L., Abraham, J. ''et al.'' {{cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=Yuying |last2=Cheng |first2=Lijing |last3=Abraham |first3=John |last4=Trenberth |first4=Kevin E. |last5=Reagan |first5=James |last6=Du |first6=Juan |last7=Wang |first7=Zhankun |last8=Storto |first8=Andrea |last9=von Schuckmann |first9=Karina |last10=Zhu |first10=Yujing |last11=Mann |first11=Michael E. |last12=Zhu |first12=Jiang |last13=Wang |first13=Fan |last14=Yu |first14=Fujiang |last15=Locarnini |first15=Ricardo |last16=Fasullo |first16=John |last17=Huang |first17=Boyin |last18=Graham |first18=Garrett |last19=Yin |first19=Xungang |last20=Gouretski |first20=Viktor |last21=Zheng |first21=Fei |last22=Li |first22=Yuanlong |last23=Zhang |first23=Bin |last24=Wan |first24=Liying |last25=Chen |first25=Xingrong |last26=Wang |first26=Dakui |last27=Feng |first27=Licheng |last28=Song |first28=Xiangzhou |last29=Liu |first29=Yulong |last30=Reseghetti |first30=Franco |display-authors=1 |title=Ocean Heat Content Sets Another Record in 2025 |journal=Advances in Atmospheric Sciences |date=9 January 2026 |volume=43 |issue=10 |page=6737 |doi=10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0 |bibcode=2026AdAtS..43.2019P |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 22 January 2026: [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]]'s ''European Electricity Review 2026'' reported that in 2025, wind and solar energy provided 30% of EU electricity, surpassing fossil power (29%) for the first time, and generating more power than fossil sources in 14 of 27 EU countries.<ref name=Ember_20260122>{{cite web |title=European Electricity Review 2026 |url=https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/01/EMBER-Report-European-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |publisher=Ember |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260123173500/https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/01/EMBER-Report-European-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |archive-date=23 January 2026 |date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 21 April 2026: [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]]'s ''Global Electricity Review 2026'' said that, in 2025, clean power growth exceeded the rise in overall global electricity demand (fossil fuel generation declining), and that renewables overtook coal power.<ref name=Ember_20260421>{{cite web |title=Global Electricity Review 2026 |url=https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/04/Global-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |publisher=Ember Energy |page=8 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260424062124/https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/04/Global-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |archive-date=24 April 2026 |date=21 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 28 July 2026: risk assessor First Street's ''Global Severe Convective Storm Risk Pricing Economic Exposure to a Rising Peril'' stated that cumulative insured losses from severe convective storms (SCS)—hail, damaging straight-line winds, tornadoes, and severe thunderstorms—overtook that of tropical cyclones, with $82 billion in economic losses and constituting nearly one-third of all natural catastrophe losses worldwide in 2025.<ref name=FirstStreet_202607>{{cite web |title=Global Severe Convective Storm Risk / Pricing Economic Exposure to a Rising Peril |url=https://hubspot.firststreet.org/hubfs/Research%20Reports/First%20Street%2019th%20Risk%20Assessment%20Global%20SCS%20Risk.pdf |publisher=First Street |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729052758/https://hubspot.firststreet.org/hubfs/Research%20Reports/First%20Street%2019th%20Risk%20Assessment%20Global%20SCS%20Risk.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2026 |date=July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Natural events and phenomena==
* 1 January: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that faster flow of the [[Antarctic Circumpolar Current]] (ACC) at higher latitudes causes upwelling of isotopically light deep waters around Antarctica, likely increasing [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|atmospheric carbon dioxide]] levels and thereby potentially constituting a critical [[positive feedback]] for future warming.<ref name=SciAdvances_20250101>{{cite journal |last1=Starr |first1=Aidan |last2=Hall |first2=Ian R. |last3=Barker |first3=Stephen |last4=Nederbragt |first4=Alexandra |last5=Owen |first5=Lindsey |last6=Hemming |first6=Sidney R. |title=Shifting Antarctic Circumpolar Current south of Africa over the past 1.9 million years |journal=Science Advances |date=1 January 2025 |volume=11 |issue=1 |article-number=eadp1692 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adp1692|pmid=39742497 |pmc=11691690 |bibcode=2025SciA...11P1692S }}</ref>
* 6 January: a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' stated that a [[Pathogenic fungus|fungal pathogen]] (''[[Entomophaga maimaiga]])'' that had successfully controlled the  defoliation of the [[Lymantria dispar|spongy moth]] in [[North America]]n forests was becoming less effective due to climate change producing hotter, drier conditions. The study predicts this will lead to significantly decreased forest [[biodiversity]] and productivity by spongy moths, evidenced by recent increases in defoliation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Jiawei |last2=Kyle |first2=Colin |last3=Wang |first3=Jiali |last4=Kotamarthi |first4=Rao |last5=Koval |first5=William |last6=Dukic |first6=Vanja |last7=Dwyer |first7=Greg |date=2025-01-06 |title=Climate change drives reduced biocontrol of the invasive spongy moth |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-024-02204-x |journal=Nature Climate Change |volume=15 |issue=2 |language=en |pages=210–217 |doi=10.1038/s41558-024-02204-x |bibcode=2025NatCC..15..210L |issn=1758-6798|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* 7 January: NOAA's ''[[Arctic Report Card]] 2024'' reported that, including the impact of increased wildfires, the [[Tundra#Arctic|Arctic tundra]] region had shifted from [[carbon sink|storing carbon in the soil]] to becoming a carbon dioxide [[Greenhouse gas emissions|source]], and that the Arctic remained a consistent source of methane—both adding to planet-warming greenhouse gases in the air.<ref name=NOAA_20250107>Moon, Twila A.;Druckenmiller, Matthew L.;Thoman, Richard L., editors. {{cite journal |last1=Moon |first1=Twila A. |last2=Druckenmiller |first2=Matthew L. |last3=Thoman |first3=Richard L. |title=Arctic Report Card 2024 |journal=Noaa Technical Report Oar Arc ; 24-01 (Arctic Report Card) |date=2024 |url=https://arctic.noaa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ArcticReportCard_full_report2024.pdf |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250311065209/https://arctic.noaa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ArcticReportCard_full_report2024.pdf |archive-date=11 March 2025 |doi=10.25923/b7c7-6431 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 8 January: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that one-quarter of 23,496 decapod [[crustacean]]s, fishes and [[Odonata|odonates]] studied, some of which provide climate change mitigation, are threatened with extinction.<ref name=Nature_20250108/> One-fifth of threatened freshwater species are affected by climate change and severe weather events.<ref name=Nature_20250108>{{cite journal |last1=Sayer |first1=Catherine A. |last2=Fernando |first2=Eresha |last3=Jiminez |first3=Randall R. |last4=Macfarlane |first4=Micholas B. W. |title=One-quarter of freshwater fauna threatened with extinction |journal=Nature |date=8 January 2025 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-08375-z |display-authors=3|volume=638 |issue=8049 |pages=138–145 |doi-access=free |pmid=39779863 |pmc=11798842 |bibcode=2025Natur.638..138S }}</ref>
* 9 January: a study published in ''[[Nature Reviews Earth & Environment]]'' estimated that since the mid-twentieth century, global-averaged 3-month and 12-month "hydroclimate whiplash" events have increased by 31–66% and 8–31%, respectively.<ref name=NatRvwEandE_20250109/> Such increases amplify hazards associated with rapid swings between wet and dry states, including flash floods, wildfires, landslides and disease outbreaks.<ref name=NatRvwEandE_20250109/> (''Hydroclimate volatility'' refers to "sudden, large and/or frequent transitions between very dry and very wet conditions".)<ref name=NatRvwEandE_20250109>{{cite journal |last1=Swain |first1=Daniel L. |last2=Prein |first2=Andreas F. |last3=Abatzoglou |first3=John T. |last4=Albano |first4=Christine M. |last5=Brunner |first5=Manuela |last6=Diffenbaugh |first6=Noah S. |last7=Singh |first7=Deepti |last8=Skinner |first8=Christopher B. |last9=Touma |first9=Danielle |display-authors=4 |title=Hydroclimate volatility on a warming Earth |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |date=9 January 2025 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=35–50 |doi=10.1038/s43017-024-00624-z|bibcode=2025NRvEE...6...35S |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/14m8f2j7 }}</ref>
* 15 January: a study published in ''[[Weather (journal)|Weather]]'' reported that the terrestrial biosphere's rate of natural carbon dioxide [[carbon sequestration|sequestration]] has fallen since its 2008 peak at a rate of 0.25% per year, a decline that will accelerate climate change.<ref name=Weather_20250115>{{cite journal |last1=Curran |first1=James C. |last2=Curran |first2=Samuel A. |title=Natural sequestration of carbon dioxide is in decline: climate change will accelerate |journal=Weather |date=15 January 2025 |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=85–87 |doi=10.1002/wea.7668|bibcode=2025Wthr...80...85C |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 16 January: an interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary study published in ''[[Communications Earth & Environment]]'' identified five key hazards of [[permafrost]] thaw: infrastructure failure, disruption of mobility and supplies, decreased water quality, challenges for food security, and exposure to diseases and contaminants.<ref name=CommsEandE_20250116>{{cite journal |last1=Gargler |first1=Susanna |last2=Scheer |first2=Johanna |last3=Meyer |first3=Alexandra |last4=Abass |first4=Khaled |last5=Bartsch |first5=Annett |last6=Doloisio |first6=Natalia |display-authors=4 |title=A transdisciplinary, comparative analysis reveals key risks from Arctic permafrost thaw |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=16 January 2025 |volume=6 |issue=21 |article-number=21 |doi=10.1038/s43247-024-01883-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=39830898 |pmc=11738985 |bibcode=2025ComEE...6...21G }}</ref>
* 21 January: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' reported an "abrupt, coherent, climate-driven transformation" from "blue" (more transparent) to "brown" (less transparent) states of lakes in [[Greenland]] after a season of both record heat and rainfall drove a [[Tipping points in the climate system|state change]] in these systems.<ref name=PNAS_20250121/> This change was said to alter "numerous physical, chemical, and biological lake features", and the state changes were said to be unprecedented.<ref name=PNAS_20250121>{{cite journal |last1=Saros |first1=Jasmine E. |last2=Hazukova |first2=Vaclava |last3=Northington |first3=Robert M. |last4=McGowan |first4=Suzanne |title=Abrupt transformation of West Greenland lakes following compound climate extremes associated with atmospheric rivers |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=21 January 2025 |volume=122 |issue=4 |article-number=e2413855122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2413855122 |doi-access=free |pmid=39835905 |pmc=11789078 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12213855S }}</ref>
* February: though [[polar bear]]s and [[grizzly bear]]s traditionally occupy distinct habitats (marine and land), arctic warming has forced polar bears inland into grizzly bear habitats, where the two species mate to produce hybrid "[[Grizzly–polar bear hybrid|grolar bears]]" that have characteristics poorly adapted to either marine or land habitats.<ref name=MSN_20250222>{{cite news |last1=Cook |first1=Chelsea |title=Scientists' stunning observation of hybrid 'grolar' bear sparks concern: 'Ill-suited to adapt' |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/weather/topstories/scientists-stunning-observation-of-hybrid-grolar-bear-sparks-concern-ill-suited-to-adapt/ar-AA1zAx50 |publisher=MSN |date=22 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250226030647/https://www.msn.com/en-us/weather/topstories/scientists-stunning-observation-of-hybrid-grolar-bear-sparks-concern-ill-suited-to-adapt/ar-AA1zAx50 |archive-date=26 February 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 4 February: a study published in ''[[Environmental Research Letters]]'' concluded that, in addition to the [[2023 Caribbean heat wave|2023 marine heat wave]], an extensive [[river plume]] caused a ~{{convert|10|-|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} thick strongly stratified barrier layer that contributed to [[Hurricane Idalia]]'s rapid intensification (Category 1 to Category 4 in less than 24 hours).<ref name="EnvRschLtrs_20250204">{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Jing |last2=Hu |first2=Chuanmin |last3=Cannizzaro |first3=Jennifer |last4=Barnes |first4=Brian |last5=Zhang |first5=Yingjun |last6=Lembke |first6=Chad |last7=Le Henaff |first7=Matthieu |date=4 February 2025 |title=Intensification of Hurricane Idalia by a river plume in the eastern Gulf of Mexico |journal=Environmental Research Letters |volume=20 |issue=24050 |page=024050 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/adad8a |bibcode=2025ERL....20b4050S |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* 21 February: a study published in ''[[List of Nature Research journals#npj series|npj Natural Hazards]]'' unified studies of climatic trends and of [[wildland–urban interface]] (WUI) expansion, and concluded that climatic factors increased the frequency of high-risk fire weather by a factor of 2.5, and that the combination of climatic factors with WUI expansion led to a 4.1-fold increase in the frequency of conditions conducive to extreme-impact wildfires from 1990 to 2022 across California.<ref name=NatHazards_20250221>{{cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Mukesh |last2=AghaKouchak |first2=Amir |last3=Abatzoglou |first3=John T. |last4=Sadesh |first4=Mojtaba |title=Compounding effects of climate change and WUI expansion quadruple the likelihood of extreme-impact wildfires in California |journal=npj Natural Hazards |date=21 February 2025 |volume=2 |issue=17 |article-number=17 |doi=10.1038/s44304-025-00067-6|bibcode=2025npjNH...2...17K |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 26 February: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (AMOC) is resilient to extreme greenhouse gas and North Atlantic freshwater forcings across 34 climate models, suggesting that an AMOC collapse is unlikely in the 21st century.<ref name=Nature_20250226/>
* 26 February: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that short-, mid-, and long-term ambient outdoor heat can significantly accelerate [[Epigenetics|epigenetic]] [[ageing|aging]] in older adults.<ref name=SciAdvances_20250226>{{cite journal |last1=Choi |first1=Eun Young |last2=Ailshire |first2=Jennifer A. |title=Ambient outdoor heat and accelerated epigenetic aging among older adults in the US |journal=Science Advances |date=26 February 2025 |volume=11 |issue=9 |article-number=eadr0616 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adr0616 |pmid=40009659 |bibcode=2025SciA...11R.616C |pmc=11864172 }}</ref>
* 5 March: a study published in ''[[Geophysical Research Letters]]'' concluded that redistribution of mass caused by melting of ice sheets and glaciers will shift the Earth's rotational poles from {{convert|12-27|m|ft}} by 2100, depending on the degree of future global warming.<ref name=GeoRschLtrs_20250305/> Changing Earth's rotational axis affects spacecraft navigation and orientation of deep space telescopes.<ref name=GeoRschLtrs_20250305>{{cite journal |last1=Shahvandi |first1=Mostafa Kiani |last2=Soja |first2=Benedikt |title=Climate-Induced Polar Motion: 1900–2100 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=5 March 2025 |volume=52 |issue=5 |article-number=e2024GL113405 |doi=10.1029/2024GL113405|bibcode=2025GeoRL..5213405K |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 10 March: a study published in ''[[Nature Sustainability]]'' projected that climate change's cooling of the atmosphere occupied by [[space debris]] in [[low Earth orbit]] will reduce the atmosphere's drag on the debris, extending the debris' lifetime and potentially causing a 50–66% reduction in [[satellite]] carrying capacity at altitudes {{convert|200|-|1000|km|mi|abbr=on}}.<ref name=NatureSust_20250311>{{cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=William E. |last2=Brown |first2=Matthew K. |last3=Linares |first3=Richard |title=Greenhouse gases reduce the satellite carrying capacity of low Earth orbit |journal=Nature Sustainability |date=10 March 2025 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=363–372 |doi=10.1038/s41893-025-01512-0|bibcode=2025NatSu...8..363P |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 19 March: an article published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' said that two major natural events occurred at the end of the last ice age: around 10,300 and 8,300 years ago, sea levels surged rapidly due to meltwater releases from the North American and Antarctic ice sheets, with peak rates of sea-level rise reaching nearly 9&nbsp;mm/year — comparable to projections for the year 2100 under high-emissions scenarios.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Khan |first=Nicole S. |date=19 March 2025 |title=Ancient peat reveals that sea level surged rapidly twice at the end of the last ice age |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-00800-1 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=639 |issue=8055 |pages=580–582 |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-00800-1 |pmid=40108316 |bibcode=2025Natur.639..580K |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* 25 March: an article published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' said that volcanic eruptions over the past 603 years have significantly impacted the strength and tilt of the Atlantic jet stream, which in turn influenced extreme weather events in Europe. These jet stream shifts contributed to increased droughts when moving north and heightened flood risks when shifting south.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dannenberg |first1=Matthew P. |last2=Wise |first2=Erika K. |date=25 March 2025 |title=How the Atlantic jet stream has changed in 600 years — and what it means for weather |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-00871-0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=640 |issue=8057 |pages=39–40 |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-00871-0 |pmid=40133451 |bibcode=2025Natur.640...39D |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* 10 April: [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]] published a statement that after a few months of [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation#La Niña phase|La Niña]] conditions, the tropical Pacific was [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|ENSO]]-neutral and was likely to remain so through autumn, stating the most recent La Niña phase was very brief.<ref name=NOAA_20250410>{{cite web |title=April 2025 ENSO update: La Niña has ended |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/april-2025-enso-update-la-nina-has-ended |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |last1=Becker |first1=Emily |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250410220328/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/april-2025-enso-update-la-nina-has-ended |archive-date=10 April 2025 |date=10 April 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 21 April: NOAA confirmed the Earth was experiencing its [[2023–2025 global coral bleaching event|fourth global coral bleaching event]], which it called the biggest to date: from 1 January 2023 to 20 April 2025, bleaching-level heat stress had impacted 83.7% of the world's coral reef area, and mass coral bleaching had been documented in at least 83 countries and territories.<ref name=NOAA_20250421>{{cite web |title=Current Global Bleaching: Status Update & Data Submission |url=https://www.coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/research/coral_bleaching_report.php |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423145045/https://www.coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/research/coral_bleaching_report.php |archive-date=23 April 2025 |date=21 April 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 30 April: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' described how melting of [[sea ice]] caused by global warming allows increased areas of open water—which passes a narrower spectrum of light than the smooth continuum of frequencies passed by sea ice—to "cause major changes in both the pigment and species composition of primary producers in polar ecosystems".<ref name=NatureComms_20250430/> These changes affect [[photosynthesis]] in ocean [[phytoplankton]].<ref name=NatureComms_20250430>{{cite journal |last1=Soja-Woźniak |first1=Monika |last2=Holtrop |first2=Tadzio |last3=Woutersen |first3=Sander |last4=van der Woerd |first4=Hendrik Jan |last5=Lund-Hansen |first5=Lars Chresten |last6=Huisman |first6=Jef |title=Loss of sea ice alters light spectra for aquatic photosynthesis |journal=Nature Communications |date=30 April 2025 |volume=16 |issue=1 |article-number=4059 |doi=10.1038/s41467-025-59386-x |doi-access=free|pmid=40307241 |pmc=12043827 |bibcode=2025NatCo..16.4059S }}</ref>
* 31 March: a study published in the [[American Geophysical Union]]'s ''[[Journal of Geophysical Research|JGR Oceans]]'' said that most climate model simulations project a decline or disappearance of the [[Beaufort Gyre]] before 2100, so that the gyre region would no longer accumulate freshwater, thus impacting oceanic properties in the Arctic and North Atlantic..<ref name=AGU_20250331>{{cite journal |last1=Athanase |first1=Marylou |last2=Köhler |first2=Raphael |last3=Heuzé |first3=Céline |last4=Lévine |first4=Xavier |last5=Williams |first5=Ryan |title=The Arctic Beaufort Gyre in CMIP6 Models: Present and Future |journal= Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans|date=31 March 2025 |volume=130 |issue=4 |article-number=e2024JC021873 |doi=10.1029/2024JC021873|bibcode=2025JGRC..13021873A |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 6 May: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' concluded that [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|glacial melt]] is accelerated even when ocean temperatures are constant, a phenomenon caused when cold fresh [[meltwater]] rushing from beneath [[glacier]]s creates upward turbulence, drawing in warm ocean water from below.<ref name=NatureComms_20250506>{{cite journal |last1=Prakash |first1=Abhay |last2=Zhou |first2=Qin |last3=Hattermann |first3=Tore |last4=Kirchner |first4=Nina |title=Enhanced subglacial discharge amplifies Petermann Ice Shelf melting when ocean thermal forcing saturates |journal=Nature Communications |date=6 May 2025 |volume=16 |issue=4213 |article-number=4213 |doi=10.1038/s41467-025-59469-9  |doi-access=free|pmid=40328747 |pmc=12056069 |bibcode=2025NatCo..16.4213P }}</ref>
* 8 May: NOAA's April 2025 U.S. Climate Report documented a slow-moving storm system that brought over 150 tornadoes to the South and Midwest, resulting in at least 24 fatalities and widespread flooding. This event underscores the increasing frequency of severe convective storms in a warming climate.<ref>{{cite web |last1=National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) |title=Assessing the U.S. Climate in April 2025 |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202504 |website=National Centers for Environmental Information |date=8 May 2025 |publisher=NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) |access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref>
* 20 May: a study published in ''[[Communications Earth & Environment]]'' concluded that merely maintaining a global average temperature of +1.5{{nbsp}}°C is inadequate to avoid extensive loss and damage to coastal populations in coming centuries, and hypothesized that "+1{{nbsp}}°C above pre-industrial, possibly even lower" is required to avoid such loss and damage.<ref name=CommsEandE_20250520 />
* 31 May: a study published in ''[[Communications Earth & Environment]]'' suggested that as [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|glacial melt]] exposes soil, glacial meltwater's net sequestration of carbon dioxide gives way to water from exposed soil that enhances methane and carbon dioxide production, switching from a negative to positive warming feedback.<ref name=NatureCommsEandE_20250531>{{cite journal |last1=Pain |first1=A. J. |last2=Martin |first2=J. B. |last3=Martin |first3=E. E. |last4=Salinas-Reyes |first4=J. T. |last5=Bennett |first5=C. |title=Glacial retreat converts exposed landscapes from net carbon sinks to sources |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=31 May 2025 |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=424 |doi=10.1038/s43247-025-02404-z |bibcode=2025ComEE...6..424P |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 9 June: a study published in ''[[Global Change Biology]]'' suggested that by 2020, global [[ocean acidification|ocean acidity conditions]] had already crossed into the [[:File:PBs2023.png|uncertainty range]] of the [[Planetary boundaries|Planetary Boundary Framework]].<ref name=GlobalChangeBiology_20250609>{{cite journal |last1=Findlay |first1=Helen S. |last2=Feely |first2=Richard A. |last3=Jiang |first3=Li-Qing |last4=Pelletier |first4=Greg |last5=Bednaršek |first5=Nina |title=Ocean Acidification: Another Planetary Boundary Crossed |journal=Global Change Biology |date=9 June 2025 |volume=31 |issue=6 |article-number=e70238 |doi=10.1111/gcb.70238 |pmid=40485607 |pmc=12147064 |bibcode=2025GCBio..3170238F }} <!-- URL provided because doi wasn't working as of 10 June 2025 --></ref>
* 16 June: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' reported a tripling in the past half-century of the number of [[Rossby wave|planetary wave events]] caused by quasi-resonant amplification (QRA).<ref name=PNAS_20250616/> Such wave events underlie extreme weather events such as heatwaves, flooding, wildfires, and heat dome events.<ref name=PNAS_20250616>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Xueke |last2=Mann |first2=Michael E. |last3=Wehner |first3=Michael F. |last4=Christiansen |first4=Shannon |title=Increased frequency of planetary wave resonance events over the past half-century |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=16 June 2025 |volume=122 |issue=25 |article-number=e2504482122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2504482122 |doi-access=free |pmid=40523169 |pmc=12207419 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12204482L }}</ref>
* 7 July: findings in a study published in  ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' suggested that current Earth system models overestimate the ability of [[Northern Hemisphere|northern]] [[temperate forest]]s to absorb carbon, because the models do not consider the impacts of shrinking snowpack and increased soil freeze/thaw cycles.<ref name=PNAS_20250707>{{cite journal |last1=Conrad-Rooney |first1=Emerson |last2=Reinmann |first2=Andrew B. |last3=Templer |first3=Pamela H. |title=Declining winter snowpack offsets carbon storage enhancement from growing season warming in northern temperate forest ecosystems |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=7 July 2025 |volume=122 |issue=28 |article-number=e2412873122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2412873122 |doi-access=free |pmid=40623184 |pmc=12280935 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12212873C }}</ref>
* 14 July: a study published in ''[[Communications Earth & Environment]]'' said that accelerated East Asian reduction in aerosol emissions unmasks greenhouse gas-driven warming, enough to be a main driver of the accelerated global warming since 2010.<ref name=CommsEandE_20250714>{{cite journal |last1=Samset |first1=Bjorn H. |last2=Wilcox |first2=Laura J. |last3=Allen |first3=Robert J. |last4=Stjern |first4=Camilla W. |last5=Lund |first5=Marianne T. |display-authors=4 |title=East Asian aerosol cleanup has likely contributed to the recent acceleration in global warming |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=14 July 2025 |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=543 |doi=10.1038/s43247-025-02527-3  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2025ComEE...6..543S |hdl=10138/601627 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 5 August: a study published in ''[[Geophysical Research Letters]]'' concluded that a slowdown in the rate of [[Arctic sea ice decline]] since 2005 is largely due to natural climate variation.<ref name=GeoRschLtr_20250805/> The study forecast that the slowdown could continue for another five to ten years, although a faster-than-average sea ice decline would be more likely thereafter.<ref name=GeoRschLtr_20250805>{{cite journal |last1=England |first1=M. R. |last2=Polvani |first2=L. M. |last3=Screen |first3=J. |last4=Chan |first4=A. C. |title=Minimal Arctic Sea Ice Loss in the Last 20 Years, Consistent With Internal Climate Variability |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=5 August 2025 |volume=52 |issue=15 |article-number=e2025GL116175 |doi=10.1029/2025GL116175|bibcode=2025GeoRL..5216175E |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 10 August (occurrence of megatsunami): a study published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' concluded that climate change had "preconditioned" a >64{{nbsp}}million cubic meter [[landslide]] in Alaska's [[Tracy Arm]] fjord that caused a 481-meter [[Tsunami#Tsunami_heights|run-up]] [[megatsunami]] after an initial 100-meter high [[breaking wave]] traveling at over {{convert|70|m/s|mph}}.<ref name=Science_20260506>{{cite journal |last1=Shugar |first1=Dan H. |last2=Barnhart |first2=Katherine R. |last3=Berdahl |first3=Mira |last4=Caplan-Auerbach |first4=Jacqueline |last5=Ekstrom |first5=Goran |last6=Fathian |first6=Aram |display-authors=4 |title=A 481-meter-high landslide-tsunami in a cruise ship–frequented Alaska fjord |journal=Science |date=6 May 2026 |volume=392 |issue=6803 |article-number=eaec3187 |doi=10.1126/science.aec3187 |pmid=42089535 |bibcode=2026Sci...392c3187S |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 2 September: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' reported that the [[Gulf of Panama]]'s seasonal [[upwelling]] failed in early 2025, breaking a >40-year record of reliability, which the researchers said "underscores how climate disruption can threaten wind-driven tropical upwelling systems".<ref name=PNAS_20250902>{{cite journal |last1=O'Dea |first1=Aaron |last2=Sellers |first2=Andrew J. |last3=Perez-Medina |first3=Carmen |last4=Diaz |first4=Javier Pardo |last5=Bloise |first5=Alexandra Buzman |last6=Pohlker |first6=Christopher |last7=Chilinski |first7=Michal t. |last8=Aardema |first8=Hedy M. |last9=Cybulski |first9=Jonathan D. |last10=Heins |first10=Lena |last11=Paton |first11=Steven R. |last12=Slagter |first12=Hans A. |last13=Schiebel |first13=Ralf |last14=Haug |first14=Gerald H. |display-authors=4 |title=Unprecedented suppression of Panama's Pacific upwelling in 2025 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=2 September 2025 |volume=122 |issue=36 |article-number=e2512056122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2512056122|pmid=40892925 |pmc=12435233 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12212056O |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 10 September: a study published in ''[[Aerospace (journal)|Aerospace]]'' assessed how a warming atmosphere could reduce aircraft [[Angle of climb|climb angles]] by 2035–2064 and concluded that the number of people affected by aircraft-generated noise pollution could increase by up to 4%, and that the effects are maximised for the most damaging and psychologically annoying (low) frequencies.<ref name=Aerospace_20250910>{{cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=Jonny |last2=Williams |first2=Paul D. |last3=Venturini |first3=Marco |last4=Padhra |first4=Anil |last5=Gratton |first5=Guy |last6=Rapsomanikis |first6=Spyridon |title=The Impacts of Climate Change on Aircraft Noise near European Airports |journal=Aerospace |date=10 September 2025 |volume=12 |issue=9 |page=815 |doi=10.3390/aerospace12090815 |bibcode=2025Aeros..12..815W |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 18 September: the [[World Meteorological Organization]]'s ''State of Global Water Resources Report 2024'' concluded that only one third of [[Drainage basin|river basin]]s had normal [[hydrology|hydrological]] conditions in 2024, and that all glacier regions lost ice for third straight year.<ref name=WMOwater_20250918>{{cite web |title=State of Global Water Resources 2024 |url=https://wmo.int/publication-series/state-of-global-water-resources-2024 |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250918122953/https://wmo.int/publication-series/state-of-global-water-resources-2024 |archive-date=18 September 2025 |date=18 September 2025 |url-status=live}} ([https://library.wmo.int/viewer/69629/download?file=WMO-1380-2025_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1 download full report])</ref>
* 24 September: a report from the [[Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research]] assessed that the Ocean Acidification Boundary had been breached for the first time, with ocean acidity entering its danger zone—the seventh of nine [[Planetary boundaries|critical Earth system boundaries]] to have been exceeded.<ref name=PotsdamInst_20250924>{{cite web |title=Seven of nine planetary boundaries now breached – ocean acidification joins the danger zone |url=https://www.pik-potsdam.de/en/news/latest-news/seven-of-nine-planetary-boundaries-now-breached-2013-ocean-acidification-joins-the-danger-zone |publisher=Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250925083655/https://www.pik-potsdam.de/en/news/latest-news/seven-of-nine-planetary-boundaries-now-breached-2013-ocean-acidification-joins-the-danger-zone |archive-date=25 September 2025 |date=24 September 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 15 October: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that Australian rainforests had transitioned from [[carbon sink]] (on balance, removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere) to carbon source (on balance, adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere).<ref name=Nature_20251015>{{cite journal |last1=Carle |first1=Hannah |last2=Bauman |first2=David |last3=Evans |first3=Michael N. |last4=Coughlin |first4=Ingrid |last5=Binks |first5=Oliver |last6=Ford |first6=Andrew |last7=Bradford |first7=Matthew |last8=Nicotra |first8=Adrienne |last9=Murphy |first9=Helen |last10=Meir |first10=Patrick |display-authors=4 |title=Aboveground biomass in Australian tropical forests now a net carbon source |journal=Nature |date=15 October 2025 |volume=646 |issue=8085 |pages=611–618 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09497-8 |pmid=41094245 |bibcode=2025Natur.646..611C |url=https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/0873e13c-73c9-491c-846c-fde91672a40d |hdl=20.500.11820/0873e13c-73c9-491c-846c-fde91672a40d |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 15 October: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that global sea-level rise rates since 1900 are faster than in any century over at least the past four millennia, with human activities causing over 94% of observed urban subsidence in southeastern China.<ref name=Nature_20251015_Lin>{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Yucheng |last2=Kopp |first2=Robert E. |last3=Xiong |first3=Haixian |last4=Hibbert |first4=Fiona D. |last5=Zheng |first5=Zhuo |last6=Yu |first6=Fengling |last7=Kumar |first7=Praveen |last8=Dangendorf |first8=Sönke |last9=Yi |first9=Hailin |last10=Zhang |first10=Yaze |display-authors=4 |title=Modern sea-level rise breaks 4,000-year stability in southeastern China |journal=Nature |date=15 October 2025 |volume=646 |issue=8086 |pages=856–864 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09600-z|pmid=41094134 |pmc=12545208 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 28 November: a study published in ''[[Scientific Reports]]'' reported that between 2010 and 2017, Africa’s forests and woody savannas transitioned from being a [[carbon sink]] to a [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon source]], a transition largely attributed to [[deforestation]].<ref name=NatureSciReports_20251128>{{cite journal |last1=Rodríguez-Veiga |first1=Pedro |last2=Carreiras |first2=Joao M. B. |display-authors=1 |title=Loss of tropical moist broadleaf forest has turned Africa's forests from a carbon sink into a source |journal=Scientific Reports |date=28 November 2025 |volume=15 |issue=1 |article-number=41744 |doi=10.1038/s41598-025-27462-3 |doi-access=free|pmid=41315646 |pmc=12663118 |bibcode=2025NatSR..1541744R }}</ref>
* 8 December: a study published in the ''[[Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry]]'' concluded that children exposed to average maximum temperatures above {{convert|32|C|F}} were less likely to be developmentally on track compared to those exposed to cooler temperatures, with  literacy and numeracy skills being most affected.<ref name=JournalChildPsych_20251208>{{cite journal |last1=Cuartas |first1=Jorge |last2=Balza |first2=Lenin H. |last3=Camacho |first3=Andrés |last4=Gómez-Parra |first4=Nicolás |title=Ambient heat and early childhood development: a cross-national analysis |journal=The Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry |date=8 December 2025 |volume=67 |issue=6 |article-number=jcpp.70081 |doi=10.1111/jcpp.70081 |pmid=41358911 |doi-access=free |pmc=13170628 }}</ref>
* 16 April 2026 (reported): an editorial published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' noted that, in 2025, [[mosquito]]s were found in [[Iceland]] for the first time, and were said to be "a warning that the Arctic lacks a system for monitoring [[arthropod]]s and anticipating biological risks before they escalate".<ref name=Science_20260416>{{cite journal |last1=Koltz |first1=Amanda M. |last2=Culler |first2=Lauren E. |title=The Arctic's growing mosquito problem |journal=Science |date=16 April 2026 |volume=392 |issue=6795 |page=235 |doi=10.1126/science.aeh9505 |pmid=41990176 |bibcode=2026Sci...392..235K }}</ref>

 |quote = {{font |font=Times New Roman |size=16px |{{nbsp|5}}  Experts believe that [[Solar power|solar]], [[Wind power|wind]], and [[Electric vehicle|EVs]] have irreversibly crossed a positive [[Tipping points in the climate system|tipping point]] and entered a virtuous cycle of cost decline and widespread adoption.}}
 |source = —Climate Action Team in the Executive Office<br>of the United Nations Secretary-General<ref name=UN_202507>{{cite web |author1=The Climate Action Team in the Executive Office of the United Nations Secretary-General |title=Seizing the moment of opportunity: Supercharging the new energy era of renewables, efficiency, and electrification |url=https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/un-energy-transition-report_2025.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250722175757/https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/un-energy-transition-report_2025.pdf |archive-date=22 July 2025 |location=New York |date=July 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><br>July 2025

* 12 February: a study published in ''[[Bird Study]]'' found that [[Photovoltaic power station|solar farm]]s can benefit bird abundance and [[biodiversity]] in arable-dominated landscapes, especially when managed with biodiversity in mind.<ref name=BirdStudy_20250212>{{cite journal |last1=Copping |first1=Joshua P. |last2=Waite |first2=Catherine E. |last3=Balmford |first3=Andrew |last4=Bradbury |first4=Richard B. |last5=Field |first5=Rob H. |last6=Morris |first6=Isobel |last7=Finch |first7=Tom |title=Solar farm management influences breeding bird responses in an arable-dominated landscape |journal=Bird Study |date=12 February 2025 |volume=72 |issue=3 |pages=217–222 |doi=10.1080/00063657.2025.2450392|bibcode=2025BirdS..72..217C |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 3 March: advising policy makers to assimilate uncertainty into decision making to increase [[Climate change mitigation|decarbonization]], a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' urged a "portfolio approach" of planting diverse species of trees, as that approach "reduces exposure to downside cost extremes".<ref name=PNAS_20250303>{{cite journal |last1=Cho |first1=Frankie H. T. |last2=Aglonucci |first2=Paolo |last3=Bateman |first3=Ian J. |last4=Lee |first4=Christopher F. |last5=Lovett |first5=Andrew |last6=Mancini |first6=Mattia C. |last7=Rapti |first7=Chrisanthi |last8=Day |first8=Brett H. |title=Resilient tree-planting strategies for carbon dioxide removal under compounding climate and economic uncertainties |journal=PNAS |date=3 March 2025 |volume=122 |issue=10 |article-number=e2320961122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2320961122|pmid=40030027 |doi-access=free |pmc=11912443 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12220961C }}</ref>
* 23 April: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' applied [[extreme event attribution]] to conclude that [[Chevron Corporation]] very likely caused between US $791 billion and $3.6 trillion in heat-related losses from 1991 through 2020.<ref name=Nature_20250423>{{cite journal |last1=Callahan |first1=Christopher W. |last2=Mankin |first2=Justin S. |title=Carbon majors and the scientific case for climate liability |journal=Nature |date=23 April 2025 |volume=640 |pages=893-901 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-08751-3}}</ref>
* May (reported): a technique involves pumping water from beneath Arctic ice and spraying it on top of the ice. It quickly refreezes, thickening the ice in that location so that it lasts longer into the warm months and increases the amount of planet-warming sunlight that is [[albedo|reflected]] back into space.<ref name=SciAm_20250520>{{cite news |last1=Luhn |first1=Alex |title=Inside the Bold Geoengineering Work to Refreeze the Arctic's Disappearing Ice |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/can-we-refreeze-the-arctics-ice-scientists-test-new-geoengineering-solutions/ |work=Scientific American |date=20 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250529004610/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/can-we-refreeze-the-arctics-ice-scientists-test-new-geoengineering-solutions/ |archive-date=29 May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* Spring:  two Chinese companies announced battery technology to enable electric vehicles to drive hundreds of miles on a five-minute [[Charging station|charge]].<ref name=NYTimes_20250819/> [[BYD Company]] developed a battery with a peak charging capacity of 1,000{{nbsp}}kilowatts, compared to U.S. chargers with peak rates of 400{{nbsp}}kilowatts or less.<ref name=NYTimes_20250819>{{cite web |last1=Brown |first1=Claire |title=Why Can't the U.S. Build 5-Minute E.V. Chargers? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/19/climate/us-electric-vehicle-chargers-china.html |work=The New York Times |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250824192418/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/19/climate/us-electric-vehicle-chargers-china.html |archive-date=24 August 2025 |date=19 August 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 15 December: the [[Copernicus Programme]]'s Earth System Science Data released the GloSAT reference analysis, a gridded data set of [[Global surface temperature|air temperature]] change across global land and ocean extending back to the 1780s, using marine air temperature observations rather than the sea surface temperature measurements.<ref name=ESSD_20251215>{{cite journal |last1=Morice |first1=Colin P. |last2=Berry |first2=David I. |display-authors=1 |title=An observational record of global gridded near-surface air temperature change over land and ocean from 1781 |journal=Earth System Science Data |date=15 December 2025 |volume=17 |issue=12 |pages=7079–7100 |doi=10.5194/essd-17-7079-2025 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2025ESSD...17.7079M |hdl=20.500.11820/9bf8a58e-a3ec-46f4-b58f-4e7b3c1ca0a2 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

===Political, economic, legal, and cultural actions===
{{quote box
 |title =Existential problem of planetary proportions
 |quote = {{font |font=Times New Roman |size=16px |{{nbsp|5}} (Climate change is) an existential problem of planetary proportions that imperils all forms of life and the very health of our planet. ... A complete solution to this daunting, and self-inflicted, problem requires the contribution of all fields of human knowledge, whether law, science, economics or any other.}}
 |source = —[[International Court of Justice]] advisory opinion<ref name=ICJ_20250726>{{cite web |title=Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change / Advisory Opinion |url=https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/187/187-20250723-adv-01-00-en.pdf |publisher=International Court of Justice |date=23 July 2025 }} <!-- could not be archived at archive.org or archive.today --></ref> regarding [[Obligations of States in respect of climate change]]<br />26 July 2025

}}
* 20 January: within hours of his inauguration, U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] signed an executive order to withdraw the country from the 2015 [[Paris Agreement]], joining Iran, Libya and Yemen as the only countries not party to the agreement.<ref name=NYTimes_20250120>{{cite news |last1=Bearak |first1=Max |title=Trump Orders a U.S. Exit From the World's Main Climate Pact |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/20/climate/trump-paris-agreement-climate.html |work=The New York Times |date=20 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121100253/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/20/climate/trump-paris-agreement-climate.html |archive-date=21 January 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 4 March: the administration of U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] withdrew the country's representatives from the board of the United Nations' [[Loss and Damage Fund]], which was formed to help poor and vulnerable nations cope with climate change-fueled disasters.<ref name=Reuters_20250307>{{cite news |last1=Abnett |first1=Kate |last2=Furness |first2=Virginia |title=United States quits board of UN climate damage fund, letter shows |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/united-states-quits-board-un-climate-damage-fund-letter-shows-2025-03-07/ |publisher=Reuters |date=7 March 2025 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250307140641/https://www.reuters.com/world/us/united-states-quits-board-un-climate-damage-fund-letter-shows-2025-03-07/ |archive-date=7 March 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 13 March: the Costa Rica-based [[Inter-American Court of Human Rights]] ordered the [[Ecuador]]ian government to protect [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous people]] from oil operations, to leave oil in the ground underneath their lands, and to ensure future oil operations do not impact Indigenous peoples living in [[Uncontacted peoples|voluntary isolation]].<ref name=InsideClimateNews_20250313>{{cite news |last1=Surma |first1=Katie |title=Landmark Ruling on Uncontacted Indigenous Peoples' Rights Strikes at Oil Industry |url=https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13032025/landmark-ruling-uncontacted-indigenous-peoples-rights-ecuador-oil-industry/ |work=Inside Climate News |date=13 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250314091905/https://insideclimatenews.org/news/13032025/landmark-ruling-uncontacted-indigenous-peoples-rights-ecuador-oil-industry/ |archive-date=14 March 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 14 March: 440 Olympic athletes from 90 countries and 50 sports published an [[open letter]] to candidates for [[President of the International Olympic Committee|President]] of the [[International Olympic Committee]], urging them to keep "the spirit of the Games alive by ensuring that sport remains accessible and safe for future generations".<ref name=Olympic_athletes>{{cite web |title=Dear IOC Presidency Candidates |url=https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/558b37ef-276d-4111-81a8-d0fea75f10fd/Copy%20of%20Letter%20to%20candidates.pdf |website=Athletes of the World |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250409224508/https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/558b37ef-276d-4111-81a8-d0fea75f10fd/Copy%20of%20Letter%20to%20candidates.pdf |archive-date=9 April 2025 |date=14 March 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 24 March: the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] declined to hear the appeal in ''[[Juliana v. United States]]'', ending the case in which youth plaintiffs asserted in their 2015 filing that the government had violated their [[constitutional right]]s by encouraging use of fossil fuels.<ref name=NYTimes_20250324/> Certain other lawsuits with similar strategies were more successful.<ref name=NYTimes_20250324>{{cite news |last1=Zraik |first1=Karen |title=A Landmark Lawsuit, Where Kids Sued America, Comes to an End |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/24/climate/supreme-court-climate-lawsuit-juliana-children.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=24 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250326164456/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/24/climate/supreme-court-climate-lawsuit-juliana-children.html |archive-date=26 March 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
[[File:20201211 Billion dollar events related to climate change - U.S. -en.svg |thumb|In May 2025, NOAA/NCEI in the Trump administration indicated that it would no longer assemble the data that forms the basis of this chart.<ref name=Guardian_20250508/> NOAA/NCEI has access to non-public data, so that any private databases would be more limited in scope.<ref name=Guardian_20250508/>]]
* 30 March: an [[open letter]] signed by 1900 researchers called on the administration of US President [[Donald Trump]] to stop its "wholesale assault on U.S. science", including its blocking of research on climate change, and causing researchers to live in a "climate of fear" amid the administration's flagging of terms such as ''climate change'' as objectionable.<ref name=OpenLetter_20250331>{{cite web |author1=((1900 Researchers)) |title=Public Statement on Supporting Science for the Benefit of All Citizens |url=https://docs.google.com/document/d/13gmMJOMsoNKC4U-A8rhJrzu_xhgS51PEfNMPG9Q_cmE/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250401201136/https://docs.google.com/document/d/13gmMJOMsoNKC4U-A8rhJrzu_xhgS51PEfNMPG9Q_cmE/edit#heading=h.b3f2t4qlidd |archive-date=1 April 2025 |date=31 March 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 28 April: U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] dismissed the scientists and experts who compile the [[National Climate Assessment]]s (NCAs) that are required by the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]], the next assessment having been planned for 2028.<ref name=NYTimes_20250428>{{cite news |last1=Plumer |first1=Brad |last2=Dzomback |first2=Rebecca |title=All Authors Working on Flagship U.S. Climate Report Are Dismissed |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/28/climate/national-climate-assessment-authors-dismissed.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=28 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250430012437/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/28/climate/national-climate-assessment-authors-dismissed.html |archive-date=30 April 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref> This decision disrupted the NCA's long-standing process of providing Congress and the public with credible, science-based climate information.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Avery |first1=Christopher W. |last2=Crimmins |first2=Allison R. |last3=Lustig |first3=Allyza R. |last4=Lamb |first4=April D. |last5=Fuller |first5=Isabel J. |last6=Lemery |first6=Ciara |last7=Grade |first7=Aaron |last8=Barrie |first8=Daniel |date=2025-03-03 |title=Navigating complex waters: Designing a process for the development of the National Climate Assessment |journal=Climatic Change |language=en |volume=178 |issue=3 |pages=44 |doi=10.1007/s10584-024-03854-8 |bibcode=2025ClCh..178...44A |issn=1573-1480|doi-access=free }}</ref> Within the week, the [[American Meteorological Society]] (AMS) and the [[American Geophysical Union]] (AGU) said that together they will produce over 29 peer-reviewed journals to cover climate change; that while not claiming they will replace the NCA, they will carry on its work.<ref name=Guardian_20250503>{{cite news |last1=Yang |first1=Maya |title=Scientific societies to do climate assessment after Trump administration dismissed authors |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/may/03/us-scientific-societies-climate-report |work=The Guardian |date=3 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250505030416/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/may/03/us-scientific-societies-climate-report |archive-date=5 May 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 7 May: a study of [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] [[Climate justice#Disproportionality between causality and burden|inequality]] from 1990 to 2020 published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' concluded that two-thirds of global warming is [[Climate justice#Disproportionality between causality and burden|attributable]] to the wealthiest 10%, and 20% of warming is attributable to the wealthiest 1%.<ref name=NatureCC_20250507>{{cite journal |last1=Schöngart |first1=Sarah |last2=Nicholls |first2=Zebedee |last3=Hoffman |first3=Roman |last4=Pelz |first4=Setu |last5=Schleussner |first5=Carl-Friedrich |title=High-income groups disproportionately contribute to climate extremes worldwide |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=7 May 2025 |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=627–633 |doi=10.1038/s41558-025-02325-x|bibcode=2025NatCC..15..627S |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/735849 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Numerous other statistics were presented.
* 8 May (reported): the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA) under U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] said that NOAA's [[National Centers for Environmental Information]] would no longer update its Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database beyond 2024, and that its information—going as far back as 1980—would be archived.<ref name=Guardian_20250508>{{cite news |agency=Associated Press |title=Noaa to stop tracking cost of climate crisis-fueled disasters: 'Major loss' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/may/08/noaa-climate-crisis-extreme-weather-disasters-trump |work=The Guardian |date=8 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250508210704/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/may/08/noaa-climate-crisis-extreme-weather-disasters-trump |archive-date=8 May 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>

* 30 June: the globalchange.gov website of the [[U.S. Global Change Research Program]], established in 1990 to host legislatively mandated reports including the [[National Climate Assessment]]s, was taken down by the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]].<ref name=NYTimes_20250701>{{cite news |last1=Dzombak |first1=Rebecca |title=National Climate Report Website Goes Dark |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/01/climate/national-climate-assessment.html |work=The New York Times |date=1 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250705202709/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/01/climate/national-climate-assessment.html/ |archive-date=5 July 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* July (widely announced): the south Pacific island of [[Tuvalu]], with an average elevation {{convert|2|m|ft}} above sea level, embarks on a plan to evacuate its entire population due to [[sea level rise]], which is projected to inundate most of the territory at high tide by 2050.<ref name=Wired_20250725/> Australia formed a migration system allownig 280 Tuvaluans per year to settle in Australia as permanent residents.<ref name=Wired_20250725>{{cite magazine |last1=Gonzalez |first1=Fernanda |title=The First Planned Migration of an Entire Country Is Underway |url=https://www.wired.com/story/the-first-planned-migration-of-an-entire-country-is-underway/ |magazine=Wired |date=25 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250731213026/https://www.wired.com/story/the-first-planned-migration-of-an-entire-country-is-underway/ |archive-date=31 July 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 29 July: the chief administrator of the US [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] announced that the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]] would rescind the 2009 [[Regulation of greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act#Endangerment|endangerment finding]], which concluded that planet-warming [[greenhouse gas]]es pose a threat to public health.<ref name=NYTimes_20250725/> (The endangerment finding is the scientific determination that underpins the U.S. government's legal authority to [[climate change mitigation|combat climate change]].<ref name=NYTimes_20250725>{{cite news |last1=Joselow |first1=Maxine |last2=Friedman |first2=Lisa |title=In Game-Changing Climate Rollback, E.P.A. (editors) {{cite web |title=Climate Experts' Review of the DOE Climate Working Group Report |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PwAR8I9YYmPhbQ6CRekHkroJGMbjbX7l/view ===Mitigation goal statements===
* March: the [[OECD]]'s ''Investing in Climate for Growth and Development'' concluded that accelerated climate action provides economic gains, specifically, that under an Enhanced [[Nationally determined contribution|NDC]]s scenario, global [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] in 2040 would be 0.2% higher than under the Current Policies Scenario.<ref name=OECD_202503>{{cite web |title=Investing in Climate for Growth and Development |url=https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/about/projects/new-ndcs-to-deliver-climate-action-for-growth/investing-in-climate-for-growth-and-development-the-case-for-enhanced-NDCs-key-messages.pdf |publisher=Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250326200701/https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/about/projects/new-ndcs-to-deliver-climate-action-for-growth/investing-in-climate-for-growth-and-development-the-case-for-enhanced-NDCs-key-messages.pdf |archive-date=26 March 2025 |page=2 |date=March 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* October: [[United Nations|UN]] Secretary General [[António Guterres]] said that based on [[Nationally determined contribution|nationally determined contribution (NDCs)]]s received so far, there is a predicted 10% reduction of [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]].<ref name=Guardian_20251027/> He said that this reduction does not meet the 60% reduction needed to stay within the 1.5{{nbsp}}°C of the [[Paris Agreement]], so that overshooting the 1.5{{nbsp}}°C threshold "is now inevitable".<ref name=Guardian_20251027>{{cite news |last1=Watts |first1=Jonathan |last2=Xipai |first2=Wajã |title='Change course now': humanity has missed 1.5C climate target, says UN head |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/oct/28/change-course-now-humanity-has-missed-15c-climate-target-says-un-head |work=The Guardian |date=27 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251028060319/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/oct/28/change-course-now-humanity-has-missed-15c-climate-target-says-un-head |archive-date=28 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 9 December: the [[European Union]] [[European Parliament|Parliament]] announced a provisional political agreement of a 90% reduction target for [[greenhouse gas emissions]] by 2040 compared with 1990 levels, to achieve [[net-zero emissions]] in the EU by 2050.<ref name=EUparliament_20251209>{{cite web |title=2040 climate target: deal on a 90% emissions reduction in EU climate law |url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20251208IPR32091/2040-climate-target-deal-on-a-90-emissions-reduction-in-eu-climate-law |publisher=European Parliament |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251210202942/https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20251208IPR32091/2040-climate-target-deal-on-a-90-emissions-reduction-in-eu-climate-law |archive-date=10 December 2025 |date=9 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Consensus==
[[File:2025 Survey re global warming - Yale Climate Communication.svg |thumb |Surveys of US adults re global warming show slowly growing agreements that global warming is occurring and is mostly human-caused. By 2025, over 70% of surveyed US adults agreed that global warming is happening, and almost 60% agree that it is mostly human-caused.<ref>Leiserowitz, A., Kotcher, J., Rosenthal, S., Goddard, E., Carman, J., Verner, M., Myers, T., Ettinger, J., Fine, J., Richards, E., Goldberg, M., Marlon, J., & Maibach, E. {{cite web |title=Climate Change in the American Mind: Beliefs & Attitudes, Fall 2025 |url=https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/app/uploads/2026/01/climate-change-american-mind-beliefs-attitudes-fall-2025.pdf |pages=5, 8 |publisher=Yale Program on Climate Communication |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260205192358/https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/app/uploads/2026/01/climate-change-american-mind-beliefs-attitudes-fall-2025.pdf |archive-date=5 February 2026 |date=27 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
* 17 April: a study published in ''[[Nature Human Behaviour]]'' found that presenting people with [[Binary opposition|binary]] climate data—for example, a lake freezing versus not freezing—significantly increases the perceived impact of climate change compared to when [[Continuous or discrete variable#Continuous variable|continuous data]] such as temperature change is presented.<ref name=NatureHumanBehaviour_20250417/> The researchers said the findings confirmed the [[boiling frog]] effect for [[climate communication|climate change communication]].<ref name=NatureHumanBehaviour_20250417>{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Grace |last2=Snell |first2=Jake C. |last3=Griffiths |first3=Thomas L. |last4=Dubey |first4=Rachit |title=Binary climate data visuals amplify perceived impact of climate change |journal=Nature Human Behaviour |date=17 April 2025 |volume=9 |issue=7 |pages=1355–1364 |doi=10.1038/s41562-025-02183-9 |pmid=40246995 }}</ref>
* 5 June: results of a 20-country survey published in ''[[Nature Human Behaviour]]'' show strong majority support—including 75% of Europeans and half of Americans—for the Global Climate Scheme (a variant of [[Cap and Share]]) a global carbon price and cash redistribution plan. The study also found widespread support for increased foreign aid or a wealth tax to fund low-income countries.<ref name=NatureHumanBehaviour_20250605>{{cite journal |last1=Fabre |first1=Adrien |last2=Douenne |first2=Thomas |last3=Mattauch |first3=Linus |title=Majority support for global redistributive and climate policies |journal=Nature Human Behaviour |date=5 June 2025 |volume=9 |issue=8 |pages=1583–1594 |doi=10.1038/s41562-025-02175-9 |pmid=40473801 |pmc=12367524 }}</ref>
* 22 August: results of a public survey of the [[Global North and Global South|global south]] published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' found that [[List of climate scientists|scientists]] are perceived as the most trusted information source in all countries surveyed except Vietnam, and that trust in scientists correlates with increased climate knowledge.<ref name=NatureCC_20250822>{{cite journal |last1=Carson |first1=Richard T. |last2=Lu |first2=Jiajun |last3=Khossravi |first3=Emily A. |last4=Köhlin |first4=Gunnar |last5=Sterner |first5=Erik |last6=Sterner |first6=Thomas |last7=Whittington |first7=Dale |title=The public's views on climate policies in seven large global south countries |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=22 August 2025 |volume=15 |issue=9 |pages=954–962 |doi=10.1038/s41558-025-02389-9|bibcode=2025NatCC..15..954C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Projections==
* 6 January: A study published in ''Scientific Reports'' comparing projected [[Heat illness|heat-related deaths]] from climate change with [[COVID-19]] mortality rates across 38 global cities found that in half, annual heat-related deaths would likely exceed COVID-19 death rates within 10 years if [[Global surface temperature|global temperatures]] rise by 3.0&nbsp;°C above [[Pre-industrial society|pre-industrial]] levels. The study projected that cities in [[North America]] and [[Europe]], particularly in [[Mediterranean basin|Mediterranean]] and [[Central Europe]]an regions, would have most dramatic increases in projected heat mortality.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Batibeniz |first1=Fulden |last2=Seneviratne |first2=Sonia I. |last3=Jha |first3=Srinidhi |last4=Ribeiro |first4=Andreia |last5=Suarez Gutierrez |first5=Laura |last6=Raible |first6=Christoph C. |last7=Malhotra |first7=Avni |last8=Armstrong |first8=Ben |last9=Bell |first9=Michelle L. |last10=Lavigne |first10=Eric |last11=Gasparrini |first11=Antonio |last12=Guo |first12=Yuming |last13=Hashizume |first13=Masahiro |last14=Masselot |first14=Pierre |last15=da Silva |first15=Susana Pereira |date=2025-01-06 |title=Rapid climate action is needed: comparing heat vs. COVID-19-related mortality |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=15 |issue=1 |page=1002 |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-82788-8  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=11704295 |pmid=39762298|bibcode=2025NatSR..15.1002B }}</ref>
* 3 February: climate risk financial modeling company First Street Foundation projected that by 2055, 70,026 U.S. neighborhoods (84% of all census tracts) may experience $1.47 trillion in net climate-related property value losses, citing insurance pressures and shifting consumer demand.<ref name=FirstStreet_20250203>{{cite web |title=Property Prices in Peril |url=https://firststreet.org/research-library/property-prices-in-peril |publisher=First Street |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250204054158/https://firststreet.org/research-library/property-prices-in-peril |archive-date=4 February 2025 |date=3 February 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 4 February: a review article published in ''[[Nature Reviews Earth & Environment]]'', linking physical climate science with heat mortality risk, projected that human-caused global warming reaching 2{{nbsp}}°C above preindustrial levels will cause tripling of global land area that is "uncompensable" (beyond which human core body temperature rises uncontrollably) for young adults.<ref name=NatureRvwEandEnv_20250204>{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=Tom |last2=Colin |first2=Raymond |last3=Foster |first3=Josh |last4=Bladwin |first4=Jane W. |last5=Ivanovich |first5=Caherine |last6=Kong |first6=Qinqin |last7=Kinney |first7=Patrick |last8=Horton |first8=Radley M. |title=Mortality impacts of the most extreme heat events |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |date=4 February 2025 |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=193–210 |doi=10.1038/s43017-024-00635-w |bibcode=2025NRvEE...6..193M |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/08b400s3 }}</ref>
* 26 February: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (AMOC) is resilient to extreme greenhouse gas and North Atlantic freshwater forcings across 34 climate models, suggesting that an AMOC collapse is unlikely in the 21st century.<ref name=Nature_20250226>{{cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=J.A. |last2=Bell |first2=M.J. |last3=Jackson |first3=L.C. |last4=Vallis |first4=G.K. |last5=Watson |first5=A.J. |last6=Wood |first6=R.A. |title=Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes |journal=Nature |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-08544-0 |volume=638 |pages=987–994 |date=26 February 2025|issue=8052 |pmid=40011721 |pmc=11864975 |bibcode=2025Natur.638..987B |hdl=10871/139390 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 28 February: based on the Earth's orbital characteristics ([[Axial precession|precession]], [[Axial tilt#Earth|obliquity]], and [[Orbital eccentricity|eccentricity]]), a study published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' concluded that [[Glacial period|glacial]]-[[interglacial]] periodicity has been largely deterministic in a ~100,000 year cycle, and projected that in the absence of human-caused forcing, the next [[ice age]] would start in ~10,000 years.<ref name=Science_20250228>{{cite journal |last1=Barker |first1=Stephen |last2=Lisiecki |first2=Lorraine E. |last3=Knorr |first3=Gregor |last4=Nuber |first4=Sophie |last5=Tzedakis |first5=Polychronis C. |title=Distinct roles for precession, obliquity, and eccentricity in Pleistocene 100-kyr glacial cycles |journal=Science |date=28 February 2025 |volume=387 |issue=6737 |page=6737 |article-number=eadp3491 |doi=10.1126/science.adp3491 |pmid=40014707 |bibcode=2025Sci...387P3491B |url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10205595/ }}</ref>
* 5 March: a paper published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' cited the [[International Energy Agency]] as stating that [[data center]]s caused 1–1.3% of world electricity demand in 2022, but that, with electricity consumption expected to grow by more than 80% by 2050 owing to all sources, data centers were projected to "account for a relatively small share of overall electricity demand growth".<ref name=Nature_20250305>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Sophia |title=How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown |journal=Nature |date=5 March 2025 |volume=639 |issue=8053 |pages=22–24 |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-00616-z |pmid=40044891 |bibcode=2025Natur.639...22C }}</ref>
* 10 March: a study published in ''[[Nature Sustainability]]'' projected that climate change's cooling of the atmosphere that is occupied by [[space debris]] in [[low Earth orbit]] will reduce the atmosphere's drag on the debris, extending the debris' lifetime and potentially causing a 50–66% reduction in [[satellite]] carrying capacity at altitudes {{convert|200|-|1000|km|mi|abbr=on}}.<ref name=NatureSust_20250311/>
* 12 March: the [[Boston Consulting Group]]'s ''Landing the Economic Case for Climate Action with Decision Makers'' concluded that the ''net'' cost of failing to invest to reduce global warming from a current forecast 3.0{{nbsp}}°C to 2.0{{nbsp}}°C equates to 11% to 27% of cumulative economic output.<ref name=BCG_2025312>{{cite web |last1=Benayad |first1=Amine |last2=Hagenauer |first2=Annalena |last3=Holm |first3=Lars |last4=Jones |first4=Edmond Rhys |last5=Kämmerer |first5=Sahradha |last6=Maher |first6=Hamid |last7=Mohaddes |first7=Kamiar |last8=Santamarta |first8=Sylvain |last9=Zawadzki |first9=Annika |display-authors=4 |title=Landing the Economic Case for Climate Action with Decision Makers |url=https://web-assets.bcg.com/d6/4b/5b54eed54d7ab7d9646da32a87bd/why-investing-in-climate-action-makes-good-economic-sense.pdf |publisher=[[Boston Consulting Group]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250506021124/https://web-assets.bcg.com/d6/4b/5b54eed54d7ab7d9646da32a87bd/why-investing-in-climate-action-makes-good-economic-sense.pdf |archive-date=6 May 2025 |date=12 March 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
