* 20 May: noting that current global temperatures have quadrupled the rate of [[ice sheet]] loss since the 1990s, a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' concluded that maintaining current global temperatures will cause several metres of [[sea level rise]] over coming centuries, "causing extensive loss and damage to coastal populations and challenging the implementation of adaptation measures".<ref name=CommsEandE_20250520>{{cite journal |last1=Stokes |first1=Chris R. |last2=Bamber |first2=Jonathan L. |last3=Dutton |first3=Andrea |last4=DeConto |first4=Robert M. |title=Warming of +1.5 °C is too high for polar ice sheets |journal=Nature Communications |date=20 May 2025 |volume=6 |issue=351 |article-number=351 |doi=10.1038/s43247-025-02299-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=40406387 |pmc=12092291 |bibcode=2025ComEE...6..351S }}</ref>
* 28 May: the [[World Meteorological Organization]] projected a 70% chance that the average global warming for 2025-2029 will be more than 1.5{{nbsp}}°C, up from 47% in last year's report for 2024-2028.<ref name=WMO_20250528>{{cite web |title=Global climate predictions show temperatures expected to remain at or near record levels in coming 5 years |url=https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/global-climate-predictions-show-temperatures-expected-remain-or-near-record-levels-coming-5-years |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250529011933/https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/global-climate-predictions-show-temperatures-expected-remain-or-near-record-levels-coming-5-years |archive-date=29 May 2025 |date=28 May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 29 May: a study published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' estimated that if temperatures remain steady, glaciers globally will lose 39% of their 2020 mass, causing a [[sea level rise]] of {{convert|113|mm|in}}.<ref name=Science_20250529/> More than twice as much glacier mass was projected to remain at the Paris Agreement's +1.5{{nbsp}}°C goal than the 2.7{{nbsp}}°C predicted from current policies (53% versus 24%).<ref name=Science_20250529>{{cite journal |last1=Zekollari |first1=Harry |last2=Schuster |first2=Lilian |last3=Maussion |first3=Fabien |last4=Hock |first4=Regine |last5=Marzeion |first5=Ben |last6=Rounce |first6=David R. |last7=Compagno |first7=Loris |last8=Fujita |first8=Koji |display-authors=4 |title=Glacier preservation doubled by limiting warming to 1.5&nbsp;°C versus 2.7&nbsp;°C |journal=Science |date=2025 |volume=388 |issue=6750 |pages=979–983 |doi=10.1126/science.adu4675 |pmid=40440393 |bibcode=2025Sci...388..979Z |url=https://hal.science/hal-05108040 }}</ref>
* 16 June: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' projected that with ≥1.8{{nbsp}}°C global warming, there would be a 1.2- to 3-fold increase in [[obstructive sleep apnea]] by 2100.<ref name=NatureComms_20250616/>
* 10 September: a report by [[Common Goal (charity)|Common Goal]] and Football for Future forecast that by 2050, 14 of 16 [[World Cup]] stadiums will face extreme heat conditions (unsafe without [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation]]), and 11 stadiums will experience unplayable heat (where matches cannot be safely staged).<ref name=PitchesInPeril_20250910/> Also, every grassroots [[Football pitch|pitch]] analyzed already breached at least three major climate risk thresholds, and two-thirds of grassroots pitches will face unsafe or unplayable heat conditions.<ref name=PitchesInPeril_20250910>{{cite web |title=Pitches in Peril |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QCIij82nPZNkiWvVm3vjo0ZS0W1XBmEK/view |publisher=Common Goal and Football for Future |page=4 |date=10 September 2025 }}</ref>
* 17 September: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' projected that if global warming exceeds {{convert|2|C-change|F-change}}, at least 99% of western Atlantic [[coral reef]]s will be eroding by 2100.<ref name=Nature_20250917>{{cite journal |last1=Perry |first1=Chris T. |last2=de Bakker |first2=Didier M. |last3=Webb |first3=Alice E. |last4=Comeau |first4=Steeve |last5=Harvey |first5=Ben P. |title=Reduced Atlantic reef growth past 2 °C warming amplifies sea-level impacts |journal=Nature |date=17 September 2025 |volume=646 |issue=8085 |pages=619–626 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09439-4|pmid=40963009 |doi-access=free |pmc=12527930 |bibcode=2025Natur.646..619P }}</ref>
* 18 September: referring to effects of [[Particulate matter|PM<sub>2.5</sub>]] (fine particulate matter), a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' projected 34,930-98,430 excess deaths per year in the US by 2050 under a high warming scenario, and suggested that "the health impacts of climate-driven [[wildfire]] smoke could be among the most important and costly consequences of a warming climate in the US".<ref name=NatureWildfires_20250918>{{cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=Minghao |last2=Li |first2=Jessica |last3=Gould |first3=Carlos F. |last4=Jing |first4=Renzhi |last5=Kelp |first5=Makoto |last6=Childs |first6=Marissa L. |last7=Wen |first7=Jeff |last8=Xie |first8=Yuanyu |last9=Lin |first9=Meiyun |last10=Kiang |first10=Mathew V. |last11=Heft-Neal |first11=Sam |last12=Diffenbaugh |first12=Noah S. |last13=Burke |first13=Marshall |display-authors=4 |title=Wildfire smoke exposure and mortality burden in the US under climate change |journal=Nature |date=18 September 2025 |volume=647 |issue=8091 |pages=935–943 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09611-w |pmid=40967551 |bibcode=2025Natur.647..935Q }}</ref>
* 23 September: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' projected that many regions may face high risk of "Day Zero [[Drought]]" (DZD) conditions by the 2020s and 2030s, with the length of time between successive DZD events being shorter DZD durations.<ref name=NatureComms_20250923>{{cite journal |last1=Ravinandrasana |first1=Vecchia P. |last2=Franzke |first2=Christian L. E. |title=The first emergence of unprecedented global water scarcity in the Anthropocene |journal=Nature Communications |date=23 September 2025 |volume=16 |issue=1 |article-number=8281 |doi=10.1038/s41467-025-63784-6  |doi-access=free|pmid=40987791 |pmc=12457592 |bibcode=2025NatCo..16.8281R }}</ref>
* 24 October: a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' projected that under current climate policies, emissions until 2050 lock in {{convert|0.3|m|ft}} ''additional'' global mean [[sea level rise]] by 2300 than historical emissions until 2020, increasing to {{convert|0.8|m|ft}} for emissions until 2090.<ref name=NatureCC_20251024>{{cite journal |last1=Nauels |first1=Alexander |last2=Nicholls |first2=Zebedee |last3=Möller |first3=Tessa |last4=Hermans |first4=Tim H. J. |last5=Mengel |first5=Mattias |last6=Kloenne |first6=Uta |last7=Smith |first7=Chris |last8=Slangen |first8=Aimée B. A. |last9=Palmer |first9=Matthew D. |display-authors=4 |title=Multi-century global and regional sea-level rise commitments from cumulative greenhouse gas emissions in the coming decades |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=24 October 2025 |volume=15 |issue=11 |pages=1198–1204 |doi=10.1038/s41558-025-02452-5|bibcode=2025NatCC..15.1198N |doi-access=free |hdl=1983/6da0cfc9-2618-4cef-b334-0bf709c12fa2 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 17 November: a study published in ''[[Environmental Research|Environmental Research: Climate]]'' examined heatwave changes after [[greenhouse gas emissions]] reach [[net zero]], simulating assuming various years in which net zero is achieved.<ref name=EnvRsch_20251117/> The research concluded that most regional trends show no decline over the entire 1000 years of each simulation, and projected that some regions will experience millennial-scale heating trends when net zero occurs on or after 2050.<ref name=EnvRsch_20251117>{{cite journal |last1=Perkins-Kirkpatrick |first1=Sarah |last2=Palmer |first2=Lucinda |last3=King |first3=Andrew |last4=Ziehn |first4=Tilo |title=Heatwaves in a net zero World |journal=Environmental Research: Climate |date=17 November 2025 |volume=4 |issue=4 |page=045015 |doi=10.1088/2752-5295/ae0ea4|bibcode=2025ERCli...4d5015P |doi-access=free |hdl=1885/733796729 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 18 November: a study published in ''[[Nature_(journal)#Communications_journals|Nature Communications Earth and Environment]]'' concluded that global warming will weaken [[Andes|Andes mountains]] [[glacier]]s' buffering role against [[megadrought]]s, estimating that Andes glacier runoff could [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|decline]] by up to 20% (annual) and 48% (summer) during end-of-century megadroughts compared to pre-2010 levels.<ref name=NatureCommsEandE_20251118>{{cite journal |last1=Ayala |first1=Álvaro |last2=Muñoz-Castro |first2=Eduardo |last3=Farinotti |first3=Daniel |last4=Farías-Barahona |first4=David |last5=Mendoza |first5=Pablo A. |last6=MacDonnell |first6=Shelley |last7=McPhee |first7=James |last8=Vargas |first8=Ximena |last9=Pellicciotti |first9=Francesca |display-authors=1 |title=Less water from glaciers during future megadroughts in the Southern Andes |journal=Nature Communications Earth & Environment |date=18 November 2025 |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=860 |doi=10.1038/s43247-025-02845-6|bibcode=2025ComEE...6..860A |doi-access=free |hdl=10092/109615 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* 19 November: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' reconstructed European summer durations over the last ten millennia and projected that by 2100, European summers could last up to 42 days longer under a business-as-usual scenario.<ref name=NatureComms_20251119>{{cite journal |last1=Martin-Puertas |first1=Celia |last2=Boyall |first2=Lauara |last3=Hernandez |first3=Armand |last4=Ojala |first4=Antti E. K. |last5=Abrook |first5=Ashley |last6=Kosonen |first6=Emilia |last7=Lincoln |first7=Paul |last8=Portmann |first8=Valentin |last9=Swingedouw |first9=Didier |title=Consistent response of European summers to the latitudinal temperature gradient over the Holocene |journal=Nature Communications |date=19 November 2025 |volume=16 |issue=1 |article-number=9969 |doi=10.1038/s41467-025-65804-x  |doi-access=free|pmid=41258292 |pmc=12630748 |bibcode=2025NatCo..16.9969M }}</ref>
* 10 December: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that, by 2100 under a high [[greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] scenario, a large part of the [[Amazon rainforest]] will shift to a hotter "hypertropical" climate in which "temperature and moisture conditions during typical dry season months will more frequently exceed identified drought mortality thresholds, elevating the risk of forest dieback".<ref name=Nature_20251210>{{cite journal |last1=Chambers |first1=Jeffrey Q. |last2=Lima |first2=Adriano José Nogueira |last3=Pastorello |first3=Gilberto |display-authors=1 |title=Hot droughts in the Amazon provide a window to a future hypertropical climate |journal=Nature |date=10 December 2025 |volume=649 |issue=8099 |pages=1190–1196 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09728-y |pmid=41372411 }}</ref>
* 17 December: the [[International Energy Agency]] forecast that global coal consumption has reached a plateau and may well decline by 2030.<ref name=IEA_20251217>{{cite web |title=Coal 2025 / Analysis and forecast to 2030 |url=https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/113a8274-500c-4684-951f-947d25bef3c9/Coal2025.pdf |publisher=International Energy Agency (IEA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251217133918/https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/113a8274-500c-4684-951f-947d25bef3c9/Coal2025.pdf |archive-date=17 December 2025 |page=7 |date=17 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

{{dynamic list}}
This article documents notable events, research findings, scientific and technological advances, and human actions to measure, predict, [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate]], and [[Climate change adaptation|adapt to]] the [[Effects of climate change|effects]] of [[Climate change|global warming and climate change]]—during the year 2026.

==Summaries==

==Measurements and statistics==
<gallery mode="packed" heights="160">
20251231 NASA Vital Signs of the Planet 2025.png |"Vital Signs of the Planet" as presented by NASA at the end of 2025 / beginning of 2026<ref>{{cite web |title=Climate change / Vital signs |url=https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/ |website=science.NASA.gov |publisher=NASA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251231210402/https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/ |archive-date=31 December 2025 |date=31 December 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>
</gallery>
[[File:1960- Damages caused by countries' emissions of greenhouse gases.svg |thumb |Non-linear growth in the global warming effect of accumulating long-lived greenhouse gases contributed to economic damage over a 60-year period estimated to be over five times as large as that of a 30-year period (shown in chart). A ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' article estimated ''future'' damages from past emissions to be at least an order of magnitude larger than ''historical'' damages from the same emissions.<ref name=Nature_20260325enhanced>
* Data source for '''''1990'''''-2020 panel: Fig. 4 of {{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B }}
* Data source for '''''1960'''''-2020 panel: Fig. S5 of {{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Nature portfolio / Supplementary information / Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |url=https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-026-10272-6/MediaObjects/41586_2026_10272_MOESM1_ESM.pdf |journal=Nature |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260406031318/https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-026-10272-6/MediaObjects/41586_2026_10272_MOESM1_ESM.pdf |archive-date=6 April 2026 |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B |quote=Same as Figure 4 except valuing damages from emissions starting in 1960 rather than 1990. |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
* 9 January: a report published in ''[[Advances in Atmospheric Sciences]]'' said that [[ocean heat content]] in 2025 had reached a new record for nine consecutive years.<ref name=AdvAtmosSci_20260109>Pan, Y., Cheng, L., Abraham, J. ''et al.'' {{cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=Yuying |last2=Cheng |first2=Lijing |last3=Abraham |first3=John |last4=Trenberth |first4=Kevin E. |last5=Reagan |first5=James |last6=Du |first6=Juan |last7=Wang |first7=Zhankun |last8=Storto |first8=Andrea |last9=von Schuckmann |first9=Karina |last10=Zhu |first10=Yujing |last11=Mann |first11=Michael E. |last12=Zhu |first12=Jiang |last13=Wang |first13=Fan |last14=Yu |first14=Fujiang |last15=Locarnini |first15=Ricardo |last16=Fasullo |first16=John |last17=Huang |first17=Boyin |last18=Graham |first18=Garrett |last19=Yin |first19=Xungang |last20=Gouretski |first20=Viktor |last21=Zheng |first21=Fei |last22=Li |first22=Yuanlong |last23=Zhang |first23=Bin |last24=Wan |first24=Liying |last25=Chen |first25=Xingrong |last26=Wang |first26=Dakui |last27=Feng |first27=Licheng |last28=Song |first28=Xiangzhou |last29=Liu |first29=Yulong |last30=Reseghetti |first30=Franco |display-authors=1 |title=Ocean Heat Content Sets Another Record in 2025 |journal=Advances in Atmospheric Sciences |date=9 January 2026 |volume=43 |issue=10 |page=6737 |doi=10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0|doi-access=free |bibcode=2026AdAtS..43.2019P }}</ref>
* 9 January (reported): an [[Oxfam]] report concluded that the richest 1% exhausted their annual [[carbon budget]] in ten days.<ref name=Oxfam_20260109>{{cite web |title=Richest 1% have blown through their fair share of carbon emissions for 2026 in just 10 days, says Oxfam |url=https://www.oxfam.org/en/press-releases/richest-1-have-blown-through-their-fair-share-carbon-emissions-2026-just-10-days |publisher=Oxfam |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260111042949/https://www.oxfam.org/en/press-releases/richest-1-have-blown-through-their-fair-share-carbon-emissions-2026-just-10-days |archive-date=11 January 2026 |date=9 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> (Carbon budget is the amount of [[greenhouse gas|carbon dioxide]] that can be emitted while keeping the planet within 1.5 °C of global warming.)
* 22 January: [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]]'s ''European Electricity Review 2026'' reported that in 2025, wind and solar energy provided 30% of EU electricity, surpassing fossil power (29%) for the first time, and generating more power than fossil sources in 14 of 27 EU countries.<ref name=Ember_20260122>{{cite web |title=European Electricity Review 2026 |url=https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/01/EMBER-Report-European-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |publisher=Ember |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260123173500/https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/01/EMBER-Report-European-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |archive-date=23 January 2026 |date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 4 February: a study published in ''[[npj Climate and Atmospheric Science]]'' estimated that a {{convert|1|C-change}} increase in summer temperature causes up to three additional weeks of Alaskan glacier melt.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wells |first1=Albin |last2=Rounce |first2=David R. |last3=Fahnestock |first3=Mark |title=Seasonal progression of melt and snowlines in Alaska from SAR reveals impacts of warming |journal=npj Climate and Atmospheric Science |date=4 February 2026 |volume=9 |issue=1 |article-number=95 |doi=10.1038/s41612-026-01321-y  |doi-access=free|pmid=41971003 |pmc=13065479 |bibcode=2026npCAS...9...95W }}</ref>
* 6 March: a study published in ''[[Geophysical Research Letters]]'' removed estimated influence of three natural variability factors and concluded with over 98% confidence that global warming from 2015 to 2025 accelerated more than during any previous decade.<ref name=AGU_20260306>{{cite journal |last1=Foster |first1=G. |last2=Rahmstorf |first2=S. |title=Global Warming Has Accelerated Significantly |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=6 March 2026 |volume=53 |issue=5 |article-number=e2025GL118804 |doi=10.1029/2025GL118804|doi-access=free |bibcode=2026GeoRL..5318804F }}</ref>
* 6 March: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that compound drought-heatwave events (CDHEs) have increased nearly eightfold since the early 2000s, from 1.6 to 13.1% per degree Celsius, with considerable regional variation.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260306>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Yong-Jun |last2=Yeh |first2=Sang-Wook |last3=Ng |first3=Benjamin |title=Nonlinear increase of compound drought-heatwave events since the early 2000s |journal=Science Advances |date=6 March 2026 |volume=12 |issue=10 |article-number=eaea3038 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aea3038 |pmid=41790886 |pmc=12965305 |bibcode=2026SciA...12a3038K }}</ref>
* 10 March: a study published in ''[[Environmental Research|Environmental Research: Health]]'' reported extensive statistics on present and projected worsening of heat- and humidity-related [[livability]] limitations.<ref name=EnvRschHealth_20260310>{{cite journal |last1=Parsons |first1=L. A. |last2=Baldwin |first2=J. W. |last3=Guzman-Echavarria |first3=G. |last4=Jay |first4=O |last5=Kalmus |first5=P. |last6=Staudmyer |first6=H. |last7=Vanos |first7=J. K. |last8=Wolff |first8=N. H. |title=Intensifying global heat threatens livability for younger and older adults |journal=Environmental Research: Health |date=10 March 2026 |volume=4 |page=015013 |doi=10.1088/2752-5309/ae3c3a|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* 25 March: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' estimated that, from 1990 through 2020, [[greenhouse gas emissions|carbon dioxide emissions]] in the US caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020, with about 30% occurring within the US itself.<ref name="Nature_20260325"/> Damages from China were estimated at $8.7 trillion, and from the EU, $6.42 trillion.<ref name="Nature_20260325"/> The researchers said that future damages from past emissions are at least an order of magnitude larger than historical damages from the same emissions.<ref name="Nature_20260325">{{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B }}</ref>
* 17 April: based on climate-driven weakening of day-night weather constraints, a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' estimated that from 1975 to 2024, annual potential burning hours for [[wildfire]]s in North America rose 36%.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260417>{{cite journal |last1=Luo |first1=Kaiwei |last2=Wang |first2=Xianli |last3=Castellanos-Acuna |first3=Dante |last4=Flannigan |first4=Mike |title=A weakened diurnal weather constraint leads to longer burning hours in North America |journal=Science Advances |date=17 April 2026 |volume=12 |issue=16 |article-number=eaed0725 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aed0725 |pmid=41996499 |pmc=13089344 |bibcode=2026SciA...12d0725L }}</ref>
* 21 April: [[Ember (non-profit organisation)|Ember]]'s ''Global Electricity Review 2026'' said that, in 2025, clean power growth exceeded the rise in overall global electricity demand (fossil fuel generation declining), and that renewables overtook coal power.<ref name=Ember_20260421>{{cite web |title=Global Electricity Review 2026 |url=https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/04/Global-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |publisher=Ember Energy |page=8 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260424062124/https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2026/04/Global-Electricity-Review-2026.pdf |archive-date=24 April 2026 |date=21 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 12 May: a study published in ''[[Environmental Research Letters]]'' considered life-cycle emissions of electric vehicles (EVs) and internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) and (acknowledging the variability of driving behaviors, climatic conditions, prices, fees, etc.) estimated that in the US battery electric vehicles (BEVs) save 40%–60% of emissions compared to ICEVs.<ref name=EnvRschLtrs_20260512>{{cite journal |last1=Miotti |first1=Marco |last2=Trancik |first2=Jessika E. |title=Determinants of electric vehicle emissions savings and costs across locations and individuals |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=12 May 2026 |volume=21 |issue=9 |doi=10.1088/1748 |doi-broken-date=1 July 2026 }}</ref>
* 13 May: a study of "compound events" (example: droughts combined with extreme heat)  published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that [[Extreme event attribution|rare and severe events]] escalate disproportionately with increasing {{CO2}} [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]].<ref name=Nature_20260513/> Accordingly, when compound events are considered, [[Carbon budget|emission levels that are considered allowable]] are substantially lower than when conventional [[Earth system science|Earth system models]] are used.<ref name=Nature_20260513>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jun |last2=Zhang |first2=Yao |last3=Ciais |first3=Philippe |last4=Zhang |first4=Hongying |last5=Wang |first5=Zhaoli |last6=Tang |first6=Hongwu |last7=Piao |first7=Shilong |title=Enhanced response of extreme compound events to cumulative CO2 emissions |journal=Nature |date=13 May 2026 |volume=654 |issue=8117 |pages=100–106 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10544-1 |pmid=42129560 }}</ref>
* 13 May: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature Health]]'' concluded that adoption in China of [[electric vehicle]]s led to a reduction in airborne pollutants that prevented about 262,000 non-accidental deaths and 75,000 all-cause deaths.<ref name=NatureHealth_20260513>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Qianqian |last2=Yuan |first2=Quan |last3=Yuan |first3=Qiangqiang |last4=Shen |first4=Huanfeng |last5=Wang |first5=Yuan |last6=Jiao |first6=Hongzan |last7=Zhaang |first7=Liangpei |last8=Gao |first8=Meng |title=Reduced urban air pollution and mortality from the transition to new energy vehicles in China |journal=Nature Health |date=13 May 2026 |volume=1 |issue=8 |pages=865–875 |doi=10.1038/s44360-026-00120-2}}</ref>
* 15 May: a study published in ''[[Nature Sustainability]]'' analyzed how [[Coal-fired power station|coal plants']] aerosol pollution reduces energy [[photovoltaics|photovoltaic]] (PV) energy production, including a 5.8% reduction in 2023, and losses from 2017 to 2023 equivalent to a third of energy added by [[Growth of photovoltaics|new PV sources]].<ref name=NatureSus_20260515>{{cite journal |last1=Song |first1=Rui |last2=Yin |first2=Feng |last3=Muller |first3=Jna-Muller |last4=Povey |first4=Adam C. |last5=Swain |first5=Basudev |last6=Huang |first6=Chenchen |last7=Grainger |first7=Roy G. |display-authors=4 |title=Coal plants persist as a large barrier to the global solar energy transition |journal=Nature Sustainability |date=15 May 2026 |volume=9 |issue=7 |pages=981–992 |doi=10.1038/s41893-026-01836-5 |bibcode=2026NatSu...9..981S }}</ref>
* 9 June: a study published in ''[[American Geophysical Union#Publications|GeoHealth]]'' forecast that, under a low [[greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] scenario, 31.5K-231K US [[heat illness|heat-related illnesses]] in 2012 would increase to 137K-314K by 2040. Under a high emissions scenario, the model predicted 42.5K-246K US illnesses in 2012 would increase to 156K-337K by 2040.<ref name=GeoHealth_20260609>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=S. E. |last2=Shandas |first2=V. |title=Predicting Urban Heat-Related Illness Across U.S. Climate Regions and Demographics |journal=GeoHealth |date=9 June 2026 |volume=10 |issue=6 |article-number=e2025GH001655 |doi=10.1029/2025GH001655 |doi-access=free |pmid=42272949 |pmc=13248521 |bibcode=2026GHeal..1001655B }}</ref>
* 10 June: 
:: — applying [[extreme event attribution]], a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' concluded that since 1900, the median frequency 1-in-100-year extreme [[coastal flooding]] events has increased ~12-fold, with human-driven [[radiative forcing]] alone quadrupling their likelihood.<ref name=NatureCC_20260610>{{cite journal |last1=Dangendorf |first1=Sonke |last2=Sun |first2=Qiang |last3=Maduwantha |first3=Pravin |last4=Wahl |first4=Thomas |last5=Marcos |first5=Marta |last6=Marzeion |first6=Ben |last7=Slangen |first7=Aimee B. A. |last8=Mitrovica |first8=Jerry X. |display-authors=4 |title=Human-driven sea-level rise has quadrupled the frequency of coastal sea-level extremes since 1900 |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=10 June 2026 |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=796–803 |doi=10.1038/s41558-026-02659-0 |bibcode=2026NatCC..16..796D }}</ref>
:: — applying [[extreme event attribution]], a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that human-caused climate change is responsible for ~58% of the daily extreme [[sea level rise|water level extremes]] over 2000–2018, and that human-caused sea level rise has caused a near-tripling of days with such extremes since the 1970s.<ref name=ScienceAdvances_20260610>{{cite journal |last1=Gilford |first1=Daniel M. |last2=Lin |first2=Yucheng |last3=Dahl |first3=Kristina |last4=Pershing |first4=Andrew |last5=Kopp |first5=Robert E. |last6=Strauss |first6=Benjamin |display-authors=4 |title=Human-caused sea level rise drives 21st-century worldwide water level extremes |journal=Science Advances |date=10 June 2026 |volume=12 |issue=24 |article-number=eadz3595 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adz3595 |pmid=42268972 |pmc=13251855 |bibcode=2026SciA...12z3595G }}</ref>
* 16 June: the [[UNICEF|United Nations Children’s Fund's]] ''Children’s Climate Risk Report 2026'' estimated that almost all children are now exposed to at least one of the following climate hazards: riverine floods (337M, "M"=million), coastal floods (33M), droughts (1.8B, "B"=billion), tropical storms (662M), heatwaves (1.5B), extreme heat (1.2B), fires (206M), and sand/dust storms (123M).<ref name=UNICEF_20260616>{{cite web |title=Children's Climate Risk Report 2026 |url=https://www.unicef.org/media/181481/file/CCRR%202026%20(1).pdf.pdf |website=UNICEF.org |publisher=United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260618155616/https://www.unicef.org/media/181481/file/CCRR%202026%20(1).pdf.pdf |archive-date=18 June 2026 |date=June 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* June: [[Energy Institute]]'s ''2026 Statistical Review of World Energy'' said that [[Renewable energy|renewables]] (solar, wind, geothermal, biofuels; excluding hydro, nuclear) were the largest source of energy supply ''growth'' (+3.3 EJ; EJ=10<sup>18</sup> [[joule]]s) for the first time outside of a recession (outpacing oil (2.5 EJ), gas (2.4 EJ) and coal (1.1 EJ)).<ref>{{cite web |title=2026 Statistical Review of World Energy |url=https://www.energyinst.org/__data/assets/file/0004/1827616/Statistical-Review-of-World-Energy-PDF-Report.pdf |publisher=Energy Institute |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260630103831/https://www.energyinst.org/__data/assets/file/0004/1827616/Statistical-Review-of-World-Energy-PDF-Report.pdf |archive-date=30 June 2026 |date=June 2026 |page=4 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 28 July: risk assessor First Street's ''Global Severe Convective Storm Risk Pricing Economic Exposure to a Rising Peril'' stated that cumulative insured losses from severe convective storms (SCS)—hail, damaging straight-line winds, tornadoes, and severe thunderstorms—overtook that of tropical cyclones, with $82 billion in economic losses and constituting nearly one-third of all natural catastrophe losses worldwide in 2025.<ref name=FirstStreet_202607>{{cite web |title=Global Severe Convective Storm Risk / Pricing Economic Exposure to a Rising Peril |url=https://hubspot.firststreet.org/hubfs/Research%20Reports/First%20Street%2019th%20Risk%20Assessment%20Global%20SCS%20Risk.pdf |publisher=First Street |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729052758/https://hubspot.firststreet.org/hubfs/Research%20Reports/First%20Street%2019th%20Risk%20Assessment%20Global%20SCS%20Risk.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2026 |date=July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 26 August: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that, based on current global temperature levels, on average, children (age 0–9) experience 9 to 10 more [[Extreme event attribution|attributable]] heat stress days than people aged 60–69 years, and that this difference is likely conservative as children spend more time outdoors.<ref name=SciAdv_20260826>{{cite journal |last1=Pietroiusti |first1=Rosa |last2=Fischer |first2=Erich |last3=Stuart-Smith |first3=Rupert |last4=Harrington |first4=Luke J. |last5=Brimicombe |first5=Chloe |last6=Mentel |first6=Matthias |last7=Savaresi |first7=Annalisa |last8=Adelman |first8=Sam |last9=Thiery |first9=Wim |display-authors=4 |title=Age-specific exposure to human-induced increases in humid heat |journal=Science Advances |date=26 August 2026 |volume=12 |issue=35 |article-number=eaeb3232 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aeb3232 |pmid=42647621 |pmc=13510599 |bibcode=2026SciA...12b3232P }}</ref>

==Natural events and phenomena==
[[File:1960- Heat storms.svg |thumb |Heat storms—generally defined as heat waves of long duration and covering wide areas—have increased in recent decades, under one definition growing from five per year in the 1960s to 102 per year in the 2020s through September 2026.<ref name=Reuters_20261020/> Spikes in heat waves have often followed within months after [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|El Niño]] events.<ref name=Reuters_20261020>{{cite news |last1=Tamman |first1=Maurice |last2=Welsh |first2=Ben |last3=McKenzie |first3=Pete |last4=Szymanski |first4=Charlie |last5=Delgerjargal |first5=Delgerzaya |last6=Corey-Boulet |first6=Robbie |last7=Coulibaly |first7=Loucoumane |last8=Horwitz |first8=Jeff |last9=Faus |first9=Joan |display-authors=4 |title=Giant ‘heat storms’ are scorching the Earth. This is the story of the biggest one on record. |url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/climate-heatstorms-science/ |agency=Reuters |date=20 October 2026}} "Sources: Reuters analysis, US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration".</ref>]]
* 4 February: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that [[wildfire]] smoke fine [[particulate matter]] (PM<sub>2.5</sub>) was responsible for ~24,100 all-cause deaths per year in the contiguous United States.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260204>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Min |last2=Castro |first2=Edgar |last3=Shtein |first3=Alexandra |last4=Peralta |first4=Adjani A. |last5=Yazdi |first5=Mahdieh Danesh |last6=Wu |first6=Xiao |last7=Schwartz |first7=Joel D. |last8=Wright |first8=Robert O. |last9=Wei |first9=Yaguang |display-authors=4 |title=Wildfire smoke PM<sub>2.5</sub> and mortality rate in the contiguous United States: A causal modeling study |journal=Science Advances |date=4 February 2026 |volume=12 |issue=6 |article-number=eadw5890 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adw5890|pmid=41637512 |pmc=12871454 |bibcode=2026SciA...12w5890Z }}</ref>
* 12 February: a study published in ''[[Nature Geoscience]]'' estimated that the contribution associated with a [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|La Niña-to-El Niño]] transition explains about 75% of the 2022-2023 extreme increase in Earth's [[Earth's energy budget|energy uptake]], contributing to the record [[global surface temperature]]s and widespread [[Extreme weather|climate extremes]] observed in 2023–2024.<ref name=Nature_20260109>{{cite journal |last1=Tsuchida |first1=Ko |last2=Kosaka |first2=Yu |last3=Minobe |first3=Shoshiro |title=Multi-year La Niña–El Niño transition influenced Earth's extreme energy uptake in 2022–2023 |journal=Nature Geoscience |date=12 February 2026 |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=432–438 |doi=10.1038/s41561-026-01921-6 |bibcode=2026NatGe..19..432T }}</ref>
* 25 February: a study published in ''[[Nature Ecology & Evolution]]'' stated that long-term global warming was associated with an annual fish biomass decline of up to 19.8% between 1993 and 2021 in major Northern Hemisphere basins.<ref name=NatureEcolandEvol_20260225>{{cite journal |last1=Chaikin |first1=Shahar |last2=Bonzalez-Trujillo |first2=Juan David |last3=Araujo |first3=Miguel B. |title=Long-term warming reduces fish biomass, but heatwaves shift it |journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution |date=25 February 2026 |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=932–941 |doi=10.1038/s41559-026-03013-5 |pmid=41741680 |bibcode=2026NatEE..10..932C }}</ref>
* 25 February: a study published in ''[[PLOS One]]'' reported that between 1794 and 2024, there was an average absolute shift in flowering of tropical plants of 2.04 days per decade (range: 0.037–14.10), comparable to changes seen in temperate, boreal and alpine desert plants, and severe enough to cause interspecific misalignment between pollinators and seed dispersers.<ref name=PLOSone_20260225>{{cite journal |last1=Graves |first1=Skylar |last2=Manzitto-Tripp |first2=Erin A. |title=Observing shifts in phenology of tropical flowering plants |journal=PLOS ONE |date=25 February 2026 |volume=21 |issue=2 |article-number=e0342105 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0342105 |doi-access=free |pmid=41739735 |pmc=12935240 |bibcode=2026PLoSO..2142105G }}</ref>
* 26 February: a study published in ''Air Quality, Atmosphere & Health'' warned that increasing [[Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth|atmospheric carbon dioxide]] levels might cause human blood's bicarbonate, calcium and phosphorus levels to reach the limits of acceptable healthy range.<ref name=AirQuality_20260226>{{cite journal |last1=Larcombe |first1=Alexander N. |last2=Bierwirth |first2=Phil N. |title=Carbon dioxide overload, detected in human blood, suggests a potentially toxic atmosphere within 50 years |journal=Air Quality, Atmosphere & Health |date=26 February 2026 |volume=19 |issue=44 |article-number=44 |doi=10.1007/s11869-026-01918-5 |bibcode=2026AQAH...19...44L }}</ref>
* 9 March: a study published in ''[[Atmospheric Science Letters]]'' estimated that, in the 3 May 2025 [[Hail|hailstorm]] in Western Europe, a 30% increase in probability of larger hail stones and a {{nbsp}}{{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} increase in hailstone size could be [[Extreme event attribution|attributed]] to climate change.<ref name=AtmosSciLtr_20260309>{{cite journal |title=Investigating the Role of Climate Change in the 3 May 2025 Western Europe Hailstorm Using Atmospheric Analogs |journal=Atmospheric Science Letters |last1=Faranda |first1=Davide |last2=Alberti |first2=Tommaso |date=9 March 2026 |volume=27 |issue=3 |article-number=e70016 |doi=10.1002/asl2.70016 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2026AtScL..2770016F }}</ref>
* 10 March: a study published in the ''[[Journal of Geophysical Research]]'' considered continental-ocean mass redistribution due to melting of polar [[Antarctic ice sheet#Ice_loss_and_accumulation|ice sheets]] and [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|global glaciers]] and changes in Earth's [[hydrology]], and said that 21st century climate change may be increasing the length of Earth's days at a rate among the highest in 3.6{{nbsp}}million years.<ref name=JGR_20260310>{{cite journal |last1=Shahvandi |first1=Mostafa Kiani |last2=Soja |first2=Benedikt |title=Climate-Induced Length of Day Variations Since the Late Pliocene |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |date=10 March 2026 |volume=131 |issue=3 |article-number=e2025JB032161 |doi=10.1029/2025JB032161 |bibcode=2026JGRB..13132161K }}</ref>
* March: the [[World Meteorological Organization]]'s ''State of the Global Climate 2025'' introduced a new indicator of the [[Earth's energy budget|Earth's energy balance]] and concluded that Earth's energy budget is more out of balance than at any previous time in the observational record.<ref>{{cite report |title=State of the Global Climate 2025 |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |year=2026 |location=Geneva |language=en |type=Flagship annual climate report |series=State of the Global Climate |number=WMO-No. 1391 |isbn=978-92-63-11391-7 |doi=10.59327/WMO/S/CRI/SOC1 |edition= 1 |page= 46 |url=https://library.wmo.int/records/item/69807-state-of-the-global-climate-2025 |format=PDF |access-date=24 March 2026}}</ref>
* 25 March: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that extreme global [[Effects of climate change|climate outcomes]] may occur even under moderate (2{{nbsp}}°C) global warming.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bevacqua |first1=Emanuele |last2=Fischer |first2=Erich |last3=Sillman |first3=Jana |last4=Zscheischler |first4=Jakob |title=Moderate global warming does not rule out extreme global climate outcomes |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=946–953 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10237-9 |pmid=41882130 |pmc=13017523 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..946B }}</ref>
* 26 March: a study published in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' concluded that environmental heat stress thresholds may be cooler and drier than previously thought, more specifically, that "non-survivable conditions" are occurring during present-day heat events that are below the six-hour 35{{nbsp}}°C wet-bulb temperature threshold that currently defines such conditions.<ref name=ClimateComms_20260326>{{cite journal |last1=Perkins-Kirkpatrick |first1=Sarah E. |last2=Gregory |first2=Catherine H. |last3=Vanos |first3=Jennifer K. |last4=Baldwin |first4=Jane W. |last5=Staudmyer |first5=Haley |last6=Guzman-Echavarria |first6=Gisel |last7=Jay |first7=Ollie |title=Deadly heat stress conditions are already occurring |journal=Nature Communications |date=26 March 2026 |volume=17 |issue=1 |article-number=2590 |doi=10.1038/s41467-026-70485-1  |doi-access=free|pmid=41888528 |pmc=13021964 }}</ref>
* 8 April: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that over the past 20 years, the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (AMOC) has weakened at four different latitudes along the western boundary of the North Atlantic Ocean, that boundary thought to constitute the "[[wikt:canary in a coal mine|canary in a coal mine]]" for the tendency of the AMOC as a whole.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260408>{{cite journal |last1=Xing |first1=Qianjiang |last2=Elipot |first2=Shane |last3=Johns |first3=William E. |last4=Smeed |first4=David A. |last5=Moat |first5=Ben I. |last6=Loder |first6=John W. |title=Meridionally consistent decline in the observed western boundary contribution to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation |journal=Science Advances |date=8 April 2026 |volume=12 |issue=15 |article-number=eadz7738 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adz7738 |pmid=41950313 |pmc=13060603 |bibcode=2026SciA...12z7738X }}</ref>
* 10 April: [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA's]] "Final La Niña Advisory" concluded that La Niña conditions had transitioned to [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|ENSO]]-neutral, which was expected to persist through Northern Hemisphere summer.<ref name=NOAA_20260410>{{cite web |title=El Niño & La Niña (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) |url=https://www.climate.gov/enso |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260410034308/https://www.climate.gov/enso |archive-date=10 April 2026 |date=10 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 15 April: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' estimated a slowdown of the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (AMOC) of 51±8%—a weakening ~60% stronger than suggested by multimodel mean estimates.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260415>{{cite journal |last1=Portmann |first1=Valentin |last2=Swingedouw |first2=Didier |last3=Khattab |first3=Omar |last4=Chavent |first4=Marie |title=Observational constraints project a ~50% AMOC weakening by the end of this century |journal=Science Advances |date=15 April 2026 |volume=12 |issue=16 |article-number=eadx4298 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adx4298 |pmid=41984958 |pmc=13082334 |bibcode=2026SciA...12x4298P }}</ref>
* 16 April (reported): an editorial published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' noted that, in 2025, [[mosquito]]s were found in [[Iceland]] for the first time, and were said to be "a warning that the Arctic lacks a system for monitoring [[arthropod]]s and anticipating biological risks before they escalate".<ref name=Science_20260416>{{cite journal |last1=Koltz |first1=Amanda M. |last2=Culler |first2=Lauren E. |title=The Arctic's growing mosquito problem |journal=Science |date=16 April 2026 |volume=392 |issue=6795 |page=235 |doi=10.1126/science.aeh9505 |pmid=41990176 |bibcode=2026Sci...392..235K }}</ref>
* 4 May: a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' estimated that airborne [[microplastics]] and [[Microplastics#nanoplastics|nanoplastics]] add direct [[radiative forcing]] of ~1.34 W/m<sup>2</sup>, exceeding that of black carbon by a factor of 4.7.<ref name=NatureCC_202260504>{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Yu |last2=Fu |first2=Hongbo |last3=Zhang |first3=Hongliang |last4=Wang |first4=Yunhang |last5=Chakrabarty |first5=Rajan K. |last6=Tu |first6=Xiang |last7=Tang |first7=Xu |last8=Laskin |first8=Alexander |last9=Carmichael |first9=Gregory R. |last10=Chen |first10=Jianmin |last11=Francisco |first11=Joseph S. |last12=Shindell |first12=Drew T. |display-authors=4 |title=Atmospheric warming contributions from airborne microplastics and nanoplastics |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=4 May 2026 |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=598–605 |doi=10.1038/s41558-026-02620-1 |bibcode=2026NatCC..16..598L }}</ref>
* 6 May: a study published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' concluded that, on 10 August 2025, climate change had "preconditioned" a >64{{nbsp}}million cubic meter [[landslide]] in Alaska's [[Tracy Arm]] fjord that caused a 481-meter [[Tsunami#Tsunami_heights|run-up]] [[megatsunami]] after an initial 100-meter high [[breaking wave]] traveling at over {{convert|70|m/s|mph}}.<ref name=Science_20260506>{{cite journal |last1=Shugar |first1=Dan H. |last2=Barnhart |first2=Katherine R. |last3=Berdahl |first3=Mira |last4=Caplan-Auerbach |first4=Jacqueline |last5=Ekstrom |first5=Goran |last6=Fathian |first6=Aram |display-authors=4 |title=A 481-meter-high landslide-tsunami in a cruise ship–frequented Alaska fjord |journal=Science |date=6 May 2026 |volume=392 |issue=6803 |article-number=eaec3187 |doi=10.1126/science.aec3187 |pmid=42089535 |bibcode=2026Sci...392c3187S }}</ref>
* 8 May: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' concluded that, even under gradual [[Effects of climate change|environmental change]], eco-evolutionary feedback can create a [[Tipping points in the climate system|tipping point]] beyond which [[Adaptive capacity|adaptation]] fails, as [[genetic drift]] overwhelms selection and species' ranges contract from the margins or fragment abruptly.<ref name=PNAS_20260508>{{cite journal |last1=Polechova |first1=Jitka |title=Evolution of species' range and niche in changing environments |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=8 May 2026 |volume=123 |issue=19 |article-number=e2604510123 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2604510123 |pmid=42101998 |pmc=13167760 |bibcode=2026PNAS..12304510P }}</ref>
* 8 May: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' applied a sea ice-ocean model identifying three distinct phases of [[Antarctic sea ice]] retreat, and suggested that "persistent [[upwelling]]-favorable conditions under anthropogenic forcing may [[Tipping points in the climate system|push]] the [[Southern Ocean]] into a prolonged low sea ice state".<ref name=SciAdv_20260508>{{cite journal |last1=Narayanan |first1=Aditya |last2=Ayres |first2=Holly |last3=England |first3=Matthew H. |last4=Haumann |first4=F. Alexander |last5=Mazloff |first5=Matthew R. |last6=Silvano |first6=Alessandro |last7=Spira |first7=Theo |last8=Zhou |first8=Shenjie |last9=Garabato |first9=Alberto C. Naveira |display-authors=4 |title=Compound drivers of Antarctic sea ice loss and Southern Ocean destratification |journal=Science Advances |date=8 May 2026 |volume=12 |issue=19 |article-number=eaeb0166 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aeb0166 |pmid=42102215 |pmc=13155358 |bibcode=2026SciA...12b0166N }}</ref>
* 11 May: a study published in ''[[Nature Geoscience]]'' concluded that stratospheric cooling atop a [[greenhouse effect|warming troposphere]] is the result of the [[spectroscopy]] of [[carbon dioxide]] and not a result of increasing optical thickness.<ref name=NatureGeosci_20260511>{{cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=Sean |last2=Pincus |first2=Robert |last3=Polvani |first3=Lorenzo M. |title=Stratospheric cooling and amplification of radiative forcing with rising carbon dioxide |date=11 May 2026 |journal=Nature Geoscience |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=507–512 |doi=10.1038/s41561-026-01965-8 |bibcode=2026NatGe..19..507C }}</ref>
* 19 May: a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' concluded that [[warm-blooded]] seabirds—unable to adjust their body temperature to ambient temperature—must reduce their geographic [[Species distribution|range]] in response to global warming, forcing them to disperse over longer distances.<ref name=NatureCC_20260519>{{cite journal |last1=Avaria-Llautureo |first1=Jorge |last2=Rvadeneira |first2=Marcelo M. |last3=Venditti |first3=Chris |last4=Luna-Jorquera |first4=Guillermo |title=Seabird range contraction and dispersal under climate change |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=19 May 2026 |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=836–842 |doi=10.1038/s41558-026-02655-4 |bibcode=2026NatCC..16..836A }}</ref>
* 20 May: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' estimated that the factors driving [[sea level rise]] since 1960 are 43% from thermal ocean expansion, 27% from glacier melting, 15% from Greenland, 12% from Antarctica, and 3% from land water storage.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260520>{{cite journal |last1=Zheng |first1=Huayi |last2=Cheng |first2=Lijing |last3=Dangendorf |first3=Sonke |last4=Meyssignac |first4=Benoit |last5=Barnoud |first5=Anne |last6=Trenberth |first6=Kevin E. |last7=Fasullo |first7=John T. |last8=Abraham |first8=John |display-authors=4 |title=Improved closure of the global mean sea level budget from observational advances since 1960 |journal=Science Advances |date=20 May 2026 |volume=12 |issue=21 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aea065 |doi-broken-date=22 June 2026 }}</ref>
* 27 May: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' forecast a 36.5–42.1% increase in global [[hail]]storm-induced damage potential by 2100, with the magnitude determined by the emission scenario.<ref name=Nature_20260527>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Shiyi |last2=Zhang |first2=Qinghong |last3=Allen |first3=John T. |last4=Lin |first4=Xiangyu |title=Rising global hail damage potential in a warming world |journal=Nature |date=27 May 2026 |volume=653 |issue=8116 |pages=1069–1077 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10543-2 |pmid=42203928 |bibcode=2026Natur.653.1069Z }}</ref>
* 28 May: a study published in ''[[Geophysical Research Letters]]'' concluded that the cooling observed in the "cold blob" south of Greenland and Iceland is due to changes in the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (ocean heat transport), and not because of variations in ocean surface heat loss.<ref name=GeophyRschLtrs_20260528>{{cite journal |last1=Rahmstorf |first1=Stefan |last2=Jendrkowiak |first2=Jan |last3=Gou |first3=Ruijian |last4=Cheng |first4=Lijing |last5=Ruiz-Angulo |first5=Angel |last6=Bjornsson |first6=Halldor |title=Multidecadal Atlantic "Warming Hole" Heat Content Variations Are Caused by Ocean Heat Transport, Not by Surface Fluxes |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=28 May 2026 |volume=53 |issue=11 |article-number=e2025GL118383 |doi=10.1029/2025GL118383 |bibcode=2026GeoRL..5318383R }}</ref>
* 28 May: a study published in ''[[Communications Earth & Environment]]'' suggested that an Arctic Ocean [[Tipping points in the climate system|regime shift]] is occurring because of [[nitrate]] reductions attributable to [[Arctic sea ice decline]].<ref name=CommsEandE_20260528>{{cite journal |last1=Santos-Garcia |first1=Marta |last2=Geneshram |first2=Raja S. |last3=Oziel |first3=Laurent |last4=Dodd |first4=Paul A. |last5=de Steur |first5=Laura |last6=Tuerena |first6=Robyn E. |last7=Stedmon |first7=Colin A. |title=Sea ice loss drives a regime shift in Arctic Ocean nitrogen biogeochemistry |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=28 May 2026 |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=442 |doi=10.1038/s43247-026-03569-x  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2026ComEE...7..442S }}</ref>
* 11 June: a [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] notice stated that "[[2026–2027 El Niño event|El Niño]] conditions are present and expected to strengthen into the Northern Hemisphere winter 2026-27".<ref name=NOAA_20260611>{{cite web |title=El Nino/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) Diagnostic Discussion issued by Climate Prediction Center/NCEP/NWS |url=https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260611151636/https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml |archive-date=11 June 2026 |date=11 June 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 12 June: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that coupling between [[photosynthesis]] and woody [[biomass]] growth (wood acting as a [[carbon sink]]) has been overestimated, so that current [[Earth system science|earth system models]] may be overestimating long-term [[carbon sequestration]] in forests.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260612A>{{cite journal |last1=Rao |first1=Mukund Palat |last2=Pacheco-Solana |first2=Arturo |display-authors=1 |title=Decoupled carbon assimilation and growth responses to aridity in temperate deciduous oaks |journal=Science Advances |date=12 June 2026 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.ady7139 |volume=12 |issue=24 |article-number=eady7139 |pmid=42284422 |pmc=13262636 |bibcode=2026SciA...12y7139R }}</ref>
* 12 June: considering "deep carbon"— at least {{convert|3|m|ft}} deep—in [[permafrost#Impacts of climate change|permafrost thaw]], a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that in high-[[greenhouse gas emissions|emission]] scenarios, northern soil carbon balance's reversal from carbon sink to carbon source should be advanced from what is predicted by existing Earth system models.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260612B>{{cite journal |last1=Xi |first1=Yi |last2=Ciais |first2=Philippe |last3=Zhu |first3=Dan |last4=Qiu |first4=Chunjing |last5=Zhang |first5=Yuan |last6=Peng |first6=Shushi |last7=Bowring |first7=Simon P. K. |last8=Goll |first8=Daniel S. |last9=Friedlingstein |first9=Pierre |last10=Hugelius |first10=Gustaf |display-authors=4 |title=Net release of CO2 from thawing permafrost soil carbon predicted to occur earlier in this century |journal=Science Advances |date=12 June 2026 |volume=12 |issue=24 |article-number=eadz8478 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adz8478 |pmid=42284397 |pmc=13262627 |bibcode=2026SciA...12z8478X }}</ref>
* 17 June: a study of UK floods and droughts published in ''[[American Geophysical Union#Publications|Earth's Future]]'' (American Geophysical Union) concluded that increased global warming will increase "hydrodynamic whiplash" (sudden shifts between wet and dry conditions), which might cause a drought to make land less able to subsequently absorb intense rain.<ref name=EarthsFuture_20260617>{{cite journal |last1=He |first1=Y. |last2=Manful |first2=D. |last3=Forstenhausler |first3=N. |last4=Huang |first4=Y. |last5=Smith |first5=B. |last6=Zha |first6=Q. |title=Escalating Hydroclimatic Extremes and Volatility in the UK Under 2°C and 4°C Warming |journal=Earth's Future |date=17 June 2026 |volume=14 |issue=6 |article-number=e2025EF007156 |doi=10.1029/2025EF007156 |bibcode=2026EaFut..1407156H }}</ref>
* 20 July: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' said that exceptionally low 2025 and 2026 [[Arctic ice pack|arctic ice]] extent indicated that 20-year [[arctic sea ice decline]] was "becoming significant again" after a period in which such declines had been insignificant.<ref name=PNAS_20260720>{{cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Duo |last2=Silvano |first2=Alessandro |last3=Josey |first3=Simon A. |title=Record-low 2025 and 2026 ice extents restore Arctic winter sea-ice decline |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=20 July 2026 |volume=123 |issue=30 |article-number=e2614134123 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2614134123 |pmid=42475559 |pmc=13415921 }}</ref>
* 27 July: a study published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' concluded that, above a certain air temperature [[Tipping points in the climate system|threshold]], the date of lake ice spring melting advances non-linearly, with the sensitivity of ice loss increasing up to 22-fold.<ref name=PNAS_20260727>{{cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Jian |last2=Wang |first2=Weijia |last3=Ma |first3=Yaru |last4=Leavitt |first4=Peter R. |title=Rapid acceleration of ice-cover loss from Northern Hemisphere lakes above critical air temperature thresholds |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=27 July 2026 |volume=123 |issue=32 |article-number=e2610752123 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2610752123 |pmid=42507911 |pmc=13462685 }}</ref>
* 5 August: a study published in ''[[Nature Ecology & Evolution]]'' concluded that 80% of [[butterfly]] species studied experienced [[Species distribution#Range|range]] expansions and 27% experienced range contractions; 79% of range shifts were associated with climate change and extreme weather events.<ref name=NatureEcolEvol_20260805>{{cite journal |last1=Chowdhury |first1=Shawan |last2=Aich |first2=Upama |last3=Antao |first3=Laura H. |last4=Pinkert |first4=Stefan |last5=Akita |first5=Perpetra |display-authors=etal |title=Extensive climate-induced range shifts in butterflies across the globe |journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution |date=5 August 2026 |doi=10.1038/s41559-026-03117-y |pmid=42557340 }}</ref>
* 5 August: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that, since the 1850s in the western US, "snow-eater heat waves"—involving abrupt snowmelt triggered by rain-on-snow events, and possibly causing flooding, initiating or accelerating snow drought, and affecting water availability—have increased in area and frequency, decreased in duration, and shifted earlier in the melt season.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260805>{{cite journal |last1=Rhoades |first1=Alan M. |last2=North |first2=Joshua Snowball |last3=Fudisill |first3=William |last4=Hatchett |first4=Benjamin J. |last5=Risser |first5=Mark |display-authors=4 |title=Snow-eater heat waves of the western United States |journal=Science Advances |date=5 August 2026 |volume=12 |issue=32 |article-number=eaeb3361 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aeb3361 |pmid=42555720 |pmc=13440393 |bibcode=2026SciA...12b3361R }}</ref>
* 12 August: a study published in ''[[Trends (journals)|Trends in Ecology & Evolution]]'' concluded that, contrary to current assumptions, water scarcity and droughts can intensify many diseases by "altering host aggregation, parasite persistence, community composition, and contact networks across space and time".<ref name=EcolEvol_20260812>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Pieter |last2=Merrill |first2=Tara Stewart |title=Plagued by drought: how water scarcity reshapes host–parasite interactions |journal=Trends in Ecology & Evolution |date=12 August 2026 |doi=10.1016/j.tree.2026.07.002 |pmid=42586806 }}</ref>
* 27 August: a study published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' reported that  geochemistry of [[Galápagos Islands|Galápagos]] [[coral]] skeletons across the past millennium shows a large recent increase in interannual variability of [[sea surface temperature]] in the eastern equatorial Pacific compared to existing paleorecords, an increase that exceeds simulated [[Climate variability and change|natural variability]] and that results from stronger [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation]] (ENSO) events.<ref name=Science_20260827>{{cite journal |last1=Cole |first1=J. E. |last2=Thompsno |first2=D. M. |last3=Tripp |first3=C. J. |last4=Edwards |first4=R. L. |display-authors=1 |title=Recent strengthening of eastern Pacific ENSO in the last millennium paleorecord |journal=Science |date=27 August 2026 |article-number=eady2660 |doi=10.1126/science.ady2660 |pmid=42658966 }}</ref>
* 10 September: a study published in ''[[Environmental Research Letters]]'' estimated that warming-induced [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] (WIE) of [[greenhouse gas]]es from natural sources (permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters, wildfire)—which are not represented by most current climate models—could add 0.2{{nbsp}}°C–0.4{{nbsp}} °C of global warming by 2100.<ref name=EnvRsch_20260910>{{cite journal |last1=Abernethy |first1=Sam |last2=Monteverde |first2=Danielle |last3=Schadel |first3=Christina |last4=Buma |first4=Brian |last5=Duffy |first5=Philip B. |last6=Jackson |first6=Robert B. |last7=Natali |first7=Susan M. |last8=Ocko |first8=Ilissa |last9=Rogers |first9=Brendan M. |last10=Poulter |first10=Benjamin |title=Projected amplification of global warming by warming-induced greenhouse gas emissions |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=10 September 2026 |volume=21 |issue=17 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/ae9e24 |bibcode=2026ERL....21q4022A }}</ref>
* 10 September: a study published in ''[[American_Geophysical_Union#Publications|AGU Advances]]'' concluded that since 1980, extreme dry and humid heat seasons have significantly expanded over 50% and 48% of the global land area, respectfully, and that the expansions are primarily asymmetric (occurring before vs after the historical extreme heat season, in different regions of the world).<ref name=AGUadvances_20260910>{{cite journal |last1=Ivanovich |first1=Catherine C. |last2=Cook |first2=Benjamin |last3=McDermid |first3=Sonali |title=Extreme Dry and Humid Heat Seasons Are Changing Asymmetrically |journal=AGU Advances |date=10 September 2026 |volume=7 |issue=6 |page=e2026AV002516 |doi=10.1029/2026AV002516Digital |doi-broken-date=4 October 2026 }}</ref>
* 16 September: a study published in ''[[Scientific Data (journal)|Scientific Data]]'' concluded that the [[Greenland ice sheet|Greenland]] and [[Antarctic ice sheet|Antarctic]] ice sheets lost 11,309 ±565 billion tonnes of ice between 1979 and 2023, with glacier dynamical imbalance driving 84% of the ice loss and surface mass balance the remainder.<ref name=SciData_20260916>{{cite journal |last1=Otosaka |first1=Ines N. |last2=Shepherd |first2=Andrew |display-authors=1 |title=Mass balance of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets from the 1970s to 2023 |journal=Scientific Data |date=16 September 2026 |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=1301 |doi=10.1038/s41597-026-08088-0 |pmid=42749744 |pmc=13582886 |bibcode=2026NatSD..13.1301O }}</ref>
* 21 September: the [[Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research]]'s ''Planetary Health Check 2026'' reported that seven out of nine [[planetary boundaries]] have been transgressed.<ref name=PIKhealthCheck2026>{{cite web |title=Planetary Health Check 2026 / A Scientific Assessment of the State of Our Planet |last1=Caesar |first1=Levke |last2=Sakschewski |first2=Boris |last3=Andersen |first3=Lauren Seaby |editor-first1=Niklas Henrik |editor-first2=Boris |editor-first3=Levke |editor-first4=Johan |editor-last1=Kitzmann |editor-last2=Sakschewski |editor-last3=Caesar |editor-last4=Rockström |display-authors=2 |url=https://publications.pik-potsdam.de/rest/items/item_35009/component/file_35022/content |page=7 |publisher=Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260921153920/https://publications.pik-potsdam.de/rest/items/item_35009/component/file_35022/content |archive-date=21 September 2026 |doi=10.48485/pik.2026.25 |date=September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 14 October: ''The 2026 state of the climate report'' published in ''[[BioScience]]'' stated that seven of sixteen climate-related indicators are currently at record extremes, and that progress in mitigation climate change "remains far below the scale and speed needed to stabilize Earth’s climate system".<ref name=BioScience_20261014>{{cite journal |last1=Ripple |first1=William J. |last2=Wolf |first2=Christopher |last3=Mann |first3=Michael E. |last4=Rockstrom |first4=Johan |last5=Pascual |first5=Unai |last6=Gregg |first6=Jillian W. |last7=Xu |first7=Chi |last8=Perkins-Kirkpatrick |first8=Sarah E. |last9=Newsome |first9=Thomas M. |last10=Bukoski |first10=Jacob |last11=Prakash |first11=Anjal |display-authors=4 |title=The 2026 state of the climate report: challenges and opportunities |journal=BioScience |date=14 October 2026 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biag125}}</ref>
* 23 October: a study published by [[Imperial College London]] estimated 50,391 heat-related excess deaths across 854 European cities during the [[2026 European heatwaves|summer heat waves]], with around two thirds [[Extreme event attribution|attributable]] to anthropogenic [[climate change]].<ref name=ImperialCollege_20261023>{{cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=Clair |last2=Masselot |first2=Pierre |last3=Xi |first3=Di |last4=Rayner |first4=Archie |last5=chen |first5=Xinyi |last6=Raju |first6=Emmanuel |last7=Mistry |first7=Malcolm |last8=Gasparrini |first8=Antonio |last9=Otto |first9=Friederike |last10=Vicedo-Cabrera |first10=Ana Maria |last11=Konstantinoudis |first11=Garyfallos |title=Heat-related urban mortality attributable to human-induced climate change in Europe in summer 2026 |journal=Nature Health (via Imperial) |date=23 October 2026 |doi=10.25560/147042 |url=https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/e8879b8a-f89b-4690-b6d5-5bfbf81f94b8/content |publisher=Imperial College London}} ([https://www.imperial.ac.uk/grantham/publications/all-publications/heat-related-urban-mortality-attributable-to-human-induced-climate-change-in-europe-in-summer-2026.php accepted for publication] in ''Nature Health'')</ref>

==Actions, and goal statements==
===Science and technology===
* January (reported): a Chinese company launched the first megawatt-level airborne wind turbine—a 60x40x40{{nbsp}}m (197x131x131{{nbsp}}ft) helium-filled [[aerostat]]—providing electricity through a [[tether]] cable from {{convert|2000|m|ft}} above the ground.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sinha |first1=Sujita |title=China's world-first megawatt-level 'windmill' airship rises 6,560 ft, feeds grid |url=https://interestingengineering.com/energy/worlds-first-megawatt-airship-rises-6560-ft |publisher=Interesting Engineering |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260115030438/https://interestingengineering.com/energy/worlds-first-megawatt-airship-rises-6560-ft |archive-date=15 January 2026 |date=13 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 14 January: at [[Concordia Station]], Antarctica, the [[Ice Memory#Ice Memory Foundation|Ice Memory Foundation]] inaugurated a global repository of mountain [[ice core]]s, to ensure that future generations will be able to study past climate conditions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Winfield |first1=Nicole |last2=Santalucia |first2=Paulo |title=A novel sanctuary in Antarctica is preserving ice samples from rapidly melting glaciers |url=https://apnews.com/article/italy-climate-global-warming-glacier-ice-antarctica-25c45a3a1e6375a1f241c825e5e63e5c |work=AP News |date=14 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260115031550/https://apnews.com/article/italy-climate-global-warming-glacier-ice-antarctica-25c45a3a1e6375a1f241c825e5e63e5c |archive-date=15 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 15 January: a study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' estimated the 2020 ocean-based [[social cost of carbon]] (SCC) to be almost double that of prior SCC estimates that didn't consider ocean-related impacts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bastien-Olvera |first1=Bernardo A. |last2=Aburto-Oropeza |first2=Octavio |last3=Brander |first3=Luke M. |last4=Cheung |first4=William W. L. |last5=Emmerling |first5=Johannes |last6=Free |first6=christopher M. |last7=Granella |first7=Francesco |last8=Tavoni |first8=Massimo |last9=Verschuur |first9=Jasper |last10=Ricke |first10=Katharine |title=Accounting for ocean impacts nearly doubles the social cost of carbon |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=15 January 2026 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=297–304 |doi=10.1038/s41558-025-02533-5 |bibcode=2026NatCC..16..297B |url=https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/eee4ec57-81f1-4e4d-92eb-09d75c7e55d4 }}</ref>
* 12 February: anomalous increases in tropical [[sea surface temperature]]s have caused [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]] to revise the threshold distinguishing [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|La Niña and El Niño (ENSO) events]] from each other.<ref name="NOAA_20260212"/> The new method replaces a dependency on a 30-year climate base period with the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI): a comparison of the ENSO region to the global tropics.<ref name="NOAA_20260212">{{cite web |title=CPC adopts Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) for reliable, responsive monitoring and tracking of ENSO |url=https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/announcement.php |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260224062958/https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/announcement.php |archive-date=24 February 2026 |date=12 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* 4 March: a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' concluded that sea level measurements that have been based on [[geoid]] models rather than actual sea level measurements have underestimated the degree of [[sea level rise]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seegeer |first1=Katharina |last2=Minderhoud |first2=Philip S. J. |title=Sea level much higher than assumed in most coastal hazard assessments |journal=Nature |date=4 March 2026 |volume=652 |issue=8110 |pages=667–674 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10196-1 |doi-access=free |pmid=41781624 |pmc=13083249 |bibcode=2026Natur.652..667S }}</ref>
* 24 April: a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' concluded that artificial closure of the [[Bering Strait]] can extend the safe carbon budget of the [[Atlantic meridional overturning circulation]] (AMOC), provided that the AMOC is strong enough at the time of closure.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260424>{{cite journal |last1=Soons |first1=Jelle |last2=Dijkstra |first2=Henk A. |title=The effects of a constructed closure of the Bering Strait on AMOC tipping behavior |journal=Science Advances |date=24 April 2026 |volume=12 |issue=17 |article-number=eaeb7887 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aeb7887 |pmid=42030387 |pmc=13108545 |bibcode=2026SciA...12b7887S }}</ref>
