======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in New Zealand
======================================================================

{{Short description|Emissions, impacts and responses of New Zealand related to climate change}}

{{Use New Zealand English|date=November 2012}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2023}}
{{POV|talk=NPOV concerns|date=October 2026}}

[[File:Baringhead co2 v9.svg|thumb|450px|Atmospheric carbon dioxide record from [[Baring Head]], Wellington, from 1977 to present.<ref>[[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]], La Jolla, California, U.S.A.</ref>]]

'''Climate change in New Zealand''' involves historical, current and future changes in the [[climate of New Zealand]]; and New Zealand's contribution and response to global [[climate change]].<ref name="climate2017">{{cite web| url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/publications/environmental-reporting/our-atmosphere-and-climate-2017| title=Our atmosphere and climate 2017| publisher=Ministry for the Environment and Statistics NZ| date=October 2017}}</ref> Summers are becoming longer and hotter, and some glaciers have melted completely and others have shrunk. In 2021, the Ministry for the Environment estimated that New Zealand's gross emissions were 0.17% of the world's total gross [[greenhouse gas emissions]]. However, on a [[per capita]] basis, New Zealand is a significant emitter, the sixth highest within the Annex I countries, whereas on absolute gross emissions New Zealand is ranked as the 24th highest emitter.<ref name="MFEcompare">{{cite web| url= https://environment.govt.nz/publications/new-zealands-greenhouse-gas-inventory-1990-2019-snapshot/how-new-zealand-compares-to-other-countries/ |title=Snapshot How New Zealand compares to other countries|work=Ministry for the Environment |date= 15 April 2021 }}</ref><ref name="outsized-climate-change-contribution">{{cite news| url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/109053475/new-zealands-outsized-climate-change-contribution| title=New Zealand's out-sized climate change contribution| publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | date=8 December 2018}}</ref>

More than half (53%) of New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions are from [[Agriculture in New Zealand|agriculture]], mainly methane from sheep and cow belches.<ref name="ghgisnapshot2021">{{citation | url=https://environment.govt.nz/publications/new-zealands-greenhouse-gas-inventory-19902022-snapshot/ |title=New Zealand's Greenhouse Gas Inventory 1990–2022 snapshot |work=Ministry for the Environment |date=18 April 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=13 April 2021|title=Agriculture emissions and climate change|url=https://environment.govt.nz/guides/agriculture-emissions-climate-change/|access-date=19 January 2022|website=Ministry for the Environment|language=en-GB}}</ref> Between 1990 and 2022, New Zealand's gross emissions (excluding removals from land use and forestry) increased by 14%. When the uptake of carbon dioxide by forests (sequestration) is taken into account, net emissions (including [[carbon removal]]s from land use and forestry) increased by 33% since 1990.<ref name="ghgisnapshot2021" />

Climate change is being responded to in a variety of ways by civil society and the [[New Zealand Government]]. This includes participation in international treaties and in social and political debates related to climate change. New Zealand has an [[New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme|emissions trading scheme]], and in 2019 the government introduced the [[Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill]] which created a [[Climate Change Commission]] responsible for advising the government on policies and [[Carbon budget|emissions budgets]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.mfe.govt.nz/climate-change/zero-carbon-amendment-bill| title=Proposed Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill| publisher=Ministry for the Environment| access-date=7 June 2019| archive-date=6 November 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106151412/https://www.mfe.govt.nz/climate-change/zero-carbon-amendment-bill}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/landmark-climate-change-bill-goes-parliament |date= 8 May 2019 |access-date= 20 May 2019 |title=Landmark climate change bill goes to Parliament |author= Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern |publisher=New Zealand Government }}</ref>

New Zealand made a number of pledges on [[climate change mitigation]] in 2019: to reduce net carbon emissions to zero by 2050, to plant 1 billion trees by 2028, and to bring pastoral agriculture (farmers) into an emissions price policy by 2025. Already in 2019, New Zealand banned new offshore oil and gas drilling and decided that climate change issues would be examined before every important decision.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ainge Roy |first1=Eleanor |date=4 December 2019 |title=Climate change to steer all New Zealand government decisions from now on |publisher=The Dunedin |agency=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/dec/04/climate-change-to-steer-all-new-zealand-government-decisions-from-now-on |access-date=4 December 2019}}</ref> In early December 2020, [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] [[Jacinda Ardern]] declared a [[Climate emergency declarations in New Zealand|climate change emergency]] and pledged that the New Zealand Government would be carbon neutral by 2025. Key goals and initiatives include requiring the public sector to buy only electric or hybrid vehicles, government buildings will have to meet new "green" building standards, and all 200 coal-fired boilers in public service buildings will be phased out.<ref name="climate-change-emergency">{{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Phil |date=2 December 2020 |title=New Zealand declares a climate change emergency |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/02/new-zealand-declares-a-climate-change-emergency |url-status=live |access-date=2 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202030445/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/02/new-zealand-declares-a-climate-change-emergency |archive-date=2 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="government-will-have-to-buy-electric-cars">{{cite news |last1=Cooke |first1=Henry |date=2 December 2020 |title=Government will have to buy electric cars and build green buildings as it declares climate change emergency |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300172852/government-will-have-to-buy-electric-cars-and-build-green-buildings-as-it-declares-climate-change-emergency |url-status=live |access-date=2 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202053524/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300172852/government-will-have-to-buy-electric-cars-and-build-green-buildings-as-it-declares-climate-change-emergency |archive-date=2 December 2020}}</ref> International assessments of New Zealand's climate change actions are either ranked as "low" on the [[Climate Change Performance Index]]<ref name="Germanwatch_CCPI-2024-Results">{{cite web |author1=Jan Burck |author2=Thea Uhlich |author3=Christoph Bals |author4=Niklas Höhne |author5=Leonardo Nascrimiento |date =20 November 2024 |publisher=Germanwatch |title=Climate Change Performance Index 2024 |url= https://ccpi.org/wp-content/uploads/CCPI-2024-Results.pdf }}</ref> or rated as "highly insufficient" by [[Climate Action Tracker]].<ref name="catnz2023">{{cite web |publisher = Climate Action Tracker |title=New Zealand |date =7 March 2023 |archive-date=14 March 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230314172923/https://climateactiontracker.org/countries/new-zealand/ |url= https://climateactiontracker.org/countries/new-zealand/}}</ref>
{{TOC level|3}}

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==
{{bar box
|title=NZ GHG Emissions Profile by Gas 2022<ref name="ghgisnapshot2021" />
|titlebar=#ddd
|left1=greenhouse gas
|right1=percent
|float=right
|bars=
{{bar percent|Carbon Dioxide|green|40}}
{{bar percent|Methane|blue|49}}
{{bar percent|Nitrous Oxide|red|9}}
{{bar percent|HFCs PFCs and SF6|yellow|2}}
}}
[[File:New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Emissions from 1990.svg|thumb|right|New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions from 1990]]{{Update section|date=December 2023|reason=needs 2022 emission estimates added and more up to date official figures}}
New Zealand has a relatively unique emissions profile. In 2022, agriculture contributed 53% of total gross emissions; energy (including transport), 37%; industry, 6%; waste, 4%. Based on the latest available Inventory data for 2022, New Zealand's gross emissions per capita were above the average for developed countries.<ref name="ghgisnapshot2021" /> In other [[Kyoto Protocol]] Annex 1 countries, agriculture typically contributes about 12% of total emissions.<ref name="MFEcompare" />

Between 1990 and 2022, New Zealand emissions of [[carbon dioxide]] (CO<sub>2</sub>) increased by 24%; [[methane]] (CH<sub>4</sub>) by 2%; and [[nitrous oxide]] (N<sub>2</sub>O) by 35%. The total of all combined [[fluorinated gases]] have increased by 87%.<ref name="ghgisnapshot2021" />

The [[New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme]], which came into effect in 2010, was intended to provide a mechanism which encouraged different sectors of the economy to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. It may have slowed the increase somewhat. Between 2007 and 2017 total national emissions decreased 0.9%, reflecting growth in [[Renewable energy in New Zealand|renewable energy generation]].<ref name="barely-budged-in-a-decade">[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/113806480/greenhouse-gas-emissions-have-barely-budged-in-a-decade-new-data-shows Greenhouse gas emissions have barely budged in a decade, new data shows] Stuff, 27 June 2019</ref> However, between 2016 and 2017, New Zealand's gross emissions jumped 2.2%, bringing the total (or gross) increase in greenhouse gas emissions between 1990 and 2017 to 23.1%.<ref name="NZH_Emissions19">[https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12221417 Rising NZ emissions sparks call for transport crackdown], NZ Herald 11 April 2019</ref>
[[File:NZ greenhouse gases by sector.svg|thumb|left|New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions projected and actual from 1990 to 2030]]
[[File:Per capita greenhouse gas emissions.svg|thumb|right|New Zealand gross greenhouse gas emissions per capita compared to United Kingdom, Europe, China, World average, India and Africa]]

In 2018, on a per capita basis, New Zealand was the 21st biggest contributor to global emissions in the world and fifth highest in the [[OECD]].<ref name="outsized-climate-change-contribution" />

=== Carbon dioxide ===
New Zealand has a long-term record of atmospheric [[carbon dioxide]] similar to the [[Keeling Curve]]. In 1970, [[Charles David Keeling|Charles Keeling]] asked [[Dave Lowe (atmospheric scientist)|David Lowe]], a physics graduate from [[Victoria University of Wellington]] to establish continuous atmospheric measurements at a New Zealand site. The south-facing [[Baring Head]], on the eastern entrance to [[Wellington Harbour]], was chosen as being representative of the atmosphere of the [[Southern Hemisphere|southern hemisphere]]. Despite the majority of CO<sub>2</sub> emissions coming from the [[Northern Hemisphere]], the atmospheric concentration in New Zealand is similar.<ref name="pmcsa.org.nz">[https://www.pmcsa.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/New-Zealands-Changing-Climate-and-Oceans-report.pdf New Zealand's changing climate and oceans: The impact of human activity and implications for the future], An assessment of the current state of scientific knowledge by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor, July 2013</ref> The Baring Head records show that CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations rose from 325 ppm in 1972 to 380 ppm in 2009,<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gibson|first=Eloise|date=5 December 2009|title=Measuring the air that we breathe|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/climate-change/news/article.cfm?c_id=26&objectid=10613515|access-date=10 January 2010}}</ref> and passed 400 ppm in 2015<ref>[https://www.niwa.co.nz/atmosphere/our-data/trace-gas-plots/carbon-dioxide Carbon dioxide], Baring Head, New Zealand, NIWA</ref> and reached a new maximum of 416 ppm in December 2023.<ref>{{cite web |first=Kate |last=Newton |title=Carbon dioxide levels reach another new record at NIWAS's monitoring site on Wellington's coast |date=31 July 2024 |access-date=17 August 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/in-depth/523651/carbon-dioxide-levels-reach-another-new-record-at-niwa-s-monitoring-site-on-wellington-s-coast}}</ref>

Modelled wind directions indicated that air flows were originating from 55 degrees south. The Baring Head data shows about the same overall rate of increase in CO<sub>2</sub> as the measurements from the [[Mauna Loa Observatory]], but with a smaller seasonal variation. The rate of increase in 2005 was 2.5 parts per million per year.<ref>{{cite book|last=Lowe|first=David|url=http://vup.victoria.ac.nz/confronting-climate-change-critical-issues-for-new-zealand/|title=Confronting Climate Change. Critical issues for New Zealand|publisher=Victoria University Press|year=2006|editor-last=Chapman|editor-first=Ralph|place=Wellington|pages=75–82|contribution=The changing composition of the Earth's atmosphere: linkages to increasing agricultural and industrial activity|editor2-last=Boston|editor2-first=Jonathan|editor3-last=Schwass|editor3-first=Margot}}</ref> The Baring Head record is the longest continuous record of atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> in the Southern Hemisphere and it featured in the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report: Climate Change 2007 in conjunction with the better-known Mauna Loa record.<ref>{{cite book|author=Forster, P.|url=http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch2s2-3.html#2-3-1|title=2.3 Chemically and Radiatively Important Gases|series=[[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report|IPCC AR4 WG1 2007]]|display-authors=etal|access-date=3 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121012045712/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch2s2-3.html#2-3-1|archive-date=12 October 2012}}</ref>

According to estimates from the International Energy Association, New Zealand's per capita carbon dioxide emissions roughly doubled from 1970 to 2000 and then exceeded the per capita carbon dioxide emissions of either the United Kingdom or the European Union.<ref>{{cite web|author=IEA|year=2009|title=CO<sub>2</sub> Emissions from Fuel Combustion|url=http://www.iea.org/co2highlights/co2highlights.xls|access-date=18 June 2011|publisher=International Energy Association|location=Paris}}</ref>  Per capita carbon dioxide emissions are in the highest quartile of global emissions.<ref>{{cite web|year=2012|title=Country Data New Zealand|url=http://co2scorecard.org/countrydata/|access-date=27 July 2012|work=CO2 Scorecard|quote=per capita CO<sub>2</sub> emissions of 9.28 metric tons per year, it is in the highest quartile globally}}</ref>

=== Methane ===

[[File:New Zealand atmospheric methane concentrations.svg|thumb|New Zealand atmospheric methane concentrations at Baring Head]]

The [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research]] (NIWA) has also recorded atmospheric concentrations of [[Methane emissions|methane]] (from 1989) and [[nitrous oxide]] (from 1997) at Baring Head.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Atmosphere – Greenhouse gas measurements in New Zealand|encyclopedia=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/atmosphere/3|access-date=2 November 2011|date=2 March 2009|author2=Katja Riedel|author3=Richard McKenzie|author4=Sylvia Nichol|author5=Tom Clarkson|author1=Bill Allan}}</ref> More than 80% of methane emissions in New Zealand come from [[enteric fermentation]] in [[ruminant]] livestock – sheep, cattle, goats and deer – with sheep the greatest single source.<ref>[https://www.nzagrc.org.nz/methane-1.html Methane], NZ Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre</ref>

This emissions profile is significantly different to that of other countries as, internationally, the dominant sources of methane are rice paddies and wetlands. As a greenhouse gas, methane is 28 times more powerful than carbon dioxide.<ref>[https://research.csiro.au/futurefeed/ FutureFeed], CSIRO</ref> A dairy cow produces between 84 and 123&nbsp;kg of methane per year from rumen fermentation.<ref>{{cite web|year=2009|title=Greenhouse Gases|url=http://sci.waikato.ac.nz/farm/content/greenhouse.html|access-date=19 March 2012|publisher=University of Waikato|archive-date=18 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318104108/http://sci.waikato.ac.nz/farm/content/greenhouse.html}}</ref> Since New Zealand has large stock numbers these emissions are significant. In 1997, New Zealand's per capita emissions of methane were almost six times the OECD average and ten times the global average.<ref>{{cite web|last=MfE|year=2007|title=State of New Zealand's Environment 1997 – Chapter 10: Conclusions|url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/publications/ser/ser1997/html/chapter10.3.html#IssueReducingtheriskofclimate|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081016011806/http://mfe.govt.nz/publications/ser/ser1997/html/chapter10.3.html#IssueReducingtheriskofclimate|archive-date=16 October 2008|access-date=15 July 2012|publisher=Ministry for the Environment|quote=New Zealand's per capita emissions of methane, another greenhouse gas, are almost six times the OECD average and ten times the global average}}</ref>

In 1997 Minister for Climate Change Issues Simon Upton stated that New Zealand's methane emissions from ruminant livestock industries were the highest per capita in the world.<ref>{{cite web|title= New Zealand's Climate Change Policy |url= https://www.beehive.govt.nz/speech/energy-federation-new-zealands-climate-change-policy |work= Speech to Energy Federation |publisher = New Zealand Government |first = Simon |last= Upton |date = 31 October 1997 |access-date= 10 April 2025 }}</ref>

=== Nitrous oxide ===
[[Nitrous oxide]] is emitted primarily from agriculture, but also comes from industrial processes and fossil fuel combustion. Over 100 years, it was 298 times more effective than CO<sub>2</sub> at trapping heat. In New Zealand in 2018, 92.5% of N<sub>2</sub>O came from agricultural soils mainly due to urine and dung deposited by grazing animals. Overall, N<sub>2</sub>O emissions increased 54% from 1990 to 2018 and now make up 19% of all agricultural emissions.<ref name="greenhouse-gas-emissions">{{cite web| url=https://www.stats.govt.nz/indicators/new-zealands-greenhouse-gas-emissions| title=New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions| date=15 October 2020| access-date=11 May 2021| publisher=Stats NZ}}</ref>

=== Agriculture ===
{{as of|2019|alt = In 2019}}, the agriculture industry was responsible for half of all emissions in New Zealand, but contributed less than 7% of the national Gross Domestic Product (GDP). In the decade prior there were modest reductions in emissions from sheep, beef, deer and poultry farms, but these were offset by a rapid growth in dairy farming which was the biggest increase in emissions of any single industry. Emissions from dairy had risen 27% over the decade such that this industry was responsible for more emissions than the manufacturing, electricity and gas supply industries combined.<ref name="barely-budged-in-a-decade" />

=== Food processing ===
In 2019, dairy collective [[Fonterra]] was responsible for 20% of New Zealand's entire greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name="newsroom.co.nz">{{cite news
 |title        = Politicking and pleading over climate crisis regulation
 |url          = https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2019/06/09/623996/oram-politicking-pleading
 |publisher    = Newsroom NZ
 |author       = Rod Oram
 |date         = 9 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref> This was largely due to Fonterra's use of coal-powered boilers to dry milk into milk powder. Clean energy expert, [[Michael Liebreich]], described the use of coal for this process as "insane". [[Genesis Energy Limited]] chief executive, Marc England, said in 2019 that Fonterra was using more coal than Genesis uses at its [[Huntly power station]] and should use electricity, which was already 85% renewable, in its milk powder factories.<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = Fonterra burning coal to dry milk 'insane' and must stop, says British energy expert
 |url          = https://www.stuff.co.nz/business/113599336/fonterra-burning-coal-to-dry-milk-insane-and-must-stop-says-british-energy-expert
 |work         = Stuff
 |publisher    = Stuff Limited
 |author       = Eloise Gibson
 |date         = 21 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

=== Electricity ===
The majority of New Zealand's [[Electricity sector in New Zealand|New Zealand's electricity]] is hydroelectric. In the 2019 calendar year, 82.4% of the country's electricity was generated from renewable or low-carbon resources: 58.2% from hydroelectricity, 17.4% from geothermal, 12.6% from [[natural gas]], 5.1% from wind, 4.9% from coal, and 1.7% from other sources.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Energy in New Zealand|url=https://www.mbie.govt.nz/building-and-energy/energy-and-natural-resources/energy-statistics-and-modelling/energy-publications-and-technical-papers/energy-in-new-zealand/|access-date=29 November 2020|publisher=Ministry of Business, Innovation & Employment}}</ref>

In 2019, the [[Huntly Power Station]] consumed about 300,000 tonnes of coal<ref name="nzherald.co.nz">{{cite news|last=Baker|first=Chris|date=12 June 2019|title=Let's talk about coal and climate change|work=[[New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/opinion/news/article.cfm?c_id=466&objectid=12239337}}</ref> and was one of the biggest carbon dioxide generators in the country contributing over half of New Zealand's emissions of greenhouse gases from electricity generation.<ref>{{cite web|author=Professor Peter Gluckman|date=13 August 2009|title=Climate change|url=http://www.pmcsa.org.nz/issues/climate_change/|access-date=7 January 2011|publisher=Office of the Prime Minister's Science Advisory Committee|quote=The coal-burning Huntly power station on the Waikato river is responsible for over half of New Zealand's emissions from electricity generation}}</ref> According to Chris Baker, chief executive of Straterra, "that scenario won't change for years to come."<ref name="nzherald.co.nz" /> Only 10% of the power from the Huntly plant was used by [[Genesis Energy Limited]] itself. The remaining 90% sold to other electricity companies to ease their own supply issues. In February 2018 Genesis Energy said it may keep burning fossil fuels until 2030.<ref>[https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2018/02/14/88961/our-inconvenient-truth-nz-will-keep-burning-coal# Our Inconvenient Truth: NZ will keep burning coal], Newsroom, 15 February 2018</ref>

A major barrier in decommissioning Huntly is ensuring continued security of supply, especially to [[Auckland]] and Northland. In June 2019, transmission grid operator [[Transpower New Zealand|Transpower]] analysed the effects of closing the two remaining coal-fired units at Huntly on its grid. It concluded that without the coal-fired units and no major new generation or transmission upgrades, voltage collapse could occur during Auckland and Northland winter peak demand from 2023 onwards with the 400 MW combined-cycle gas turbine Huntly Unit 5 out of service, or from 2019 onwards with both Huntly Unit 5 and any one of the 220,000-volt transmission lines from [[Whakamaru Dam|Whakamaru]] out of service.<ref>{{Cite web|date=June 2019|title=Waikato and Upper North Island Voltage Management Investigation – Attachment A: Power Systems Analysis Report|url=https://www.transpower.co.nz/sites/default/files/projects/resources/WUNIVM%20Power%20System%20Analysis%20Report%20-%20June%202019.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=9 August 2021|website=Transpower New Zealand|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210809033321/https://www.transpower.co.nz/sites/default/files/projects/resources/WUNIVM%20Power%20System%20Analysis%20Report%20-%20June%202019.pdf |archive-date=9 August 2021 }}</ref>

=== Households ===

The bulk of household emissions stem from New Zealanders' reliance on combustion engine cars for transport, with relatively small amounts coming from heating and cooling.<ref name="barely-budged-in-a-decade" /> In 2019, there were less than 10,000 electric vehicles on New Zealand roads leading the [[New Zealand Productivity Commission]] to recommend a rapid and comprehensive switch from petrol cars to EVs. Professor David Frame, director of Victoria University's New Zealand Climate Change Research Institute says "the growth (in use) of electric cars has been nowhere fast enough to get to where we've said we want to be by 2030".<ref name="NZH_Emissions19" />

In the last ten years,{{When|date=April 2021}} New Zealand and Australia were among a handful of developed nations where household emissions are increasing. The others are all Eastern European countries.<ref name="barely-budged-in-a-decade" /> A New Zealand study conducted in 2019 says housing must shrink its carbon footprint by 80% to meet New Zealand's commitment to the [[Paris Agreement]] - adding that a typical new Kiwi home emits five times as much carbon dioxide as it should if the world is to stay below 2&#x20;°C warming.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Chandrakumar | first1=Chanjief | last2=McLaren | first2=Sarah J. | last3=Dowdell | first3=David | last4=Jaques | first4=Roman | title=A science-based approach to setting climate targets for buildings: The case of a New Zealand detached house | journal=Building and Environment | date=2020 | volume=169 | article-number=106560 | doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2019.106560 | bibcode=2020BuEnv.16906560C | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360132319307723 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Transportation ===
==== Road ====
{{further|Plug-in electric vehicles in New Zealand}}
Due to the growth in the number of vehicles on New Zealand roads (now more than four million vehicles) emissions from transport have grown 78% since 1990<ref name="ReferenceB">[https://www.stuff.co.nz/motoring/news/106901060/what-the-productivity-commissions-feebate-could-mean-for-car-prices What the Productivity Commission's 'feebate' could mean for car prices], Stuff, 10 September 2018</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=nzcpe|date=28 December 2019|title=Should I ditch my fossil-fueled car?|url=https://blog.planetaryecology.org/2019/12/28/should-i-ditch-my-fossil-fueled-car/|access-date=15 January 2020|website=Planetary Ecology|language=en-GB}}</ref>{{Update inline|date=April 2021}} and are now the second-largest source of the country's greenhouse gas emissions. Road transport contributes 45% of all emissions from the burning of fossil fuels in New Zealand.<ref name=":0" /> New Zealanders tend to buy big cars, [[SUV|SUVs]] and [[Utility vehicle|utes]],<ref name="ReferenceB" /> and for this reason our average vehicle CO<sub>2</sub> emissions per head of population is high compared to other developed nations,<ref name="pmcsa.org.nz" /> such that the country's transport emissions per person are the fourth highest in the world.<ref name="ReferenceB" />

One reason for this is that New Zealand is one of only three countries without fleet-wide vehicle emissions standards<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/114068301/government-proposes-massive-feebate-car-scheme-that-would-make-cleaner-cars-up-to-8k-cheaper-and-dirtier-cars-more-expensive?rm=m Government scheme could slash prices on cleaner cars, and make dirtier cars more expensive], Stuff, 9 July 2019</ref> leading the [[New Zealand Productivity Commission]] to argue the country is "becoming a dumping ground for high-emitting cars from other nations busy decarbonising their highways".<ref name="NZH_Emissions19" /> As a result, there has been little incentive for the public to buy electric cars or hybrids; as at May 2019, only 61,000 hybrid vehicles were registered in New Zealand.<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/motoring/news/113716461/are-we-finally-accepting-hybrids Are we finally accepting hybrids?] Stuff 12 July 2019</ref>{{Update inline|date=April 2021}}

However, in July 2019, Associate Transport Minister [[Julie Anne Genter]] announced a government proposal to impose substantial price discounts on imported cars with low emissions and price penalties on those with high emissions. This would knock about $8,000 off the price of new or near-new imported electric vehicles (EVs) while the heaviest petrol using polluters would cost $3,000 more. The scheme is expected to remove more than five million tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> from New Zealand's emissions even though it only applies to (new and used) vehicles coming into the country and does not apply to the 3.2 million vehicles already on the roads which account for 74% of annual sales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Editorial: Clean cars the right road forward |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/editorial-clean-cars-the-right-road-forward/N32INMVGBHDO5MRVUZLLIB2QVE/ |access-date=16 May 2026 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=McCulloch |first=Craig |last2= |first2= |date=9 July 2019 |title=Government's 'clean car discount': Fees for high-emission vehicles would offset efficiency subsidy |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/393928/government-s-clean-car-discount-fees-for-high-emission-vehicles-would-offset-efficiency-subsidy |access-date=16 May 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

====Rail====
Around {{Convert|589|km||abbr=on}} of New Zealand's {{Convert|4128|km||abbr=on}} of railway track is [[Railway electrification system|electrified]]. This includes the majority of the [[Public transport in Auckland|Auckland]] and [[Public transport in the Wellington Region|Wellington]] regional commuter networks (with the notable exception of the [[Wairarapa Connection|Wellington to Masterton]] service), and the central section of the North Island Main Trunk between Hamilton and Palmerston North. There is no electrified track in the South Island.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

==== Air travel ====
[[File:New Zealand aviation emissions of greenhouse gases.svg|thumb|left|New Zealand emissions of greenhouse gases from aviation]]New Zealand's aviation emissions have resumed increasing rapidly after a decline in 2020 caused by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. From 1990 to 2019 New Zealand's aviation emissions increased by 116% to 4.9 Mt CO<sub>2</sub>. New Zealand ranks 4th highest in the world for per-capita domestic aviation emissions and 6th highest in the world for per-capita international aviation emissions, which are about 10 times the world average. From 2015 to 2019 international aviation emissions rose more rapidly at more than 40%. In summary, New Zealand has particularly high aviation emissions and has been on a very rapid growth path that is incompatible with the Paris Agreement on climate change.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 =Callister | first1 = Paul | last2 = McLachlan | first2 = Robert | title = Managing Aotearoa New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions from aviation | journal = Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand | pages = 412–432 | publisher = Taylor & Francis | location = New Zealand | date = 2024 | volume = 54 | issue = 4 | doi = 10.1080/03036758.2023.2212174 | pmid = 39559259 | doi-access = free | pmc = 11573339 | bibcode = 2024JRSNZ..54..412C }}</ref>
[[Air New Zealand]] is one of the country's largest climate polluters, emitting more than 3.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere every year. This represents about 4% of New Zealand's total greenhouse gas emissions. [[Air New Zealand]] offers a voluntary scheme, called FlyNeutral, which allows passengers to buy carbon credits to offset their flights. Currently customers offset less than 1.5% of the airline's total carbon emissions. Air New Zealand's domestic emissions are regulated through the [[New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme]] and it has to purchase and surrender emission units for its domestic emissions.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.stuff.co.nz/business/industries/113919272/air-new-zealands-kiwi-customers-half-as-likely-to-buy-carbon-credits-than-those-in-the-united-kingdom |title =Air New Zealand's Kiwi customers half as likely to buy carbon credits than those in the United Kingdom |work= Stuff |date= 2 July 2019 |first =John |last=Anthony}}</ref>

In 2022, Air New Zealand adopted a 2030 target to cut its emissions by almost 29%.<ref>{{cite web |url =  https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/czrjzvep41ro |title = Air NZ becomes first big carrier to drop climate goal |work=  BBC |date= 30 July 2024 |access-date= 19 February 2024 |first = João |last = da Silva}}</ref>

In July 2024, Air NZ announced the withdrawal of its 2030 climate target and that it would withdraw from the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi). The Spinoff website reported that this raises serious credibility questions for Air New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web
|url =  https://thespinoff.co.nz/business/31-07-2024/air-nz-abandoning-its-2030-climate-target-raises-serious-credibility-questions  |title = Air NZ abandoning its 2030 climate target raises serious credibility questions |work=  The Spinoff |date= 31 July 2024 |access-date= 19 February 2024 |first = Danny |last = Rood }}</ref>

=== Ten biggest polluters ===
{{as of|2019}}, the ten companies which emit the most greenhouse gases in New Zealand were [[Fonterra]], [[Z Energy]], [[Air New Zealand]], [[Methanex]], [[Marsden Point Oil Refinery]], BP, Exxon Mobil, [[Genesis Energy Limited]], [[Contact Energy]], and [[Fletcher Building]]. These companies emit around 54.5 million tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> each year – more than two thirds of New Zealand's total emissions.<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = NZ's biggest greenhouse gas emitters and their struggle to pollute less
 |url          = https://www.stuff.co.nz/business/114431409/nzs-biggest-greenhouse-gas-emitters-and-their-struggle-to-pollute-less
 |work         = Stuff
 |publisher    = Stuff Limited
|last1 =Gibson
 |first1      = Eloise 
 |date         = 26 July 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

==== Favourable treatment for high polluters ====
The seven biggest industrial emitters in New Zealand are [[Fonterra]], [[NZ Steel]], [[New Zealand Aluminium Smelters]] (which operates the [[Tiwai Point Aluminium Smelter]]), [[Marsden Point Oil Refinery|NZ Refining]], [[Golden Bay Cement]], [[Methanex]] and [[Pan Pac Forest Products]]. According to business journalist [[Rod Oram]], for years these companies have been the main beneficiaries of favourable Government policies designed to minimise the impact of the [[New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme]] on companies which are emissions intensive and trade exposed (EITE). In 2017 these companies (plus another three of the largest emitters) received 90% of the free credit allocations—essentially a licence to continue polluting—offered by the Government under the scheme.<ref name="newsroom.co.nz" />{{Update inline|date=April 2021}}
