This global warming level most closely matches country emissions reduction pledges made for the Paris Climate Agreement..." |doi-access=free |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1899837 }}</ref><ref name="Phiddian2022">{{Cite web |last=Phiddian |first=Ellen |date=5 April 2022 |title=Explainer: IPCC Scenarios |url=https://cosmosmagazine.com/earth/climate/explainer-ipcc-scenarios/ |website=[[Cosmos (magazine)|Cosmos]] |access-date=30 September 2023 |quote="The IPCC doesn't make projections about which of these scenarios is more likely, but other researchers and modellers can. [[The Australian Academy of Science]], for instance, released a report last year stating that our current emissions trajectory had us headed for a 3°C warmer world, roughly in line with the middle scenario. [[Climate Action Tracker]] predicts 2.5 to 2.9°C of warming based on current policies and action, with pledges and government agreements taking this to 2.1°C. |archive-date=20 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230920224129/https://cosmosmagazine.com/earth/climate/explainer-ipcc-scenarios/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
}}

New Zealand has reliable air temperature records going back to the early 1900s. Temperatures are taken from seven climate stations throughout the country and combined into an average.

According to [[NIWA]], the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research, 2022 was Aotearoa New Zealand's warmest year on record. The nationwide average temperature for 2022 was +1.15&nbsp;°C above the 1981–2010 annual average. From 1909 to 2022 the air around New Zealand has warmed by 1.37&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://niwa.co.nz/climate/summaries/annual-climate-summary-2022| title=Annual Climate Summary 2022| publisher=NIWA| date=11 January 2023}}</ref> That record succeeded 2021 as the warmest year on record.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://niwa.co.nz/climate/summaries/annual-climate-summary-2021| title=Annual Climate Summary 2021|publisher=NIWA| date=11 January 2022}}</ref>

Temperatures are expected to warm by at least 2&nbsp;°C by the end of the century<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.climatehotmap.org/global-warming-locations/tasman-glacier-new-zealand.html| title=Tasman Glacier, New Zealand| work=Climate Hot Map| publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists}}</ref> although an Australian report released in 2019 called [[Breakthrough - National Centre for Climate Restoration|Breakthrough]], says the plans that countries have put forward for cutting emissions for the [[Paris Agreement]] will lead to around 3&nbsp;°C of warming. Breakthrough says warming will be even higher than that because the model used does not include long-term [[carbon cycle]] feedback loops.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2205741-is-it-true-climate-change-will-cause-the-end-of-civilisation-by-2050/| title=Is it true climate change will cause the end of civilisation by 2050?| publisher=New Scientist| date=6 June 2019}}</ref>

=== Ecosystems ===
The [[Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society of New Zealand]] has pointed out that New Zealand's native plants and animals are vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. More frequent storms combined with rising sea levels will make it harder for seabirds like [[hoiho]] (yellow-eyed penguin) to find food. Warmer temperatures will lead to more frequent ''mast events'' (sudden abundance of food in an area of forest leading to huge population irruptions of mice, rats and stoats). This puts greater pressure on native species like [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] which are already in trouble. Warmer temperatures also allow pests and weeds will extend their range, and new pests and diseases will begin to appear. [[Tuatara]] eggs are also sensitive to temperature: fewer female tuatara will hatch, threatening the survival of New Zealand's largest reptile.<ref>[https://www.forestandbird.org.nz/what-we-do/climate Climate] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507104211/https://www.forestandbird.org.nz/what-we-do/climate |date=7 May 2019 }}, Forest & Bird</ref>

Research done in [[Wellington|Wellington, New Zealand]] in 2018 showed that the effects of climate change in conjunction with their rapid growth affect plant and animal life. Natural habitats are getting smaller and smaller, reducing the opportunity for certain plants to survive. Alongside this, researchers are noticing that with an increase in temperature, predation and invasive species are becoming more common. Researchers advise introducing more pest-free urban [[wildlife sanctuaries]] as they have seen success with them on the island in the past. Doing this would ensure that highly important native animals, like the [[kererū]] and [[tūī]], are conserved while keeping invasive species out, ultimately preserving New Zealand's biodiversity in the face of climate change.<ref name=":05">{{Cite web |last=Rastandeh |first=Amin |date=2018 |title=Urban biodiversity in an era of climate change: Towards an optimised landscape pattern in support of indigenous wildlife species in urban New Zealand |url = https://openaccess.wgtn.ac.nz/articles/thesis/Urban_biodiversity_in_an_era_of_climate_change_Towards_an_optimised_landscape_pattern_in_support_of_indigenous_wildlife_species_in_urban_New_Zealand/17134823 |doi = 10.26686/wgtn.17134823.v1 }}</ref>

=== Glaciers ===
[[File:Fox Franz Ivory Glaciers NZ fig6.gif|thumb|right|400px|Measured variations in the position of the termini of the Fox, Franz Josef, and Ivory Glaciers, 1870 to 1988<ref name=usgs>{{Cite book
 | first = Trevor.J.
 | last = Chinn
 | editor-last = Williams
 | editor-first = R.S.
 | editor2-last = Ferrigno
 | editor2-first = J.G.
 | title=Glaciers of New Zealand
 | url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/prof/p1386h/nzealand/nzealand2.html
 | series=U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1386-H
 | year=1989
 | page=48
 | publisher=U.S. Geological Survey
 | isbn=978-0-607-71457-9}}</ref>]]

New Zealand has over 3,000 [[glacier]]s, most of which are in the South Island.<ref>[https://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/jpl/pia21509/new-zealand-glaciers New Zealand Glaciers], NASA 2017</ref> Since 1977, the [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research]] (NIWA) has been using aerial surveys of late summer snowline to estimate the [[Glacier mass balance|mass balance]] of 50 index glaciers.  The snowline marks the equilibrium line of a glacier; above the line the glacier is accumulating snow and below the line the glacier is melting. The mass balance is the net gain or loss of snow and ice.<ref name='wa'>{{Cite journal
  | last1 =Salinger
  | first1 = Jim
  | author-link =Jim Salinger
  | last2 = Chinn
  | first2 = Trevor
  | last3 = Willsman
  | first3 = Andrew
  | last4 = Fitzharris
  | first4 = Blair
  | title = Glacier response to climate change
  | journal = Water & Atmosphere
  | volume = 16
  | issue = 3
  | pages = 16–17
  | publisher = [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research]]
  | location = New Zealand
  |date=September 2008
  | url = http://www.niwa.co.nz/news-and-publications/publications/all/wa/16-3/glacier
  | access-date =20 January 2010 }}</ref> A survey by [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research|NIWA]] in 2009 says the volume of ice in [[Glaciers of New Zealand|New Zealand's glaciers]] declined by about 50% in the last century, while New Zealand's average temperature increased by about 1&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Glaciers Continue to Shrink | url = http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/SC0911/S00044.htm |publisher = [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research]] (NIWA)|date=23 November 2009|access-date=5 January 2010}}</ref>

In 2017, [[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research|NIWA]] published new research in the scientific journal, ''[[Nature Communications]]'', showing that between 1983 and 2008, regional climate variability caused more than 50 of New Zealand's glaciers to grow in contrast to international trends. Lead author Associate Professor Andrew Mackintosh from Victoria's [[Antarctic Research Centre]] said: "Glaciers advancing is very unusual—especially in this period when the vast majority of glaciers worldwide shrank in size as a result of our warming world." Mackintosh said glaciers grew because temperatures dropped as a result of variability in the climate system specific to New Zealand. He does not expect this unusual trend to continue saying: "If we get the two to four degrees of warming expected by the end of the century, our glaciers are going to mostly disappear."<ref name="phys.org">[https://phys.org/news/2017-02-zealand-unusual-glaciers.html Explaining New Zealand's unusual growing glaciers], 15 February 2017</ref>

New Zealand's largest glacier, the [[Tasman Glacier]], has retreated about 180 metres a year on average since the 1990s and the glacier's terminal lake, [[Tasman Lake]], is expanding at the expense of the glacier. [[Massey University]] scientists expect that Lake Tasman will stabilise at a maximum size in about 10 to 19 years, and eventually the Tasman Glacier will disappear completely. In 1973 the Tasman Glacier had no terminal lake and by 2008 Tasman Lake was 7&nbsp;km long, 2&nbsp;km wide and 245 m deep.<ref>{{cite web
| title = Tasman Glacier retreat extreme
| publisher = [[Massey University]]
| date =  23 April 2008
| url = http://www.massey.ac.nz/massey/about-massey/news/article.cfm?mnarticle=tasman-glacier-retreat-extreme-23-04-2008
| access-date = 24 April 2008 }}</ref> Between 1990 and 2015, Tasman Glacier retreated 4.5 kilometres (2.8 miles),  mostly from calving.<ref>[https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/89901/tasman-glacier-retreats Tasman Glacier Retreats], NASA Earth Observatory</ref>

Climate change has caused [[Glaciers of New Zealand|New Zealand's glaciers]] to shrink in total volume by one third in the last four decades. Some glaciers have already disappeared completely. As at 2017, the area covered by New Zealand's glaciers shrank from 1240sq km to 857sq km, a decrease of 31% since the late 1970s. This is a loss of just under 1% a year, although the rate is speeding up with the biggest melt occurring in a record-hot summer of 2017/18.<ref>[https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12249079 Climate change: New Zealand's glaciers hit hard by another big melt], NZ Herald, 13 July 2019</ref> Climate scientist, [[Jim Salinger]] said the decline will affect skiing and tourism, and cause problems for South Island farmers in particular. He also said: "This would mean that ice melt from our mountain glaciers will predominate during the 21st century with Aotearoa, land of the long white cloud, becoming Aoteapoto – the land of the short white cloud."<ref>[https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12220542 'Land of the short white cloud' – NZ glaciers' huge loss of ice in just 42 years], NZ Herald, 9 April 2019
</ref>

===Sea level rise===
{{excerpt|Sea level rise in New Zealand|paragraphs=1-2}}

=== Wildfires ===
Summers are getting longer and hotter such that four of the last six years have been New Zealand's warmest on record. Scion Rural Fire Research Group fire scientist, Grant Pearce, says the number of days that the risk of dangerous fires breaking out in some parts of New Zealand could double by 2050. The [[Pigeon Valley Fire|Pigeon Valley fire]] in Nelson in 2019 was New Zealand's largest forest fire in 60 years. It covered more than 2,300 hectares prompting an independent review of fire risk which found wildfires would occur more frequently because of drier conditions. The risk will escalate due to increases in temperature, wind speed and lower rainfall associated with global warming. [[The Lancet]] reports that the health effects of wildfires range from burns and death, to the exacerbation of acute and chronic conditions.<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/117446174/severe-fire-weather-days-could-double-by-2050-in-some-regions-fire-scientist-warns Severe fire weather days could double by 2050 in some regions, fire scientist warns], Stuff 15 November 2019
</ref>

==Impacts on people==
The combined [[effects of climate change]] will result in a multitude of irreversible impacts on New Zealand. By the end of this century New Zealand will experience higher rainfalls, more frequent extreme weather events, rising sea levels and higher temperatures.<ref name="Overview2018">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/climate-change/likely-impacts-of-climate-change/overview-of-likely-climate-change-impacts|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180227210332/https://www.mfe.govt.nz/climate-change/likely-impacts-of-climate-change/overview-of-likely-climate-change-impacts|archive-date=27 February 2018| title=Overview of likely climate change impacts in New Zealand| publisher=Ministry for the Environment| website=www.mfe.govt.nz| language=en|access-date=28 May 2018}}</ref> Such effects will significantly impact New Zealand, with higher temperatures resulting in dry summers, consequently limiting New Zealand's water supply and intensifying droughts.<ref name="Overview2018" /> The Ministry for the Environment says the greatest effect of climate change is likely to be on New Zealand's water resources, with higher rainfall in the west and less in the east. Extreme climate events such as droughts could become more frequent in eastern areas, with increased flooding after major downpours.<ref name="mfe.govt.nz">{{cite web |url=https://www.environment.govt.nz/assets/Publications/Files/impacts-report-jun01.pdf |title= Climate change impacts on New Zealand |publisher=Ministry for the Environment |page=12 |access-date=26 October 2024}}</ref>

Higher temperatures are likely to increase problems such as heat stress in summer and mortality is expected to rise due to harsher living environments. Disease-transmitting insects such as mosquitoes could become established more easily as the climate warms.<ref name="mfe.govt.nz"/> Rising temperatures will also have devastating effects on New Zealand's flora and fauna, with climate threatening both animal and plant chances of survival.<ref name="Overview2018" /> New Zealand experienced its warmest year on record in 2022, and at that point eight out of 10 warmest years ever recorded in New Zealand have been within the last decade.<ref>{{Cite web |date=27 September 2023 |title=Eight of 10 warmest years in New Zealand recorded in last decade |url=https://www.stats.govt.nz/news/eight-of-10-warmest-years-in-new-zealand-recorded-in-last-decade/ |access-date=31 October 2025 |website=Stats NZ}}</ref>

Sir Peter Gluckman, the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor, noted in 2013 that even "the magnitude of environmental changes (in New Zealand) will depend in part on the global trajectories of greenhouse gas emissions and land use change, (and that) effective risk management requires consideration of the possibility of experiencing more extreme components of the predictive range".<ref name="pmcsa.org.nz"/>

=== Economic impacts ===

Droughts and lack of water will not only affect the environment, this will also impact on the economy as New Zealand's agricultural export sector strongly relies on an environment conducive to growing crops and livestock.<ref>{{Cite web|last=EPA, OA|first=US|title=Climate Impacts on Agriculture and Food Supply|url=https://19january2017snapshot.epa.gov/climate-impacts/climate-impacts-agriculture-and-food-supply_.html|access-date=28 May 2018|website=19january2017snapshot.epa.gov|language=en}}</ref> For instance, higher temperatures could cause problems for fruit growers in northern areas because plants such as kiwifruit require cold winters. Pests and diseases could spread more easily under warmer conditions and pasture composition may change with the spread of subtropical grasses. Increased costs will be incurred by farmers as land-use activities shift while adapting to changes in the climate.<ref name="mfe.govt.nz" />

==== Loss of insurance cover ====

The Insurance Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) says houses and buildings in vulnerable areas will eventually become uninsurable. In the [[Bay of Plenty]] some properties have already been declared "unliveable" due to severe flooding risk.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.noted.co.nz/currently/science/rising-sea-levels-new-zealand-impact/| title=The impact rising sea levels will have on New Zealand| publisher=Noted| date=22 October 2018| access-date=10 June 2019| archive-date=26 June 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190626052754/https://www.noted.co.nz/currently/science/rising-sea-levels-new-zealand-impact/}}</ref> The Hutt City Council has issued a report which says large parts Petone including Seaview, Alicetown and Moera could be under water before the end of the century and suggests home owners in these suburbs could find their homes uninsurable in as little as 30 years.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/108862230/lower-hutt-suburb-could-be-swallowed-up-by-sea-level-rise-in-just-80-years| title=Lower Hutt suburb could be swallowed up by sea level rise in just 80 years| publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | date=28 November 2018| first1=Nicholas| last1=Boyack}}</ref>

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) reports that over $5 billion in local government infrastructure is at risk of damage from a one-metre sea level rise.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.lgnz.co.nz/assets/Uploads/d566cc5291/47716-LGNZ-Sea-Level-Rise-Report-3-Proof-FINAL-compressed.pdf| title=Vulnerable: the quantum of local government infrastructure exposed to sea level rise| date=30 January 2019| first1=Tom| last1=Simonson| first2=Grace| last2=Hall| publisher=LGNZ}}</ref> However, this does not include the exposure of houses, businesses or central government assets and ICNZ claims full exposure for a one-metre rise in sea level is likely to be closer to $40 billion<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/nz/news/environmental/rising-sea-level-damage-could-cost-up-to-40-billion--icnz-123744.aspx| title=Rising sea level damage could cost up to $40 billion – ICNZ| publisher=Insurance Business| date=1 February 2019| first1=Ksenia| last1=Stepanova}}</ref> affecting 125,000 buildings. Another $26 billion and a further 70,490 buildings would be at risk if seas rose between one and two metres. If the increase was up to three metres, which is projected in some scenarios, another 65,530 buildings would be at risk costing an additional $20 billion. So in the worst-case scenario, by the end of the century, over 260,000 buildings in coastal areas could be destroyed with projected losses of around $84 billion.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2018/11/20/329590/125000-buildings-worth-38bn-at-risk-from-first-1m-sea-level-rise-draft-report#| title=125,000 buildings at risk from first metre of sea level rise| publisher=Newsroom| date=21 November 2018| first1=Eloise| last1=Gibson}}</ref>

==== Potential costs ====

The economic loss associated with soil erosion and landslides is already estimated at up to $300 million a year. Freshwater scientist Mike Joy says that in the last 20 years or so, the loss of sediment into waterways has also had a significant detrimental effect on water quality.<ref>[https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/387424/erosion-is-costing-nz-up-to-300m-a-year Erosion is costing NZ up to $300m a year], RNZ, 19 April 2019</ref>

In April 2019 Judy Lawrence from Victoria University's Climate Change Research unit suggested a climate change fund similar to the Earthquake Commission needed to be set up to pay for [[climate change adaptation]]. She said that "Local Government New Zealand have done a recent assessment of the costs and they are talking of $14 billion" although "we think that is an underestimate of the real cost". James Palmer, chief executive of the Hawke's Bay Regional Councils, said local authorities were already facing up to the dangers from coastal erosion, but "What we don't know is what contribution the Crown would be willing to make, both to safeguard its own assets, but also,  more broadly, on behalf of the wider communities."<ref>[https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/386638/calls-for-special-fund-for-likely-costs-of-climate-change Calls for special fund for likely costs of climate change], RNZ 9 April 2019</ref>

==== Agriculture ====
As temperatures rise, more frequent and severe water extremes, including droughts and floods, will impact on agricultural production. Rising temperatures will also lead to increased water demand for farming and agriculture. Due to chronic water shortages and desertification in food growing regions, internationally, crop yields are predicted to drop by 20% by 2050 combined with a decline in nutritional content.<ref>[https://www.breakthroughonline.org.au/papers Existential climate-related security risk: A scenario approach], Breakthrough, p. 9.</ref> Prices are likely to skyrocket, while job losses and reduced incomes will further reduce people's capacity to purchase food. New Zealand researcher, associate professor [[Carol Wham]], says malnutrition is "associated with higher infection rates, loss of muscle mass, strength and function, longer hospital stays, as well as increasing morbidity and mortality."<ref>{{cite web|date=26 May 2017|title=Almost a quarter of elderly New Zealanders malnourished, new study finds|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11923626|access-date=16 June 2019|publisher=[[New Zealand Herald]] }}</ref>

=== Health impacts ===
In 2018, the American Psychological Association issued a report about the [[effects of climate change on mental health|impact of climate change on mental health]]. It said that "gradual, long-term changes in climate can also surface a number of different emotions, including fear, anger, feelings of powerlessness, or exhaustion".<ref>[https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2017/03/climate-mental-health Climate Change's Toll On Mental Health], APA, 29 March 2017</ref><ref name="ReferenceC">[https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/opinion/113500475/kids-dont-let-climate-grief-stop-you-looking-forward-to-the-future Kids, don't let climate grief stop you looking forward to the future], Stuff 17 June 2019</ref> The NZ Psychological Society reports similar findings. It says clients are presenting with "a lot of helplessness, a lot of anxiety and some depression" brought about by climate change. In 2014, the Psychological Society set up a 'Climate Psychology Taskforce'. Task force co-convener, Brian Dixon, said psychologists were seeing the effects of climate change showing up in people of all ages. However, young people are most at risk, including the risk of suicide because of climate change.  Dr Margaret O'Brien says some young people are saying, "what's the use, if this is going to happen, why should I go ahead?" The society says taking action to address the issue is the best "antidote".<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/113973585/kiwis-suffering-depression-anxiety-and-hopelessness-because-of-climate-change Kiwis suffering depression, anxiety and hopelessness because of climate change], Stuff, 14 July 2019</ref>

A report titled ''The Human Health Impacts of Climate Change for New Zealand'' points out that the most vulnerable sectors are children, the elderly, those suffering with disabilities or chronic disease, and those on low-incomes.  Also at risk are those who have an economic base invested in primary industries, those who experience housing and economic inequalities, especially low income housing in areas vulnerable to flooding and sea level rise.<ref name=":1" /> Environmental concerns are even affecting New Zealanders' plans for the future leading some young women to decide not to have children. Those who make this decision believe any children they might bring into the world would face lives full of hardship and conflict due to a lack of natural resources and, by adding to the population, would actually cause more harm to the planet.<ref name="ReferenceC" />

==== Heat related deaths ====
If greenhouse gas emissions continue at current levels, many places in New Zealand will see more than 80 days per year above 25&nbsp;°C by 2100. Currently most parts of the country typically see between 20 and 40 days per year above 25&nbsp;°C. The elderly populations are particularly vulnerable to heatwaves. In Auckland and Christchurch, a total of 14 heat-related deaths already occur each year amongst those over 65 when temperatures exceed 20&nbsp;°C.  Approximately a quarter of New Zealanders are projected to be 65 and over by 2043, so heat-related deaths are likely to rise.<ref name=":1">[https://royalsociety.org.nz/assets/documents/Report-Human-Health-Impacts-of-Climate-Change-for-New-Zealand-Oct-2017.pdf The Human Health Impacts of Climate Change for New Zealand], The Royal Society, October 2017 [[File:CC BY-SA icon.svg|50x50px]] This article contains quotations from this source, which is available under the [[creativecommons:by/3.0/nz/|Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 New Zealand (CC BY 3.0 NZ)]] license.</ref>

=== Impacts on indigenous peoples ===
A report in 2017, Adapting to Climate Change in New Zealand, identifies [[Māori people|Māori]] as among the most vulnerable groups to climate-change in New Zealand due to their "significant reliance on the environment as a cultural, social and economic resource".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mfe.govt.nz/sites/default/files/media/adapting-to-climate-change-stocktake-tag-report-final.pdf|title=Adapting to Climate Change in New Zealand|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211102194121/https://environment.govt.nz/sites/default/files/media/adapting-to-climate-change-stocktake-tag-report-final.pdf |archive-date=2 November 2021 |website=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref> Māori tend to be involved in primary industries, and many Māori communities were near the coast. The report states that urupā (burial grounds) and marae are already being flooded or washed into the sea.

[[Mike Smith (activist)|Mike Smith]], of Ngāpuhi and Ngāti Kahu, says the Government is failing in its duties under the Treaty of Waitangi to protect Māori, who are particularly vulnerable, from the "catastrophic effects of climate change". Smith has filed proceedings in the High Court "on behalf of my children, grandchildren and the future generations of Māori children, whose lives are threatened by the climate crisis".<ref>[https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12250045 Iwi leader suing Government over 'failure' to protect Māori from climate change], NZ Herald, 16 July 2019</ref>

Smith brought a lawsuit against Fonterra, New Zealand Steel, Z Energy and other high greenhouse gas emitters,  [[Smith v Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd]], which argued for the new [[tort]] of climate change damage and the [[Supreme Court of New Zealand|New Zealand Supreme Court]] duly ruled in 2024 that this novel civil wrong can be asserted in future proceedings. However, in May 2026 the New Zealand government countered this decision by introducing legislation to prevent climate lawsuits.<ref>{{cite news
 | title      = Government changes climate law to prevent lawsuits
 | newspaper  = Radio New Zealand
 | date       = 10 June 2026
 | url        = https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment_climate/594922/government-changes-climate-law-to-prevent-lawsuits
}}</ref> Following the government's decision it emerged that the defendants had lobbied the Prime Minister's office for civil climate lawsuits to be banned, however documentation surrounding this had been left out of an earlier [[Official Information Act 1982|Official Information Act]] request.<ref>{{cite news
 |title      = More details revealed over climate case briefing
 |url        = https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/598241/more-details-revealed-over-climate-case-briefing
 |publisher  = Radio New Zealand
 |date       = 17 June 2026
|access-date = 17 June 2026}}
</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hanly |first=Lillian |date=25 May 2026 |title='A co-ordinated campaign of secret lobbying' - climate activist |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596197/a-co-ordinated-campaign-of-secret-lobbying-climate-activist |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

=== Impacts on migration ===
If the atmosphere warms by two degrees Celsius, small island countries in the Pacific will be inundated by sea level rise. These islands do not have the populations or resources to deal with weather related disasters. As of 2019, 180,000 people living in low-lying islands like Kiribati, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands are the most threatened. More extreme projections suggest that by 2050, 75 million people from the wider Asia-Pacific region will be forced to shift.<ref name="ReferenceD">{{cite news
 |title        = Climate refugees pose challenges to mental health services
 |url          = https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12245227
 |work         = The New Zealand Herald
 |publisher    = NZME
 |author       = Nicholas Jones
 |date         = 30 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

Pacific islanders forced to relocate will be at higher risk of developing mental health problems because of losing their homes, their culture and the stress of climate-induced migration.<ref name="ReferenceD"/> The New Zealand Defence Force is predicting an increase in the number of humanitarian and disaster relief operations it will attend in the Pacific due to climate change.<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = Why does NZ need a military? For more reasons than you might think
 |url          = https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/113389596/why-does-nz-need-a-military-for-more-reasons-than-you-might-think
 |publisher    = Stuff Limited
 |first1      = Thomas 
|last1=Manch
 |date         = 11 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

One analysis suggests that as one of the few habitable areas left on the planet, New Zealand "would likely become overcrowded, under constant threat of flood and cyclone, and increasingly infested by flies and other insects."<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = 407 and rising: the basics of the climate emergency
 |url          = https://interactives.stuff.co.nz/2019/07/407-and-rising/
 |work         = Stuff interactive
 |publisher    = Stuff Limited
 |date         = 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

== Policies and legislation ==

===International commitments===

==== UNFCC and Kyoto Protocol ====
[[File:New Zealand's comparative emissions 1990-2012.png|thumbnail|A comparison between New Zealand emissions (net and gross) and those of other countries from 1990 to 2012]]
New Zealand ratified the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (the UNFCCC) in September 1993.<ref>[https://www.mfe.govt.nz/more/international-environmental-agreements/multilateral-environmental-agreements/united-nations United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)], Ministry for the Environment</ref> The purpose of this convention was to collectively bring countries together to discuss how to best address climate change and handle the impacts of it.<ref name="UNFCC">{{Cite web|url=https://environment.govt.nz/what-government-is-doing/international-action/nz-united-nations-framework-convention-climate-change/|title=New Zealand and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change|date=17 June 2022|website=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref>

In July 1994, four months after the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC) came into force, the [[Fourth National Government of New Zealand|Fourth National Government]] announced a number of priorities related to New Zealand's emissions. Environment Minister, [[Simon Upton]] published the Environment 2010 Strategy which included a goal to reduce net carbon dioxide emissions to 20 percent less than 1990 levels by the year 2000 if cost-effective and to reduce other emissions, particularly methane, by the year 2000.<ref>{{cite web|last=RT Hon Simon Upton|date=24 July 1996|title=Environment 2010 Strategy|url=http://www.beehive.govt.nz/feature/environment-2010-strategy|access-date=12 July 2012|publisher=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref>

===== Kyoto Protocol First commitment period 2008–2012 =====
New Zealand signed the Kyoto Protocol on 24 May 1998.<ref>{{cite web|first = Simon |last=Upton|url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/new-zealand-signs-kyoto-protocol-climate-change |title=New Zealand Signs Kyoto Protocol On Climate Change  |publisher = New Zealand Government |date = 24 May 1998 |access-date =9 April 2025 }}</ref> New Zealand ratified the [[Kyoto Protocol]] to the UNFCCC in December 2002.<ref name="UNFCC"/>

New Zealand's Kyoto target was to ensure that emissions of net greenhouse gases between 2008 and 2012 did not exceed 1990 gross emissions (the baseline).<ref>{{cite web |year=2012 |title=Annex B Party Quantified emission limitation or reduction commitment |url=http://unfccc.int/essential_background/kyoto_protocol/items/1678.php |access-date=16 December 2012 |work=Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change |publisher=UNFCCC}}</ref> The [[Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (New Zealand)|Ministry for Foreign Affairs and Trade]] (MFAT) believed New Zealand would be able to increase emissions and still comply with the Kyoto Protocol as long as more [[Removal Units]] were obtained from forest carbon sinks between 2008 and 2012.<ref name="p2e">{{cite web |year=2002 |title=National Interest Analyses Kyoto Protocol Part II Emissions accounting under the Protocol |url=http://www.mfat.govt.nz/Treaties-and-International-Law/03-Treaty-making-process/2-National-Interest-Analyses/0-Kyoto-Protocol-Part-2.php#emissions |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130209114212/http://www.mfat.govt.nz/Treaties-and-International-Law/03-Treaty-making-process/2-National-Interest-Analyses/0-Kyoto-Protocol-Part-2.php |archive-date=9 February 2013 |access-date=9 January 2013 |publisher=NZ Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade}}</ref>

<nowiki>In June 2005, a financial liability under the Kyoto Protocol for a shortfall of emission units of 36.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent was first recognised in the Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand. It was estimated as a liability of $NZ310 million.</nowiki><ref>{{cite web |date=June 2005 |title=Note 15: Payables and Provisions |url=http://www.treasury.govt.nz/government/financialstatements/yearend/jun05/45.htm#_toc15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724215838/http://www.treasury.govt.nz/government/financialstatements/yearend/jun05/45.htm#_toc15 |archive-date=24 July 2011 |access-date=14 October 2010 |work=Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the Year Ended 30 June 2005 |publisher=The Treasury – New Zealand}}</ref> New Zealand's net balance under the Kyoto Protocol remained in deficit from 2005 (a deficit of 36 million units)<ref>{{cite web |author=MfE |date=October 2005 |title=Review of New Zealand's net position |url=http://mfe.govt.nz/publications/climate-change/review-new-zealands-net-position |access-date=5 January 2016 |publisher=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref> until May 2008 (a deficit of 21.7 million units).<ref>{{cite web |author=MfE |date=May 2008 |title=Net Position Report 2008 Projected balance of Kyoto Protocol units during the first commitment period Executive Summary |url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/publications/climate/net-position-report-projected-balance-emissions-may08/html/page1.html |access-date=12 January 2013 |publisher=Ministry for the Environment |quote=As at May 2008 the net position is projected to be a deficit of 21.7 million units during the first commitment period}}</ref>

On 18 December 2015 Minister for Climate Change [[Paula Bennett]] announced that New Zealand met the "target for the period from 2008-2012 through a combination of emissions reductions, carbon removal by forests, and international trading".<ref>{{cite web |first = Paula |last= Bennett |url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/new-zealand-meets-kyoto-climate-target |title= New Zealand meets Kyoto climate target |publisher = New Zealand Government |date=18 December 2015 | access-date=9 April 2025 }}</ref>

==== Doha Amendment 2013–2020 ====
The second commitment period (2013–20) was established in Doha in 2012, although New Zealand refused to take on any new targets during this period. Instead, in November 2012, the New Zealand Government announced it would make climate pledges for the period from 2013 to 2020 under the UNFCCC process rather than agree to a second commitment under the Kyoto Protocol.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://beehive.govt.nz/release/new-zealand-commits-un-framework-convention |title=New Zealand Commits to UN Framework Convention |publisher=New Zealand Government |date=9 November 2012 |access-date=12 November 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=AP |date=9 November 2012 |title=NZ says no to second stage of Kyoto Protocol |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10846322 |access-date=12 November 2012 |work=The Herald}}</ref>

This announcement angered environmentalists and was reported internationally as New Zealand avoiding legally binding obligations.<ref>{{cite web |author=The Associated Press |date=9 November 2012 |title=New Zealand won't sign 'Kyoto 2' climate treaty |url=http://www.sacbee.com/2012/11/08/4972617/new-zealand-wont-sign-kyoto-2.html |access-date=12 November 2012 |work=The Sacramento Bee}}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Green Party climate change spokesman Kennedy Graham said the Government's announcement was about hot air at talks instead of legally binding measures to reduce emissions.<ref>{{cite web |last=Small |first=Vernon |date=9 November 2012 |title=New Zealand Government Rejects Second Kyoto Commitment |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/politics/7929559/Government-shuns-second-Kyoto-commitment |access-date=3 January 2013 |work=[[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]]}}</ref> The decision was also heavily criticised by the [[World Wildlife Fund]].<ref>{{cite news |date=26 November 2012 |title=Government challenged to do more at Doha talks |work=3 News NZ |url=http://www.3news.co.nz/Government-challenged-to-do-more-at-Doha-talks/tabid/1160/articleID/278085/Default.aspx |access-date=25 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729111546/http://www.3news.co.nz/Government-challenged-to-do-more-at-Doha-talks/tabid/1160/articleID/278085/Default.aspx |archive-date=29 July 2013}}</ref> Prime Minister John Key said New Zealand should not lead the way on climate change, but instead be a "fast follower".<ref>{{cite news |date=26 November 2012 |title=Rebuild trust in Doha, says WWF |work=3 News NZ |url=http://www.3news.co.nz/Rebuild-trust-in-Doha-says-WWF/tabid/1160/articleID/278053/Default.aspx |access-date=25 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729104131/http://www.3news.co.nz/Rebuild-trust-in-Doha-says-WWF/tabid/1160/articleID/278053/Default.aspx |archive-date=29 July 2013}}</ref> The Alliance of Small Island States voiced disappointment at New Zealand's decision.<ref>{{cite web |date=30 November 2012 |title=NZ government no commitment to Kyoto Protocol |url=http://www.radioaustralia.net.au/international/radio/program/pacific-beat/nz-government-no-commitment-to-kyoto-protocol/1053818 |access-date=14 January 2013 |publisher=Radio Australia}}</ref>

In August 2013, the National Government announced a target to reduce New Zealand's emissions to 5% less than total emissions in 1990 by the year 2020. Tim Groser, the Minister for Climate Change issues noted that New Zealand would still honour its conditional offer made in 2009 to reduce emissions to 10 – 20% below 1990 levels – but only if other countries come on board.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://beehive.govt.nz/release/new-zealand-commits-2020-climate-change-target |title=New Zealand commits to 2020 climate change target |first=Tim |last=Groser |publisher=New Zealand Government |date=16 August 2013}}</ref>

Labelling the National Government's commitment, to an emissions reduction of 5% below 1990 levels by 2020, as a 'failure', Global conservation organisation, [[World Wide Fund for Nature|WWF]], pointed out that a 5% reduction is well below the level recommended by scientists in order reduce the damage of anthropogenic climate change.<ref>{{cite web |date=16 August 2013 |title=NZ Government's climate target 'a failure' |url=http://www.wwf.org.nz/?11042/NZ-Governments-climate-target-a-failure |publisher=WWF}}</ref> The changes to the scheme also allowed an influx of cheap, imported international emission units that collapsed the price of the New Zealand unit. This effectively undermined the whole scheme.<ref name="ReferenceE">Climate Change, New Zealand Labour Party Manifesto 2017</ref>

====Paris Climate Agreement targets or National Determined Contributions====
The 2015 [[Paris Agreement]] is the successor to the 1998 [[Kyoto Protocol]] and has set a target to keep temperature rises within 2&nbsp;°C this century, with the hope of limiting it to 1.5&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Paris Agreement|url=https://unfccc.int/process/the-paris-agreement/what-is-the-paris-agreement|access-date=10 May 2018|publisher=United Nations Climate Change}}</ref> The [[Paris Agreement]] negotiations concluded on 12 December 2015 and the Agreement took effect in 2020.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last         = Christoff
 |first        = Peter
 |title        = The promissory note: COP 21 and the Paris Climate Agreement
 |journal      = Environmental Politics
 |volume       = 25
 |issue        = 5
 |year         = 2016
 |pages        = 765–787
 |doi          = 10.1080/09644016.2016.1191818
}}</ref>

The key difference between the [[Paris Agreement]] and the [[Kyoto Protocol]] is that the latter prescribed goals that were to be achieved by each signatory country and offered monetary support for developing countries. The [[Paris Agreement]] allows each country to determine its own goals, defined as [[Intended Nationally Determined Contributions|Nationally Determined Contributions]] (NDCs). The treaty uses the term 'expectations' in regard to reducing emissions and there are obligations on each signatory country to communicate and review their progress (NDCs) every 5 years. Countries are expected to meet their expectations, but there is no obligation to do so – and no mechanism describing how any country should go about achieving this. The [[Paris Agreement]] also has financial incentives available to support countries achieve their goals towards keeping the global temperature rises to below 2&nbsp;°C and down towards 1.5&nbsp;°C.<ref name="The Paris Agreement" />

In October 2015 New Zealand submitted its first [[Nationally Determined Contribution]] or international target for 2021 to 2030 under the Paris Agreement (NDC),<ref>{{citation |title=The Paris Agreement|url=https://www.mfat.govt.nz/en/environment/climate-change/working-with-the-world/building-international-collaboration/#bookmark2 |publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade|date=2015|access-date=21 October 2023}}</ref> to reduce 2030 net greenhouse gas emissions to 30% less than gross 2005 emissions.<ref name="The Paris Agreement">{{cite web|title=The Paris Agreement|url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/climate-change/why-climate-change-matters/global-response/paris-agreement|access-date=10 May 2018|publisher=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref> In October 2021 the Government announced a more ambitious target; to reduce 2030 net greenhouse gas emissions to 50% less than gross 2005 emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 June 2022 |title=Nationally Determined Contribution |url=https://environment.govt.nz/what-government-is-doing/areas-of-work/climate-change/nationally-determined-contribution/ |access-date=17 January 2023 |website=Ministry for the Environment |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=13 October 2021 |title=Govt increases contribution to global climate target|url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/govt-increases-contribution-global-climate-target |access-date=8 June 2023 |website=New Zealand Government |language=en-GB}}</ref> The updated target represents a 41% reduction in 2030 net emissions compared to gross 2005 emissions when using the same (budget) accounting methodology used for the 2015 NDC submission.<ref>{{cite report |url=https://environment.govt.nz/assets/publications/2-Cabinet-Paper-Agreement-to-Update-New-Zealands-First-Nationally-Determined-Contribution-NDC1-under-the-Paris-Agreement.pdf |title=Agreement to update New Zealand's first Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement |author=Office of the Minister of Climate Change |date=2021 |publisher= |page= }}</ref>

On 30 January 2025 the Government announced the second NDC target out to 2035; to reduce emissions by 51 to 55 per cent compared to 2005 gross emission by 2035.<ref>{{citation |url=https://environment.govt.nz/news/second-international-climate-target-under-the-paris-agreement/
|title=Government announces second international climate target under the Paris Agreement
|date= 30 January 2025 |access-date= 1 February 2025 |publisher = New Zealand Government}}</ref>

=== Domestic initiatives ===
In 1988, the same year as the United Nations established the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]], the [[Fourth Labour Government of New Zealand]] started developing policy for climate change. This was coordinated between agencies by the [[Ministry for the Environment (New Zealand)|Ministry for the Environment]].<ref name="senz99c5">{{cite web |author=MfE |year=2007 |title=Chapter 5: Responses to atmospheric change |url=http://www.mfe.govt.nz/publications/ser/ser1997/html/chapter5.9.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130314190226/http://www.mfe.govt.nz/publications/ser/ser1997/html/chapter5.9.html |archive-date=14 March 2013 |access-date=15 July 2012 |work=State of New Zealand's Environment 1997 |publisher=Ministry for the Environment}}</ref> The Government asked the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]] to report on the scientific basis of climate change. A short report, 'Climate Change in New Zealand', was published in 1988 and the full report 'New Zealand Climate Report 1990' was published in 1989.<ref>{{cite web |year=2010 |title=New Zealand Climate Expert Panel |url=http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/panels/climate/ |access-date=29 July 2012 |publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand}}</ref>

==== Carbon tax ====
{{See also|Agricultural emissions research levy}}

[[New Zealand]] Governments have unsuccessfully attempted to enact a carbon tax.
In 2005, the [[Fifth Labour Government]] had proposed a carbon tax of [[New Zealand dollar|NZ]]$15 per tonne of [[Global warming potential|CO<sub>2</sub> equivalent]] ([[United States dollar|US]]$14.47 after adjusting for inflation in 2021) to meet obligations under the [[Kyoto Protocol]]. The tax was scheduled to take effect from April 2007 and apply across most economic sectors, with an exemption for [[methane]] [[Methane emissions from livestock|emissions from farming]] and provisions for special exemptions from carbon-intensive businesses if they adopted best-practice standards.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hodgson |first=Pete |date=4 May 2005 |title=Speech announcing carbon tax detail |url=http://www.beehive.govt.NZ/?q=node/22886 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081016190835/http://www.beehive.govt.nz/?q=node%2F22886 |archive-date=16 October 2008 |access-date=18 September 2009 |publisher=Minister of Climate Change Issues, The Beehive, NZ Parliament}}</ref>

After the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], two coalition parties supporting the [[Fifth Labour Government]], [[NZ First]] and [[United Future]], opposed the proposed tax, and it was abandoned in December 2005.<ref>{{cite news |author=NZPA |date=5 December 2005 |title=Carbon tax ditched |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10360930 |access-date=24 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511191839/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10360930 |archive-date=11 May 2011}}</ref> The Green Party described the carbon tax backdown as "giving up on climate change" and "capitulating" to the anti-Kyoto lobby.<ref>{{Cite press release |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0512/S00327.htm |title=Govt gives up on the climate |publisher=Green Party of Aotearoa |date=5 December 2005 |access-date=24 September 2009}}</ref>

The [[Environmental Defence Society]] described the withdrawal of the carbon tax as "pathetic" and a result of the NZ Government Climate Change Office being "captured" by vested interests such as energy intensive businesses and the Greenhouse Policy Coalition.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO0512/S00173.htm |title=Government dropping carbon tax labelled pathetic |publisher=The Environmental Defence Society |date=21 December 2005 |access-date=1 March 2010}}</ref>

==== Methane policies ====
In 2003, the Government proposed an [[Agricultural emissions research levy]] to fund research into reducing ruminant emissions. The proposal, popularly called a "fart tax", was strongly opposed by Federated Farmers<ref>{{cite news |date=4 September 2003 |title=Farmers invade capital for 'fart tax' protest |publisher=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |agency=NZPA |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/farmers-invade-capital-for-fart-tax-protest/6OAPZ5KHG2OT2O5EVCGIOKN4IU/ |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref> and was later abandoned.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Atmosphere – Methane tax petition|encyclopedia=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/atmosphere/2/3|access-date=2 November 2011|date=24 September 2011|author2=Katja Riedel|author3=Richard McKenzie|author4=Sylvia Nichol|author5=Tom Clarkson.|author1=Bill Allan}}</ref> The [[Livestock Emissions and Abatement Research Network]] (LEARN) was launched in 2007 to address livestock emissions.<ref>{{cite web|last=Parker|first=David|author-link=David Parker (New Zealand politician)|date=27 November 2007|title=Leading the way to pastoral emissions reductions|url=http://www.beehive.govt.nz/speech/leading+way+pastoral+emissions+reductions|access-date=22 August 2009|publisher=[[List of ministers of climate change#N|Minister of Climate Change, New Zealand Government]]}}</ref> The [[Pastoral Greenhouse Gas Research Consortium]] between the New Zealand government and industry groups seeks to reduce agricultural emissions through the funding of research.
At the [[2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference]] in Copenhagen, the New Zealand government announced the formation of the Global Research Alliance involving 20 other countries. New Zealand will contribute NZ$45 million over four years towards research on agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/45-million-global-research-alliance|title=$45 million for Global Research Alliance|publisher=New Zealand Government|date=17 December 2009|access-date=9 January 2010}}</ref>

In 2019, it was announced that the government had awarded funding to cultivate and research a red native seaweed known as ''[[Asparagopsis armata]]'' to the [[Cawthron Institute]] in Nelson. This particular seaweed has been found to reduce methane emissions from animals by as much as 80% when small amounts (2%) are added as a supplement to animal food.<ref>{{cite news|date=31 December 2019|title=From red seaweed to climate-smart cows: New Zealand leads the fight against methane|work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/jan/01/from-red-seaweed-to-climate-smart-cows-new-zealand-leads-the-fight-against-methane}}</ref>

On 13 October 2025, the New Zealand government announced a significant revision to its biogenic methane emission reduction targets for 2050.<ref>{{cite news |date=13 October 2025 |title=Government lowers methane target, rules out methane taxes |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/top/575686/government-lowers-methane-target-rules-out-methane-taxes |work=Radio New Zealand |access-date=14 October 2025}}</ref> The new target range of 14–24% below 2017 levels replaced the previous legislated goal of a 24–47% reduction, representing a substantial lowering of climate commitments. The government stated the revision reflected findings from the independent Methane Science Review released in 2024, though the Climate Change Commission had previously recommended even greater reductions of 35–47% by 2050. Agriculture and Trade Minister Todd McClay defended the change as a "practical, fair pathway" that would protect jobs and production while maintaining climate commitments. The announcement drew criticism from environmental groups and the opposition Labour Party, with Labour climate spokesperson Deborah Russell arguing the government had "moved the goalposts" rather than developing policies to meet existing targets. The government also confirmed it would not pursue a tax on agricultural methane emissions and would instead rely on technology development and industry partnership to achieve reductions.

On 11 June 2024, the New Zealand Government announced that it would invest NZ$400 million over four years to accelerate the commercialisation of tools and technology that reduce on-farm emissions.<ref name=rnz>{{cite news |title=Coalition exempts farmers from ETS, sets up fresh working group |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/519248/coalition-exempts-farmers-from-ets-sets-up-fresh-working-group |work=RNZ |date=11 June 2024 |access-date=8 October 2026}}</ref> The announcement was made alongside the government's decision to keep agriculture out of the New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme.<ref name=rnz /> The package included an additional NZ$50.5 million over five years for the New Zealand Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre.<ref>{{cite web |last=Brunskill |first=Dan |title=NZ farmers will be spared paying for their emissions |url=https://www.interest.co.nz/economy/128194/government-delivers-six-year-delay-farm-emissions-pricing-promised-during-election |website=Interest.co.nz |date=11 June 2024 |access-date=8 October 2026}}</ref>

==== Emissions trading scheme ====
{{main|New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme}}

{{excerpt|New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme|paragraphs=1-5}}The [[Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment]] also criticised the Scheme for its generous free allocations of emission units and the lack of a carbon price signal.<ref name="pce1">{{cite press release |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO0910/S00231.htm |title=New bill 'weakens ETS' says Environment Commissioner |publisher=Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment |date=15 October 2009 |access-date=15 October 2009 |quote=The allocation of free carbon credits to industrial processes is extremely generous and removes the carbon price signal where New Zealand needs one the most}}</ref> [[Greenpeace Aotearoa New Zealand]] criticised it for its total ineffectiveness at reducing emissions.<ref name="greenpeace">{{cite press release |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO0909/S00153.htm |title=Revised ETS an insult to New Zealanders |date=14 September 2009 |publisher=Greenpeace New Zealand |access-date=12 October 2009 |quote=We now have on the table a pathetic ETS which won't actually do anything to reduce emissions}}</ref> In May 2011, the climate scientist [[James Hansen]] visited New Zealand for a speaking tour. Hansen drew huge crowds for his public talks. He said he did not agree with schemes like the NZETS which included forestry offsets. "In my opinion you have to have the simplest, transparent scheme so I just say it should be a flat fee proportional to the amount of carbon in the fuel."<ref>{{cite web |last=Williams |first=David |date=20 May 2011 |title=Kiwi climate change policy 'close' |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/5031880/Kiwi-climate-change-policy-close |access-date=21 August 2012 |work=[[The Press]]}}</ref>

In 2014, the New Zealand Climate Party stated the emissions trading scheme "degenerated into a farce because the current emissions charges are far too low to address our steadily climbing emissions levels or to cover the damage these emissions are causing".<ref name="ClimateParty14">{{cite web |last1=Whitmore |first1=Peter |title=NZ Climate Party Launched |url=http://www.climate.org.nz/nz-climate-party-launched/ |access-date=25 August 2014 |website=climate.org.nz |date=10 August 2014 |publisher=NZ Climate Party}}</ref> In June 2019, Peter Whitmore, executive member of Engineers for Social Responsibility and founder of the Climate Party said: " We need to rapidly phase out the provision of free emissions units to trade exposed industries" as, in practice, they incentivise these industry to continue polluting.<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = Peter Whitmore: Climate change – NZ needs to do better
 |url          = https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12241108
 |work         = The New Zealand Herald
 |publisher    = NZME
 |last1        = Whitmore
 |first1       = Peter
 |date         = 18 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

====Financed emissions disclosure====
Financed emissions are [[greenhouse gas]] emissions linked to a bank's or other financial institution's lending and investments, rather than to its own operations. under the [[GHG Protocol Corporate Standard]] they are counted as scope 3 category 15 emissions .<ref name="Atlason2023">{{cite journal |last1=Atlason |first1=Reynir Smári |last2=Gunnarsson |first2=Gunnar |last3=Pálsson |first3=Kjartan |last4=Sigurjonsson |first4=Throstur Olaf |date=19 September 2023 |title=Accounting for time when estimating financed greenhouse gas emissions from investment and lending portfolios |journal=Current Research in Environmental Sustainability |volume=6 |article-number=100232 |doi=10.1016/j.crsust.2023.100232 |doi-access=free |issn=2666-0490|hdl=10398/928dbd3f-94e8-44d3-9ce5-8ba301f819e6 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 requires registered banks, building societies, credit unions, licensed insurers, listed issuers and managed investment scheme managers to publish annual climate statements if they meet size thresholds. Banks published their first statements for 2024.<ref name="FSCRD2021">{{cite web |title=Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 |url=https://legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2021/39/en/latest/ |website=New Zealand Legislation |publisher=Parliamentary Counsel Office |access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref>

In October 2025, the government agreed to narrow the regime. The threshold for listed issuers rose from $60 million to $1 billion, investment scheme managers were removed, and automatic personal liability for directors was relieved. The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment estimated that the number of reporting entities would fall from about 164 to 76. Thresholds for banks and insurers were not changed. In May 2026, Cabinet agreed to exclude nine health and life insurers.<ref name="Spinoff2025">{{cite news |last=Waiwiri-Smith |first=Lyric |date=28 October 2025 |title=Why many big businesses will no longer have to disclose their climate-related risks |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/28-10-2025/why-many-big-businesses-will-no-longer-have-to-disclose-their-climate-related-risks |work=The Spinoff |access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="IBNZ2026">{{cite news |last=Libatique |first=Roxanne |date=10 October 2026 |title=NZ insurers' climate reporting in limbo as election stalls legislation |url=https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/nz/news/life-insurance/nz-insurers-climate-reporting-in-limbo-as-election-stalls-legislation-592995.aspx |work=Insurance Business NZ |access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref>

==== Offshore oil & gas permits ====
{{Update|section|date=June 2026}}
In 2018 when the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand]] came to power, it ceased issuing new offshore oil and gas exploration permits and only permitted onshore permits in the Taranaki region.<ref name="no-new-permits">{{cite web |date=2 April 2018 |title=Planning for the future – no new offshore oil and gas exploration permits |url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/planning-future-no-new-offshore-oil-and-gas-exploration-permits |access-date=2 January 2019 |publisher=New Zealand Government}}</ref> Currently Taranaki is the only oil and gas producing region in New Zealand's with more than 20 fields, on and offshore. The Petroleum Exploration and Production Association of New Zealand (PEPANZ) which lobbies on behalf of the industry has been highly critical of the exploration ban. PEPANZ points out that the oil and gas sector contributes $1.5bn to Taranaki's GDP and makes up 40% of the regional economy.<ref name="rnz.co.nz">{{cite news
 |title        = Beyond gas and oil: Can alternative energy save Taranaki?
 |url          = https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/insight/audio/2018696911/beyond-gas-and-oil-can-alternative-energy-save-taranaki
 |work         = Insight
 |publisher    = Radio New Zealand
 |last1        = Young
 |first1       = Conan
 |date         = 2 June 2019
 |access-date  = 17 June 2026
}}</ref>

The Government's decision does not affect the reserves or potential finds from these active exploration permits.<ref name="no-new-permits" /> Energy Minister at the time [[Megan Woods]] said this will lead to a long-term, managed transition away from oil and gas production over the next 30 years.<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = The Government's ban on oil and gas exploration could cost up to $30b by 2050, NZIER say
 | work        = New Zealand Herald
 | date        = 19 February 2019
 | url         = https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12205320
}}</ref> In 2018, [[Simon Bridges]] said the National Party "would bring back oil and gas exploration immediately if National was returned to government". He said: "[It's] no good us doing everything and no-one else doing anything. That will still mean the world gets warmer..."<ref>{{cite news |date=17 December 2018 |title=UN climate conference agreement: Mixed reactions |publisher=[[Radio NZ]] |url=https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/378434/un-climate-conference-agreement-mixed-reactions}}</ref>

==== Tree planting ====
The Labour led coalition has established a goal to plant one billion trees within ten years (by 2028)<ref name=one-billion-trees>{{cite web |title=Planting one billion trees |url=https://www.mpi.govt.nz/funding-and-programmes/forestry/planting-one-billion-trees/ |access-date=10 May 2018 |publisher=Ministry for Primary Industries}}</ref> because trees absorb carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) from the atmosphere in a process known as [[carbon sequestration]] potentially helping New Zealand to become carbon neutral. According to the Forest Owners Association, in 2015 New Zealand forests held 283 million tonnes of carbon.<ref>{{cite report
 | title       = Facts & Figures 2017/18
 | publisher   = New Zealand Forest Owners Association
 | url         = http://www.nzfoa.org.nz/images/stories/pdfs/facts_figures_2017_2018v2.pdf
 | pages       = 54
 | year        = 2018
}}</ref>

Under the new scheme, $120 million has been allocated for landowners to plant new areas and $58 million to establish Te Uru Rākau forestry service in Rotorua. The plan is also designed to encourage farmers and Maori land holders to include trees on their property.<ref name=one-billion-trees /> However, Bay of Plenty and Taupo contractors are struggling to find workers to do the planting, even though the pay is $300 to $400 a day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chalmers |first=Heather |date=16 January 2019 |title=$400 a day to plant trees but no-one wants the job |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/business/farming/109810764/400-a-day-to-plant-trees-but-no-one-wants-the-job |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> As at 27 July 2018, nine million trees, 13% of them native species had been planted.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fox |first=Andrea |title=Ten years, 1 billion trees - making the numbers add up |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/companies/agribusiness/ten-years-1-billion-trees-making-the-numbers-add-up/ZG7MZSXN5AOT27PJ72SHTX4O5E/ |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref>

Concerns''':''' New Zealand emits over 80 million tonnes of greenhouse gases (measured in CO<sub>2</sub>-equivalents) every year, approximately 45% of which (36 million tonnes) is CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gudsell |first=Kate |date=26 May 2017 |title=NZ seventh-worst on emissions of 41 nations |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/331646/nz-seventh-worst-on-emissions-of-41-nations |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> Between 1990 and 2016, the net uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere by land use, [[land-use change]], and forestry (LULUCF) decreased by nearly 23% (down to 23 million tonnes a year) due to more intensive harvesting of planted forests.<ref name="greenhouse-gas-emissions" /> On top of this, a typical hardwood tree takes about 40 years to remove approximately one ton of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 November 2024 |title=Could Atmosphere CO2 Levels be Reduced by Planting Trees? |url=https://www.co2meter.com/blogs/news/could-global-co2-levels-be-reduced-by-planting-trees |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=CO2 Meter |language=en}}</ref>

Climate scientist [[Jim Salinger]] and anthropologist and environmentalist [[Anne Salmond|Dame Anne Salmond]] have criticised the plan to plant one billion trees because only 13% of the trees that have been planted are natives. Salmond says two thirds of the trees being planted are supposed to be natives.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Church |first=Logan |date=17 July 2019 |title=Exotic trees being planted instead of natives – Dame Anne Salmond |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/audio/2018704571/exotic-trees-being-planted-instead-of-natives-dame-anne-salmond |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> Salinger points out that pine forests store far less carbon than natives as they are harvested after a few decades; the trees end up as pulp and paper and the carbon goes back into the atmosphere. Natural (native) forests store 40 times more carbon than and plantations like pine trees.<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 July 2019 |title=One billion tree plan flawed, says climate scientist |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/393832/one-billion-tree-plan-flawed-says-climate-scientist |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> A report released by the Productivity Commission in August 2018 also found that one billion tree plan is only a fraction of what is required to offset the amount carbon being released in New Zealand. The Commission says the planting rate needs to double, from 50,000 hectares to 100,000ha per year and the length of the programme needs to be extended from 10 to 30 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Matt |date=18 December 2018 |title=Billions more trees needed for NZ to be carbon neutral |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/108820042/billions-more-trees-needed-for-nz-to-be-carbon-neutral |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> Conservation charity, Trees That Count, monitors the number of native trees planted throughout New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://treesthatcount.co.nz/|title=Restoring nature for biodiversity and climate resilience|website=Trees That Count}}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=March 2026}}

In response to New Zealand's forestry-based [[climate change mitigation]] strategies, significant critiques have emerged regarding the sustainability of these approaches. A report by the [[Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment]], [[Simon Upton]], particularly challenges the current practice of predominantly utilizing [[Pinus radiata#Cultivation#New Zealand|''Pinus radiata'']] for [[afforestation]] to offset fossil fuel emissions. According to Upton's analysis, while this strategy initially accelerates carbon sequestration, it may not sustain long-term [[ecological stability]]. The report advocates for a more balanced afforestation approach, which incorporates both immediate [[Carbon capture and storage|carbon capture]] and long-term environmental sustainability. This critique aligns with broader environmental concerns that suggest a reevaluation of forestry practices is necessary to ensure they contribute effectively to New Zealand's climate goals.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Thomson |first1=Ainsley |last2=Withers |first2=Tracy |date=28 May 2024 |title=Millions More Trees Isn't the Climate Fix New Zealand Thought |url=
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-05-27/after-planting-millions-of-trees-nz-reviews-its-controversial-climate-fix

|access-date=30 May 2024 |website=www.bloomberg.com}}</ref>

==== Zero Carbon Act ====
In 2019, the Labour led coalition introduced the [[Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act]] which sets a target of net zero carbon emissions (except biogenic methane) for New Zealand by 2050. The Bill passed into law in November 2019 with almost unanimous support.<ref>{{cite news |date=7 November 2019 |title=119 of 120 MPs just voted to pass NZ's historic Zero Carbon Bill into law. Here's the best of what they said |work=[[The Spinoff]] |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/07-11-2019/119-of-120-mps-just-voted-to-pass-nzs-historic-zero-carbon-bill-into-law-heres-the-best-of-what-they-said/ |url-status=live |access-date=14 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201021012433/https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/07-11-2019/119-of-120-mps-just-voted-to-pass-nzs-historic-zero-carbon-bill-into-law-heres-the-best-of-what-they-said/ |archive-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> It establishes an independent [[Climate Change Commission]] to advise the Government of the day on emissions reduction pathways, progress towards targets and develop regular five-year emission budgets. The act sets a separate target for methane gas emissions which mostly come from the agricultural sector – requiring a 10% reduction in biological methane by 2030 and a provisional reduction between 24%–47% by 2050.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lyons |first1=Kate |date=7 May 2019 |title=New Zealand introduces bill for zero carbon emissions by 2050 |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/may/08/new-zealand-introduces-bill-for-zero-carbon-emissions-by-2050 |url-status=live |access-date=14 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125101235/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/may/08/new-zealand-introduces-bill-for-zero-carbon-emissions-by-2050 |archive-date=25 November 2020}}</ref>

The National Party said that they opposed the 24–47% methane reduction target<ref name="NZH 7 Nov 2019">{{cite news |last1=Young |first1=Audrey |date=7 November 2019 |title=Zero Carbon Bill passes with almost unanimous support in Parliament |work=[[New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12283372 |access-date=7 November 2019}}</ref> and that they would remove the methane target<ref name="Stuff 7 Nov 2019">{{cite news |last1=Cooke |first1=Henry |date=7 November 2019 |title=Zero Carbon Bill passes with near-unanimous support, setting climate change targets into law |work=[[Stuff.co.nz]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/117244331/national-will-support-climate-change-zero-carbon-bill |access-date=7 November 2019}}</ref> when they next form a government.<ref name="Passed">{{cite web |last=Tibshraeny |first=Jenée |date=7 November 2019 |title=James Shaw's Zero Carbon Bill passes with near-unanimous support, however National commits to making tweaks if elected into government |url=https://www.interest.co.nz/news/102476/national-throws-its-support-behind-james-shaws-zero-carbon-bill-commits-tweaking |access-date=7 November 2019 |website=Interest.co.nz}}</ref> [[Greenpeace New Zealand]] executive director, [[Russel Norman]] criticised the bill because the targets are voluntary and have no enforcement mechanisms. He says: "What we've got here is a reasonably ambitious piece of legislation that's then had the teeth ripped out of it. There's bark, but there's no bite."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mazengarb |first1=Michael |date=8 May 2019 |title=NZ unveils carbon goal, but goes soft on sheep emissions |url=https://reneweconomy.com.au/nz-unveils-zero-carbon-goal-but-goes-soft-on-sheep-emissions-52937/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028095356/https://reneweconomy.com.au/nz-unveils-zero-carbon-goal-but-goes-soft-on-sheep-emissions-52937/ |archive-date=28 October 2020 |access-date=14 December 2020 |publisher=Renew Economy}}</ref>

In December 2020, an independent scientific analysis by Climate Action Tracker<ref>{{cite web |date=30 July 2020 |title=New Zealand |url=https://climateactiontracker.org/countries/new-zealand/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201207234034/https://climateactiontracker.org/countries/new-zealand/ |archive-date=7 December 2020 |access-date=14 December 2020 |website=Climate Action Tracker}}</ref> stated that "The Bill does not introduce any policies to actually cut emissions". It also rated New Zealand's [[emissions target]]s as "insufficient" meaning that the goals were not "consistent with holding warming below 2C, let alone with the Paris Agreement's stronger 1.5C limit".<ref>{{cite news |date=22 June 2019 |title=Climate Change action: How NZ's 'insufficient' targets stack up against other countries |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/113673075/climate-change-action-how-nzs-insufficient-targets-stack-up-against-other-countries |url-status=live |access-date=14 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201004090139/https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/113673075/climate-change-action-how-nzs-insufficient-targets-stack-up-against-other-countries |archive-date=4 October 2020}}</ref> That was the sixth time in a row that New Zealand's responses had been ranked as "insufficient".<ref>{{cite news |date=5 December 2019 |title=Scathing international report marks NZ's climate action 'insufficient' |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/117967162/scathing-international-report-marks-nzs-climate-action-insufficient |url-status=live |access-date=15 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191206181112/https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/117967162/scathing-international-report-marks-nzs-climate-action-insufficient |archive-date=6 December 2019}}</ref>

=== Climate emergency declarations ===
As at January 2020, 1,315 jurisdictions and local governments around the world covering 810 million citizens had declared climate emergencies.<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = Climate emergency declarations in 1,315 jurisdictions and local governments cover 810 million citizens
 | work        = Climate Emergency Declaration
 | date        = 19 January 2020
 | url         = https://climateemergencydeclaration.org/climate-emergency-declarations-cover-15-million-citizens/
}}</ref> What this means varies for each community and country, but common themes include a commitment to be carbon neutral as quickly as possible, limiting global warming to below 1.5 degrees Celsius, and a willingness to share solutions and join global movements that encourage climate action.<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = Are councils walking the talk with the 'climate emergency'?
 | work        = Stuff
 | date        = 25 May 2019
 | url         = https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/112794608/are-councils-walking-the-talk-with-the-climate-emergency?rm=a
}}</ref>
