Making the declaration for Auckland, Mayor [[Phil Goff]] said: ''"Our obligation is to avoid our children and grandchildren inheriting a world devastated by global heating. Scientists tell us that if we don't take action, the effects of heating will be catastrophic, both environmentally and economically. In declaring an emergency, we are signalling the urgency of action needed to mitigate and adapt to the impact of rising world temperatures and extreme weather events. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change says we have only around 12 years to reduce global carbon emissions to limit temperature rises to 1.5 degrees. While international and national actions are critical, at a local and personal level we need to play our role in achieving that target."''<ref name="ourauckland.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz"/>

The declaration by the Auckland City Council also obliges dozens of council committees to include a climate change impact statement in their reports. This has the advantage of keeping diverse teams working for the Council focused on the issue.<ref name="rnz_mean-anything-sure">{{Cite web |last=Roughan |first=Greg |date=13 June 2019 |title=Opinion: Does a council climate emergency mean anything? Sure |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/on-the-inside/391942/opinion-does-a-council-climate-emergency-mean-anything-sure |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

==== Financial justification ====

Financial liability for the damage caused by rising sea levels and climate related disasters will largely fall on city councils. In July 2019, a review of local government funding by the Productivity Commission has found more funding and support is required from central government because of the significant challenges councils are having to face adapting to sea level rise and flooding. The review found that many local councils are frustrated by the lack of leadership from Government; in particular councils want advice, guidance and legal frameworks to support decisions they need to make about land use in areas that are, or will become, prone to flooding."<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 July 2019 |title=Local govt needs climate change help - Productivity Commission review |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/393594/local-govt-needs-climate-change-help-productivity-commission-review |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

An example of the difficulties that will likely arise is the decision by National MP, [[Judith Collins]] and her husband David Wong-Tung to sue the Nelson City Council for $180,000 for remedial works and lost rental income after a slip damaged their property during heavy rain in Nelson in 2011. At the time the flooding which occurred that day was described as a one in 250 year event.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gee |first=Samantha |date=20 June 2019 |title=National's Judith Collins sues Nelson council, residents over 2011 slip |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/113575823/nationals-judith-collins-sues-nelson-council-residents-over-2011-slip |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> Global warming increases the frequency of such events. Collins is claiming that omissions by the Council caused the landslide which damaged their property. The Council has accepted some of the claims and denied others.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Neal |first=Tracy |date=21 June 2019 |title=Judith Collins takes legal action over damage to her rental home |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/392577/judith-collins-takes-legal-action-over-damage-to-her-rental-home |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

Media commentator, Greg Roughan, points out that as the frequency of such events increases, the cost to business, and councils will only get worse. He also points to the negative impact on property prices if, for example, a low stretch of motorway just north of the Auckland harbour bridge gets washed out multiple times each year, preventing thousands of people from getting to work; and to the legal and financial ramifications if a council grants consent for beachfront properties to be built in an area that a few years later insurers decide not to underwrite. Roughan argues that by declaring a climate emergency, forward-looking Councils are making the point – "this is going to get expensive".<ref name="rnz_mean-anything-sure"/>

==== National government ====
In May 2019, Green MP [[Chlöe Swarbrick]] requested leave to pass a motion in Parliament declaring a climate emergency. Such a motion required the unanimous consent of parliament – but was blocked by the National Party. Prime Minister, Jacinda Ardern said: "We're not opposed to the idea of declaring [a climate change] emergency in Parliament, because certainly I'd like to think our policies and our approach demonstrates that we do see it as an emergency." Radio New Zealand reports that "the climate change declaration has been signed by 90 percent of the country's mayors and council chairs around New Zealand, and it calls for the government to be ambitious with its climate change mitigation measures".<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = Council taken to court over lack of action on climate change
 | work        = RNZ
 | date        = 2 July 2019
 | url         = https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/393547/council-taken-to-court-over-lack-of-action-on-climate-change
}}</ref> However, on 18 July 2019, youth MPs demonstrated the importance of this issue to young people and "beat their actual MPs to the punch by declaring a climate change emergency at (the triennial) Youth Parliament 2019."<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = Youth Parliament 2019 declares climate emergency
 | work        = RNZ
 | date        = 18 July 2019
 | url         = https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/395237/youth-parliament-2019-declares-climate-emergency
}}</ref>

Building on previous campaigning for the decarbonisation of public transport in Auckland a coalition of 17 groups, called All Aboard Aotearoa, was formed in 2020. Using a combination of public education, lobbying and legal action it persuaded Auckland's council to adopt an evidence-based policy to achieve an emissions reductions target for transport of 64% by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gulliver |first=Robyn |date=20 March 2023 |title=Auckland Transport Decarbonisation Campaign (2020 - 2022) |url=https://commonslibrary.org/auckland-transport-decarbonisation-campaign/ |access-date=5 July 2023 |website=The Commons Social Change Library |language=en-AU}}</ref>

On 14 May 2019, Wellington inhabitant [[Ollie Langridge]] began sitting on the lawn outside Parliament holding a sign calling on the Government to declare a climate change emergency.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Iles |first1=Julie |title=Parliament's lone protester will be on its lawn until a climate emergency is declared |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/112826745/parliaments-lone-protester-will-be-on-its-lawn-until-a-climate-emergency-is-declared |access-date=24 August 2019 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=18 May 2019}}</ref> From 28 July, Langridge set a record as the longest running protest outside Parliament in New Zealand's history.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/father-five-clocks-up-74-days-climate-change-protest-outside-parliament | title=Father of five clocks up 74 days of climate change protest outside Parliament | work=[[1News]] | date=28 July 2019 |access-date=24 August 2019 }}</ref> Langridge's protest achieved international attention. After protesting outside Parliament every day for 100 days, Langridge cut back his presence to Fridays only, saying he wanted to spend more time with his wife and children.<ref name="100 days">{{cite news | url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/115208213/climate-vigil-at-parliament-called-off-after-100-days-of-no-action | title=Climate vigil at parliament scaled back to Fridays after 100 days of no action | first=Amber-Leigh | last=Woolf |date=23 May 2019 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | access-date=24 August 2019 }}</ref>

On 2 December 2020, Prime Minister [[Jacinda Ardern]] declared a [[climate change]] emergency in New Zealand and sponsored a parliamentary motion pledging that the New Zealand Government would aim to be "carbon neutral" by 2025 in line with the goals of the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act. As part of the Government's "carbon neutral" goals, the public sector will be required to buy only electric or hybrid vehicles, government buildings will have to meet new building standards, and all 200 coal-fired boilers in public service buildings will be phased out. This motion was supported by the governing centre-left [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] and left-wing [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green]] parties and the opposition [[Māori Party]] but was opposed by the centre-right opposition [[New Zealand National Party|National]] and libertarian [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] parties.<ref name="climate-change-emergency" /><ref name="government-will-have-to-buy-electric-cars" />

On 14 December 2020, Swedish climate change activist [[Greta Thunberg]] criticised the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour Government]]'s climate change emergency declaration as "[[virtue signalling]]," stating that the Government had only committed to reducing less than one percent of New Zealand's carbon emissions by 2025.<ref>{{cite news|author1=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=14 December 2020|title='Nothing unique': Greta Thunberg hits out at NZ over climate emergency|work=[[Newstalk ZB]]|url=https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/national/greta-thunberg-calls-out-new-zealand-over-lack-of-climate-change-action/|url-status=live|access-date=14 December ==== Opinion polls ====

On 13 June 2019 a 1 NEWS Colmar Brunton poll found that a majority of New Zealanders (53%) believe the Government should declare a climate emergency. 39% said no, and 8% did not know.<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = It's time for NZ to declare a climate emergency, majority of Kiwis say in new poll
 | work        = 1 News
 | date        = 13 June 2019
 | url         = https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/its-time-nz-declare-climate-emergency-majority-kiwis-say-in-new-poll
}}</ref> More than 50 of the country's top researchers have also called on New Zealand politicians to declare a climate emergency. Their appeal to government states: "The scientific consensus is that the world stands on the verge of unprecedented environmental and climate catastrophe for which we are little prepared, and which affords us only a few years for mitigating action. We, the undersigned, urge the New Zealand House of Representatives to declare a climate emergency, now."<ref>{{cite news
 | title       = We must face climate emergency head-on
 | work        = Stuff
 | date        = 4 July 2019
 | url         = https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/113984415/we-must-face-climate-emergency-headon
}}</ref>

==== Support for national declaration ====
The Labour Party Climate Change manifesto lists one of its goals as "[Making] New Zealand a leader in the international fight against climate change, and in ensuring that the 2015 [[Paris Agreement]] is successfully implemented."<ref>[https://d3n8a8pro7vhmx.cloudfront.net/nzlabour/pages/8493/attachments/original/1504847668/Climate_Change_Manifesto.pdf?1504847668 Climate Change], New Zealand Labour Party Manifesto 2017</ref> As at June 2019, four countries had formally declared a climate emergency: the UK, France, Canada and Ireland. (Despite these declarations, these countries still provide subsidies of $27.5bn annually which support fossil fuel industries.)<ref>[https://www.climatechangenews.com/2019/06/24/four-countries-declared-climate-emergencies-give-billions-fossil-fuels/ Four countries have declared climate emergencies, yet give billions to fossil fuels], Climate Home News, 24 June 2019.</ref> If the Labour Party wants New Zealand to be a world leader in this area, the Government will need to follow or do better than the example set by these four.

Tom Powell of Climate Karanga Marlborough argues that it is only when we recognise we are facing an actual emergency that our local and national governments get away from "business as usual".<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/113548349/climate-emergency-call-promotes-political-will?rm=m Climate emergency call promotes political will], Stuff, 17 June 2019</ref> Greg Roughan agrees arguing that it takes time for 'out there ideas' (such as a climate crisis) to become mainstream so that political action can be implemented. A declaration that there is a climate emergency from a reputable source such as a city council or national government brings "mainstream cred to the need for urgent action – even if it doesn't spell out how that looks."<ref name="rnz_mean-anything-sure"/>

Climate Change Minister, [[James Shaw (New Zealand politician)|James Shaw]], says "This is obviously not a civil defence emergency, but it creates civil defence emergencies and is increasing civil defence emergencies. It is a meta-emergency. It is quite weird not to call it an emergency, given its consequences."<ref name="ReferenceG">{{Cite web |last=Gorman |first=Paul |date=22 July 2019 |title='Taking stock' before second attempt at declaring New Zealand-wide climate emergency |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/114264612/taking-stock-before-second-attempt-at-declaring-new-zealandwide-climate-emergency |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref> Introducing a "feebate" scheme for car imports in July 2019, associate transport minister, [[Julie Anne Genter]], spoke about fronting up to climate change by comparing it to fighting World War II.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cooke |first=Henry |date=12 July 2019 |title=We don't need a climate emergency. We need a climate war |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/114192119/we-dont-need-a-climate-emergency-we-need-a-climate-war |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=Stuff |language=en}}</ref>

At the Just Transition Community Conference sponsored by the New Plymouth District Council on 15 June 2019,<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Plymouth District Council |url=https://www.npdc.govt.nz/ |access-date=3 June 2026 |website=www.npdc.govt.nz |language=en-NZ}}</ref> Victoria University professor and keynote speaker, [[James Renwick (climate scientist)|James Renwick]], said the situation was dire. He continued: "Last year saw the highest emissions globally on record and emissions have been going up, up and up for the past 30 years. If the world continues to emit greenhouse gasses it will lock in a further 3C of global warming and 10m of sea level rise... There's been a lot of talk about a climate emergency lately and it really is an emergency situation."<ref>[https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/392131/greenhouse-gas-emissions-climate-scientist-warns-of-dangers-ahead Greenhouse gas emissions: Climate scientist warns of dangers ahead], RNZ, 15 June 2019</ref>

==== Opposed to national declaration ====
The decision by local councils to declare climate emergencies has led to debate in the media about what a declaration of an emergency really means and whether or not such declarations will be backed up by significant action to address the problem.<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/112942182/councils-are-declaring-climate-emergencies--but-what-does-that-mean?rm=a Councils are declaring climate emergencies – but what does that mean?] Stuff, 23 May 2019</ref><ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/113747732/councils-declare-climate-emergencies-but-will-it-result-in-any-real-change?rm=a Councils declare climate emergencies, but will it result in any real change?] Stuff 28 June 2019</ref>

National MP, [[Paula Bennett]], called the Prime Minister "ridiculous" because of her willingness to declare a "climate emergency". Bennett said declarations of emergency should only be used for "very serious events" such as the [[2011 Christchurch earthquake|earthquakes]] which occurred in Christchurch in 2011.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20190708015123/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2019/07/paula-bennett-scorns-jacinda-ardern-over-ridiculous-openness-to-climate-emergency.html Paula Bennett scorns Jacinda Ardern over 'ridiculous' openness to 'climate emergency'], Newshub 8 July 2019</ref> National's climate change spokesman, Todd Muller, says "This is a 30, 40, 50-year, multi-generational transition for the economy away from fossil fuels. It's not an emergency in that context – to say it's an emergency is absolutely ridiculous. When you call something from a government – central or local – an emergency, you are saying you are pursuing this above all else."<ref name="ReferenceG"/>

=== National adaptation plan ===
In August 2022, the Ministry for the Environment published Aotearoa New Zealand's first National Adaptation Plan, covering the years 2022–2028, titled: "Adapt and thrive: Building a climate-resilient New Zealand".  The plan includes a range of adaptation options: Avoid, Protect, Accommodate and Retreat.<ref>{{Cite web |date=3 August 2022 |title=Aotearoa New Zealand's first national adaptation plan |url=https://environment.govt.nz/publications/aotearoa-new-zealands-first-national-adaptation-plan/ |access-date=4 August 2022 |website=Ministry for the Environment |language=en-NZ}}</ref>

=== International ranking of climate change policies ===
In 2023 the [[Climate Action Tracker]] project gave New Zealand's climate policies and actions an overall rating of "highly insufficient".<ref name="catnz2023" /> In November 2024, New Zealand's ranking on the 20th [[Climate Change Performance Index]] dropped by seven places to 41st out of 67 nations. The report stated that New Zealand had "taken significant backwards steps in climate policy" due to the Government scrapping policies boosting public transportation and delaying pricing greenhouse gas emissions from farming.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gibson |first1=Eloise |title=New Zealand drops seven places, to 41st, in global climate change league table |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/534411/new-zealand-drops-seven-places-to-41st-in-global-climate-change-league-table |access-date=21 November 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=21 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241120232005/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/534411/new-zealand-drops-seven-places-to-41st-in-global-climate-change-league-table |archive-date=20 November 2024}}</ref> Germanwatch rated New Zealand's overall climate change performance as 'low'.<ref name="Germanwatch_CCPI-2024-Results"/>

== Society and culture ==

=== Activism ===
In March 2019, inspired by Greta Thunberg, tens of thousands of school students took to the streets across NZ calling for action on climate change. The main protests took place on 15 March 2019, however had to be abandoned for safety reasons due to the [[Christchurch mosque shootings]] on the same day. For many young people, it was the first time they felt compelled to become politically active.<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/wellington/111298009/tens-of-thousands-of-school-students-demonstrate-across-nz-calling-for-action-on-climate-change Tens of thousands of school students demonstrate across NZ calling for action on climate change], Stuff 16 March 2019</ref> With the headline, ''We need to listen to young people about climate change'', an editorial on Stuff in March 2019 noted that "Many decision-makers in the governments, businesses, community organisations and churches of the world won't be alive to experience the impact of climate change. But today's school students will be."<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/111220374/we-need-to-listen-to-young-people-about-climate-change We need to listen to young people about climate change], Stuff 13 March 2019</ref> Indeed, some teenagers are wondering "whether or not they will have a planet on which to live out their lives".

A Stuff survey of 15,000 readers in July 2019 shows that New Zealanders aged between 10 and 19 rated climate change as a more important issue than any other age group. Those aged between 20 and 29 were also very concerned about the issue, with the level of concern decreasing with age.<ref>[https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/114288879/tell-me-again-how-the-school-climate-strike-was-just-a-day-off Tell me again how the school climate strike was 'just a day off'], Stuff 18 July 2019</ref> On 18 July, Radio New Zealand reported that youth MPs took a "bold stance" on the issue by declaring a climate change emergency at the triennial Youth Parliament for 2019.<ref>[https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/the-house/audio/2018704687/youth-parliament-2019-declares-climate-emergency Youth Parliament 2019 declares climate emergency], RNZ 18 July 2019</ref>

===<span class="anchor" id="Media_reporting_and_public_opinion"></span>Media messaging===
The Climate Reality Project, founded by [[Al Gore]] after the release of his 2006 documentary ''[[An Inconvenient Truth]]'', appoints and trains 'Climate Reality Leaders' from around the world. At a conference in Brisbane in June 2019, Gore appointed 40 New Zealanders as "apprentices" of his global climate change movement. [[James Shaw (New Zealand politician)|James Shaw]], who is now Minister for Climate Change Issues attended a similar conference in 2013. Part of the messaging taught at these seminars is to use the terms 'climate emergency' and 'climate crisis' rather than 'climate change'.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/113501335/al-gore-names-40-kiwis-apprentices-of-his-climate-change-movement| title=Al Gore names 40 Kiwis apprentices of his climate change movement| publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | date=19 June 2019}}</ref> ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper has also decided to use the terms climate emergency, or crisis instead of [[climate change]]; and [[global heating]] instead of [[global warming]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2019/jun/16/urgency-climate-crisis-robust-new-language-guardian-katharine-viner| title=The urgency of climate crisis needed robust new language to describe it| work=[[The Guardian]] | date=16 June 2019}}</ref>

Media website [[Stuff.co.nz|Stuff]] has a dedicated section focused on the climate crisis called ''Quick! Save the Planet''. When publishing climate related stories, Stuff includes this disclaimer: "Stuff accepts the overwhelming scientific consensus that climate change is real and caused by human activity. We welcome robust debate about the appropriate response to climate change, but do not intend to provide a venue for denialism or hoax advocacy. That applies equally to the stories we will publish in Quick! Save the Planet."<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/environment/climate-news/108819497/quick-save-the-planet-we-must-confront-climate-change| title=Quick! Save the Planet: We must confront climate change| publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | date=28 November 2018}}</ref>

Radio New Zealand points out that "Talk radio broadcasters are still happy to put hosts (such as [[Mike Hosking]], [[Tim Wilson (broadcaster)|Tim Wilson]] and Ryan Bridge) on the air who airily admit they don't understand the science of climate change."<ref>[https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/mediawatch/audio/2018705763/climate-scepticism-boosted-by-broadcasters Climate scepticism boosted by broadcasters] 28 July 2019</ref>

===Opinion polls===

Surveys carried out on public attitudes to climate change show a dramatic shift in concern between 2007 and 2019. The percentage of the public perceiving it to be an urgent problem has jumped by 35% – from 8% to 43%. The number seeing it as a problem already has gone up 10% – from 16% to 26%.<ref>[https://www.horizonpoll.co.nz/page/541/public-conc Public concern over climate change hits new high], HorizonPoll 9 May 2019</ref>

::{| class="wikitable"

|-
| An urgent and immediate problem ||  08% || 43%
|-
|A problem now || 16% ||26% 
|-
|A problem for the future || 37% ||13%
|-
|Not really a problem|| 37% ||11%
|-
|Don't know || 02% ||08%
|}

In August 2012, a Horizons poll showed that 64.4% of respondents wanted Parliament to do more to respond to global warming. 67.5% of respondents wanted business to do more to address global warming. Horizons commented that the poll "makes a strong case for more political action".<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.horizonpoll.co.nz/page/244/people-want |title=People want more action on climate change
|publisher=Horizonpoll 
|date=10 August 2012 |quote=The poll, of 2829 New Zealanders aged 18-plus, taken between July 5 and July 16, also makes a strong case for more political action |access-date=20 January 2013}}</ref>

In 2014, Motu Economic and Public Policy Research surveyed 2200 New Zealanders (over the age of 18) and found that at least 87% of participants are "somewhat concerned" about the effects of climate change to society in general. 63% also believed that climate change would affect themselves and 58% believed that climate change would affect society.<ref name="Motu">{{Cite web| url=https://motu.nz/about-us/news/majority-of-new-zealanders-are-concerned-about-climate-change-and-taking-actions-that-reduce-emissions/| title=Majority of New Zealanders are concerned about climate change and taking actions that reduce emissions| date=15 May 2015| website=Motu| language=en| access-date=31 May 2018}}</ref>

=== Political parties stance on climate change===
{{Update section|date=September 2025|reason=outdated information}}
{{Anchor|Politics of climate change in New Zealand}}
==== ACT Party ====

The [[ACT New Zealand|ACT Party]] promotes policies associated with [[climate change denial]]. They went into the 2008 election with a policy that in part stated "New Zealand is not warming" and that their policy goal was to ensure: "That no New Zealand government will ever impose needless and unjustified taxation or regulation on its citizens in a misguided attempt to reduce global warming or become a world leader in [[carbon neutrality]]"<ref>{{cite web |year=2008 |title=ACT Climate Change Policy |url=http://www.act.org.nz/climate-change-policy |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100818044115/http://www.act.org.nz/climate-change-policy |archive-date=18 August 2010 |access-date=12 January 2010 |publisher=The ACT Party}}</ref> In September 2008, ACT Party Leader [[Rodney Hide]] stated "that the entire climate change – global warming hypothesis is a hoax, that the data and the hypothesis do not hold together, that Al Gore is a phoney and a fraud on this issue, and that the emissions trading scheme is a worldwide scam and swindle".<ref>{{cite web |last=Hide |first=Rodney |date=3 September 2008 |title=Hide: Emissions Trading Bill Speech |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0809/S00042.htm |access-date=12 January 2010 |work=Press Release ACT Party Speech to Parliament |publisher=Scoop}}</ref> In October 2012, in response to a speech on climate change by Green Party MP Kennedy Graham, ACT leader [[John Banks (New Zealand politician)|John Banks]] said he had "never heard such claptrap in this parliament... a bogeyman tirade, humbug."<ref>{{cite news |date=26 October 2012 |title=Climate change policy splits main parties |work=3 News NZ |url=http://www.3news.co.nz/Climate-change-policy-splits-main-parties/tabid/1607/articleID/274244/Default.aspx |access-date=25 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729113311/http://www.3news.co.nz/Climate-change-policy-splits-main-parties/tabid/1607/articleID/274244/Default.aspx |archive-date=29 July 2013}}</ref> In 2016, ACT's only MP, David Seymour, deleted climate change policy from their website. Prior to that their website claimed New Zealand was not warming and pledged to withdraw the country from the Kyoto Protocol.<ref>{{cite news |last=Cooke |first=Henry |date=27 February 2016 |title=ACT deletes climate change policy from their website |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/77338800/act-delete-climate-change-policy-from-their-website}}</ref>

However at the 2017 election, ACT did commit to replace petrol tax with a user-pays road pricing system to reduce congestion on the roads by only charging those who use them. In their transport policy, ACT argued this would make public transport faster and reduce carbon emissions.<ref name="Policies"/>{{rp|at=[https://policy.nz/topic/Environment#Conservation Conservation]}} Under the leadership of David Seymour the ACT party has since toned back its anti-climate change stance in favour of committing to policies that combat climate change while doing the least amount of damage to the economy. ACT was the only political party to oppose the Zero Carbon Act.<ref>{{cite web |title=Act's Real Solutions for the Environment and the Climate |url=https://www.act.org.nz/environment |access-date=13 December 2020 |publisher=ACT}}</ref> It is ACT's policy to repeal the ban on oil and gas exploration.<ref name="Policies"/>{{rp|at=[https://policy.nz/topic/Environment#Emissions%20reduction Emissions reduction]}}

==== Climate Change Party ====
In August 2014, Peter Whitmore launched the NZ Climate Party, although it was never formally registered. Whitmore says there is "global scientific agreement that the world's temperature increase must be limited to 2 degrees Celsius to avoid major catastrophe"<ref>[http://www.climate.org.nz/the-issue/ The Issue], NZ Climate Party</ref> and that current & past New Zealand Governments have not been taking the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions nearly seriously enough.<ref name="ClimateParty14"/> In a NZ Herald opinion piece in 2017, Whitmore wrote: "It is clear from the above that New Zealand's current Paris commitment is pathetically feeble. We are not actually undertaking to make any reduction in our emissions by 2030, even compared to today's levels".<ref>[https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11908137 Peter Whitmore: Emissions target is giving wrong impression], NZ Herald 22 August 2017</ref>

==== Green Party ====
Since 2014, [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]] policy has been to "establish a clear strategy, action plan and [[Emissions budget|carbon budget]] for the transition to a net zero emissions, fossil-fuel free economy and support a 100% reduction in net greenhouse gas emissions from 1990 levels within New Zealand by 2050".<ref>[https://www.greens.org.nz/sites/default/files/climatechange_20140601.pdf Climate Change Policy], Green Party Policy document, 1 June 2014</ref>

At the 2017 general election the Green Party leader [[James Shaw (New Zealand politician)|James Shaw]] also announced that the Green Party also wanted to establish an independent climate commission. The Green Party proposed a Kiwi Climate Fund to replace the Emissions Trading Scheme, charging individuals responsible for contributing to climate change pollution. Commitment was also made to New Zealand having [[100% renewable energy]] by 2030, as well as planting 1.2 billion trees, allocating 40 million dollars to native forest regeneration and creating a 100 million dollar [[green infrastructure]] fund.<ref name="CPP">{{Cite news |date=8 September 2017 |title=Climate Protection Plan |language=en |work=Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand |url=https://www.greens.org.nz/climate-protection-plan |access-date=28 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180529135003/https://www.greens.org.nz/climate-protection-plan |archive-date=29 May 2018}}</ref>

==== Labour Party ====
The [[New Zealand Labour Party]] under Jacinda Ardern set a target of net zero for greenhouse gases by the year 2050. Labour committed to creating an independent climate change commission to address carbon monitoring and budgeting, and also to provide comment and guidance when set targets or goals weren't met. Labour also committed to bringing agriculture into the emissions trading scheme to ensure that the agricultural sector operates with improved environmental practice. Overall, Labour pledged to create a sustainable [[low-carbon economy]], and become a leading nation in addressing climate change, successfully achieving its commitments as made under the 2015 [[Paris Agreement]].<ref name="RAOCC">{{Cite news |title=Real Action on Climate Change |language=en |work=New Zealand Labour Party |url=https://www.labour.org.nz/climatechange |access-date=28 May 2018}}</ref>

==== Te Pāti Māori ====

In 2017, [[Te Pāti Māori]] (the Māori Party) committed to developing renewable energy and alternative fuels, including subsidised solar panels for all homes in New Zealand and championing their installation in schools, marae, hospitals and government agencies. It also wanted to set legally binding emission reduction targets, close all coal run power plants by 2025, support the development of renewable resources and plant 100,000 hectares of forest over the next 10 years. Te Pāti Māori also agreed to the establishment of an independent Climate Commission established to ensure this occurs, but also wanted subsidised electric vehicles for community groups. They also proposed a new visa category for Pacific climate change refugees.<ref name="Policies">{{Cite web |title=Environment Policies {{!}} NZ Election 2017 {{!}} Policy |url=https://policy.nz/topic/Environment |access-date=28 May 2018 |website=policy.nz |language=en}}</ref>{{rp|at=[https://policy.nz/topic/Environment#Climate%20Change Climate change]}} However, the Te Pāti Māori lost all its seats at this election.

==== National Party ====
According to Colin James, the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] "herded with" the climate change sceptics up to 2006. In May 2007, National stopped opposing the Kyoto Protocol and adopted a policy of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2050.<ref>{{cite web |last=James |first=Colin |date=8 May 2007 |title=National bids to outflank Labour on climate change |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/climate-change/news/article.cfm?c_id=26&objectid=10438313 |access-date=20 September 2012 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]}}</ref> At the 2008 election, National's policy was to honour New Zealand's Kyoto Protocol obligations and the emissions target of a 50% reduction in emissions by 2050. National proposed changing the [[Climate Change Response (Emissions Trading) Amendment Act 2008|Labour Party's emissions trading scheme]] to align it with the Australian Carbon Pollution Reduction Scheme so that consumers and small businesses would not be penalised.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 September 2008 |title=National Party Environment Policy |url=http://national.org.nz/files/2008/environment%20policy.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100525072027/http://www.national.org.nz/files/2008/environment%20policy.pdf |archive-date=25 May 2010 |access-date=22 August 2009}}</ref>

Prior to the 2017 election, the National Party made a commitment to reduce carbon emissions by 30% below 2005 levels by 2030. The National Party also committed to achieving 90% of New Zealand's energy as renewable, alongside investing 4 million dollars into New Zealand becoming closer to a low carbon economy. The National government also focused on transport, committing to invest in public transport, electric vehicles and cycleways to reduce use of non-renewable energy run vehicle use.<ref name="NationalCC">{{Cite web |title=Climate change |work=NZ National Party |url=https://www.national.org.nz/climate_change |access-date=28 May 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2019, ''New Zealand Herald'' journalist Simon Wilson, argued that the National Party is New Zealand's biggest threat to addressing climate change. Writing for his newspaper, he said: "National's position on climate change will undermine our economy and damage us socially. Delays now will lead to crisis management later and the people worst affected will include farmers, coastal dwellers and the poor. As long as National holds to this position, to me it demonstrates it is unfit to govern."<ref>{{cite news |last=Wilson |first=Simon |date=19 July 2019 |title=Why National is our biggest climate change threat |publisher=[[New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/opinion/news/article.cfm?c_id=466&objectid=12250757}}{{subscription required}}</ref>

During the [[Sixth National Government of New Zealand]], climate reporting rules for large businesses were eased, with the threshold for reporting raised to companies worth $1b from current $60m meaning fewer businesses would be required to report their emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beckford |first=Gyles |date=22 October 2025 |title=Climate reporting rules for large businesses to be eased |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/576637/climate-reporting-rules-for-large-businesses-to-be-eased |access-date=31 October 2025 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref> In 2025, the National Party announced a plan to lower the methane emission reductions target, from between 24 and 47% to between 14 and 24% by 2050, compared to 2017 levels.<ref>{{Cite news |last=France-Presse |first=Agence |date=13 October 2025 |title=New Zealand accused of 'full-blown climate denial' over cuts to methane reduction targets |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/13/new-zealand-government-accused-climate-denial-methane-reduction-targets |access-date=31 October 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The reduction was criticised in an open letter to Prime Minister [[Christopher Luxon]] signed by 26 international climate change scientists, accusing the government of "ignoring scientific evidence" over the move.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gibson |first=Eloise |date=3 June 2025 |title=Climate change scientists accuse government of 'ignoring scientific evidence' |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/562938/climate-change-scientists-accuse-government-of-ignoring-scientific-evidence |access-date=31 October 2025 |website=RNZ |language=en-nz}}</ref>

==== NZ First ====

At the 2017 election, the NZ First Party committed to setting legally binding emission reduction targets; to require electricity retailers to purchase power generated by customers at retail price; to replace the ETS with carbon budgets; and to require all government vehicles to be electricity run by the year 2025/2026.<ref name="Policies"/>{{rp|at=[https://policy.nz/topic/Environment#Climate%20Change Climate change]}}

==== Opportunities Party ====

The [[The Opportunities Party|Opportunity Party]]'s policies were to set a legally binding target of carbon neutrality by 2050; reform the Emissions Trading Scheme to create a firm limit on emissions; require all large new investments take into account the goal of being carbon neutral by 2050; aim for 100% renewable electricity by 2035; and reforest all erosion-prone land by 2030.<ref name="Policies"/>{{rp|at=[https://policy.nz/topic/Environment#Climate%20Change Climate change]}}

|url-status=live}}</ref> Turkey will host the [[2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference]] and its president [[Murat Kurum]] says that [[climate finance]] is the most important issue.<ref>{{Cite April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Turkey's annual [[greenhouse gas emissions]] are over 1% of the global total,<ref>{{cite web |title=Each Country's Share of CO2 Emissions |url=https://www.ucsusa.org/global-warming/science-and-impacts/science/each-countrys-share-of-co2.html |publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists |access-date=16 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181124214635/https://www.ucsusa.org/global-warming/science-and-impacts/science/each-countrys-share-of-co2.html |archive-date=24 November 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[energy policy of Turkey|energy policy]] includes [[energy subsidies#Turkey|subsidizing]] both [[fossil gas in Turkey|fossil gas]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ergur |first=Semih |date=2023-05-12 |title=Turkey Spent Over $200,000,000 in Fossil Fuel Subsidies in 2022 |url=https://www.climatescorecard.org/2023/05/turkey-spent-over-200000000-in-fossil-fuel-subsidies-in-2022/ |access-date=2023-11-30 |website=Climate Scorecard |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231212202730/https://www.climatescorecard.org/2023/05/turkey-spent-over-200000000-in-fossil-fuel-subsidies-in-2022/ |archive-date=12 December 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[coal in Turkey|coal]].<ref name="OECD">{{Cite web |title=Fossil Fuel Support - TUR |url=https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=FFS_TUR |access-date=2023-11-30 |website=stats.oecd.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112004527/https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=FFS_TUR |archive-date=12 November 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> Per person emissions since the late-2010s have varied around six and a half&nbsp;[[tonne]]s a year,<ref name=":46">{{Cite web |title=Greenhouse Gas Emissions Statistics, 1990-2024 |url=https://veriportali.tuik.gov.tr/en/press/58000 |access-date=2026-04-22 |website=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260425234106/https://veriportali.tuik.gov.tr/en/press/58000 |archive-date=25 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> which is about [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per person|the global average]].<ref name="Website-3">{{Cite web |title=Are per capita CO₂ emissions above or below the global average? |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/per-capita-co2-vs-average |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Our World in Data |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260220201646/https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/per-capita-co2-vs-average |archive-date=20 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> However historical emissions are less than 1% of the global total.<ref>{{Cite web |website=Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Cumhurbaşkanlıği |title=2053 yılı itibarıyla net sıfır emisyon hedefini gerçekleştirmeyi öngörüyoruz |url=https://www.tccb.gov.tr/haberler/410/150389/-2053-yili-itibariyla-net-sifir-emisyon-hedefini-gerceklestirmeyi-ongoruyoruz- |access-date=2023-12-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231202050714/https://www.tccb.gov.tr/haberler/410/150389/-2053-yili-itibariyla-net-sifir-emisyon-hedefini-gerceklestirmeyi-ongoruyoruz- |archive-date=2 December 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change#Directorate of Climate Change|Directorate of Climate Change]] co-ordinates [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation to climate change]], which has been planned for water resources by [[river basin]], and for [[Agriculture in Turkey|agriculture]]. Certificate caps in [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|the emission trading system]] are unclear as of 2026. Housing is not energy efficient, the pathway to the 2053 [[Net-zero emissions|net zero]] target is unclear, and there is no plan for [[coal phase-out]].<ref name="Bosse1">{{Cite web |last=Bosse |first=Jolana |date=2025-11-18 |title=Türkiye – Climate Performance Ranking 2026 {{!}} Climate Change Performance Index |url=https://ccpi.org/country/tur/ |access-date=2026-07-26 |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251228025452/https://ccpi.org/country/tur/ |archive-date=28 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>__TOC__

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==
[[File:Control room of Zetes-3 power station.jpg|thumb|Coal-fired power stations, such as the [[ZETES power stations]], are the largest source of greenhouse gas.<ref name="2021report">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Turkish Greenhouse Gas Inventory 1990 - 2021 [TurkStat report]
 |date=14 April 2023
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/627786
 }}</ref>{{Rp|459}}]]

[[Coal in Turkey|Coal]], cars and lorries vent more than a third of [[Turkey]]'s annual [[greenhouse gas emissions]], which total about six hundred million tonnes.<ref name=":46" /><ref name=":53">{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory - Turkey |url=https://climatetrace.org/inventory?region=T%C3%BCrkiye+%28TUR%29%3A247%3ATUR%3Acountry&timeframe=100 |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008170024/https://climatetrace.org/inventory?region=T%C3%BCrkiye+(TUR):247:TUR:country&timeframe=100 |archive-date=8 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>  They are mostly [[carbon dioxide]] and part of the cause of climate change in Turkey. A quarter of the emissions are from [[Electricity sector in Turkey|electricity generation]].<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.1}}

The government estimated 2024 emissions at 517.4 Mt with and 584.5 Mt without LULUCF,<ref name="2026report">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Greenhouse Gas Inventory of Türkiye 1990 - 2024
 |date=April 2026
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/656425
 }}
 </ref>{{Reference page|page=v}} and uncertainty at 7.9%, or 5.1% without LULUCF.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=23}} [[Climate Trace]] estimate 646 million tonnes (Mt) of GHG was emitted in 2025 excluding [[land use, land-use change, and forestry]],<ref name=":53" /> and 43 Mt from LULUCF.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory - Turkey |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en}}</ref> Their estimate of 72 Mt of GHG from waste in 2023 and 2024 and 2025<ref name="Climate TRACE">{{Cite web |title=Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=Climate TRACE |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260122113914/https://climatetrace.org/ |archive-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> is much higher than the official figure of 15 Mt in 2023 and 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Official figures do not detail individual sources, but the largest in 2025 according to Climate Trace were [[ZETES power stations]], [[Istanbul Airport]], [[Cenal power station]], [[İÇDAŞ Biga power station]] and [[Isdemir Payas steel plant]].<ref name="Climate TRACE" /> The [[Transnational Institute]] estimated 2023 military emissions at 4.7 million tonnes,<ref>{{Cite web| title=Climate in the crosshairs - The planetary impact of NATO's spending increases | url=https://www.tni.org/files/2024-07/Climate%20in%20the%20Crosshairs.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240709130109/https://www.tni.org/files/2024-07/Climate%20in%20the%20Crosshairs.pdf | archive-date=2024-07-09}}</ref> but this estimate may not have used official [[NATO]] methodology.<ref>{{Cite web| title=The NATO Greenhouse Gases Emission Mapping and Analytical Methodology | url=https://www.nato.int/nato_static_fl2014/assets/pdf/2023/7/pdf/230710-NATO-GHG-Methodology.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230712125955/https://www.nato.int/nato_static_fl2014/assets/pdf/2023/7/pdf/230710-NATO-GHG-Methodology.pdf | archive-date=2023-07-12}}</ref> 

The energy sector, including [[Transport in Turkey|transport]], emitted 420 million tonnes in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> [[List of active coal-fired power stations in Turkey|The nation's coal-fired power stations]] emit the most carbon dioxide, and road vehicles running on [[gasoline|petrol]] or [[diesel fuel|diesel]] are also significant. After coal<ref name=":49">{{Cite news |date=15 November 2022 |title=Turkey's Climate Plan Points to 32% Rise in Emissions by 2030 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-15/turkey-s-climate-plan-points-to-32-rise-in-emissions-by-2030?leadSource=uverify%20wall |access-date=2022-11-15 |newspaper=Bloomberg |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221115142245/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-15/turkey-s-climate-plan-points-to-32-rise-in-emissions-by-2030?leadSource=uverify%20wall |archive-date=15 November 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[oil in Turkey|oil]] the third most polluting [[fossil fuel|fuel]] is [[gas in Turkey|fossil gas]]; which is burnt in [[List of power stations in Turkey#Natural Gas|Turkey's gas-fired power stations]], homes and workplaces. Much [[methane emissions from livestock|methane is belched by livestock]]; cows alone produce half of the greenhouse gas from [[agriculture in Turkey]].<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cells I12 and I20}}

Economists say that major reasons for Turkey's greenhouse gas emissions are [[Coal subsidies in Turkey|subsidies for coal-fired power stations]],<ref name=":43">{{Cite web|title=Still Not Getting Energy Prices Right: A Global and Country Update of Fossil Fuel Subsidies|url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2021/09/23/Still-Not-Getting-Energy-Prices-Right-A-Global-and-Country-Update-of-Fossil-Fuel-Subsidies-466004|access-date=2021-10-06|website=IMF|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230111182236/https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2021/09/23/Still-Not-Getting-Energy-Prices-Right-A-Global-and-Country-Update-of-Fossil-Fuel-Subsidies-466004|archive-date=11 January 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|18}}<ref>{{Cite web |author=Prashant Vaze |author2=Archie Gilmour |author3=Bengisu Ozenc |author4=Evrim Ozyorulmaz-Akcura |date=2024-12-25 |title=Low-Carbon Transition Risks Facing Coal in Türkiye |url=https://sefia.org/en/publications/low-carbon-transition-risks-facing-coal-in-turkiye/ |access-date=2025-04-06 |website=SEFiA |language=en-US |quote=These capacity payments have grown markedly over time and now provide an important revenue line for local coal (1.16 billion Turkish lira (TL) in 2023) and gas power (TL2.5 billion). |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251210205842/https://sefia.org/en/publications/low-carbon-transition-risks-facing-coal-in-turkiye/ |archive-date=10 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the lack of a [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|price on carbon pollution]].<ref name=":44">{{Cite journal|last1=Steckel|first1=Jan C.|last2=Dorband|first2=Ira I.|last3=Montrone|first3=Lorenzo|last4=Ward|first4=Hauke|last5=Missbach|first5=Leonard|last6=Hafner|first6=Fabian|last7=Jakob|first7=Michael|last8=Renner|first8=Sebastian|date=23 September 2021|title=Distributional impacts of carbon pricing in developing Asia|journal=Nature Sustainability|volume=4|issue=11|language=en|pages=1005–1014|doi=10.1038/s41893-021-00758-8|s2cid=237611447|issn=2398-9629|quote=|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021NatSu...4.1005S |hdl=1887/3238835|hdl-access=free}}</ref>{{Rp|1}}

Turkey's [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions|share of current global greenhouse gas emissions]] is slightly over 1%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EDGAR - The Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research |url=https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103095711/https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/report_2025 |archive-date=2026-01-03 |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref> Annual per person emissions are six and a half&nbsp;[[tonne]]s,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-28 |title=Total greenhouse gas emissions (without LULUCF) |url=https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/total-greenhouse-gas-emissions |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=www.eea.europa.eu |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260214224505/https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/total-greenhouse-gas-emissions |archive-date=14 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> which is around [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per person|the global average]].<ref name="Website-3" /> Although greenhouse gas totals are reported some details, such as the split between cars and lorries, are not published.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=Table1.A(a)s3 Col G}}

The government supports [[Reforestation#Turkey|reforestation]], [[Automotive industry in Turkey|electric vehicle manufacturing]] and [[Low-carbon power|low-carbon]] [[Electricity sector in Turkey|electricity generation]]; and is aiming for [[Carbon neutrality|net zero carbon emissions]] by 2053. But its long-term plan omits [[coal phase-out]],<ref name=":55">{{Cite report |date=November 2024 |title=2053 long term climate strategy |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Turkiye_Long_Term_Climate_Strategy.pdf |publisher=[[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251113110826/https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Turkiye_Long_Term_Climate_Strategy.pdf |archive-date=13 November 2025 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":39">{{Cite web |date=2024-11-11 |title=Türkiye iklim yol haritasını paylaştı, 2053'e kadar 'net sıfır' gerçekçi mi? |url=https://www.bbc.com/turkce/articles/cjw092p8356o |access-date=2024-11-11 |website=BBC News Türkçe |language=tr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251218234853/https://www.bbc.com/turkce/articles/cjw092p8356o |archive-date=18 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> and there is no clear pathway to net zero.<ref name="Bosse1" /> Turkey's [[Nationally Determined Contributions|nationally determined contribution]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=NDC 3.0 {{!}} UNFCCC |url=https://unfccc.int/ndc-3.0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250204033728/https://unfccc.int/ndc-3.0 |archive-date=2025-02-04 |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=unfccc.int |language=en}}</ref> to the [[Paris Agreement]] on [[Climate change mitigation|limiting climate change]] is 643 million tonnes in 2035,<ref>{{Cite news |title=Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan BM İklim Zirvesi'nde konuştu |url=https://www.iletisim.gov.tr/turkce/haberler/detay/cumhurbaskani-erdogan-bm-iklim-zirvesinde-konustu |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729153917/https://www.iletisim.gov.tr/turkce/haberler/detay/cumhurbaskani-erdogan-bm-iklim-zirvesinde-konustu |archive-date=2026-07-29 |access-date=2026-07-29 |language=tr-TR}}</ref> which has been criticised as an increase on current emissions. In 2024 environment minister [[Murat Kurum]] said that by Turkey's [[Net-zero emissions|net zero]] year of 2053 half of primary energy would be from renewables and 30% from [[Nuclear power in Turkey|nuclear]], but did not explain how the remaining 20% could be decarbonised.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye plans to increase renewable energy to reach 50% of primary energy by 2053 |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/environment/turkiye-plans-to-increase-renewable-energy-to-reach-50-of-primary-energy-by-2053/3392926 |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=www.aa.com.tr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251211102206/https://www.aa.com.tr/en/environment/turkiye-plans-to-increase-renewable-energy-to-reach-50-of-primary-energy-by-2053/3392926 |archive-date=11 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Paris in dreams, Baku in reality {{!}} Heinrich Böll Stiftung {{!}} Derneği Türkiye Temsilciliği |url=https://tr.boell.org/en/2024/12/17/paris-in-dreams-baku-in-reality |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=tr.boell.org |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260208203325/https://tr.boell.org/en/2024/12/17/paris-in-dreams-baku-in-reality |archive-date=8 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Although [[Turkish Emissions Trading System|carbon emission trading]] is due to start its pilot phase,<ref>{{Cite report |title=Why a weak Turkish ETS fails both the climate and Turkish exporters |url=https://carbonmarketwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Turkish-ETS_final-version.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260513174711/https://carbonmarketwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Turkish-ETS_final-version.pdf |archive-date=13 May 2026 |access-date=26 July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> unless Turkey's climate and energy policies are changed the 2053 net zero target may be missed.<ref>{{cite web |title=Global climate policy forecast predicts 'well below 2°C' Paris Agreement climate goals will be met |work=PRI |url=https://www.unpri.org/news-and-press/global-climate-policy-forecast-predicts-well-below-2c-paris-agreement-climate-goals-will-be-met/11790.article |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727053329/https://www.unpri.org/news-and-press/global-climate-policy-forecast-predicts-well-below-2c-paris-agreement-climate-goals-will-be-met/11790.article |archive-date=27 July 2025 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
[[File:Ghg pie chart Turkey.svg|thumb|alt=Chart showing the top sources of greenhouse gases are, in order: coal-fired electricity, road transport, home fuel, cement, cattle and gas-fired electricity|Coal-fired power stations emit the most, followed by diesel fuel burned in lorries and other road vehicles.]]

Turkey emitted 585&nbsp;Mt of GHG in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Istanbul Policy Center has suggested a total national [[carbon budget]] of about 13 Gt after 2023, as a part of the global carbon budget to keep below 2 degrees.<ref name=":30">{{Cite report |title=Turkey's Decarbonization Roadmap: Towards Net Zero by 2053 |url=https://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/Content/Images/CKeditorImages/20251001-15101101.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260426222314/https://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/Content/Images/CKeditorImages/20251001-15101101.pdf |archive-date=26 April 2026 |access-date=22 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=5}} Per-person emissions are around the world average,<ref name="Website-3" /> at around 7 t in 2024.<ref name=":46" /> Turkey's cumulative CO<sub>2</sub> emissions are estimated at around 13&nbsp;Gt, which is less than 1% of the world's cumulative total (Turkey's population is about 1% of world population).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/cumulative-co-emissions?country=~TUR|title=Cumulative CO₂ emissions &#124; Our World in Data}}</ref> Turkey's emissions can be looked at differently to the standard IPCC classification: for example a 2021 study by [[İzmir University of Economics|Izmir University of Economics]] estimated that food, "from farm to fork", accounts for about a third of national emissions,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Üçtuğ|first1=Fehmi Görkem|last2=Günaydin|first2=Dorukhan|last3=Hünkar|first3=Beliz|last4=Öngelen|first4=Cansu|date=1 April 2021|title=Carbon footprints of omnivorous, vegetarian, and vegan diets based on traditional Turkish cuisine|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352550920314263|journal=Sustainable Production and Consumption|volume=26|pages=597–609|doi=10.1016/j.spc.2020.12.027|bibcode=2021SusPC..26..597G |s2cid=230577702|issn=2352-5509|access-date=16 February 2021|archive-date=17 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417022658/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352550920314263|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> which is similar to the global emissions share of food.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lynch|first=John|title=Global food system emissions alone threaten warming beyond 1.5°C – but we can act now to stop it|url=http://theconversation.com/global-food-system-emissions-alone-threaten-warming-beyond-1-5-c-but-we-can-act-now-to-stop-it-149312|access-date=17 March 2021|website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]|date=5 November 2020 |archive-date=1 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210301234607/https://theconversation.com/global-food-system-emissions-alone-threaten-warming-beyond-1-5-c-but-we-can-act-now-to-stop-it-149312|url-status=live}}</ref>
=== Monitoring, reporting and verification ===

[[File:Ghg gases by year Turkey.svg|thumb|alt=Graph showing the types of greenhouse gases emitted by Turkey |As in most countries carbon dioxide, mostly from burning fossil fuels, is the main GHG]]

[[Greenhouse gas monitoring|Monitoring]], reporting and verification (MRV) includes tracking national GHG emissions and action to limit them,<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is MRV? {{!}} MRV |url=http://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv |access-date=2026-10-06 |website=carbon-turkey.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829171647/http://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv |archive-date=29 August 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and sharing information and lessons learned.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is MRV?|url=https://www.carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv|access-date=6 September 2021|website=www.carbon-turkey.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729215239/https://carbon-turkey.org/en/what-is-mrv|archive-date=29 July 2021|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[Directorate of Climate Change]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=iklim.gov.tr |title=About Us - İklim Değişikliği Başkanlığı |url=https://iklim.gov.tr/en/about-us-i-75#:~:text=Directorate%20of%20Climate%20Change&text=It%20is%20responsible%20for%20determining,change%20mitigation%20and%20adaptation%20efforts. |access-date=2024-12-16 |website=iklim.gov.tr |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260217074919/https://iklim.gov.tr/en/about-us-i-75#:~:text=Directorate%20of%20Climate%20Change&text=It%20is%20responsible%20for%20determining,change%20mitigation%20and%20adaptation%20efforts. |archive-date=17 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Turkish Statistical Institute|Turkish government's Statistical Institute]] (Turkstat) follow the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC) reporting guidelines, so use [[Greenhouse gas emissions accounting#Production-based accounting|production-based GHG accounting]] to compile the country's [[greenhouse gas inventory]]. Using [[Greenhouse gas emissions accounting#Consumption-based accounting|consumption-based accounting]] would give a similar total.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Territorial and consumption-based CO₂ emissions, Turkey |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/production-vs-consumption-co2-emissions?country=~TUR |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241218195010/https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/production-vs-consumption-co2-emissions?country=~TUR |archive-date=18 December 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Turkstat sends the data to the UNFCCC annually during the second year following the reported year, for example 2023 emissions were reported in 2025 in the annual National Inventory Document (NID) and Common Reporting Tables (CRT).<ref>{{cite web|title=Reporting requirements|url=https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/transparency-and-reporting/reporting-and-review-under-the-convention/greenhouse-gas-inventories-annex-i-parties/reporting-requirements|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200810200216/https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/transparency-and-reporting/reporting-and-review-under-the-convention/greenhouse-gas-inventories-annex-i-parties/reporting-requirements|archive-date=10 August 2020|access-date=8 October 2019|website=[[UNFCCC]]}}</ref> In years when a [[Biennial transparency report]] (BTR) is submitted to the UNFCCC the data may be included with the report, as was done in 2024 with Turkey's first BTR.<ref name=":48">{{Cite report |date=November 2024 |title=First Biennial Transparency Report of Türkiye |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/T%C3%BCrkiye_1BTR.pdf |publisher=[[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241111090312/https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/T%C3%BCrkiye_1BTR.pdf |archive-date=11 November 2024 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Emissions from fuels sold in the country for international aviation and shipping are accounted separately in reports to the UNFCCC, and are not included in a country's total.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|46}} In 2024 [[jet kerosene]], supplied at Turkish airports and burnt by international flights, emitted 15&nbsp;Mt [[Global warming potential|{{CO2}}e (carbon dioxide equivalent)]];<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=54}} (there are also indirect effects from [[Contrail|contrails]] and [[ozone]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Carbon Footprint and Environmental Health Impacts of Airline Fleets: The Case of Turkish Airlines |url=https://jast.msu.edu.tr/index.php/JAST/article/view/685/464}}</ref>) and [[diesel oil]] and [[residual fuel oil]] from Turkish ports powering international shipping 2 Mt&nbsp;{{CO2}}e.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=55}}

The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) defines three methodological tiers to measure emissions. Tier 1 uses global defaults and simplified assumptions, so is the easiest but least accurate. Tier 2 uses country specific values and more detailed data. Tier 3 uses the most detailed data and modelling, so is the most difficult to compile but the most accurate. To make best use of human resources each nation may decide to only use higher tiers to estimate its particular "key categories". Turkstat selects these categories depending on either the absolute level of emissions from that category, or whether it is trending, or uncertain.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|439}} For example, CO2 from [[Lime (material)|lime]] production was a key category for 2024 solely because of its quickly rising emissions: most of the key categories selected in 2024 are both trending up and the largest emitting sectors, [[Cement kiln|cement production]] for example.<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=22}} Turkey uses Tier 2 and Tier 3 methodology for some key categories, for example a power plant might [[Coal assay|analyse the lignite]] it burns, which differs from mine to mine.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|72}} Turkey has a high rate of car ownership even in urban areas,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=OECD |date=2025-09-25 |title=Decarbonising Health Systems Across OECD Countries |url=https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/decarbonising-health-systems-across-oecd-countries_5ac2b24b-en.html |journal=OECD Health Policy Studies |language=en |doi=10.1787/5ac2b24b-en |isbn=978-92-64-89270-5 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260114133316/https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/decarbonising-health-systems-across-oecd-countries_5ac2b24b-en.html |archive-date=14 January 2026 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{Reference page|page=31}}and although road transport is a key category, it is not split between cars and lorries as is done in some countries. In 2021 the UNFCCC asked Turkey why it reported negligible indirect GHGs ([[carbon monoxide]], [[nitrogen oxides]], non-methane [[volatile organic compounds]] and [[sulfur oxides]]) in 2018.<ref name=":24">{{cite tech report |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/trr4_TUR.pdf |title=Report on the technical review of the fourth biennial report of Turkey |date=2 June 2021 |work=[[UNFCCC]] |id=FCCC/TRR.4/TUR}}</ref>{{Rp|12}} Legislation for the [[Turkish Emissions Trading System]] to monitor some private sector emissions was passed in 2026, but does not include methane from [[biomass]] such as [[Waste management in Turkey|waste]].<ref name=":31">{{Cite news |last1=Carrington |first1=Damian |last2=Michaelson |first2=Ruth |last3=Aldatmaz |first3=Ayça |date=2026-10-05 |title=Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/05/methane-mega-leaks-from-un-climate-summit-host-turkey |access-date=2026-10-05 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Greenhouse gas sources ===
==== Fossil fuels ====
{{See also|Energy in Turkey}}
[[File:CO₂ emissions by fuel or industry, Turkey, OWID chart.png|thumb|alt=Graph shows carbon dioxide emitted by coal, oil, and natural gas over the years from 1990|Emissions from gas increased, but remain far below coal. Emissions from oil products, such as petrol and diesel, increased more slowly than gas and coal.]]

Burning [[coal in Turkey]] was the largest emitter in 2024, followed by [[Oil in Turkey|oil]] then [[Gas in Turkey|gas]].<ref name="2026report" />{{Reference page|page=52}} That year, Turkey's energy sector emitted over 70% of the country's GHG,<ref name=":46" /> mostly through electricity generation,<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s1 Cell G31}} followed by road transport.{{efn|1=Under IPCC guidelines, the energy sector includes fuel for transport.}}<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cell G20}} In contrast agriculture contributed 13% of emissions and industrial processes and product use (IPPU) also 13%.<ref name=":46" /> [[Carbon capture and storage]] is not economically viable.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Esmaeili |first1=Danial |date=June 2018 |title=Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage in the Context of Turkish Energy Market |publisher=[[Sabancı University]] |url=http://research.sabanciuniv.edu/36807/1/1806_IICECE%26CPaperCCUSinTurkey_0.pdf |page=15 |quote=Having an emissions trading market is critical for a successful implementation of the carbon capturing technology in Turkey. |access-date=14 May 2019 |archive-date=14 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514155754/http://research.sabanciuniv.edu/36807/1/1806_IICECE%26CPaperCCUSinTurkey_0.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The GHG [[emission intensity]] of energy consumption is higher than in the EU.<ref>{{Cite web |title=European Innovation Scoreboard 2022 |url=https://ec.europa.eu/assets/rtd/eis/2022/ec_rtd_eis-country-profile-tr.pdf |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251112164850/https://ec.europa.eu/assets/rtd/eis/2022/ec_rtd_eis-country-profile-tr.pdf |archive-date=12 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Turkey expects to greatly increase gas production.<ref>{{cite web|last=O'Byrne|first=David|date=21 April 2021|title=Turkey to begin field tests at Sakarya gas find next month: minister|url=https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/natural-gas/042121-turkey-to-begin-field-tests-at-sakarya-gas-find-next-month-minister|access-date=15 May 2021|website=[[S&P Global Platts]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515110955/https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/natural-gas/042121-turkey-to-begin-field-tests-at-sakarya-gas-find-next-month-minister|archive-date=15 May 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2021, IEA head [[Fatih Birol]] called for fossil-fuel producing countries to include limits on [[methane leaks]] in their climate pledges,<ref>{{cite web|title=IEA calls on companies, governments and regulators to take urgent action to cut methane emissions from oil and gas sector|url=https://www.iea.org/news/iea-calls-on-companies-governments-and-regulators-to-take-urgent-action-to-cut-methane-emissions-from-oil-and-gas-sector|access-date=15 May 2021|website=[[International Energy Agency|IEA]]|date=18 January 2021 }}</ref> but {{As of|2026|lc=y}} Turkey has not signed the [[Global Methane Pledge|global methane pledge]].<ref name=":31" />

Production of public heat and electricity emitted 150 [[Tonne#Symbol and abbreviations|megatonnes]] of {{CO2}}e in 2024,<ref name="2026table" />{{Rp|table 1 cell B10}} mainly through coal burning.{{efn|The carbon content ([[tonne|t]]/[[Terajoule|TJ]]), oxidation factor and CO<sub>2</sub> [[emission intensity]] (t/TJ [[Heat of combustion#Lower heating value|NCV]]), respectively, of lignite burnt in Turkish power stations in 2021 was as follows:<ref name=2021report/>{{Rp|50 & 51, table 3.5, 3.6, 3.7}}
* [[lignite]]: 30, 0.97, 104

The extremely low-quality lignite is explained in detail in [[Coal in Turkey]]. The {{CO2}} emission intensity (or emission factor) shown above is the mass of {{CO2}} emitted for each unit of heat produced by burning a fuel. In contrast, the grid emission intensity is the mass of {{CO2}}e produced per unit of electricity supplied to the [[electrical grid]]. Because [[thermal power station]]s generally convert less than half of the heat energy into electrical energy,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zhang|first=Tongjun|date=2020|title=Methods of Improving the Efficiency of Thermal Power Plants|journal=J. Phys.: Conf. Ser.|language=en|volume=1449|issue=1|article-number=012001|doi=10.1088/1742-6596/1449/1/012001|bibcode=2020JPhCS1449a2001Z|doi-access=free}}</ref> their numbers for grid emission intensity are much greater than the emission intensity figures shown above.}} Investment in wind and [[Solar power in Turkey|solar]] is hampered by subsidies for coal.<ref>{{Cite report

{{anchor|Fuel to heat buildings and cook}}

Subsidised coal burnt by poor families contributes a bit to climate change, and more importantly its [[soot]] [[air pollution in Turkey|pollutes local air]]. Residential fuel, such as natural gas and coal, contributed 51&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s4 G37}} Burning [[fossil fuels]] such as coal and natural gas for commercial and institutional buildings, such as for heating, emitted 13&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s4 Cell G17}} According to the [[Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources (Turkey)|Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources]], "The energy sector, which is an emission-intensive and resource-intensive sector, will be one of the sectors that will be most affected by the regulations brought or to be brought by [the Paris and UNFCCC] agreements. In this context, our country is determined to use its energy resources effectively, efficiently and with the least impact on the environment, within the framework of sustainable development goals.".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Change and International Negotiation |url=https://enerji.gov.tr/infobank-climate-change-and-international |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=[[Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714212811/https://enerji.gov.tr/infobank-climate-change-and-international |archive-date=14 July 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{efn|The goals they are referring to may be [[Sustainable Development Goal 7]] and [[Sustainable Development Goal 13]]}}

===== <span class="anchor" id="Coal fired power stations"></span>Coal-fired power stations =====
[[File:Yatağan Termik Santrali.jpg|thumb|Some old power stations like [[Yatağan power station|Yatağan]] pollute but are subsidised.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey's electricity supply security and Akbelen |url=https://www.birgun.net/haber/turkeys-electricity-supply-security-and-akbelen-734155 |access-date=2026-10-07 |website=birgun.net |language=Turkish |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260911195835/http://www.birgun.net/haber/turkeys-electricity-supply-security-and-akbelen-734155 |archive-date=11 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>|alt=white smoke rises into a blue sky from 3 large chimneys]]
[[List of coal fired power stations in Turkey|Turkey's coal-fired power stations]] are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions by Turkey, at 123 Mt (over 20% of national emissions) in 2024.<ref name="2026table">{{cite tech report 
 |work=[[Turkish Statistical Institute]]
 |title=Türkiye. 2026 Common Reporting Table (CRT)
 |date=14 April 2026
 |url=https://unfccc.int/documents/656426
 |format=TUR-CRT-2026-V1.0-2024
 }}</ref>{{Rp|table 1.A(a)s1 cell G26 "solid fuels"}} Over a kilogram of {{CO2}} is emitted for every [[Kilowatt-hour|KWh]] of electricity generated in Turkey by coal-fired power stations.<ref name="AtAz">{{cite journal |last1=Atilgan |first1=Burcin |last2=Azapagic |first2=Adisa |date=2016 |title=An integrated life cycle sustainability assessment of electricity generation in Turkey |journal=Energy Policy |volume=93 |pages=168–186 |bibcode=2016EnPol..93..168A |doi=10.1016/j.enpol.2016.02.055 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{Rp|177}} 

Almost all coal burnt in power stations is local [[lignite]] or imported [[Bituminous coal|bituminous (hard) coal]]. [[Coal analysis]] of Turkish lignite shows that it is high in ash and moisture, low in [[energy value of coal|energy value]] and high in [[emission intensity]];<ref name=":38" /> that is Turkish lignite emits more {{CO2}} than other countries' lignites.<ref name=":38">{{Cite web|url=https://www.powerengineeringint.com/coal-fired/cfb-in-turkey-the-right-timing-for-the-right-technology/|title=CFB in Turkey: The right timing for the right technology|website=www.powerengineeringint.com|date=December 2017|access-date=8 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801065509/https://www.powerengineeringint.com/coal-fired/cfb-in-turkey-the-right-timing-for-the-right-technology/|archive-date=1 August 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> When carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) from coal used by industry and for heating buildings, and [[methane emissions]] from [[coal mining]], are added to those from coal-fired electricity generation, over 30% of Turkey's annual emissions come from coal. In 2024, burning coal emitted 159&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}} in total.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s1 Cell G12}} Methane leaks from coal mines in 2024 were equivalent to 7&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 1 Cell I39}} [[Eren Holding]] (via Eren Enerji's coal-fired [[ZETES power stations]]) emits over 2% of Turkey's GHG, and [[İÇDAŞ]] emits over 1% from its Bekirli coal-fired power stations.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pearce|first1=Rosamund|last2=Evans|first2=Simon|title=Global coal power map|url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/mapped-worlds-coal-power-plants|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190205154748/https://www.carbonbrief.org/mapped-worlds-coal-power-plants|archive-date=5 February 2019|access-date=14 May 2020|website=[[Carbon Brief]]}}</ref> Emissions of [[black carbon]] are not published for individual power stations,<ref name=":21">{{Cite report|title=Cobenefits Policy Report: Unlocking the co-benefits of decarbonising Turkey's power sector|url=https://www.cobenefits.info/country-studies-infographics/studies/turkey/|date=December 2020|publisher=International Climate Initiative: IASS IPC/UfU|editor1-last=Akyazı|editor1-first=Pınar Ertör|editor2-last=Sperfeld|editor2-first=Franziska|editor3-last=Helgenberger|editor3-first=Sebastian|editor4-last=Şahin|editor4-first=Ümit|editor5-last=Nagel|editor5-first=Laura|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251201064032/https://www.cobenefits.info/country-studies-infographics/studies/turkey/|archive-date=1
