===== <span class="anchor" id="Gas fired power stations"></span>Gas-fired power stations =====

[[List of power stations in Turkey#Natural Gas|Gas-fired power stations]] emitted 27&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Rp|table 1.A(a)s1 cell G27}} Electricity generation from gas tends to increase when hydropower is limited by droughts.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Turkey's power output from gas up 21 pct due to drought – Latest News|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkeys-power-output-from-gas-up-21-pct-due-to-drought-162258|access-date=6 September 2021|website=Hürriyet Daily News|date=8 February 2021|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211204012327/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkeys-power-output-from-gas-up-21-pct-due-to-drought-162258|archive-date=4 December 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> The cost of natural gas is expected to fall in the late 2020s with the expiry of expensive import agreements with Russia and Iran, and increasing production from the [[Sakarya Gas Field]] in the [[Black Sea]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sellars |first=William |date=2025-01-03 |title=Turkey hopes to offer Russia a gas route into Europe |url=https://www.agbi.com/oil-and-gas/2025/01/turkey-hopes-to-offer-russia-gas-route-into-europe/ |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=AGBI |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251119074152/https://www.agbi.com/oil-and-gas/2025/01/turkey-hopes-to-offer-russia-gas-route-into-europe/ |archive-date=19 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-01 |title=Strength in LNG? The gas market in Turkey |url=https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2024-10-01/strength-lng-gas-market-turkey |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=OSW Centre for Eastern Studies |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260417053510/https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2024-10-01/strength-lng-gas-market-turkey |archive-date=17 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===== Transport =====
[[File:Traffic jam in Istanbul's road.JPG|thumb|alt=Photograph of two lanes of cars, buses and taxis at a standstill in a traffic jame|A traffic jam in [[Istanbul]], one of the few major European cities without a [[low-emission zone]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Urban Access Regulations in Europe|url=https://urbanaccessregulations.eu/|url-status=live|access-date=14 March 2021|website=Urban Vehicle Access Regulations & Low Emission Zones|archive-date=10 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310071240/https://urbanaccessregulations.eu/}}</ref>]]

Transport emitted 101&nbsp;Mt of {{CO2}}e in 2024, a bit over one tonne per person, over 90% from [[Road transport in Turkey|road transport in the country]] (and agricultural vehicles).<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cells G10/21}} Over half of Turkey's transport emissions come from [[diesel fuel]] burnt in road vehicles, but the proportion from cars compared to other vehicles such as lorries is not known.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=Table1.A(a)s3 Col G}} The train network is underused and, unlike some other countries, {{As of|2026|lc=y}} Turkey has no binding transport specific targets.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 March 2026 |title=Türkiye's Net Zero Emission Target: Road Map for Transport |url=https://emisyonsuzulasim.uab.gov.tr/api/reports/Best-Practices-and-Benchmarking-Report.pdf}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=21}} Fuel quality and emissions standards for new cars are less strict than those in the EU.<ref name="EC2020">{{Cite report |url=https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/sites/near/files/turkey_report_2020.pdf |title=Turkey 2020 Report (see chapters: 15 Energy, 27 Environment and Climate change) |publisher=[[European Commission]] |year=2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201103090805/https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/sites/near/files/turkey_report_2020.pdf |archive-date=3 November 2020 |access-date=28 February 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|102}} Domestic flights{{efn|1=Emissions from international trips are not included in a country's emissions total, but fuel sales for international aviation can be found in Common Reporting Format category 1.A.3.a.1A. Turkey has joined the [[Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation]].}} emitted 4&nbsp;Mt of {{CO2}}e in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=|location=Table1.A(a)s3 Cell G18}}

==== Industry ====

2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Some sugar factories, such as some owned by Türkşeker<ref>{{cite news|date=3 July 2018|title=45.000 ton kömür alacak|language=tr|trans-title=They will buy 45,000 tonnes [[Process heat|heat needed to make]] sugar and sometimes to generate electricity.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Algedik|first1=Önder|title=Coal & Climate Change – |archive-date=18 July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=5}}

===== Cement =====
Turkey is the sixth-largest [[cement]] producer in the world and the largest in Europe,<ref name=":42">{{cite web |date=21 December 2020 |title=Turkey cement exports reach US$1bn in 2020 |url=https://www.cemnet.com/News/story/170047/turkey-cement-exports-reach-us-1bn-in-2020.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222000537/https://www.cemnet.com/News/story/170047/turkey-cement-exports-reach-us-1bn-in-2020.html |archive-date=22 December 2020 |access-date=16 March 2021 |website=International Cement Review}}</ref> and by far the largest exporter to the EU.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=EU Cement Industry Trade Statistics |url=https://cembureau.eu/media/5irpnycs/cembureau-trade-report-first-6-months-2024.pdf |access-date=2025-01-13 |publisher=Cembureau, The European Cement Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251116161308/https://www.cembureau.eu/media/5irpnycs/cembureau-trade-report-first-6-months-2024.pdf |archive-date=16 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Cement (clinker) production in 2024 emitted 45&nbsp;Mt {{CO2}},<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 2(I) Cell N12}} 8% of the country's total GHG. [[Climate TRACE|Climate Trace]] has estimated the contributions of individual factories, sometimes from kiln heat visible from satellites,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cement |website=[[GitHub]] |url=https://github.com/climatetracecoalition/methodology-documents/blob/main/Manufacturing/Manufacturing%20sector-%20Cement%20Methodology.pdf |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415124204/https://github.com/climatetracecoalition/methodology-documents/blob/main/Manufacturing/Manufacturing%20sector-%20Cement%20Methodology.pdf |archive-date=15 April 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> and says that Nuh, Göltaş, and  [[Eren Holding|Medcem cement plants]] emitted more than 1 Mt each in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Explore map - Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/explore/#admin=Turkey%20(TUR):247:TUR:country&gas=co2e&year=2023&timeframe=100&sector=manufacturing,cement&asset=3165683 |access-date=2024-11-25 |website=[[Climate trace]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126002146/https://climatetrace.org/explore/#admin=Turkey%20(TUR):247:TUR:country&gas=co2e&year=2023&timeframe=100&sector=manufacturing,cement&asset=3165683 |archive-date=26 November 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Nuh publish information about their emissions and say some of their cement is low emission,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our Carbon Footprint |url=https://www.nuhcimento.com.tr/en/our-carbon-footprint/ |access-date=2024-11-25 |website=Nuh Çimento |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260306114113/https://www.nuhcimento.com.tr/en/our-carbon-footprint/ |archive-date=6 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> and Medcem publishes some figures<ref>{{Cite web |title=2023 Sustainability Report |url=https://medcem.com.tr/uploads/Medcem-SR-EN.pdf |page=39}}</ref> whereas Göltaş has less GHG info.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Göltaş Çimento A.Ş. |url=https://www.goltas.com.tr/en/surdurulebilirlik/cevreci-yaklasim/ |access-date=2024-11-25 |website=www.goltas.com.tr |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251110135414/https://www.goltas.com.tr/en/surdurulebilirlik/cevreci-yaklasim/ |archive-date=10 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> {{As of|2026}} most producers report about 0.8 tonnes CO2eq per tonne cement.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-14 |title=CBAM uncertainty stalls Turkish cement pricing {{!}} Latest Market News |url=https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2775803-cbam-uncertainty-stalls-turkish-cement-pricing |access-date=2026-01-21 |website=www.argusmedia.com |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260127185317/https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2775803-cbam-uncertainty-stalls-turkish-cement-pricing |archive-date=27 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Turkish construction and contracting industry|Turkey's construction sector]] uses cement. Cement producers in the EU have to buy [[EU Allowance|EU carbon credits]], and say the CBAM is needed to protect them from unfair competition, as Turkish companies pay no carbon price as of 2026. The CBAM could be up to 50% on the cement price.<ref>{{Cite report|date=12 August 2021|title=Turkey could face over $900 million in CBAM-related export costs: Report|url=https://ihsmarkit.com/research-analysis/turkey-could-face-over-900-million-in-cbamrelated-export-costs.html|website=[[IHS Markit]]}}</ref> The proportion of clinker in publicly procured cement is being reduced.<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.2.1}}

===== Iron, steel and aluminium =====
Turkish steel, primarily from [[minimill]]s, averages about one tonne of {{CO2}} per tonne of steel produced.<ref name=":40">{{cite web|title=How an EU Carbon Border Tax Could Jolt World Trade|url=https://www.bcg.com/en-tr/publications/2020/how-an-eu-carbon-border-tax-could-jolt-world-trade.aspx|access-date=15 July 2020|website=[[Boston Consulting Group]]|archive-date=15 July average is less polluting than China,<ref name=":40" /> three steelworks—[[Erdemir]], [[İsdemir]] and [[Kardemir]]—use [[blast furnaces]] and thus emit more than those using [[electric arc furnace]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ricardo |date=2026-02-11 |title=Hasan Akbulut: Türkiye's steel industry has a competitive advantage with its low emission production structure - EUROMETAL |archive-date=25 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> The EU [[Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism]] (CBAM) includes a carbon tariff on Turkish steel produced in blast furnaces,<ref>{{Cite Emissions|journal=Celal Bayar University Journal of Science|volume=17|issue=1|pages=17–29|doi=10.18466/cbayarfbe.823265|doi-access=free}}</ref> but the CBAM could help arc furnaces compete against products such as Chinese steel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/SHURA_Agora_Border_Carbon_Adjustment_Turkey_EU.pdf|title=The European Green Deal's Border Carbon investing in [[solar power in Turkey]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=INFOGRAPHIC: Turkish steel sector lowers energy costs, carbon footprint with massive solar investments |url=https://www.spglobal.com/commodity-insights/en/news-research/latest-news/metals/082025-turkish-steel-sector-lowers-energy-costs-carbon-footprint-with-massive-solar-investments |access-date=22 |archive-date=22 August 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Aluminium is carbon-intensive at almost 9 tCO₂e per tonne.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-07 |title=The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Considerations for Türkiye - SHURA |url=https://shura.org.tr/en/the-eus-carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism-considerations-for-turkiye/ |access-date=2026-09-02 |language=en-US ==== Agriculture and fishing ====

[[File:Jersey cattle in Sisdağı 04.jpg|thumb|alt=brown Jersey cow wearing a fancy halter in a green field|Around half of agricultural emissions are from cows.]]

Agriculture accounted for 74&nbsp;Mt which was 13% of Turkey's total 2024 GHG, including 62% of its methane emissions and 78% of its [[nitrous oxide]] emissions.<ref name=":46" /> These are due primarily to [[enteric fermentation]], [[Agricultural soil science|agricultural soils]], and [[fertilizer|synthetic fertilizer]] application.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate TRACE |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=Climate TRACE |language=en}}</ref> Cattle emit about half of the GHG from agriculture, made up in 2024 of 30 Mt from enteric fermentation<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cell I12}} and 7 Mt from manure management.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|location=Table 3 Cell I20}}

About three quarters of red meat production in Turkey is beef.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Red Meat sector|url=http://www.turkishanimalpro.org/en-US/uyeler-sektorler/et-urunleri/23|access-date=1 October 2021|website=Turkish Animal Pro|language=}}</ref> Turks eat an average of {{convert|15|kg}} of [[beef]] per person each year (which is more than the world average<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Beef Consumption Per Capita (Ranking of Countries) |url=https://beef2live.com/story-world-beef-consumption-per-capita-ranking-countries-0-111634 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160114181559/http://beef2live.com/story-world-beef-consumption-per-capita-ranking-countries-0-111634 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=14 January 2016 |access-date=2022-05-01 |website=beef2live.com |language=en}}</ref>), and the country produced 1 million tonnes of beef in 2021.<ref name=":3">{{Cite report|date=7 April 2022|title=Turkey Livestock and Products Semiannual|url=https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/turkey-livestock-and-products-semi-annual|website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250228060335/https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/turkey-livestock-and-products-semi-annual|archive-date=28 February 2025|access-date=22 January 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> Cattle are subsidized by the "Rural Prosperity, Livestock Support Project" until 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Livestock and Products Annual Türkiye |url=https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=Livestock+and+Products+Annual_Ankara_Turkiye_TU2025-0044.pdf |access-date=28 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260205015228/https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=Livestock+and+Products+Annual_Ankara_Turkiye_TU2025-0044.pdf |archive-date=5 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> VAT on meat and dairy is 1% like other "staple foods". Being [[ruminant]]s sheep, goats and cattle belch methane. Fertilizers can emit the GHG nitrous oxide, but estimates of the effects of government policy on the agricultural and waste sectors' emissions are lacking.<ref name=":25">{{cite tech report |url=https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/idr7_TUR.pdf |title=Report on the technical review of the seventh national communication of Turkey |date=17 June 2019 |work=[[UNFCCC]] |id=FCCC/IDR.7/TUR}}</ref>{{Rp|28}} Turkey is one of the top ten nitrous oxide emitters.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.leeds.ac.uk/news-environment/news/article/5592/study-warns-of-alarming-rise-in-long-lived-greenhouse-gas | title=Study warns of 'alarming rise' in long-lived greenhouse gas | date=13 2025 | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Plastic pollution#Plastic pollution as a cause of climate change|Production of plastic]], such as for agriculture, may release significant GHG in future.<ref>{{Cite GHG inventories do not yet include [[bottom trawling]], such as in parts of the [[Black Sea]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yildiz |first1=Taner |last2=Cömert |first2=Nurdan |last3=Ferrà |first3=Carmen add "huge" fish trawling emissions to national inventories|url=https://www.climatechangenews.com/2021/03/17/scientists-push-add-huge-fish-trawling-emissions-national-inventories/|access-date=27 May 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2024 the government said that farming subsidies would be "reviewed through the lens of climate change".<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.6.1}}

==== Waste ====
Municipalities collect about 1&nbsp;kg of waste per person per day.<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.5}} The government says the waste sector contributed 15&nbsp;Mt (3%) of Turkey's 2024 GHG,<ref name=":46" /> with almost half of that from the tenth of waste sent to unmanaged [[landfill]]s.<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.5}} However Climate Trace estimates CO2e from solid waste disposal at 68 Mt in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Country/Territory Inventory |url=https://climatetrace.org/inventory?sector=waste&region=Türkiye+%28TUR%29%3A247%3ATUR%3Acountry&timeframe=100 |access-date= |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en}}</ref> Senem Abak at [[Boğaziçi University]] has suggested possible reasons for this large discrepancy; perhaps the differences in methodology, or official figures could be missing some open burning.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Abak |first=Senem |title=Comparison of the national-contributed emissions with the climate trace's global emissions inventory |date=2025-01-01 |degree=Thesis |publisher=Boğaziçi University |url=https://thesis.rawdatalibrary.net/thesis/comparison-national-contributed-emissions-climate-trace-s-global-emissions |language=en}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Section 4.5}}

Satellite methane measurements in 2025 and 2026 highlight [[landfill]] sites serving Istanbul (such as one in [[Seymen, Silivri]]) and [[İzmir|Izmir]] as large emitters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spotlight on the Top 25 Methane Plumes in 2025: Landfills {{!}} UCLA Law |url=https://law.ucla.edu/news/spotlight-top-25-methane-plumes-2025-landfills |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=law.ucla.edu |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260930200022/https://law.ucla.edu/news/spotlight-top-25-methane-plumes-2025-landfills |archive-date=30 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Completely phasing out the little remaining open dumping is important, and in 2026 an academic claimed that MSW could become a carbon sink by 2035 by recovering materials and energy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maçin |first1=Kadriye Elif |title=Decarbonizing municipal solid waste management in Türkiye: A scenario-based life cycle assessment from historical baseline to 2035 recovery targets |journal=Environmental Pollution and Management |date=2026 |volume=3 |page=328 |doi=10.1016/j.epm.2026.06.003 |bibcode=2026EnvPM...3..328M |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2950305126000239|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Landfilling is the most common waste-disposal method.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Yaman |first1=Cevat |title=Investigation of greenhouse gas emissions and energy recovery potential from municipal solid waste management practices |journal=[[Environmental Development]] |date=March 2020 |volume=33 |article-number=100484 |doi=10.1016/j.envdev.2019.100484 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020EnvDe..3300484Y }}</ref> Climate Trace estimate [[Istanbul Waste Power Plant|Odayeri]] (even though it has a [[biogas]] facility<ref>{{Cite web |title=Odayeri Çöp Gazı Santrali - Biyogaz |url=https://www.enerjiatlasi.com/biyogaz/odayeri-cop-gazi-santrali.html |access-date=2022-11-12 |website=Enerji Atlası |language=tr-TR |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260121134424/https://www.enerjiatlasi.com/biyogaz/odayeri-cop-gazi-santrali.html |archive-date=21 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>) on the European side of Istanbul to have been by far the biggest single emitter of methane from waste in 2025 with 3.6 Mt CO2e.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Odayeri |url=https://climatetrace.org/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=[[Climate TRACE]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260122113914/https://climatetrace.org/ |archive-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Organic waste sent to landfills emits methane, but the country is working to improve [[Waste management in Turkey|its waste and resource management]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lo |first=Joe |date=2026-02-13 |title=Turkiye prioritises cleaning up garbage emissions for COP31 |url=https://www.climatechangenews.com/2026/02/13/turkiye-prioritises-cleaning-up-garbage-emissions-in-cop31-action-agenda/ |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=Climate Home News |language=en-GB}}</ref> One third of organic waste is [[compost]]ed,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=İkizoğlu|first1=Bahar|last2=Koçak|first2=Emel|date=15 December 2020|title=Types of waste in the context of waste management and general overview of waste disposal in Turkey|journal=International Journal of Agriculture Environment and Food Sciences|language=en|volume=4|issue=4|pages=520–527|doi=10.31015/jaefs.2020.4.17|doi-access=free}}</ref> but others argue for [[incineration]].<ref name=":1" /> Some refrigerants are sent to Turkey from other countries for destruction.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2023 |title=Workshop on Kigali Implementation Plans |url=https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2023-07/KIP2023-Session%208.pdf |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260117164902/https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2023-07/KIP2023-Session%208.pdf |archive-date=17 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Climate ==
{{Excerpt|Climate of Turkey}}

==Impacts on the natural environment==
According to [[Boğaziçi University]]'s Center for Climate Change and Policy Studies, human-caused climate change in Turkey started in the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite news|date=9 October 2020|title=Turkey in the midst of climate change, says climate expert|newspaper=[[Hürriyet Daily News]]|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-in-the-midst-of-climate-change-says-climate-expert-158990|access-date=2020-11-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124023116/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-in-the-midst-of-climate-change-says-climate-expert-158990|archive-date=24 January 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Turkey is forecast to be more severely affected than many other countries,<ref name="TPQ">{{cite web|title=Warming a Frozen Policy: Challenges to Turkey's Climate Politics After Paris|work=Turkish Policy Quarterly|url=http://turkishpolicy.com/article/818/warming-a-frozen-policy-challenges-to-turkeys-climate-politics-after-paris|access-date=25 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903060552/http://turkishpolicy.com/article/818/warming-a-frozen-policy-challenges-to-turkeys-climate-politics-after-paris|archive-date=3 September 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="3rd BR">{{cite report
 |work=[[Ministry of Environment and Urban Planning (Turkey)|Ministry of Environment and Urban Planning]]
 |title=Seventh National Communication of Turkey under the UNFCCC
 |version=V. 2
 |date=August 2019
 |url=https://www.tr.undp.org/content/turkey/en/home/library/environment_energy/NC7-2019.html
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501221745/https://www.tr.undp.org/content/turkey/en/home/library/environment_energy/NC7-2019.html
 |archive-date=1 May 2021
 |access-date=28 November 2020
 |url-status=dead 
 }}</ref> but effects vary considerably across its regions.<ref name="TemaWWF" /> [[Coupled Model Intercomparison Project#CMIP Phase 6]] (CMIP6) models it well,<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2021-07-01 |title=Intercomparison of the expected change in the temperature and the precipitation retrieved from CMIP6 and CMIP5 climate projections: A Mediterranean hot spot case, Turkey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169809521001289 |journal=Atmospheric Research |language=en |volume=256 |article-number=105576 |doi=10.1016/j.atmosres.2021.105576 |issn=0169-8095 |last1=Bağçaci |first1=S. One example of climate change's impact will be on the distribution of rainfall: the expansion of the [[Hadley cell]] (an area of circulation near the equator) may move the descending edge northwards towards Turkey, whose southern border is around 36 degrees north, and this may reduce rainfall.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Daher |first1=Houraa |last2=Kirtman |first2=Ben P. |date=2025-11-07 |title=Future climate assessment in the Mediterranean region using downscaled CMIP6 data |journal=Frontiers in Climate |language=English |publisher=Frontiers |volume=7 |article-number=1691944 |doi=10.3389/fclim.2025.1691944 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2025FrCli...791944D |issn=2624-9553}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boza |first1=Burcu |last2=Ezber |first2=Yasemin |last3=Sen |first3=Omer Lutfi |title=A Seesaw of Anatolian Winter Precipitation from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Future |url=https://essopenarchive.org/doi/full/10.22541/essoar.15001810/v1 |journal=ESS Open Archive |volume=2026 |issue=409 |doi=10.22541/essoar.15001810/v1|hdl=11527/81071 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

hottest year (since international standard measurements began in 1971) was 2024, followed by 2010, 2018, 2023 and 2025.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=2025-01-15 |title=Türkiye records hottest year in More floods are predicted, due to rainfall replacing snow.<ref name="HDN">{{cite news |title=Temperature to increase significantly in Turkey in 30 years due to global warming, warns climate expert |url=http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/temperature-to-increase-significantly-in-turkey-in-30-years-due-to-global-warming-warns-climate-expert-128980 |work=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |date=19 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919221619/http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/temperature-to-increase-significantly-in-turkey-in-30-years-due-to-global-warming-warns-climate-expert-128980 |archive-date=19 September 2019 |access-date=18 September 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> Total precipitation did not change much in the 35 years before 2025,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=i̇Slam |first1=Yașa |last2=Turgay |first2=Partal |title=Türkiye's climate change: rising temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns |journal=Theoretical and Applied Climatology |date=2025 |volume=156 |issue=12 |page=685 |doi=10.1007/s00704-025-05938-6 |bibcode=2025ThApC.156..685I |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ThApC.156..685I/abstract}}</ref>  but may decrease and become more variable.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MGM |title=Türkiye İçin İklim Projeksiyonları - Meteoroloji Genel Müdürlüğü |url=https://mgm.gov.tr/iklim/iklim-degisikligi.aspx?s=projeksiyonlar |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260610061313/https://mgm.gov.tr/iklim/iklim-degisikligi.aspx?s=projeksiyonlar |archive-date=10 June 2026 |access-date=2026-08-30 |website=www.mgm.gov.tr |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Water===

[[File:Mount Ararat from Armash (3).jpg|thumb|[[Mount Ararat#Summit ice cap|Mount Ararat's glacier]] is [[Retreat of glaciers since 1850|retreating]] due to climate change,<ref name="Baldasso1" /> and will be gone before the end of the century.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Azzoni|first1=Roberto Sergio|last2=Sarıkaya|first2=Mehmet Akif|last3=Fugazza|first3=Davide|date=2020-04-01|title=Turkish glacier inventory and classification from high-resolution satellite data|journal=Mediterranean Geoscience Reviews|volume=2|issue=1|pages=153–162|doi=10.1007/s42990-020-00029-2|bibcode=2020MGRv....2..153A |issn=2661-8648|hdl=2434/745029|s2cid=216608789|hdl-access=free}}</ref>|alt=not very sharp snow-capped mountain peak in the distance, under a blue sky with a few small clouds]]
[[File:Turkey_river_basins.svg|thumb|River basins of Turkey also showing where they extend into neighbouring countries]]
Climate change has reduced rainfall in some regions and has made it less regular,  which has put stress on [[Hydroelectricity in Turkey|hydroelectric power plants]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Bulut |first1=U |last2=Sakalli |first2=A |date=2021 |title=Impacts of climate change and distribution of precipitation on hydroelectric power generation in Turkey |doi=10.1088/1757-899X/1032/1/012043|journal=IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering|volume=1032|issue=1 |bibcode=2021MS&E.1032a2043B |s2cid=234299802 |at=Article 012043|doi-access=free }}</ref> Between 1979 and 2019 annual precipitation fluctuated from over 60&nbsp;cm to under 45&nbsp;cm,<ref name=":6" /> and average annual temperatures varied by 4 degrees.<ref name=":6" /> Dams are collecting less drinking water due to reduced pricipitation due to climate change.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Demirbaş |first1=Furkan |last2=Özbaş |first2=Emine Elmaslar |last3=Can Sarıkap |first3=Mehmet |last4=Nur Ciner |first4=Mirac |last5=Yurtseven |first5=Hüseyin |last6=Özcan |first6=Hüseyin Kurtuluş |date=2026-03-12 |title=Modelling the Impact of Climate Change on the Reservoir Filling Rates of Dams Used for Drinking Water Supply Through Artificial Neural Networks |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-026-04527-0 |journal=Water Resources Management |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=187 |doi=10.1007/s11269-026-04527-0 |bibcode=2026WatRM..40..187D |issn=1573-1650|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Turkey is already a [[water stress]]ed country, because the amount of water per person is only about {{convert|1,500|m3}} a year: and due to [[Turkey#Demographics|population increase]] and climate change it is highly likely the country will suffer [[water scarcity]] (less than 1,000 m³) by the 2070s.<ref name=":13" /> Higher temperatures can increase evaporation from lakes, making them more saline.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ClimateChangePost |title=Fresh water resources |url=https://www.climatechangepost.com/countries/turkey/fresh-water-resources/ |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=www.climatechangepost.com |language=en-us |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250905214459/https://www.climatechangepost.com/countries/turkey/fresh-water-resources/ |archive-date=5 September 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Little change has been forecast for water resources in the northern [[Drainage basin|river basins]], but a substantial reduction has been forecast for the southern river basins.<ref name=":13" /> [[Konya]] in central Turkey is also vulnerable.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gedik |first=Furkan |date=2021 |title=Meteorological Drought Analysis in Konya Closed Basin |url=https://iupress.istanbul.edu.tr/en/journal/jgeography/article/konya-kapali-havzasinda-meteorolojik-kuraklik-analizi |journal=Journal of Geography |issue=42 |pages=295–308 |doi=10.26650/JGEOG2021-885519 |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.12428/3876 |hdl-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231212160919/https://iupress.istanbul.edu.tr/en/journal/jgeography/article/konya-kapali-havzasinda-meteorolojik-kuraklik-analizi |archive-date=12 December 2023 |access-date=21 March 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> Charging for water used by agriculture has been suggested.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.suverimliligi.gov.tr/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/su-vermliligi-eylem-plani-en.pdf|title=Water Efficiency Strategy Document and Action Plan in the Framework of Adaptation to the Changing Climate (2023 – 2033)}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=64–66}}

Over 200 thousand people live in areas at risk if [[sea level rise]]s by 1 meter.<ref name=":6b">{{Cite web|title=Potential Impacts of Sea Level Rise on the Coasts of Turkey|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/327151922.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501150532/https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/327151922.pdf |archive-date=2021-05-01 }}</ref> The [[Aegean Sea|Aegean]] rose by an estimated 4&nbsp;mm a year in the early 21st century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Calafat |first1=F. M. |last2=Frederikse |first2=T. |last3=Horsburgh |first3=K. |date=September 2022 |title=The Sources of Sea-Level Changes in the Mediterranean Sea Since 1960 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans |language=en |volume=127 |issue=9 |article-number=e2022JC019061 |doi=10.1029/2022JC019061 |issn=2169-9275|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022JGRC..12719061C }}</ref> [[Istanbul]] is at risk from [[sea level rise]];<ref name="Website-4">{{Cite web|title=Coastal floods in Turkey|url=https://www.climatechangepost.com/turkey/coastal-floods/|access-date=2021-02-11|website=Climatechangepost.com|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170416164144/http://www.climatechangepost.com/turkey/coastal-floods/|archive-date=16 April 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> for example, [[Kadıköy (Istanbul Metro)|Kadıkoy metro station]] is threatened with flooding.<ref name="HDN" /> [[Tectonic uplift]] has decreased sea level rise between [[Samsun]] and [[Alanya]], whereas several large river deltas have subsided.<ref name="Website-4" />

===Ecosystems===
In coastal areas permanent wetlands, croplands and grassland are affected.<ref name=":6" /> Climate models predict that extreme weather events will increase in the [[Mediterranean region, Turkey|Mediterranean Region]].<ref name="3rd BR" />{{Rp|151}} [[List of glaciers in Turkey|Glaciers in Turkey]] are retreating:<ref name="Baldasso1">{{cite journal |last1=Baldasso |first1=V. the largest remaining are the [[glaciers]] on [[Mount Ararat]] and these are forecast to be gone before the end of the century,<ref>{{Cite journal|title= A GIS-Based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis Model for Determining Glacier Vulnerability|year=2020|doi=10.3390/ijgi9030180|doi-access=free|last1=Yalcin|first1=Mustafa|journal=ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information|volume=9|issue=3|page=180|bibcode=2020IJGI....9..180Y}}</ref> as they are melting much faster than mountain glaciers in many other parts of the world.<ref name=":7" /> The [[Mount Cilo|Cilo]] glaciers are also shrinking.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Azzoni |first1=Roberto Sergio |last2=Bollati |first2=Irene Maria |last3=Pelfini |first3=Manuela |last4=Sarıkaya |first4=Mehmet Akif Because the climate in the south is forecast to become hotter and drier it may be very difficult to keep the current southern [[Forest in Turkey|forests in Turkey]].<ref name=":13" /> In the [[Marmara ==Impacts on people==

=== Health impacts ===
Climate change may impact [[health in Turkey]], for example due to increased [[heatwaves]],<ref name="Website-2">{{Cite web |date=2025-11-03 |title=Türkiye to identify climate-linked diseases under health action plan - Türkiye News |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiye-to-identify-climate-linked-diseases-under-health-action-plan-215299 |access-date=2026-10-26 |website=Hürriyet Daily News |language=en}}</ref> especially elderly and chronically ill people and children.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Bayram|first1=Hasan|chapter=Global Climate Change, Desertification, and Its Consequences in Turkey and the Middle East|date=2021|title=Climate Change and Global Public Health|pages=445–458|editor-last=Pinkerton|editor-first=Kent E.|series=Respiratory Medicine|place=Cham|publisher=Springer International Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-54746-2_21|isbn=978-3-030-54746-2 |last2=Öztürk|first2=Ayşe Bilge|editor2-last=Rom|editor2-first=William N.}}</ref> [[Wildfires in Turkey]] were the worst in the history of the republic in 2021 and killed several people and injured hundreds. Droughts risk [[Mosquito-borne disease|mosquito borne diseases]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Polat |first1=Yeşim |last2=Yanikoğlu |first2=Atila |last3=Çeti̇n |first3=Hüseyin |date=2017-08-31 |title=Effects of Climate Change on Mosquito-Borne Diseases |journal=Anadolu University Journal of Science and Technology C - Life Sciences and Biotechnology |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=86–94 |doi=10.18036/aubtdc.296680 |issn=2146-0264|doi-access=free }}</ref> The [[Ministry of Health (Turkey)|Health Ministry]] will plan.<ref name="Website-2" /> 

===Economic impacts===
Although climate related economic losses are much lower than in the EU they increased over the early 2020s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-28 |title=Climate-related economic losses |url=https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/climate-related-economic-losses |access-date=2025-10-16 |website=www.eea.europa.eu |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251005130238/https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/climate-related-economic-losses |archive-date=5 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Environment Minister Murat Kurum estimated in 2021 that losses due to disasters, such as floods,<ref>{{Cite news |title=Pandemic stresses need for green transformation: Minister |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/pandemic-stresses-need-for-green-transformation-minister-158332 |access-date=2021-04-29 |website=Hürriyet Daily News |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926160346/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/pandemic-stresses-need-for-green-transformation-minister-158332 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> caused by climate change would amount to billions of [[Turkish lira|lira]] (hundreds of millions of dollars).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Bakan Kurum: İklim Değişikliğiyle Mücadele Raporu'nu Meclise sunacağız|url=https://www.aa.com.tr/tr/ekonomi/bakan-kurum-iklim-degisikligiyle-mucadele-raporunu-meclise-sunacagiz/2148006|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217125056/https://www.aa.com.tr/tr/ekonomi/bakan-kurum-iklim-degisikligiyle-mucadele-raporunu-meclise-sunacagiz/2148006 |archive-date=2021-02-17 }}</ref> The [[World Bank]] has estimated the cost and benefits of stopping net carbon emissions, but has suggested government do far more detailed planning.<ref name="World Bank">{{Cite report |url=https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/37521 |title=Türkiye - Country Climate and Development Report |date=2022-06-13 |publisher=[[World Bank]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615154314/https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/37521 |archive-date=15 June 2022 |access-date=11 July 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> Companies which responded to the [[Carbon Disclosure Project]] in 2025 saw somewhat more climate opportunity than risk.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CDP Türkiye 2025 Climate and Nature Report {{!}} CORPORATE GOVERNANCE FORUM OF TÜRKİYE |url=https://cdpturkey.sabanciuniv.edu/en/content/cdp-turkiye-2025-climate-and-nature-report |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=cdpturkey.sabanciuniv.edu}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=6}}

According to the [[United Nations Development Programme]], decreasing rainfall is exacerbating the wide social and regional disparities within Turkey, and the gap between [[Southeastern Anatolia Region|south-eastern provinces]] and the rest of the country is widening.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey {{!}} UNDP Climate Change Adaptation |url=https://www.adaptation-undp.org/explore/europe-and-central-asia/turkey |access-date=2021-03-24 |website=www.adaptation-undp.org |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415172620/https://www.adaptation-undp.org/explore/europe-and-central-asia/turkey |archive-date=15 April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> 

====Agriculture====
[[File:Çıralı_Gölü_(Karapinar,_Provinz_Konya).jpg|thumb|[[Karst lake|Karst lakes]] like {{Interlanguage link|Çıralı Lake|tr|Çıralı Obruğu}} are drying due to climate change and excessive groundwater extraction<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poyraz |first1=Murat |last2=Öztürk |first2=Muhammed Zeynel |date=2026-07-06 |title=Spatial distribution, hydrological status of Karst Lakes in Türkiye |journal=Carbonates and Evaporites |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=109 |doi=10.1007/s13146-026-01313-2 |bibcode=2026CarEv..41..109P |issn=1878-5212|doi-access=free }}</ref> ]]
[[File:Turkish_Agriculture,_Forestry_and_Fishing_Industry_.jpg|thumb|Wheat may be severely affected.<ref>{{Cite book|date=2020-01-01|chapter=Assessing climate change impacts on wheat production in Turkey and various adaptation strategies|chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128195277000030|language=en|pages=43–54|doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-819527-7.00003-0|last1=Koç|first1=Esra|title=Climate Change and Food Security with Emphasis on Wheat|publisher=Science Direct|isbn=978-0-12-819527-7|s2cid=216269049|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210816103558/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128195277000030|archive-date=16 August 2021|access-date=16 August 2021|url-status=live }}</ref>|alt=large cylindrical bales in a field which has been cut, lit by a low golden sun]]
Unless global emissions are greatly reduced [[agriculture in Turkey]], such as [[wheat]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Reducing emissions could mitigate worst effects of climate change, study finds |url=https://airqualitynews.com/2019/03/14/reducing-emissions-could-mitigate-worst-effects-of-climate-change-study-finds/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190408083349/https://airqualitynews.com/2019/03/14/reducing-emissions-could-mitigate-worst-effects-of-climate-change-study-finds/ |archive-date=8 April 2019 |access-date=8 April 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rojas|first1=Maisa|last2=Lambert|first2=Fabrice|last3=Ramirez-Villegas|first3=Julian|last4=Challinor|first4=Andrew J.|date=2019-04-02|title=Emergence of robust precipitation changes across crop production areas in the 21st century|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=116|issue=14|pages=6673–6678|doi=10.1073/pnas.1811463116|issn=0027-8424|pmc=6452695|pmid=30858318|bibcode=2019PNAS..116.6673R|doi-access=free}}</ref> is expected to be severely affected after the late 2030s, especially in areas with rain fed agriculture.<ref name="Hasan Dudu & Erol H. Çakmak (2018)" /> Arid and semi-arid areas are at risk of [[desertification]].<ref>{{Cite report|last=|first=|date=|title=Desertification and Erosion in Turkey|url=https://www.tarimorman.gov.tr/CEM/Belgeler/collesme%20belgeleri%20arsiv/Sayfa02/CEMxBROSxINGxMAIL.pdf|website=|archive-date=22 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231022133519/https://www.tarimorman.gov.tr/CEM/Belgeler/collesme%20belgeleri%20arsiv/Sayfa02/CEMxBROSxINGxMAIL.pdf}}</ref> Water is lost through evaporation due to outdated irrigation techniques used by the [[Southeastern Anatolia Project]], increasing the risk of severe water shortage.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Will Turkey's thirst for dam building add an element of combustibility to a regional water crisis?|url=https://www.equaltimes.org/will-turkey-s-thirst-for-dam|access-date=2020-02-13|website=Equal Times|date=10 February 2020|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200213183326/https://www.equaltimes.org/will-turkey-s-thirst-for-dam|archive-date=13 February 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

Damage to agriculture<ref name="ipc2018">{{cite web |last1=Ağaçayak |first1=Tuğba |last2=Keyman |first2=E. Fuat |title=Water and Food Security in Turkey in a Changing Climate |url=http://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/WaterAndFoodSecurity_PolicyBrief_web.pdf |publisher=Istanbul Policy Center, Sabancı University |access-date=16 September 2018 |archive-date=16 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180916164315/http://ipc.sabanciuniv.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/WaterAndFoodSecurity_PolicyBrief_web.pdf }}</ref> is predicted to greatly increase,<ref name="Hasan Dudu & Erol H. Çakmak (2018)">{{cite journal |last1=Dudu |first1=Hasan |last2=Çakmak |first2=Erol H. |title=Climate change and agriculture: an integrated approach to evaluate economy-wide effects for Turkey |journal=Climate and Development |date=2018 |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=275–288 |doi=10.1080/17565529.2017.1372259 |bibcode=2018CliDe..10..275D |doi-access=free }}</ref> for example due to "false spring" [[germination]] or [[blossom]]ing followed by a cold snap.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Climate change responsible for spring and winter within weeks |url=https://www.trtworld.com/life/climate-change-responsible-for-spring-and-winter-within-weeks-43363 |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=Climate change responsible for spring and winter within weeks |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428025042/https://www.trtworld.com/life/climate-change-responsible-for-spring-and-winter-within-weeks-43363 |archive-date=28 April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> The increase in early blooming, which is happening due to climate change, can be a problem for crops such as fruit trees.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Climate change bares its many faces in Turkey|url=https://www.trtworld.com/life/climate-change-bares-its-many-faces-in-turkey-42852|access-date=2021-04-29|website=Climate change bares its many faces in Turkey|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231215180047/https://www.trtworld.com/life/climate-change-bares-its-many-faces-in-turkey-42852|archive-date=15 December 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Turkish wine|Vineyards in Thrace]] are being affected.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gurbey|first=Alev Perihan|date=July 2020|title=Climate Change Problems in Agricultural Landscape Areas: Eastern Thrace Vineyards|journal=Journal of Environmental Protection and Ecology |volume=21 |pages=1090–1097 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342736330}}</ref> 

A significant decline in agricultural production is transmitted throughout the economy and reduces national welfare.<ref name="Hasan Dudu & Erol H. Çakmak (2018)" /> More [[Agricultural technology|agritech]] co-operation with the EU and [[United Arab Emirates|UAE]] has been suggested.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Change Threatens Turkey's Role as a Food Supplier to Europe and the Middle East |url=https://www.turkeyanalyst.org/publications/turkey-analyst-articles/item/710-climate-change-threatens-turkey%E2%80%99s-role-as-a-food-supplier-to-europe-and-the-middle-east.html |access-date=2023-12-16 |website=www.turkeyanalyst.org |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240220062510/https://www.turkeyanalyst.org/publications/turkey-analyst-articles/item/710-climate-change-threatens-turkey%E2%80%99s-role-as-a-food-supplier-to-europe-and-the-middle-east.html |archive-date=20 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Fisheries and aquaculture====
[[File:Engraulis encrasicol, Istanbul.jpg|thumb|[[Anchovies]] may no longer grow properly in Turkish waters.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Commercial fishing of anchovy banned for 10 days|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/commercial-fishing-of-anchovy-banned-for-10-days-161483|access-date=2021-04-25|website=Hürriyet Daily News|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260610100533/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/commercial-fishing-of-anchovy-banned-for-10-days-161483|archive-date=10 June 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>|alt=small silver fish in open polystyrene boxes labelled "Karadeniz hamsi kilo 7 lira"]]
Warming seas and [[Lessepsian migration|invasive marine species, such as from the Red Sea]], have received little media coverage. [[Fishing in Turkey|Fishing]] in the [[Black Sea]] is sensitive to the impacts of climate change,<ref>{{Cite book |editor1=Barange, Manuel |editor2=Bahri, Tarûb |editor3=Beveridge, Malcolm C. M. |editor4=Cochrane, K. L. |editor5=Funge Smith, S. ====Tourism====
[[Tourism in Turkey]] may become too hot in the summer for some people, for example [[Antalya]] could become too hot for some visitors during some school holidays.<ref>{{Cite web|title=How hot summers and disease could impact tourism in the Mediterranean {{!}} McKinsey & Company|url=https://www.mckinsey.com/business-functions/sustainability/our-insights/sustainability-blog/hot-summers-and-disease-threaten-tourism-in-the-mediterranean|access-date=2021-02-11|website=www.mckinsey.com|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210728141027/https://www.mckinsey.com/business-functions/sustainability/our-insights/sustainability-blog/hot-summers-and-disease-threaten-tourism-in-the-mediterranean|archive-date=28 July 2021|url-status=dead}}</ref> Development of [[ski resort]]s in the [[Taurus Mountains|Central Taurus]] and eastern Black Sea region mountains may not be possible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Demiroglu|first1=Osman Cenk|last2=Turp|first2=Mustafa Tufan|last3=Kurnaz|first3=Mehmet Levent|last4=Abegg|first4=Bruno|date=2020-08-26|title=The Ski Climate Index (SCI): fuzzification and a regional climate modeling application for Turkey|journal=International Journal of Biometeorology|volume=65|issue=5|pages=763–777|language=en|doi=10.1007/s00484-020-01991-0|pmid=32845376|pmc=8116266|issn=1432-1254|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Impacts on housing===
New highways and building concrete are hindering absorption of floodwater by the land.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why does Istanbul flood so easily? Experts explain |url=https://www.turkiyetoday.com/nation/why-does-istanbul-flood-so-easily-experts-explain-3230416 |access-date=2026-10-21 |website=Türkiye Today |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-16|title=New homes, highways boost flood risk on Turkey's northern coast|url=https://arab.news/w9vhy|access-date=2021-04-25|website=Arab News|language=en}}</ref> [[Urban heat islands]] are also a problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dihkan |first1=Mustafa |last2=Karsli |first2=Fevzi |last3=Guneroglu |first3=Nilgun |last4=Guneroglu |first4=Abdulaziz |title=Evaluation of urban heat island effect in Turkey |journal=Arabian Journal of Geosciences |date=2018 |volume=11 |issue=8 |article-number=186 |doi=10.1007/s12517-018-3533-3 |bibcode=2018ArJG...11..186D |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/324700506}}</ref> Because of the increase in temperature, existing buildings will need more energy for cooling.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dino|first1=Ipek Gursel|last2=Akgul|first2=Cagla Meral|date=2019|title=Impact of climate change on the existing residential building stock in Turkey: An analysis on energy use, greenhouse gas emissions and occupant comfort|journal=Renewable Energy |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/332213083|volume=141 |pages=828–846 |doi=10.1016/j.renene.2019.03.150|bibcode=2019REne..141..828D |s2cid=132673003 |hdl=11511/38528|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

== Mitigation ==
[[File:Greenhouse gas emissions in Turkey by sector.png|500x500px|right|alt=Graph showing that most emissions are from energy and heat production, and they have increased a lot since 1990 but decreased in 2019 and 2020]]

The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) defines ''mitigation'' (of climate change) as "a human intervention to reduce [[Greenhouse gas emissions|emissions]] or enhance the [[Carbon sink|sinks]] of [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]]".<ref name="IPCC AR6 WGI Glossary2">IPCC, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_AnnexVII.pdf Annex VII: Glossary] [Matthews, J.B.R., V. Möller, R. van Diemen, J.S. Fuglestvedt, V. Masson-Delmotte, C. Méndez, S. Semenov, A. Reisinger (eds.)]. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2215–2256, doi:10.1017/9781009157896.022.</ref>{{rp|2239}}According to [[Climate Action Tracker]] Turkey's GHG emissions are not in line with the Paris Agreement objective to limit temperature rise to well below 2&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{cite web |last=Timperley |first=Jocelyn |date=3 May 2018 |title=Carbon Brief Profile: Turkey |url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/carbon-brief-profile-turkey |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413143655/https://www.carbonbrief.org/carbon-brief-profile-turkey |archive-date=13 April 2020 |website=[[Carbon Brief]]}}</ref>

A long-term climate strategy was published in 2024 but omits [[coal phase-out]].<ref name=":39" /><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Congratulations Türkiye: The 2053 Long-Term Climate Strategy is a Key Roadmap to Achieve the Net Zero Target! - MLGP4Climate |url=https://mlgp4climate.com/news/congratulations-turkiye-the-2053-long-term-climate-strategy-is-a-key-roadmap-to-achieve-the-net-zero-target |access-date=2025-01-23 |website=mlgp4climate.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":55" /> The [[United Nations Environment Programme]] says a faster decarbonisation is needed, and emissions per person per year should be cut by more than half to about 2–2.5&nbsp;t {{CO2}}e by 2030.<ref name="UNEP">{{Cite report |url=https://www.unep.org/emissions-gap-report-2020 |title=Emissions Gap Report 2020 |date=9 December 2020 |publisher=[[UN Environment Programme]] |isbn=978-92-807-3812-4 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201209220237/https://www.unep.org/emissions-gap-report-2020 |date=March 2021 |publisher=[[International Energy Agency]]}}</ref>{{Rp|42}}{{efn|1=In 2015, Turkey submitted its [[emissions target]] to the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC), "up to 21 percent reduction in greenhouse gas (GhG) emissions from the Business as Usual level by 2030" and aiming to emit 929 Mt of {{CO2}} (before subtracting {{CO2}} absorbed by forests) in 2030.<ref>{{cite web|website=United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change|url=https://www4.unfccc.int/sites/submissions/INDC/Published%20Documents/Turkey/1/The_INDC_of_TURKEY_v.15.19.30.pdf|title=Republic of Turkey Intended Nationally Determined 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> The country will probably meet this "unambitious" [[Intended Nationally Determined Contributions]] (INDC) which it submitted to the UNFCCC.<ref name="Climate Transparency 2018">{{cite web|date=2018|title=Brown to Green: the G20 Transition to a Low-carbon {{anchor|Comparison with the European Union target}}
Unless Turkey's energy policy is changed, European Union (EU) emissions per person are forecast to fall below Turkey's during the 2020s.<ref name="UNEP" />{{Rp|22}} Since the EU is Turkey's main trading partner, a comparison with targets in the [[European Green Deal]] is important to help Turkish businesses avoid future EU [[carbon tariff]]s, on exports such as steel<ref>{{Cite news |date=9 October 2019 |title=EU mills push for tariffs on Turkish flats |url=https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news/1992413-eu-mills-push-for-tariffs-on-turkish-flats |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801065541/https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news/1992413-eu-mills-push-for-tariffs-on-turkish-flats |archive-date=1 August 2020 |access-date=20 April 2020 |website=[[Argus Media]]}}</ref> and cement.<ref name=":18">{{Cite news |date=12 March 2021 |title=John Kerry warns EU against carbon border tax |url=https://www.ft.com/content/3d00d3c8-202d-4765-b0ae-e2b212bbca98 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321204949/https://www.ft.com/content/3d00d3c8-202d-4765-b0ae-e2b212bbca98 |archive-date=21 March 2021 |access-date=19 March 2021 |newspaper=[[Financial Times]]}}</ref> Public and private sector working groups discussed the [[European Green Deal]],<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Arseven |first1=E. Benan |last2=Baydar |first2=C. Hazal |date=17 August 2021 |title=Turkey Adopts Action Plan to Comply with European Green Deal |url=https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=1d5cf7b3-0fc7-40b1-9385-caddd2760443 |access-date=7 September 2021 |website=Lexology |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210907103722/https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=1d5cf7b3-0fc7-40b1-9385-caddd2760443 |archive-date=7 September 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[Ministry of Trade (Turkey)|Trade Ministry]] published an action plan in response to its [[Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=16 July 2021 |title=Yeşil Mutabakat Eylem Planı Yayımlandı |trans-title=Green Deal Action Plan published |url=https://ticaret.gov.tr/haberler/yesil-mutabakat-eylem-plani-yayimlandi |website=[[Ministry of Trade (Turkey)]] |language=tr |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251012184527/https://ticaret.gov.tr/haberler/yesil-mutabakat-eylem-plani-yayimlandi |archive-date=12 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> A [[green taxonomy]] has been published,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Minute |first=Turkish |date=2026-09-24 |title=Turkey sets green investment standards ahead of COP31 climate summit |url-status=live}}</ref> but criticised for including fossil gas, cement and blast furnaces.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Green Taxonomy paradox ahead of COP31: ‘Nuclear energy and fossil gas are unacceptable’ |url=https://bianet.org/haber/green-taxonomy-paradox-ahead-of-cop31-nuclear-energy-and-fossil-gas-are-unacceptable-324254 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=bianet.org |language=en}}</ref>[[File:Greenhouse gas emission and absorption by Turkey.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|Burning coal, petrol, diesel and natural gas is putting far more carbon dioxide into the air than [[Forests in Turkey|forests]] can take out. There is some correlation with the [[economic history of Turkey]], such as a dip during the [[2001 Turkish economic crisis|2001 economic crisis]].]]
[[File:Ghg per person Turkey.svg|thumb|alt=From 1990 the net emissions per person graph line rises in jagged parallel somewhat below gross emissions, until it dips more sharply in 2019|Greenhouse gas per person, before and after absorption by forests. The greater net dip in 2019 is because forest cover was resurveyed and found to be more than previously thought.]]

Turkey is aiming for [[Carbon neutrality|net zero carbon emissions]] by 2053.<ref name=":30" /> The [[World Bank]] has estimated the cost and benefits, but has suggested government do far more detailed planning.<ref name="World Bank"/> The long-term climate change strategy published by the [[Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change]] in 2024 does not specifically mention coal, but says that the "infrastructure of existing fossil fuel-based facilities will be reviewed".<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.8}}

Thinktank [[Istanbul Policy Center]] doubts that the target of 643 million tonnes in 2035 is compatible with the 2053 net zero target,<ref name=":30" />{{Reference page|page=23}} and several [[Non-governmental organization|NGOs]] criticised the 2035 target as being set without consultation and an increase on 2023 emissions.<ref>{{Cite news |last=ÜNLÜ |first=Didem Eryar |date=2025-09-26 |title=Türkiye'nin yeni iklim taahhüdü net sıfır hedefiyle çelişiyor |url=https://www.ekonomim.com/kose-yazisi/turkiyenin-yeni-iklim-taahhudu-net-sifir-hedefiyle-celisiyor/845323 |newspaper=Ekonomim |language=tr-TR |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251111042324/https://www.ekonomim.com/kose-yazisi/turkiyenin-yeni-iklim-taahhudu-net-sifir-hedefiyle-celisiyor/845323 |archive-date=11 November 2025 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> 

=== Energy ===
{{see also|Energy in Turkey#Energy transition|Coal_in_Turkey#Coal_phase-out}}
Emissions could be reduced considerably by switching from coal to existing gas-fired power stations:<ref>{{cite web |title=Country Focus: Turkey: LNG Intake Rises [LNG Condensed] |url=https://www.naturalgasworld.com/country-focus-turkey-lng-intake-rises-lng-condensed-77710 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200407073000/https://www.naturalgasworld.com/country-focus-turkey-lng-intake-rises-lng-condensed-77710 |archive-date=7 April 2020 |access-date=29 April 2020 |website=naturalgasworld.com}}</ref> as there is enough generating capacity to allow the decommissioning of all coal-fired power stations and still meet peak energy demand, as long as hydropower as well as gas is used to meet peaks in demand.<ref>{{cite web |date=12 July 2019 |title=All coal plants can be shut down! |url=https://www.duvarenglish.com/columns/2019/12/07/all-coal-plants-can-be-shut-down/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200705120354/https://www.duvarenglish.com/columns/2019/12/07/all-coal-plants-can-be-shut-down/ |archive-date=5 July 2020 |access-date=5 May 2020 |website=[[Gazete Duvar]]}}</ref> [[Solar power in Turkey|Solar]] and [[Wind power in Turkey|wind power]] are the cheapest generating technologies,<ref name=":14a">{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=Optimum electricity generation capacity mix for Turkey towards 2030 |url=https://www.shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ExecutiveSum.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417022702/https://www.shura.org.tr/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ExecutiveSum.pdf |archive-date=17 April 2021 |website=shura.org}}</ref> but are underdeveloped.<ref name=":26">{{cite web |author=Susi Dennison |author2=Asli Aydıntaşbaş |date=22 August 2021 |title=New energies: How the European Green Deal can save the EU's relationship with Turkey – European Council on Foreign Relations |url=https://ecfr.eu/publication/new-energies-how-the-european-green-deal-can-save-the-eus-relationship-with-turkey/ |access-date=22 June 2021 |website=[[European Council on Foreign Relations|ECFR]] |language=en-GB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210622102824/https://ecfr.eu/publication/new-energies-how-the-european-green-deal-can-save-the-eus-relationship-with-turkey/ |archive-date=22 June 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2026 Ember suggested that [[Planning permission|permitting]] should be improved for hybrid solar and for solar and wind with storage.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Renewables save Using [[International Civil Aviation Organization]] methodology [[Turkish Airlines]] offers [[carbon offset]]s certified to [[Verified Carbon Standard]] and [[Gold Standard (carbon offset standard)|Gold Standard]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 August 2022 |title=Turkish Airlines launches new carbon offset programme |url=https://www.businesstraveller.com/business-travel/2022/08/02/turkish-airlines-launches-new-carbon-offset-programme/ |access-date=2022-08-04 |website=Business Traveller |language=en-GB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240418163633/https://www.businesstraveller.com/business-travel/2022/08/02/turkish-airlines-launches-new-carbon-offset-programme/ |archive-date=18 April 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Turkey is participating in the [[Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Who volunteers for CORSIA |url=https://aviationbenefits.org/environmental-efficiency/climate-action/offsetting-emissions-corsia/corsia/who-volunteers-for-corsia/ |access-date=2022-08-04 |website=aviationbenefits.org |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231208000619/https://aviationbenefits.org/environmental-efficiency/climate-action/offsetting-emissions-corsia/corsia/who-volunteers-for-corsia/ |archive-date=8 December 2023 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Flights between Turkey and the EU may be charged in the EU ETS unless they avoid creating contrails.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-17 |title=What the 2026 ETS review means for transport |url=https://www.transportenvironment.org/articles/what-the-2026-ets-review-means-for-transport |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=T&E |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260913212041/https://www.transportenvironment.org/articles/what-the-2026-ets-review-means-for-transport |archive-date=13 September 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2024 the UNFCCC again asked Turkey to separate international from national aviation and shipping in its inventory.

=== Buildings ===
There are almost 10 million [[Turkish construction and contracting industry|buildings in Turkey]],<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.3}} and as they are the largest energy consumers there are substantial opportunities for energy savings in both new build and renovations.<ref name=":20">{{Cite report |url=https://www.tepav.org.tr/en/yayin/s/1539 |title=Decarbonization of Turkey's economy: long-term strategies and immediate challenges |last=Ayas |first=Ceren |date=August 2020 |publisher=[[Climate Action Network]] Europe, SEE Change Net, TEPAV |id=TR2015/DG/01/A5-02/147A |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250907021632/https://tepav.org.tr/en/yayin/s/1539 |archive-date=7 September 2025 |access-date=22 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> There is a roadmap, which says that as of 2021 three quarters of building stock is pre-21st century, that is pre energy standards.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Türki̇ye building sector decarbonization roadm | url=https://wrisehirler.org/sites/default/files/Turkiye%20Building%20Sector%20Decarbonization%20Roadmap...pdf | typical residential building emits almost 50 kgCO2eq/m2/year, mostly due to the energy used by residents.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Atmaca |first1=Adem |last2=Atmaca |first2=Nihat |date=2022-03-15 [[OECD|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] (OECD) has said that more could be done to improve the energy efficiency of buildings, and that tax incentives offered for this would create jobs.<ref name="OECD2021" />{{Rp|62}} Turkey was a co-leader of the group discussing [[Zero-energy building|zero-carbon buildings]] at the [[2019 UN Climate Action Summit]], and the city of [[Eskişehir]] has pledged to convert all existing buildings to zero emissions by 2050.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 September 2019 |title=12 global initiatives to beat back climate threats efficiency improvements can be made in the same programme as increasing resilience to [[earthquakes in Turkey]].<ref>{{cite web |title=World Bank Provides $265 million Boost to Improve Earthquake Resilience and Energy Efficiency of Public Buildings in Turkey |archive-date=10 June 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> However, as of 2026 gas is subsidized.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Türkiye raises electricity, gas bills by up to 25% on rising energy costs Istanbul Policy Center estimate that most of the additional cost of net zero is for buildings.<ref name=":30" />{{Reference page|page=20}} Although [[low-energy house]]s, [[zero-energy building]]s and There is no data on the [[carbon intensity]] of cement.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turkey 2020 |url=https://www.climate-transparency.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Turkey-CT-2020-WEB.pdf |publisher=Climate Transparency |access-date=22 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251112114854/https://www.climate-transparency.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Turkey-CT-2020-WEB.pdf |archive-date=12 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|13}} Emissions from cement production could be lessened by reducing its [[Cement clinker|clinker]] content<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cement – Fuels & Technologies |url=https://www.iea.org/fuels-and-technologies/cement |access-date=23 August 2021 |website=[[International Energy Agency]] |language=en-GB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210820165101/https://www.iea.org/fuels-and-technologies/cement |archive-date=20 August 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>—for example, by making [[Limestone Calcined Clay Cement]], which is only half clinker. The second-largest reduction could be made by switching half the fuel from hard coal and [[petroleum coke]] (petcoke) to a mixture of rubber from waste tires, [[refuse-derived fuel]] and [[biomass]].<ref name="Cementis2018">{{cite web |title=Abstract on the potential GHG emissions reduction in Turkey through the cement industry |url=http://www.cementis.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Turkey-GHG-from-Cement.pdf |url-status=live |publisher=Cementis GmbH}}</ref> Although the country has enough of these materials, most cement kilns (there are 54<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|156}}) use coal, petcoke or lignite as their primary energy source.<ref name="2021report" />{{Rp|154}} More [[cross-laminated timber]] could be used for building, instead of concrete.<ref>{{cite web |title=Promoting Low Cost Energy Efficient Wooden Buildings in Turkey |url=https://www.thegef.org/sites/default/files/web-documents/10090_PIFReviewSheet.pdf |url-status=live |website=[[Global Environment Facility]]}}</ref> Further decarbonisation of cement production would depend heavily on carbon capture,<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.2.1}} perhaps storing in a [[salt dome]] near [[Lake Tuz]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Glomazic |first1=Rade |last2=Raptsun |first2=Mykola |title=EU Carbon Capture and Storage Directive Preliminary Regulatory Impact Assessment or in [[Diyarbakır Province]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Firtina Ertiş |first=İrem |title=Application of Multi-criteria Decision Making for Geological Carbon Dioxide Storage Area in Turkey === Carbon sinks ===
{{See also|Reforestation#Turkey}}
[[File:Orman.JPG|thumb|alt=conifer trees covering a mountainside|These existing trees are being added to by [[Reforestation#Turkey|reforestation]].]]
Turkey has 23&nbsp;million hectares of forest covering quarter of the country, though over 40% is [[degraded forest|degraded woodland.]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Resmi İstatistikler |trans-title=Official Statistics |url=https://www.ogm.gov.tr/tr/ormanlarimiz/resmi-istatistikler |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210314235459/https://www.ogm.gov.tr/tr/ormanlarimiz/resmi-istatistikler |archive-date=14 March 2021 |access-date=16 March 2021 |website=General Directorate of Forestry |publisher=[[:tr:Orman Genel Müdürlüğü]] |language=tr}}</ref> [[Forest in Turkey|Turkey's forests]] are its main [[carbon sink]] and offset 55 Mt of the country's emissions in 2024.<ref name="2026table" />{{Reference page|page=table 4 B11}} The government said in 2015 that by 2050 "forests are envisioned to stretch across over four-fifths of the country's territory".<ref>{{cite news |last=Ngalame |first=Elias Ntungwe |date=29 October 2015 |title=What can Africa learn from Turkey's reforestation? |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/what-can-africa-learn-from-turkeys-reforestation/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190122192832/https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/what-can-africa-learn-from-turkeys-reforestation/ |archive-date=22 January 2019 |access-date=24 February 2019 |publisher=[[World Economic Forum]]}}</ref> However warmer and drier air in the south and west may make it difficult to sustain the present forest cover.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ömer Lütfi |first=Şen |title=Province-based Forest Cover (%) |url=http://climatechangeinturkey.com/effects-of-climate-change-forests.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180517191309/http://climatechangeinturkey.com/effects-of-climate-change-forests.html |archive-date=17 May 2018 |access-date=24 February 2019 |website=Climate Change in Turkey}}</ref> Due to forest fires and reduced productivity due to climate change trees are becoming less of a sink but,<ref name=":55" />{{Rp|location=section 4.2.7}} despite regional variations, forests are expected to remain an overall carbon sink.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berberoglu |first1=Suha |last2=Donmez |first2=Cenk |last3=Cilek |first3=Ahmet |date=5 April 2021 |title=Modelling climate change impacts on regional net primary productivity in Turkey |journal=[[Environmental Monitoring and Assessment]] |language=en |volume=193 |issue=5 |page=242 |bibcode=2021EMnAs.193..242B |doi=10.1007/s10661-021-09031-z |issn=1573-2959 |pmid=33818693 |s2cid=233026508}}</ref> Almost all Turkey's forest land belongs to the state and cannot be privatised. Private [[afforestation]] permits have been issued however, to encourage tree planting in areas where tree density is low.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gençay |first=Gökçe |date=1 July 2020 |title=Legal framework of private afforestation: The case of Turkey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264837719320794 |url-status=live |journal=Land Use Policy |volume=96 |bibcode=2020LUPol..9604673G |doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2020.104673 |issn=0264-8377 |s2cid=218962170 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417022706/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264837719320794 |archive-date=17 April 2021 |access-date=16 March 2021 |article-number=104673}}</ref> [[Non-governmental organization|Civil society organization]]s, such as the [[Turkish Foundation for Combating Soil Erosion]] and the [[Foresters' Association of Turkey]], are also encouraging reforestation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forester's Association of Turkey |url=https://www.ormancilardernegi.org/en/index.asp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180422120149/http://www.ormancilardernegi.org/en/index.asp |archive-date=22 April 2018 |access-date=22 March 2021 |website=[[Foresters' Association of Turkey]]}}</ref> In 2019, an annual "National Forestation Day" every 11 November was established by President Erdoğan.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Turkey plants 11 million saplings on National Forestation Day |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-plants-11-million-saplings-for-greener-future-148558 |access-date=16 May 2021 |newspaper=[[Hürriyet Daily News]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210516071918/https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-plants-11-million-saplings-for-greener-future-148558 |archive-date=16 May 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Junipers]] have been suggested for reforestation because of their hardiness, but are said to need help to regrow quickly.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yücedağ |first1=Cengiz |last2=Ayan |first2=Sezgin |last3=Farhat |first3=Perla |last4=Özel |first4=Halil Barış |date=2021 |title=Juniperus L. for Restoration of Degraded Forest Lands in Turkey |journal=South-East European Forestry |volume=12 |issue=1 |doi=10.15177/seefor.21-01 |doi-broken-date=17 September 2026 |doi-access=free}}</ref> But, according to [[Ege University]] associate professor Serdar Gökhan Senol, the [[Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (Turkey)|Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry]] sometimes replants when it should wait for regrowth instead.<ref>{{cite web |last=Verri |first=Selene |date=7 January 2020 |title=Wildfires in Izmir: a green plan for the city, an urban plan for the forests |url=http://www.youris.com/environment/biodiversity/wildfires-in-izmir-a-green-plan-for-the-city-an-urban-plan-for-the-forests.kl |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125081231/http://www.youris.com/environment/biodiversity/wildfires-in-izmir-a-green-plan-for-the-city-an-urban-plan-for-the-forests.kl |archive-date=25 January 2020 |access-date=21 January 2020 |website=youris.com}}</ref> In 2023 about 15 Mt was locked up in [[wood products]].{{Reference page|page=337}}{{Better source needed|reason=This from report published 2025 need to check and cite next report in April 2026|date=January 2026}} [[Wildfires in Turkey|Wildfires]] emit carbon dioxide such as 10 Mt in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-28 |title=Greenhouse gas emissions and removals in land and forests |url=https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/turkiye/lulucf-emissions |access-date=2026-01-11 |website=www.eea.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

[[Soil in Turkey]] contains [[soil organic carbon]], which is estimated to total 3.5&nbsp;billion tonnes at {{convert|30|cm}} soil depth, with 36&nbsp;t/ha in [[Agriculture in Turkey|agricultural]] fields.<ref name=":22">{{Cite report |url=https://www.tarimorman.gov.tr/CEM/Belgeler/yay%C4%B1nlar/yay%C4%B1nlar%202018/Karbon%20Proje%2027Eyl%C3%BCl2018.pdf |title=Toprak Organik Karbonu Projesi Teknik Özet |trans-title=Sol Organic Carbon Project technical summary |last=Karagöz |year=2018 |publisher=[[Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (Turkey)|Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry]] |display-authors=et al |lang=tr}}</ref> Soil organic carbon has been mapped:<ref name="FAO">{{cite journal |last1=Sonmez |display-authors=et al |date=March 2017 |title=Turkey's National Geospatial Soil Organic Carbon Information System |url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-br972e.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Global Symposium on Soil Organic Carbon |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181011172947/http://www.fao.org/3/a-br972e.pdf |archive-date=11 October 2018 |access-date=24 February 2019}}</ref><ref name=":22" /> this is important because carbon emissions from soil are directly related to climate change, but vary according to soil interaction<ref>{{Cite report |url=http://www.toprak.org.tr/files/Proceeding-Soil-2019.pdf |title=Proceedings 10th International Soil Congress: Successful Transformation toward Land Degradation Neutrality: Future Perspective |year=2019 |location=[[Ankara]] |isbn=978-605-63090-4-5 |editor1-last=Namlı |editor1-first=Dr. Ayten |editor2-last=Turgay |editor2-first=Prof. Dr. Oğuz Can |editor3-last=Akça |editor3-first=Muhittin Onur}}</ref>{{Rp|107}} with low levels of soil organic carbon increasing the risk of [[soil erosion]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berberoglu |first1=Suha |last2=Cilek |first2=Ahmet |last3=Kirkby |first3=Mike |last4=Irvine |first4=Brian |last5=Donmez |first5=Cenk |date=7 July 2020 |title=Spatial and temporal evaluation of soil erosion in Turkey under climate change scenarios using the Pan-European Soil Erosion Risk Assessment (PESERA) model |url=https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/163284/1/Berberoglu2020_Article_SpatialAndTemporalEvaluationOf.pdf |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |language=en |volume=192 |issue=8 |page=491 |bibcode=2020EMnAs.192..491B |doi=10.1007/s10661-020-08429-5 |issn=1573-2959 |pmid=32638113 |s2cid=220375323}}</ref> Turkey is a major producer of [[marble]]; it has been suggested that waste from the industry could capture carbon (such as from cement production<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0196890426004176|title=Decarbonization of cement production in Türkiye: a techno-economic and risk analysis of CO2 capture technologies - ScienceDirect}}</ref>) by [[calcium looping]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nawar |first1=Azra |last2=Ghaedi |first2=Hosein |last3=Ali |first3=Majid |last4=Zhao |first4=Ming |last5=Iqbal |first5=Naseem |last6=Khan |first6=Rashid |title=Recycling waste-derived marble powder for CO<sub>2</sub> capture |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336616607 |access-date=23 August 2021 |journal=Process Safety and Environmental Protection |date=2019 |volume=132 |pages=214–225
