======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change in the United States
======================================================================

{{Short description|Emissions, impacts and responses of the United States related to climate change}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2026}}
[[File:1900- Temperature change in the United States (color-coded map).png|thumb|upright=1.5| Average temperatures in almost all regions in the U.S. have increased in the last 120 years.<ref name="EPAmap_1901-2020">{{cite web |title=Climate Change Indicators: U.S. and Global Temperature |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-us-and-global-temperature |website=EPA.gov |publisher=Environmental Protection Agency |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211230101600/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-us-and-global-temperature |archive-date=30 December 2021 |date=2021 |quote=(FIg. 3) EPA's data source: NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration). 2021. Climate at a glance. Accessed February 2021. ncdc.noaa.gov/cag. |url-status=live }} ([https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/temperature_figure3_2021.png Direct link to graphic]; [https://web.archive.org/web/20220101115841/https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/temperature_figure3_2021.png archive])</ref>]]
[[File:1895- Temperature change in the United States - Ed Hawkins - climate change.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5| Annual temperatures averaged across the U.S. have exceeded the 1971–2000 average almost every year in the 21st century.<ref name=WarmingStripesUSA>{{cite web |last1=Hawkins |first1=Ed |title=Temperature change in the USA |url=https://showyourstripes.info/c/northamerica/usa/all/ |website=ShowYourStripes.info |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225071857/https://showyourstripes.info/c/northamerica/usa/all/ |archive-date=25 February 2023 |date=2023 |url-status=live }} — Based on [[warming stripes]] concept.</ref>]]
[[Climate change]] has led to the United States warming up by 2.6{{nbsp}}°F (1.4{{nbsp}}°C) since 1970. In 2023, the global average near-surface temperature reached 1.45 °C above pre-industrial levels, making it the warmest year on record.<ref>{{cite web |title=Climate change indicators reached record levels in 2023: WMO |url=https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/climate-change-indicators-reached-record-levels-2023-wmo |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |date=2024-04-21}}</ref><ref name="ClimateCentral_20220420" /> The [[climate of the United States]] is shifting in ways that are widespread and varied between [[Regions of the United States|regions]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sixth Assessment Report|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/#SPM|access-date=2021-08-20|website=www.ipcc.ch}}</ref><ref name="Heidari 2020 e2020EF001657">{{Cite journal|last1=Heidari|first1=Hadi|last2=Arabi|first2=Mazdak|last3=Warziniack|first3=Travis|last4=Kao|first4=Shih-Chieh|date=2020|title=Assessing Shifts in Regional Hydroclimatic Conditions of U.S. River Basins in Response to Climate Change over the 21st Century|journal=Earth's Future|language=en|volume=8|issue=10|article-number=e2020EF001657|doi=10.1029/2020EF001657|bibcode=2020EaFut...801657H|s2cid=225251957|issn=2328-4277|doi-access=free}}</ref> From 2010 to 2019, the United States experienced its hottest decade on record.<ref>{{Cite web|last=US EPA|first=OAR|date=2016-06-27|title=Climate Change Indicators: U.S. and Global Temperature|url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-us-and-global-temperature|access-date=2021-08-20|website=www.epa.gov|language=en}}</ref> [[Extreme weather]] events, [[Invasive species in the United States|invasive species]], [[Lists of floods in the United States|floods]] and [[Droughts in the United States|droughts]] are increasing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heidari |first1=Hadi |last2=Arabi |first2=Mazdak |last3=Ghanbari |first3=Mahshid |last4=Warziniack |first4=Travis |date=June 2020 |title=A Probabilistic Approach for Characterization of Sub-Annual Socioeconomic Drought Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) Relationships in a Changing Environment |journal=Water |language=en |volume=12 |issue=6 |page=1522 |doi=10.3390/w12061522 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020Water..12.1522H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2015-11-06 |title=Climate Change Indicators in the United States |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators |access-date=2022-07-29 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Casagr |first=Tina |date=2022-02-16 |title=Climate Change and Invasive Species - NISAW |url=https://www.nisaw.org/climatechange/ |access-date=2022-07-29 |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Tropical cyclones and climate change|Climate change's impacts on tropical cyclones]] and [[sea level rise]] also affect regions of the country.

Cumulatively since 1850, the [[Greenhouse gas emissions by the United States|U.S. has emitted]] a larger share than any country of the greenhouse gases causing current climate change, with some 20% of the global total of carbon dioxide alone.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-10-05 |title=Analysis: Which countries are historically responsible for climate change? |url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-which-countries-are-historically-responsible-for-climate-change |access-date=2021-12-30 |website=Carbon Brief |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211223055902/https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-which-countries-are-historically-responsible-for-climate-change |archive-date=December 23, 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref> Current [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per person|US emissions per person]] are among the largest in the world.<ref name="watch">[https://www.climatewatchdata.org/ghg-emissions?calculation=PER_CAPITA&end_year=2018&start_year=1990 www.climatewatchdata.org] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624200743/https://www.climatewatchdata.org/ghg-emissions?calculation=PER_CAPITA&end_year=2018&start_year=1990 |date=2021-06-24 }}, at ''Calculations'' select ''per capita.''</ref> Various [[Climate change policy of the United States|state and federal climate change policies]] have been introduced, and the US has ratified the [[Paris Agreement]] despite [[United States withdrawal from the Paris Agreement|temporarily withdrawing]]. In 2021, the country set a target of halving its annual greenhouse gas emissions by 2030,<ref name="CAT">{{cite web|title=New momentum reduces emissions gap, but huge gap remains - analysis|url=https://climateactiontracker.org/press/new-momentum-reduces-emissions-gap-but-huge-gap-remains-analysis/|website=[[Climate Action Tracker]]|access-date=27 April 2021}}</ref> however oil and gas companies still get [[tax breaks]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=The Zombies of the U.S. Tax Code: Why Fossil Fuels Subsidies Seem Impossible to Kill |work=The New York Times |date=15 March 2024 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/15/climate/tax-breaks-oil-gas-us.html |last1=Friedman |first1=Lisa }}</ref>

Climate change is having considerable impacts on the environment and society of the United States. This includes implications for [[Climate change and agriculture in the United States|agriculture]], the [[Economic impacts of climate change|economy]] (especially the [[Climate change and insurance in the United States|affordability and availability of insurance]]), [[Effects of climate change on human health|human health]], and [[Climate change and indigenous peoples|indigenous peoples]], and it is seen as [[climate security|a national security threat]].<ref>{{cite web |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=March 29, 2016 |title=Climate Change and US National Security: Past, Present, Future |url=https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/publications/reports/climate-change-and-us-national-security-past-present-future |access-date=September 21, 2016 |website=atlanticcouncil.org |publisher=[[Atlantic Council]]}}</ref> US States that emit more [[carbon dioxide]] per person and introduce policies to oppose [[climate change mitigation|climate action]] are generally experiencing greater impacts.<ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal |last1=Tollefson |first1=Jeff |date=12 February 2019 |title=US climate costs will be highest in Republican strongholds |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-00327-2 |journal=Nature |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-00327-2 |access-date=28 October 2020 |s2cid=188147110}}</ref><ref name="ecowatch.com">{{cite news |date=October 29, 2019 |title=States Blocking Climate Action Hold Residents Who Suffer the Most From Climate Impacts |agency=Climate Nexus, Ecowatch |url=https://www.ecowatch.com/states-climate-action-consequences-2641152322.html |access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> 2020 was a historic year for billion-dollar weather and climate disasters in U.S.<ref name="NCEI_thru202009" /> In 2024, the United States experienced 27 separate weather and climate disasters, each causing over  $1 billion in damages, in total, it caused $27 billion in damages. This set a record for the most billion dollars disasters in a single year.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-01-10 |title=2024: An active year of U.S. billion-dollar weather and climate disasters |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/beyond-data/2024-active-year-us-billion-dollar-weather-and-climate-disasters |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250111134623/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/beyond-data/2024-active-year-us-billion-dollar-weather-and-climate-disasters |archive-date=January 11, 2025 |access-date=2025-05-10 |website=www.climate.gov |language=en}}</ref>

Although historically a [[Nonpartisanism|non-partisan]] issue, climate change has become [[Global warming controversy|controversial]] and [[Politicization of science|politically divisive]] in the country in recent decades. [[Petroleum industry|Oil companies]] have known since the 1970s that burning [[fossil fuels|oil and gas]] could cause global warming but nevertheless [[ExxonMobil climate change controversy|funded deniers for years]].<ref name="NYT-20151105">{{cite news |last=Egan |first=Timothy |author-link=Timothy Egan |title=Exxon Mobil and the G.O.P.: Fossil Fools |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/11/06/opinion/fossil-fools.html |date=November 5, 2015 |work=The New York Times |access-date=November 9, 2015}}</ref><ref name="TG-20150708">{{cite news|last=Goldenberg|first=Suzanne|date=July 8, 2015|title=Exxon knew of climate change in 1981, email says – but it funded deniers for 27 more years|work=[[The Guardian]]|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2015/jul/08/exxon-climate-change-1981-climate-denier-funding|access-date=November 9, 2015}}</ref> Despite the support of a clear [[Scientific consensus on climate change|scientific consensus]], as recently as 2021 one-third of Americans [[Climate change denial|deny that human-caused climate change exists]]<ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-07-08|title=A third of Americans deny human-caused climate change exists|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2021/07/08/a-third-of-americans-deny-human-caused-climate-change-exists|access-date=2021-12-30|issn=0013-0613}}</ref> although the majority are concerned or alarmed about the issue.<ref name=":5">{{cite news |last1=Yang |first1=Maya |date=13 January 2021 |title=Six in 10 Americans 'alarmed' or 'concerned' about climate change – study |newspaper=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jan/13/record-number-americans-alarmed-about-climate-crisis |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220114032315/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jan/13/record-number-americans-alarmed-about-climate-crisis |archive-date=14 January 2022}}</ref> {{TOC level|3}}

== Greenhouse gas emissions ==

==Impact on the natural environment==
{{See also|Tropical cyclones and climate change}}
According to the [[Fifth National Climate Assessment]], climate change has many different impacts on the natural environment in the USA. Especially important are the effects on water: in some places there is a lack of water ([[drought]]) while in others there is too much ([[flooding]]).<ref name=CNN>{{cite news |last1=Nilsen |first1=Ella |title=No place in the US is safe from the climate crisis, but a new report shows where it's most severe |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2023/11/14/us/national-climate-assessment-extreme-weather-costs/index.html |access-date=7 December 2023 |agency=CNN |date=14 November 2023}}</ref>

=== Temperature and weather changes ===
{{multiple image | total_width=650
| image1= 1950- Springtime average temperature changes - US contiguous 48.svg |caption1= As a result of [[Climate change|global warming]], average springtime temperatures have risen in the 48 contiguous states since the middle of the 20th century.<ref name=YahooNews_20250320>{{cite news |last1=Bebernes |first1=Mike |title=How climate change is making spring warmer, rainier and earlier |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/how-climate-change-is-making-spring-warmer-rainier-and-earlier-213740724.html |agency=Yahoo News |date=20 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250322223840/https://www.yahoo.com/news/how-climate-change-is-making-spring-warmer-rainier-and-earlier-213740724.html |archive-date=22 March 2025 |url-status=live }} News source cites data source: NOAA.</ref>
| image2= Wildfire acres burned in the United States, OWID.svg |caption2= Average U.S. acreage burned annually by wildfires has almost tripled in three decades.<ref name=NIDX>{{cite web |title=Wildfires and Acres / Total Wildland Fires and Acres (1983-2024) |url=https://www.nifc.gov/fire-information/statistics/wildfires |website=National Interagency Fire Center |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251019191739/https://www.nifc.gov/fire-information/statistics/wildfires |archive-date=19 October 2025 |date=2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>
| image3= 1956- Number of freezing nights.svg |caption3= Analyzing >250 US cities, all but two experienced fewer freezing days in 2025 than in 1956. In 2025, on average, freezing days began 11 days later and ended 26 days earlier.<ref name=USAtoday_20260422>Data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) as presented by {{cite news |last1=Calderon |first1=Ignacio |last2=Padilla |first2=Ramon |last3=Bravo |first3=Veronica |last4=Loehrke |first4=Janet |title=Winter is shorter. See why it matters |url=https://www.usatoday.com/graphics/interactives/how-climate-change-is-impacting-winters/ |work=USA Today |date=22 April 2026}}</ref>
}}
Human-induced climate change has the potential to alter the prevalence and severity of [[extreme weather]] events such as heat waves, [[cold wave]]s, [[storm]]s, [[flood]]s and [[drought]]s.<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121212042523/http://www.epa.gov/climatechange/|title=EPA Climate Change}}  and {{cite web|url=http://epa.gov/climatechange/effects/extreme.html|title=Help finding information &#124; US EPA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110915034725/http://www.epa.gov/climatechange//effects/extreme.html|archive-date=2011-09-15|access-date=2011-09-14}} about [[Extreme weather]]</ref>  A 2012 [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) report confirmed that a strong body of evidence links global warming to an increase in heat waves, a rise in episodes of heavy rainfall and other precipitation, and more frequent [[coastal flooding]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gillis |first1=Justin |last2=Foster |first2=Joanna M. |title=Arctic Sea Ice Eyed for Clues to Weather Extremes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/29/science/earth/arctic-sea-ice-eyed-for-clues-to-weather-extremes.html |access-date=25 December 2019 |work=The New York Times |agency=The New York Times |date=28 March 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/14/science/earth/study-rising-sea-levels-a-risk-to-coastal-states.html|title=Rising Sea Levels a Growing Risk to Coastal U.S., Study Says|last=Gillis|first=Justin|date=2012-03-13|work=The New York Times}}</ref> 

According to the American government's [[Climate Change Science Program]], "With continued global warming, heat waves and heavy downpours are very likely to further increase in frequency and intensity. Substantial areas of North America are likely to have more frequent droughts of greater severity. Hurricane wind speeds, rainfall intensity, and storm surge levels are likely to increase. The strongest cold season storms are likely to become more frequent, with stronger winds and more extreme wave heights."<ref>[http://downloads.climatescience.gov/sap/sap3-3/sap3-3-final-all.pdf Weather and Climate Extremes in a Changing Climate] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110915154830/http://downloads.climatescience.gov/sap/sap3-3/sap3-3-final-all.pdf|date=September 15, 2011}} US Climate Change Science Programme June 2008 [http://www.climatescience.gov/Library/sap/sap3-3/final-report/Brochure-CCSP-3-3.pdf Summary] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111017191531/http://www.climatescience.gov/Library/sap/sap3-3/final-report/Brochure-CCSP-3-3.pdf|date=October 17, 2011}}</ref> Also, based on [[climate change|climate]]-driven weakening of day-night weather constraints, a study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' estimated that from 1975 to 2024, annual potential burning hours for [[wildfire]]s in North America rose 36%.<ref name=SciAdvances_20260417>{{cite journal |last1=Luo |first1=Kaiwei |last2=Wang |first2=Xianli |last3=Castellanos-Acuna |first3=Dante |last4=Flannigan |first4=Mike |title=A weakened diurnal weather constraint leads to longer burning hours in North America |journal=Science Advances |date=17 April 2026 |volume=12 |issue=16 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aed0725}}</ref>

In 2022, [[Climate Central]] reported that, since 1970, the U.S. is 2.6{{nbsp}}°F (1.4{{nbsp}}°C) warmer, all 49 states analyzed<sup>(Hawaii data not available)</sup> warmed by at least 1.8{{nbsp}}°F (1.0{{nbsp}}°C), and 244 of 246 U.S. cities analyzed warmed.<ref name=ClimateCentral_20220420/> Many of the fastest-warming locations were in the drought-prone Southwest, with Reno, Nevada, warming by +7.7{{nbsp}}°F (4.3{{nbsp}}°C).<ref name=ClimateCentral_20220420/> Alaska warmed by 4.3°{{nbsp}}F (2.4{{nbsp}}°C), where melting glaciers contribute to sea level rise, and permafrost melt releases greenhouse gases.<ref name=ClimateCentral_20220420>{{cite web |title=Earth Day: U.S. Warming Rankings |url=https://medialibrary.climatecentral.org/resources/earth-day-warming-rankings |website=Climate Central |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220420161432/https://medialibrary.climatecentral.org/resources/earth-day-warming-rankings |archive-date=April 20, 2022 |date=April 20, 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> Ninety percent of U.S. counties experienced a federal climate disaster between 2011 and 2021, with some having as many as 12 disasters during that time.<ref name=RebuildByDesign_20221116>{{cite web |title=Atlas of Disaster |url=https://rebuildbydesign.org/atlas-of-disaster/ |website=Rebuild by Design |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116121146/https://rebuildbydesign.org/atlas-of-disaster/ |archive-date=16 November 2022 |date=16 November 2022 |url-status=live}} ([https://rebuildbydesign.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/ATLAS-OF-DISASTER.pdf PDF of full report] and [https://web.archive.org/web/20221116141403/https://rebuildbydesign.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/ATLAS-OF-DISASTER.pdf archive thereof])</ref>

=== Extreme weather events ===
{{Update section|date=December 2021}}
{{multiple image |total_width=600
|image1= 1980- Cost of billion dollar hurricanes - US - variwide chart - NOAA data.svg |caption1= The number of $1 billion Atlantic hurricanes almost doubled from the 1980s to the 2010s, and inflation-adjusted costs have increased more than elevenfold.<ref name=NYTimes_20221202>{{cite news |last1=Philbrick |first1=Ian Pasad |last2=Wu |first2=Ashley |title=Population Growth Is Making Hurricanes More Expensive |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/02/briefing/why-hurricanes-cost-more.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=2 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221206130032/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/02/briefing/why-hurricanes-cost-more.html |archive-date=6 December 2022 |url-status=live }} Newspaper states data source: NOAA.  The increases have been attributed to climate change and to greater numbers of people moving to coastal areas.</ref>
|image2= 1910- Portion of U.S. experiencing extreme precipitation events - chart - EPA.svg |caption2= Extreme precipitation events have become more common over recent decades.<ref name=EPA_USprecipitation>Data from {{cite web |title=Climate Change Indicators: Heavy Precipitation |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-heavy-precipitation |website=EPA.gov |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220205213831/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-heavy-precipitation |archive-date=5 February 2022 |date=April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>
| image3= 2024 Climate change increasing Atlantic hurricane peak wind speeds.svg |caption3= Climate change's increase of water temperatures intensified peak wind speeds in all eleven 2024 Atlantic hurricanes.<ref name=EnvRschClimate_20241120>● {{cite journal |last1=Gilford |first1=Daniel M. |last2=Giguere |first2=Joseph |last3=Pershing |first3=Andrew J. |title=Human-caused ocean warming has intensified recent hurricanes |journal=Environmental Research: Climate |date=20 November 2024 |volume=3 |issue=4 |page=045019 |doi=10.1088/2752-5295/ad8d02|doi-access=free |bibcode=2024ERCli...3d5019G }}<br />● Explained in {{cite web |url=https://assets.ctfassets.net/cxgxgstp8r5d/gbIn7ANc1uAzb5cbwQMXC/58c45b96cac793be4cbc215502d4b4bd/Climate_Central_2024_hurricane_attribution_report.pdf |title=Climate change increased wind speeds for every 2024 Atlantic hurricane: Analysis |publisher=Climate Central |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241120111425/https://assets.ctfassets.net/cxgxgstp8r5d/gbIn7ANc1uAzb5cbwQMXC/58c45b96cac793be4cbc215502d4b4bd/Climate_Central_2024_hurricane_attribution_report.pdf |archive-date=20 November 2024 |date=20 November 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
}}
The number and severity of high-cost extreme weather events has increased in the 21st century in the United States, and some of these are [[Extreme event attribution|because of global warming]]. By August 2011 alone, the [[NOAA]] had registered nine distinct [[extreme weather]] disasters for that year, each totalling $1&nbsp;billion or more in economic losses. Total losses for 2011 were evaluated as more than $35&nbsp;billion before [[Hurricane Irene (2011)|Hurricane Irene]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Boykoff|first1=Jules|date=9 September 2011|title=Opinion: Hurricanes, floods and wildfires – but Washington won't talk global warming {{!}} Jules Boykoff|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/cifamerica/2011/sep/09/extreme-weather-climate-change|access-date=25 December 2019}}</ref>

Though the costs and frequency of cyclones have increased on the east coast, it remains unclear whether these effects have been driven primarily by climate change.<ref name="seattle" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Knutson|first1=Thomas|last2=Vecchi|first2=Gabriel|title=Historical Atlantic Hurricane and Tropical Storm Records: How well do we know the historical cyclone record?|url=https://www.gfdl.noaa.gov/historical-atlantic-hurricane-and-tropical-storm-records/|access-date=25 December 2019|website=Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory|publisher=National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration}}</ref> When correcting for this, a comprehensive 2006 article in ''[[Geophysical Research Letters]]'' found "no significant change in global net tropical cyclone activity" during past decades, a period when considerable warming of ocean water temperatures occurred. However, the study found major regional shifts, including a general rise of activity in the [[North Atlantic]] area, including on the U.S. eastern coast.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Klotzbach|first1=P.J.|year=2006|title=Trends in global tropical cyclone activity over the past twenty years (1986-2005)|journal=Geophysical Research Letters|volume=33|issue=10|page=L010805|bibcode=2006GeoRL..3310805K|doi=10.1029/2006GL025881|s2cid=18388967 }}</ref>

From 1898 through 1913, there have been 27 [[cold wave]]s which totalled 58 days. Between 1970 and 1989, there were about 12 such events. From 1989 until January 6, 2014, there were none. The one on the latter date caused consternation because of decreased frequency of such experiences.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Borenstein|first=Seth|date=January 10, 2014|title=Winters aren't colder; we're just softer|pages=8A|newspaper=Florida Today|location=Melbourne, Florida|url=http://www.bnd.com/2014/01/09/2996864/scientists-americans-are-becoming.html|access-date=January 12, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140113033838/http://www.bnd.com/2014/01/09/2996864/scientists-americans-are-becoming.html|archive-date=January 13, 2014}}</ref>

Looking at the lack of certainty as to the causes of the 1995 to present increase in Atlantic extreme storm activity, a 2007 article in ''Nature'' used proxy records of vertical wind shear and [[sea surface temperature]] to create a long-term model. The authors found that "the average frequency of major hurricanes decreased gradually from the 1760s until the early 1990s, reaching anomalously low values during the 1970s and 1980s." As well, they also found that "hurricane activity since 1995 is not unusual compared to other periods of high hurricane activity in the record and thus appears to represent a recovery to normal hurricane activity, rather than a direct response to increasing sea surface temperature."  The researches stated that future evaluations of climate change effects should focus on the magnitude of vertical wind shear for answers.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nyberg|first1=Johan|last2=Malmgren|first2=Björn A.|last3=Winter|first3=Amos|last4=Jury|first4=Mark R.|last5=Kilbourne|first5=K. Halimeda|last6=Quinn|first6=Terrence M.|year=2007|title=Low Atlantic hurricane activity in the 1970s and 1980s compared to the past 270 years|journal=Nature|volume=447|issue=7145|pages=698–702|bibcode=2007Natur.447..698N|doi=10.1038/nature05895|pmid=17554304|s2cid=4373395}}</ref>

The frequency of tornadoes in the U.S. has increased, and some of this trend takes place due to climatological changes though other factors such as better detection technologies also play large roles. According to a 2003 study in ''Climate Research'', the total tornado hazards resulting in injury, death, or economic loss "shows a steady decline since the 1980s." The authors reported that tornado "deaths and injuries decreased over the past fifty years." They state that additional research must look into regional and temporal variability in the future.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Boruff|first1=B. J.|last2=Easoz|first2=J. A.|last3=Jones|first3=S. D.|last4=Landry|first4=H. R.|last5=Mitchem|first5=J. D.|last6=Cutter|first6=S. L.|author6-link=Susan Cutter|year=2003|title=Tornado hazards in the United States|url=https://www.int-res.com/articles/cr2003/24/c024p103.pdf|journal=Climate Research|volume=24|pages=103–117|bibcode=2003ClRes..24..103B|doi=10.3354/cr024103}}</ref>

==== Heat waves ====
{{multiple image |total_width=450
|image1= 1920s -- Record high and low temperatures - U.S. - Climate Central.svg |caption1= In recent decades in the U.S., the number of record daily high temperatures has grown to more than twice that of record daily lows.<ref name=ClimateCentral_20191007>{{cite web |title=United States - Records Set By Decade |url=https://www.climatecentral.org/gallery/download/2019-fall-record-heat |website=ClimateCentral.org |publisher=Climate Central |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811225440/https://www.climatecentral.org/gallery/download/2019-fall-record-heat |archive-date=11 August 2020 |date=7 October 2019 |url-status=live }} ([https://assets.climatecentral.org/images/uploads/gallery/2019LocalRecords_US_en_title_lg.jpg Related chart] in source, and [https://web.archive.org/web/20210515050127/https://assets.climatecentral.org/images/uploads/gallery/2019LocalRecords_US_en_title_lg.jpg archive thereof]). Climate Central credits "Guy Walton and NOAA/NCEI" for data.</ref>
|image2= 1999- Heat-related mortality rate (age-adjusted, U.S.).svg |caption2= The heat-related death rate in the U.S. (heat being either an underlying or a contributing cause) has increased since the mid 2010s.<ref name=JAMA_20240826>{{cite journal |last1=Howard |first1=Jeffrey T. |last2=Androne |first2=Nicole |last3=Alcover |first3=Karl C. |last4=Santos-Lozada |first4=Alexis R. |title=Trends of Heat-Related Deaths in the US, 1999-2023 |journal=The Journal of the American Medical Association |date=26 August 2024 |volume=332 |issue=14 |pages=1203–1204 |doi=10.1001/jama.2024.16386|pmid=39186311 |pmc=11348089 }}</ref>
}}
{{ multiple image | total_width=450
| image1 = 1960- Heat wave indicators - US.svg |caption1= US heat waves have increased in frequency, average duration, and intensity.<ref name=EPA_202406/> <br /><br />Also, heat wave ''seasons'' have grown in length.<ref name=EPA_202406>{{cite web |title=Climate Change Indicators: Heat Waves |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-heat-waves |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007114317/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-heat-waves |archive-date=7 October 2024 |date=June 2024 |url-status=live }} EPA cites data source: NOAA, 2024.</ref>
| image2 = 1960- Annual average number of days spent in heat waves - US.svg |caption2= Over decades, the average number of days spent in heat waves in the U.S. annually has increased, based on increases in both the average annual number of heat waves and on their average durations.<ref name=EPA_202406/>
}}
From the 1960s the amount and longevity of heat waves have increased in the contiguous United States. The general effect of climate changes has been found in the journal ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' to have caused increased likelihood of [[heat wave]]s and extensive downpours.<ref name="seattle">{{cite news|url=http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/nationworld/2017895407_climate03.html|title=Scientists cite global warming for more heat waves, heavier rainfall|date=2 April 2012|access-date=3 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406025335/http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/nationworld/2017895407_climate03.html|archive-date=6 April 2012 |last1=Eilperin |first1=Juliet |last2=Vastag |first2=Eiperin |website=The Seattle Times}}</ref>  Concerns exist that, as stated by a [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) study in 2003, increasing "heat and humidity, at least partially related to anthropogenic climate change, suggest that a long-term increase in heat-related mortality could occur." However, the report found that, in general, "over the past 35 years, the U.S. populace has become systematically less affected by hot and humid weather conditions" while "mortality during heat stress events has declined despite increasingly stressful weather conditions in many urban and suburban areas." Thus, as stated in the study, "there is no simple association between increased heat wave duration or intensity and higher mortality rates" with current death rates being largely preventable, the NIH deeply urging [[Health care in the United States|American public health officials]] and physicians to inform patients about mitigating heat-related weather and climate effects on their bodies.<ref>Davis et al., [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1241712/pdf/ehp0111-001712.pdf Changing Heat-Related Mortality in the United States] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103172215/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1241712/pdf/ehp0111-001712.pdf |date=2017-01-03 }}, [[National Institutes of Health]]</ref>
[[File:West coast wildfires ESA22200484.jpeg|left|thumb|218x218px|Hotter temperatures and drier weather due to climate change has been linked to [[Climate change and wildfires|wildfires]], such as those in [[2020 California wildfires|California in 2020]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=A. Park |last2=Abatzoglou |first2=John T. |last3=Gershunov |first3=Alexander |last4=Guzman-Morales |first4=Janin |last5=Bishop |first5=Daniel A. |last6=Balch |first6=Jennifer K. |last7=Lettenmaier |first7=Dennis P. |date=August 2019 |title=Observed Impacts of Anthropogenic Climate Change on Wildfire in California |journal=Earth's Future |language=en |volume=7 |issue=8 |pages=892–910 |doi=10.1029/2019EF001210 |bibcode=2019EaFut...7..892W |s2cid=199105541 |issn=2328-4277|doi-access=free }}</ref>]]
In 2021 an [[2021 Western North America heat wave|unprecedented heat wave occurred in the northwest]] linked to climate change.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Anne C. |first1=Mulkern |title=Unprecedented Heat Wave in Pacific Northwest Driven by Climate Change |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/unprecedented-heat-wave-in-pacific-northwest-driven-by-climate-change/ |website=Scientific American |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref> The heatwave brought temperatures close to {{convert|122|F|abbr=on}} to many areas that generally do not experience such heat like [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] and [[Seattle]], killed 500 people and caused 180 wildfires in British Columbia in Canada. The heat wave was made 150 times more likely by climate change.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schiermeier |first1=Quirin |title=Climate change made North America's deadly heatwave 150 times more likely |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-021-01869-0 |journal=Nature |year=2021 |doi=10.1038/d41586-021-01869-0 |pmid=34239114 |s2cid=235775516 |access-date=20 July 2021}}</ref> According to [[World Weather Attribution]] such events occur every 1,000 years in today climate but if the temperature will rise by 2 degrees above preindustrial levels, such events will occur each 5–10 years. However, it was more severe than predicted climate models. Significant impacts in that area were expected in the Pacific Northwest only by the middle of the 21st century.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chow |first1=Denise |title=How climate change 'loads the dice' for heat waves |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/environment/heat-wave-west-coast-hints-climate-change-scientists-say-rcna1297 |access-date=20 July 2021 |agency=NBC |date=30 June 2021}}</ref> Currently, scientists search ways to make the predictions more accurate because: "researchers need to assess whether places such as North America or Germany will face extremes like the heat dome and the floods every 20 years, 10 years, 5 years – or maybe even every year. This level of accuracy currently isn't possible".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harrabin |first1=Roger |title=Climate change: Science failed to predict flood and heat intensity |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-57863205 |access-date=20 July 2021 |agency=BBC |date=16 July 2021}}</ref>

The leading cause of animal extinction rates within the United States is due to rising temperatures and heat waves. ''Science'' writer Mark C. Urban states, "Species must disperse into newly suitable habitats as fast as climate shifts across landscapes."<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Urban |first=Mark C. |date=2015 |title=Accelerating extinction risk from climate change |journal=Science |volume=348 |issue=6234 |pages=571–573 |doi=10.1126/science.aaa4984 |jstor=24747394 |pmid=25931559 |bibcode=2015Sci...348..571U |s2cid=206634789 |issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free }}</ref> The risk of extinction among species isn't as detrimental in the United States as compared to other countries such as, "South America, Australia, and New Zealand."<ref name=":1" /> Due to these species needing to adapt as fast as rising temperature, Urban stresses the idea of countries who are at great risk, and even those who aren't to adapt strategies to limit further advances in rising temperatures and climate change.<ref name=":1" />

{{Further|Droughts in the United States|Southwestern North American megadrought|2020–21 North American drought}}
A 2006 study suggested that drought conditions appear to be worsening in the [[American southwest|southwest]] while improving in the [[Northeastern United States|northeast]].<ref name="letters">{{Cite journal |last1=Andreadis |first1=K. M. |last2=Lettenmaier |first2=D. P. |author2-link=Dennis P. Lettenmaier |year=2006 |title=Trends in 20th century drought over the continental United States |journal=[[Geophysical Research Letters]] |volume=33 |issue=10 |pages=n/a |bibcode=2006GeoRL..3310403A |doi=10.1029/2006GL025711 |s2cid=133980280|doi-access=free }}</ref> In the years 2000–2021 the [[southwestern North American megadrought]] persisted. Climate change increased temperature, reduced the amount of precipitation, decreased snowpack and increased the ability of air to soak humidity, helping to create arid conditions. As of 2021 the drought was the most severe in the last 500 years.<ref>{{cite web |last1=BORUNDA |first1=ALEJANDRA |title='Megadrought' persists in western U.S., as another extremely dry year develops |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/megadrought-persists-in-western-us-as-another-extremely-dry-year-develops |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507162414/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/megadrought-persists-in-western-us-as-another-extremely-dry-year-develops |archive-date=May 7, 2021 |website=National Geographic |date=7 May 2021 |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> As of 30 June 2021 61% of continental USA were in drought conditions. Demand for water and cooling rose.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Buchholz |first1=Katharina |title=40 weeks and counting: This chart shows the severity of the U.S. drought |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2021/06/drought-us-climate-change-environment-weather |website=World Economic Forum |date=30 June 2021 |access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref> In June 2021 water restrictions entered into force in [[California]]. A 2007 peer-reviewed study found that climate-induced droughts in regions like California have already caused observable ecological disruptions, including reduced plant productivity, altered species distributions, and increased mortality in amphibians and small mammals.<ref>Parmesan, C., Root, T. L., & Willig, M. R. (2007). Impacts of extreme weather and climate on terrestrial biota. Climatic Change, 82(1), 537–550. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-007-9377-6</ref> Climate change is responsible for 50% of the severity of the drought in California.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Canon |first1=Gabrielle |title='Truly an emergency': how drought returned to California – and what lies ahead |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/jun/07/california-drought-oregon-west-climate-change |access-date=8 June 2021 |agency=The Guardian |date=7 June 2021}}</ref> Water restrictions are expected to expand on many states in the US west, farmers are already affected. In San Francisco a hydropower plant can stop work due to lack of water.<ref>{{cite news |last1=B. Wolf |first1=Zachary |title=The American West is drying out. Things will get ugly |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2021/06/19/politics/what-matters-climate-change-western-drought/index.html |access-date=16 July 2021 |agency=CNN |date=20 June 2021}}</ref>


A study published in ''[[Nature Climate Change]]'' concluded that 2000–2021 was the driest 22-year period in southwestern North America since at least 800 CE.<ref name=NatureClimateChange_20220214>{{cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=A. Park |last2=Cook |first2=Benjamin I. |last3=Smerdon |first3=Jason E. |title=Rapid intensification of the emerging southwestern North American megadrought in 2020–2021 |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=February 2022 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=232–234 |doi=10.1038/s41558-022-01290-z |bibcode=2022NatCC..12..232W |s2cid=246815806 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-022-01290-z.epdf}}</ref> One of the study's researchers said that, without climate change, the drought would probably have ended in 2005.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fountain |first1=Henry |title=How Bad Is the Western Drought? Worst in 12 Centuries, Study Finds. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/14/climate/western-drought-megadrought.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=14 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220217114116/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/14/climate/western-drought-megadrought.html |archive-date=17 February 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> 42% of the megadrought's severity is said to be attributable to temperature rise as a result of climate change, with 88% of the area being drought-stricken.<ref name=LATimes_20220214/> In 2020–2021, the Colorado River, feeding seven states, shrank to the lowest two-year average in more than a century of record keeping.<ref name=LATimes_20220214>{{cite news |last1=James |first1=Ian |title=Western megadrought is worst in 1,200 years, intensified by climate change, study finds |url=https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2022-02-14/western-megadrought-driest-in-1200-years |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=14 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220217160134/https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2022-02-14/western-megadrought-driest-in-1200-years |archive-date=17 February 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====Megafloods====
A study published in ''[[Science Advances]]'' in 2022 stated that climate-caused changes in [[atmospheric river]]s affecting California had already doubled the likelihood of [[Outburst flood|megaflood]]s—which can involve {{convert|100|in|cm}} of rain and/or melted snow in the mountains per month, or {{convert|25 to 34|ft|m}} of snow in the [[Sierra Nevada]]—and runoff in a future extreme storm scenario is predicted to be 200 to 400% greater than historical values in the Sierra Nevada.<ref name=ScienceAdvances_20220812>{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Xingying |last2=Swain |first2=Daniel L |title=Climate change is increasing the risk of a California megaflood |journal=Science Advances |date=12 August 2022 |volume=8 |issue=32 |article-number=eabq0995 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.abq0995 |pmid=35960799 |pmc=9374343 |bibcode=2022SciA....8..995H }} Explained by {{cite news |last1=Cappucci |first1=Matthew |title=A 'megaflood' in California could drop 100 inches of rain, scientists warn |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2022/08/12/megaflood-california-flood-rain-climate/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=12 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814063213/https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2022/08/12/megaflood-california-flood-rain-climate/ |archive-date=14 August 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Weakened polar vortex jet stream ====
Climate scientists have hypothesised that the stratospheric [[polar vortex]] [[jet stream]] will gradually weaken as a result of global warming and thus influence U.S. conditions.<ref>Baek-Min Kim, et al., ''Weakening of the stratospheric polar vortex by Arctic sea-ice loss,'' Nature Communications 5, Article number: 4646 {{doi|10.1038/ncomms5646}}</ref><ref name="norm">[http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/a-wacky-jet-stream-is-making-our-weather-severe/ ''A Wacky Jet Stream Is Making Our Weather Severe; Extreme summers and winters of the past four years could become the norm''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150214021249/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/a-wacky-jet-stream-is-making-our-weather-severe/ |date=2015-02-14 }} Jeff Masters [[Scientific American]] December 2014 issue Volume 311, Issue 6</ref><ref>[http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/persistent-warming-drives-big-arctic-changes/ ''Persistent Warming Drives Big Arctic Changes; The latest Arctic Report Card details the changes due to long-term climate change''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150116030811/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/persistent-warming-drives-big-arctic-changes/ |date=2015-01-16 }} December 17, 2014 [[Scientific American]]</ref> This trend could possibly cause changes in the future such as increasing frost in certain areas. The magazine ''[[Scientific American]]'' noted in December 2014 that ice cover on the [[Great Lakes]] had recently "reached its second-greatest extent on record", showing climate variability.<ref name="norm" /> In February 2021 when the United States, officially rejoined the Paris Agreement, [[John Kerry]] spoke about it, mentioning the [[February 13–17, 2021 North American winter storm|latest extreme cold events in the USA]] that in his opinion: "related to climate because the polar vortex penetrates further south because of the weakening of the jet stream related to warming."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Finnegan |first1=Conor |title='The decisive decade': Biden climate envoy John Kerry sounds alarm as US rejoins Paris climate accord |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/decisive-decade-biden-climate-envoy-john-kerry-sounds/story?id=76002336 |access-date=21 February 2021 |agency=ABC News |date=19 February 2021}}</ref> This opinion is shared by many climate scientists.<ref>{{cite news |last1=BERARDELLI |first1=JEFF |title=Climate change and record cold: What's behind the arctic extremes in Texas |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/climate-change-texas-winter-storms-arctic-cold/ |access-date=22 February 2021 |agency=CBC News |date=20 February 2021}}</ref>

=== Sea level rise ===
[[File:2050 Projected sea level rise - United States coasts - NOAA.svg |thumb|NOAA predicts different levels of sea level rise through 2050 for the various U.S. coastlines (shown), further projecting that a failure to curb future emissions could cause a total of 3.5-7 feet (1.1-2.1 m) rise by 2100.<ref name=NOAA_SeaLevelRiseTechReport_20220200/>]]
{{multiple image |total_width=600
| image1= 1950- High tide flooding, by year - NOAA tide gauges (U.S.).svg | caption1= High tide flooding, also called tidal flooding, has become much more common in the past seven decades.<ref name=N0AA_HighTideFlooding_201802>{{cite web |last1=Sweet |first1=William V. |last2=Dusek |first2=Greg |last3=Obeysekera |first3=Jayantha |last4=Marra |first4=John J. |title=Patterns and Projections of High Tide Flooding Along the U.S. Coastline Using a Common Impact Threshold |url=https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/publications/techrpt86_PaP_of_HTFlooding.pdf |website=tidesandcurrents.NOAA.gov |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221015221519/https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/publications/techrpt86_PaP_of_HTFlooding.pdf |archive-date=15 October 2022 |page=4 |date=February 2018 |quote=Fig. 2b |url-status=live }}</ref>
| image2= 20201112 Tidal flooding graph - Annapolis, Maryland.svg | caption2= Adaptation measures for tidal flooding, such as sea walls and building up roadway heights, are predicted to last only a few decades.<ref name=NASA_BeatingBackTides>{{cite web |title=Beating Back the Tides |url=https://sealevel.nasa.gov/news/203/beating-back-the-tides |website=SeaLevel.NASA.gov |publisher=NASA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111230934/https://sealevel.nasa.gov/news/203/beating-back-the-tides |archive-date=November 11, 2020 |date=November 11, 2020 |url-status=live }} High-tide flooding is also known as tidal flooding, sunny day flooding and nuisance flooding.</ref>
| image3=2000- Declared flood disasters - US.svg | caption3= The number of floods declared to be disasters by the [[Federal Emergency Management Agency]] (FEMA) has increased, especially since 2010.<ref name=NYTimes_20241022>{{cite news |last1=Flavelle |first1=Christopher |title=America's Flooding Problem |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/22/briefing/americas-flooding-problem.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=22 October 2024 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241022105521/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/22/briefing/americas-flooding-problem.html |archive-date=22 October 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>
}}
[[Sea level rise]] has taken place in the U.S. for decades, going back to the 19th century. 40% of the U.S. population live near a coast, and are vulnerable to sea level rise. For almost all coastal areas of the US, except for Alaska, the future rise in sea level is expected to be higher than the global average.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lindsey |first1=Rebecca |title=Climate Change: Global Sea Level |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level |date=14 August 2020 |website=Climate.gov |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220216080655/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level |archive-date=16 February 2022 }}</ref> [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]]'s ''Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios'' said in February 2022 that relative sea level along the contiguous U.S. coastline is expected to rise on average as much over the next 30 years—{{convert|25|to|30|cm|in}}—as it has over the preceding 100 years.<ref name=NOAA_20220215>{{cite web |title=Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United States / Updated Mean Projections and Extreme Water Level Probabilities Along U.S. Coastlines / NOAA Technical Report NOS 01 / Executive Summary |url=https://aambpublicoceanservice.blob.core.windows.net/oceanserviceprod/hazards/sealevelrise/EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY.pdf |website=NOAA.gov |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220216014443/https://aambpublicoceanservice.blob.core.windows.net/oceanserviceprod/hazards/sealevelrise/EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY.pdf |archive-date=16 February 2022 |date=15 February 2022 |url-status=live}} ([https://web.archive.org/web/20220216054626/https://aambpublicoceanservice.blob.core.windows.net/oceanserviceprod/hazards/sealevelrise/noaa-nos-techrpt01-global-regional-SLR-scenarios-US.pdf Full report])</ref>

More specifically, NOAA's February 2022 ''Sea Level Rise Technical Report'' estimated that rise in the following three decades is anticipated to be, on average: 10-14 inches (0.25-0.35 m) for the East coast; 14-18 inches (0.35-0.45 m) for the Gulf coast; 4-8 inches (0.1-0.2 m) for the West coast; 8-10 inches (0.2-0.25 m) for the Caribbean; 6-8 inches (0.15-0.2 m) for the Hawaiian Islands; and 8-10 inches (0.2-0.25 m) for northern Alaska.<ref name=NOAA_SeaLevelRiseTechReport_20220200/> Also, by 2050, "moderate" (typically damaging) flooding is expected to occur, on average, more than 10 times as often as it does today, and "major" (often destructive) flooding is expected to occur five times as often as it does today.<ref name=NOAA_SeaLevelRiseTechReport_20220200>{{cite web |title=2022 Sea Level Rise Technical Report |url=https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/hazards/sealevelrise/sealevelrise-tech-report.html |publisher=National Ocean Service, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129070303/https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/hazards/sealevelrise/sealevelrise-tech-report.html |archive-date=November 29, 2022 |date=February 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[United States Geological Survey|U.S. Geological Survey]] has conducted research on sea level rise, addressing coastal vulnerability, and incorporating six physical variables to analyze the changes in sea level: geomorphology, coastal slope (percent), rate of relative sea level rise (mm/yr), shoreline erosion and acceleration rates (m/yr), mean tidal range (m), and mean wave height (m).<ref>"[https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/risk.html National Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability to Sea-Level Rise: Preliminary Results for the U.S. Pacific Coast] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191006085214/https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/risk.html |date=2019-10-06 }}," USGS</ref> The research was conducted on the various coastline areas of the United States. Along the Pacific coast, the most vulnerable areas are low-lying beaches, and "their susceptibility is primarily a function of geomorphology and coastal slope."<ref>[https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/res.html National Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability to Sea-Level Rise: Preliminary Results for the U.S. Pacific Coast] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220119094648/http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/res.html |date=2022-01-19 }}, USGS</ref> From research along the Atlantic coast, the most vulnerable areas to sea level rise were found to be along the Mid-Atlantic coast (Maryland to North Carolina) and Northern Florida, since these are "typically high-energy coastlines where the regional coastal slope is low and where the major landform type is a barrier island."<ref>"[https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1999/of99-593/pages/res.html National Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability to Sea-Level Rise: Preliminary Results for the U.S. Atlantic Coast] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220119043426/http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1999/of99-593/pages/res.html |date=2022-01-19 }}," USGS</ref> For the Gulf coast, the most vulnerable areas are along the Louisiana-Texas coast. According to the results, "the highest-vulnerability areas are typically lower-lying beach and marsh areas; their susceptibility is primarily a function of geomorphology, coastal slope and rate of relative sea-level rise."<ref>"[https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-179/pages/res.html National Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability to Sea-Level Rise: Preliminary Results for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico Coast] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220209090953/https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-179/pages/res.html |date=2022-02-09 }}," USGS</ref>

Coastal regions would be most affected by rising sea levels. The increase in sea level along the coasts of continents, especially [[North America]] are much more significant than the global average. According to 2007 estimates by the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC), "global average sea level will rise between 0.6 and 2 feet (0.18 to 0.59 meters) in the next century.<ref name="EPA">"[http://www.epa.gov/climatechange/effects/coastal/index.html Coastal Zones and Sea Level Rise] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120511021904/http://www.epa.gov/climatechange/effects/coastal/index.html |date=2012-05-11 }}," U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 14 April 2011</ref> Along the U.S. [[Mid-Atlantic states|Mid-Atlantic]] and Gulf Coasts, however, the sea level rose {{convert|5|to|6|in|abbr=on}} in the last century, which is more than the global average. This is due to the subsiding of coastal lands.<ref name="EPA" /> The sea level along the U.S. Pacific coast has also increased more than the global average, but less than along the Atlantic coast. This can be explained by the varying continental margins along both coasts; the Atlantic type continental margin is characterized by a wide, gently sloping continental shelf, while the Pacific type continental margin incorporates a narrow shelf and slope descending into a deep trench.<ref>Tripati, Aradhna, Lab 5¬-Istostasy, Physiography Reading, E&SSCI15-1, [[UCLA]], 2012</ref> Since low-sloping coastal regions should retreat faster than higher-sloping regions, the Atlantic coast is more vulnerable to sea level rise than the Pacific coast.<ref>"[https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/risk.html National Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability to Sea-Level Rise: Preliminary Results for the U.S. Pacific Coast] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191006085214/https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2000/of00-178/pages/risk.html |date=2019-10-06 }}," [[U.S. Geological Survey]], 2001</ref>

A rise in sea level will have a negative impact not only on coastal property and economy, but on our supply of fresh water. According to the EPA, "Rising sea level increases the salinity of both surface water and ground water through salt water intrusion."<ref name="CoastalZones">"Coastal Zones and Sea Level Rise," EPA</ref> Coastal estuaries and aquifers are therefore at a high risk of becoming too [[Saline water|saline]] from rising sea levels. With respect to estuaries, an increase in salinity would threaten aquatic animals and plants that cannot tolerate high levels of salinity. Aquifers often serve as a primary water supply to surrounding areas, such as Florida's Biscayne aquifer, which receives freshwater from the Everglades and then supplies water to the Florida Keys. Rising sea levels would submerge low-lying areas of the Everglades, and salinity would greatly increase in portions of the aquifer.<ref name="CoastalZones" /> The considerable rise in sea level and the decreasing amounts of freshwater along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts would make those areas rather uninhabitable. Many economists predict that global warming will be one of the main economic threats to the West Coast, specifically in California. "Low-lying coastal areas, such as along the Gulf Coast, are particularly vulnerable to sea-level rise and stronger storms—and those risks are reflected in rising insurance rates and premiums. In Florida, for example, the average price of a homeowners' policy increased by 77 percent between 2001 and 2006."<ref>{{cite web|last=Coplin|first=Kelly|title=How Climate Change Will Affect Home Value|url=http://alumni.stanford.edu/get/page/magazine/article/?article_id=30265|access-date=2013-10-27|publisher=Stanford University|archive-date=2019-06-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190611113804/https://alumni.stanford.edu/get/page/magazine/article/?article_id=30265}}</ref>

Another important coastal habitat that is threatened by sea level rise is [[wetland]]s, which "occur along the margins of estuaries and other shore areas that are protected from the open ocean and include swamps, tidal flats, coastal marshes and bayous."<ref>{{harv|Thurman|Trujillo|2005|p=335}}</ref> Wetlands are extremely vulnerable to rising sea levels, since they are within several feet of sea level. The threat posed to wetlands is serious, due to the fact that they are highly productive [[ecosystem]]s, and they have an enormous impact on the economy of surrounding areas. Wetlands in the U.S. are rapidly disappearing due to an increase in housing, industry, and agriculture, and rising sea levels contribute to this dangerous trend. As a result of rising sea levels, the outer boundaries of wetlands tend to erode, forming new wetlands more inland. According to the EPA, "the amount of newly created wetlands, however, could be much smaller than the lost area of wetlands— especially in developed areas protected with bulkheads, dikes, and other structures that keep new wetlands from forming inland."<ref name="CoastalZones"/> When estimating a sea level rise within the next century of 50&nbsp;cm (20 inches), the U.S. would lose 38% to 61% of its existing coastal wetlands.<ref>{{harv|Thurman|Trujillo|2005|p=336}}</ref>

Beachfront property is at risk from eroding land and rising sea levels. Since the threat posed by rising sea levels has become more prominent, property owners and local government have taken measures to prepare for the worst. For example, "Maine has enacted a policy declaring that shorefront buildings will have to be moved to enable beaches and wetlands to migrate inland to higher ground."<ref name="Titus-1989-p119">{{harv|Titus|1989|page=119}}</ref> Additionally, many coastal states add sand to their beaches to offset shore [[erosion]], and many property owners have elevated their structures in low-lying areas. As a result of the erosion and ruin of properties by large storms on coastal lands, governments have looked into buying land and having residents relocate further inland.<ref name="Robertson">{{cite news|last=Robertson|first=Ricky|title=Crop Changes National Geographic|work=[[National Geographic Society|National Geographic]]|location=Madison|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/climate-change/how-to-live-with-it/water.html|access-date=3 March 2016}}</ref>

=== Freshwater ecosystems ===
A study published in 2009 delves into the effects to be felt by [[River ecosystem|lotic]] (flowing) and [[Lake ecosystem|lentic]] (still) [[freshwater ecosystem]]s in the American Northeast. According to the study, persistent rainfall, typically felt year round, will begin to diminish and rates of evaporation will increase, resulting in drier summers and more sporadic periods of precipitation throughout the year.<ref name="Brooks2009">{{cite journal |last1=Brooks |first1=Robert T. |date=6 January 2009 |title=Potential impacts of global climate change on the hydrology and ecology of ephemeral freshwater systems of the forests of the northeastern United States |journal=Climatic Change |volume=95 |issue=3–4 |pages=469–483 |bibcode=2009ClCh...95..469B |doi=10.1007/s10584-008-9531-9 |s2cid=154713741}}</ref> Additionally, a decrease in snowfall is expected, which leads to less runoff in the spring when snow thaws and enters the watershed, resulting in lower-flowing fresh water rivers.<ref name="Brooks2009" /> This decrease in snowfall also leads to increased runoff during winter months, as rainfall cannot permeate the frozen ground usually covered by water-absorbing snow.<ref name="Brooks2009" /> These effects on the water cycle will wreak havoc for indigenous species residing in fresh water lakes and streams.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brooks |first=Robert T. |date=2021-08-01 |title=Potential impacts of global climate change on the hydrology and ecology of ephemeral freshwater systems of the forests of the northeastern United States |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10584-008-9531-9 |journal=Climatic Change |language=en |volume=95 |issue=3 |pages=469–483 |doi=10.1007/s10584-008-9531-9 |bibcode=2009ClCh...95..469B |issn=1573-1480}}</ref>

== Socioeconomic impacts ==
[[File:20210824 Survey - climate change impact on daily life - European Investment Bank.svg|thumb|right| At least 72% of Chinese, American and European respondents to a 2020−2021 [[European Investment Bank]] climate survey stated that climate change had an impact on everyday life.]]

The [[Fifth National Climate Assessment]] states that climate change impacts communities over all the territory of the United States. The impacts differ from state to state. The human and economic toll is high. Scientists now can say with relatively high confidence how much climate change impacted a specific meteorological event. The impacts mentioned in the report include, increase in frequency and magnitude of [[heat wave]]s, [[drought]]s, [[flooding|floods]], [[hurricanes]] and more.<ref name=CNN/>

An article in ''Science'' predicts that the [[Southern United States|Southern states]], such as Texas, Florida, and the [[Deep South]] will be economically affected by climate change more severely than northern states (some of which would even gain benefits), but that economic impacts of climate change would likely exacerbate preexisting [[Income inequality in the United States|economic inequality]] in the country.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hsiang|first1=Solomon|last2=Kopp|first2=Robert|last3=Jina|first3=Amir|last4=Rising|first4=James|last5=Delgado|first5=Michael|last6=Mohan|first6=Shashank|last7=Rasmussen|first7=D. J.|last8=Muir-Wood|first8=Robert|last9=Wilson|first9=Paul|last10=Oppenheimer|first10=Michael|last11=Larsen|first11=Kate|date=2017-06-30|title=Estimating economic damage from climate change in the United States|journal=Science|language=en|volume=356|issue=6345|pages=1362–1369|doi=10.1126/science.aal4369|issn=0036-8075|pmid=28663496|bibcode=2017Sci...356.1362H|s2cid=217546780|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Heidari|first1=Hadi|last2=Arabi|first2=Mazdak|last3=Warziniack|first3=Travis|last4=Kao|first4=Shih-Chieh|date=June 2021|title=Shifts in hydroclimatology of US megaregions in response to A 2021 survey of 1,422 members of the [[American Economic Association]] found that 86 percent of professional economists generally agreed with the statement: "Climate change poses a major risk to the US economy."<ref name="2021 AEA survey">{{cite journal|last1=Geide-Stevenson|first1=Doris|last2=La Parra-Perez|first2=Alvaro|year=2024|title=Consensus among economists 2020—A sharpening of the 2024}}</ref>

A 2026 study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' estimated that, from 1990 through 2020, [[greenhouse gas emissions|carbon dioxide emissions]] in the US caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020, with about 30% occurring within the US itself.<ref name=Nature_20260325/> The researchers said that future damages from past emissions are at least an order of magnitude larger than historical damages from the same emissions.<ref name=Nature_20260325>{{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6}}</ref>
