===Cost of disaster relief===
[[File:20201211 Billion dollar events related to climate change - U.S. -en.svg |thumb| NOAA's [[National Centers for Environmental Information]] (NCEI) has reported growing numbers of weather and climate-related events costing at least a billion dollars,<ref name=BillionDollarDisastersNOAA_2023>Annual data: {{cite web |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters / United States Billion-Dollar Disaster Events 1980- (CPI-Adjusted) |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/time-series/US |publisher=National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240113044752/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/time-series/US |archive-date=13 January 2024 |url-status=live }} Click "Access data".</ref> exceeding the 1980–2019 [[Consumer price index|inflation-adjusted]] average of 6.6 such events.<ref name=NCEI_thru202009>{{cite journal |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: Overview / 2020 in Progress |url=https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/billions/ |website=NCDC.NOAA |publisher=National Centers for Environmental Information (NCDC, part of NOAA) |access-date=11 December 2020 |doi=10.25921/stkw-7w73 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210044128/https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/billions/ |archive-date=10 December 2020 |date=December 2020 |url-status=live|last1=Smith |first1=Adam B. |author2=NOAA National Centers For Environmental Information }} and {{cite web |title=Contiguous U.S. ranked fifth warmest during 2020; Alaska experienced its coldest year since 2012 / 2020 Billion Dollar Disasters and Other Notable Extremes |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202012 |website=NCEI.NOAA.gov |publisher=NOAA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108185719/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202012 |archive-date=8 January 2021 |date=January 2021 |url-status=live }} For 2021 data: {{cite web |title=Calculating the Cost of Weather and Climate Disasters / Seven things to know about NCEI's U.S. billion-dollar disasters data |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/calculating-cost-weather-and-climate-disasters |website=ncei.noaa.gov |date=6 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111143455/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/calculating-cost-weather-and-climate-disasters |archive-date=11 January 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
Since 1980, the United States has experienced 323 in climate and weather related disasters, which have cost more than $2.195 trillion in total.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NCEI.Monitoring.Info@noaa.gov |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters {{!}} National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/ |access-date=2022-05-26 |website=www.ncei.noaa.gov |language=en}}</ref> According to NOAA's [[National Centers for Environmental Information]] (NCEI), 2021 witnessed 20 climate-related disasters, each exceeding losses of $1 billion.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last= |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: Overview {{!}} National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) |url=https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/billions/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510033505/http://www.ncdc.noaa.gov:80/billions/ |archive-date=2012-05-10 |access-date=2021-12-05 |website=www.ncdc.noaa.gov |language=en}}</ref>

These increasingly common and severe weather events have put pressure on existing disaster-relief efforts. For instance, the increasing rate of wildfires, the increasing length of the fire season, and increasing severity have put pressure on national and international resources. In the US, federal firefighting efforts surpassed $2 billion a year for the first time in 2017, and this expense was repeated in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Suppression Costs {{!}} National Interagency Fire Center |url=https://www.nifc.gov/fire-information/statistics/suppression-costs |access-date=2022-03-10 |website=www.nifc.gov}}</ref> At the same time, internationally shared capital, such as firefighting planes, has experienced increasing demand, requiring new investment.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Cave|first1=Damien|date=21 November 2019|title=The World Burns All Year. Are There Enough Planes to Douse the Flames?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/11/21/world/australia/fires-water-tankers-climate-change.html|access-date=12 December 2019|work=The New York Times}}</ref>

=== Culture ===
[[File:Portland skyline during 2015 Oregon wildfires - Big Pink, Portland sign from Burnside Bridge.jpg|thumb|Air pollution on the Portland skyline, 2015 wildfires]]
By August 2022, an increasing number of outdoor theater and musical performances, including the [[Oregon Shakespeare Festival]] and ''[[Eureka Springs, Arkansas#20th century|The Great Passion Play]]'' in Arkansas, were being canceled due to wildfire smoke, extreme heat, and heavy rains.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Paulson |first=Michael |date=2022-08-11 |title=Too Darn Hot: How Summer Stages Are Threatened by Climate Change |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/11/arts/climate-change-outdoor-theater.html |access-date=2022-08-11 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

===Health impacts===
Climate change is expected to pose increased [[Effects of climate change on human health|threats to human health]].<ref name=StateOfKnowledge /> The physical and psychological effects of climate change in the United States on human health will likely depend on specific location. Researchers have determined that locations of concern are "coastal regions, islands, deserts in the southwest, vector-borne and zoonotic disease border regions, cities, and the U.S. Arctic (Alaska)".<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=Jeremy J. |last2=Malilay |first2=Josephine N. |last3=Parkinson |first3=Alan J. |date=2008-11-01 |title=Climate Change: The Importance of Place |url=https://www.ajpmonline.org/article/S0749-3797(08)00689-2/abstract |journal=American Journal of Preventive Medicine |language=English |volume=35 |issue=5 |page=473 |doi=10.1016/j.amepre.2008.08.024 |pmid=18929973 |issn=0749-3797|doi-access=free }}</ref> Physical impacts include injury and illness from both initial incidents and secondary effects of major weather events or the changing climate. Psychological impacts include post-traumatic stress disorder, forced emigration and social loss related to people's attachment to place and identity.<ref name=":2" /> The impacts these have on the individual are felt throughout the community as well. Displacement after a major weather event harms a community's capacity to engage and become resilient.<ref name=":2" />

===Immigration===
[[Climate change]] has increased migration to the United States from [[Central America]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Lee|first1=Deborah Jian|title=How climate change influences immigration to the United States|url=https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2019/12/how-climate-change-influences-immigration-to-the-united-states/|access-date=3 November 2020|website=Yale Climate Connections|date=4 December 2019|publisher=ChavoBart Digital Media}}</ref> Due to [[Sea level rise|rising sea levels]] in coastal areas in the [[United States]], it is projected that 13 million Americans will be forced to move away from submerged coastlines.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Abrahm |last=Lustgarten|author-link=Abrahm Lustgarten|title=Climate Change Will Force a New American Migration |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/climate-change-will-force-a-new-american-migration?token=-L_tfnbCuURPOGrhh5EWTKvU7C44wJHC |access-date=2022-05-27 |website=ProPublica |date=15 September 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

===Indigenous peoples===
{{see also|Climate change and Indigenous peoples}}
According to Indigenous scholars such as Daniel Wildcat, [[Zoe Todd]], and [[Kyle Powys Whyte|Kyle Whyte]], the experience of modern climate change echoes previous experiences of environmental damage and territorial displacement brought about by European settlement.<ref name=DavisTodd_Decolonizing/><ref name="WhyteDecolonizing" /> Colonial practices such as damming and deforestation forced Indigenous peoples to adapt to unfamiliar climates and environments.<ref name=DavisTodd_Decolonizing>{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Heather |last2=Todd |first2=Zoe |title=On the Importance of a Date, or Decolonizing the Anthropocene |url=https://acme-journal.org/index.php/acme/article/view/1539/1303 |journal=ACME: An International Journal for Critical Geographies |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=761–780 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201222417/https://acme-journal.org/index.php/acme/article/view/1539/1303 |archive-date=December 1, 2021 |date=June 2016 |url-status=live }} Archive has download button.</ref> Thus, the impacts of global climate change are viewed as being not separate from but rather an intensification of the impacts of [[settler colonialism]].<ref name=WhyteDecolonizing>{{Cite journal|last=Whyte|first=Kyle Powys|date=Fall 2017|title=Indigenous Climate Change Studies: Indigenizing Futures, Decolonizing the Anthropocene|url=https://www.academia.edu/31177682 |journal=English Language Notes |volume=55|issue=1–2|pages=153–162|doi=10.1215/00138282-55.1-2.153|s2cid=132153346}}</ref>

Indigenous scholars and activists argue that colonialist policies—prioritizing [[Exploitation of natural resources|exploitation]] and [[Extractivism|commoditization]] of resources over Indigenous teachings favoring [[Ecological stability|environmental stability]] and seeking a [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] relation with nature<ref name=EMBO_200605>{{cite journal |last1=Mazzocchi |first1=Fulvio |title=Western science and traditional knowledge: Despite their variations, different forms of knowledge can learn from each other |journal=[[EMBO Reports]] |date=May 2006 |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=463–466 |doi=10.1038/sj.embor.7400693 |pmid=16670675 |pmc=1479546}}</ref>—have fueled climate change.<ref name=WhyteDistopiaNow>{{Cite journal |last=Whyte |first=Kyle Powys |title=Our Ancestors' Dystopia Now: Indigenous Conservation and the Anthropocene |website=SSRN.com |url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2770047 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210612025959/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2770047 |archive-date=June 12, 2021 |url-status=live |date=2016 |ssrn=2770047 |quote=(In) ''Routledge Companion to the Environmental Humanities'', Forthcoming }} Full article is free, but requires online registration.</ref> The United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs has stated that "Indigenous peoples are among the first to face the direct consequences of climate change, due to their dependence upon, and close relationship, with the environment and its resources."<ref name="UN_2017">{{cite web |title=Climate change / The effects of climate change on indigenous peoples |url=https://www.un.org/development/desa/indigenouspeoples/climate-change.html |website=UN.org |publisher=United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113073917/https://www.un.org/development/desa/indigenouspeoples/climate-change.html |archive-date=November 13, 2017 |date=2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> More specifically, North American tribes' present-day lands are on average more exposed to extreme heat and receive less precipitation, nearly half of tribes experience heightened wildfire hazard exposure, and tribes' present-day lands have less mineral value potential.<ref name=Science_20211029>{{cite journal |last1=Farrell |first1=Justin |last2=Burow |first2=Paul Berne |last3=McConnell |first3=Kathryn |last4=Bayham |first4=Jude |last5=Whyte |first5=Kyle |last6=Koss |first6=Gal |title=Effects of land dispossession and forced migration on Indigenous peoples in North America |journal=Science |date=October 29, 2021 |volume=374 |issue=6567 |article-number=eabe4943 |doi=10.1126/science.abe4943 |pmid=34709911 |s2cid=240153327 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abe4943 }}</ref>

Native peoples residing on the Gulf and West Coasts are affected by the rising sea temperatures because that makes the fish and shellfish, that they rely on for food and cultural activities, more susceptible to contamination.<ref name="auto1" /> In California, climate change has wiped out much of the [[Salmonidae|salmonids]] and [[acorn]]s that were a significant portion of the [[Karuk]] people's traditional diet.<ref name="nca2014.globalchange.gov">{{cite web|last1=Bennet|first1=T.M. Bull|last2=Maynard|first2=Nancy G|display-authors=1|date=2014|title=National Climate Assessment: Indigenous Peoples, Lands, and Resources|url=http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/sectors/indigenous-peoples#|access-date=13 March 2017|website=Global Change|publisher=US Global Change Research Program|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140507040148/http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/sectors/indigenous-peoples |archive-date=2014-05-07 }}</ref> Exploitation practices produce pollution and introduce non-native species, promoting the intensity of climate change.<ref name=WhyteDistopiaNow /> Conservation efforts of the [[Great Lakes]] ecosystems are necessary in order to prevent climate change from doing further damage to the environment and the Indigenous communities living there.<ref name=WhyteDistopiaNow/> Increasing temperatures have stunted the growth of wild rice, negatively impacting the [[Anishinaabe]] and [[Ojibwe]] people's health and culture.<ref name="nca2014.globalchange.gov" /><ref name="auto1">{{cite web|date=May 2016|title=Climate Change and the Health of Indigenous Populations|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-03/documents/indigenous-11x17.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=5 April 2017|website=EPA United States Environmental Protection Agency|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220103164810/https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-03/documents/indigenous-11x17.pdf |archive-date=2022-01-03 }}</ref> The [[Navajo Nation]] will experience increasing droughts and air pollution from dust.<ref name="auto1"/> In Arizona, rising temperatures and more severe rain events will likely exacerbate existing water purity problems, resulting in increased diarrhea and stomach problems, especially among children.<ref name="auto1"/> In [[Maine]], habitat loss and increasing temperatures, especially in the colder seasons, encourage the survival of ticks. This harms moose populations that Indigenous people have historically relied on.<ref name="nca2014.globalchange.gov" />

The Status of Tribes and Climate Change (STACC) report is a US-based report informing on indigenous impacts to climate change, indigenous methods that offer solutions, and how these methods can be implemented in a well-informed and appropriate way. Established in 1992, it takes into consideration Indigenous land sovereignty and personal narratives from Indigenous peoples to ensure that mitigation and adaptation of climate change involves Indigenous people and practices.<ref>{{Cite web |title=STACC |url=https://sites.google.com/view/staccreport/home?authuser=0 |access-date=2025-03-19 |website=sites.google.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

====Hawaii====
In the last century, climate change has played a part in causing "between 90 and 95 percent of [[Hawaii|Hawaiʻi]]'s dryland forests" to disappear, which is especially important because many of the native species that exist in Hawaiʻi cannot be found anywhere else on earth.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last=Sproat|first=Kapua' ala|title=An Indigenous People's Right to Environmental Self-Determination: Native Hawaiians and the Struggle Against Climate Change Devastation |url=https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstream/10125/46075/1/35StanEnvtlLJ157.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=2021-12-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210320003543/https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstream/10125/46075/1/35StanEnvtlLJ157.pdf |archive-date=2021-03-20 }}</ref> Indigenous communities developed agroecosystems that could have had production levels comparable to consumption today.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|last=Kurashima|first=Natalie|date=2019|title=The Potential of Indigenous Agricultural Food Production under Climate Change in Hawaiʻi|url=https://www.iccaconsortium.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/2019_Kurashima-et-al_The-potential-of-indigenous-agricultural-food-production-under-climate-change-in-Hawai%CA%BBi.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211209195541/https://www.iccaconsortium.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/2019_Kurashima-et-al_The-potential-of-indigenous-agricultural-food-production-under-climate-change-in-Hawai%CA%BBi.pdf |archive-date=2021-12-09 }}</ref>  As such, Indigenous agroecosystems may help climate change mitigation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Keeler|first=Kyle|date=2021-08-09|title=Before colonization (BC) and after decolonization (AD): The Early Anthropocene, the Biblical Fall, and relational pasts, presents, and futures |journal=Environment and Planning E: Nature and Space |volume=5 |issue=3 |language=en |pages=1341–1360 |doi=10.1177/25148486211033087 |s2cid=238671275|issn=2514-8486}}</ref>

====Alaska====
[[File:Kivalina 2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35| [[Kivalina]], Alaska, is threatened by [[sea level rise|rising sea levels]] and [[coastal erosion]].]]
[[Arctic sea ice decline|Thinning sea ice]] on which some Alaskan tribes traditionally rely for hunting<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vinyeta|first1=Kirsten|last2=Whyte|first2=Kyle Powys|last3=Lynn|first3=Kathy|date=2015|title=Climate change through an intersectional lens: gendered vulnerability and resilience in indigenous communities in the United States|url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/49888|journal=Gen. Tech. Rep. PNW-GTR-923. Portland, OR: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station. 72 P.|language=en|volume=923|doi=10.2737/PNW-GTR-923|doi-access=free}}</ref> contributes to ''climigration''—[[migration caused by climate change]], a term originally was coined for Arctic Alaska towns and villages.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hamilton|first1=Lawrence C.|last2=Saito|first2=Kei|last3=Loring|first3=Philip A.|last4=Lammers|first4=Richard B.|last5=Huntington|first5=Henry P.|date=2016|title=Climigration? Population and climate change in Arctic Alaska|journal=Population and Environment|volume=38|issue=2|pages=115–133|issn=0199-0039|doi=10.1007/s11111-016-0259-6 |jstor=44132371|pmid=27829694|pmc=5080311|bibcode=2016PopEn..38..115H |quote=Some historical movements have been attributed to climate change, but closer study tends to find multiple causes, making it difficult to quantify the climate contribution. }}</ref> The policy advisor for the National Congress of American Indians has stated that "among indigenous peoples in North America, the Native Americans who continue to practice traditional and subsistence lifestyles to perhaps the highest degree are those in Alaska, where 80% of the diet comes from the immediate surroundings".<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Weinhold|first=Bob|date=2010-02-01|title=HEALTH DISPARITIES: Climate Change and Health: A Native American Perspective|journal=Environmental Health Perspectives|volume=118|issue=2|pages=A64–A65|doi=10.1289/ehp.118-a64|pmc=2831938|pmid=20123636}}</ref>

[[Coastal erosion]] and [[Sea level rise|rising sea levels]] caused by climate change have threatened coastal communities.<ref name=":113">{{Cite journal|last=Bender|first=Brian A.|date=2010-05-20|title=Greenhouse Gas Politics and Climate Change Public Nuisance Litigation|journal=Environmental Claims Journal|volume=22|issue=2|pages=78–90|doi=10.1080/10406021003766115|bibcode=2010EnvCJ..22b..78B |issn=1040-6026|s2cid=153465306}}</ref> For example, reports suggest that melting [[permafrost]], repeated storms, and decrease of land could make [[Kivalina]] unlivable by 2025,<ref name=":142">{{Cite web|last1=April 1|first1=Anna V. Smith|last2=Now|first2=2020 From the print edition Like Tweet Email Print Subscribe Donate|date=2020-04-01|title=Tribal nations demand response to climate relocation|url=https://www.hcn.org/issues/52.4/indigenous-affairs-justice-tribal-nations-demand-response-to-climate-relocation|access-date=2020-12-04|website=www.hcn.org|language=en-us}}</ref> though some residents do not have the enough money to relocate.<ref name=":113" /> Sea ice that historically sheltered the town has retreated, and storms that would have previously hit the ice now reach the town.<ref name=":113" /> The [[Arctic sea ice decline|decline in ice sheets]] has been directly linked to a decline in the population of polar bears on which many Indigenous people rely.<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal|last=Tsosie|first=Rebecca|date=2007|title=Indigenous People and Environmental Justice: The Impact of Climate Change|url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/P?h=hein.journals/ucollr78&i=1648|journal=University of Colorado Law Review|volume=78|pages=1625–1678}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.north-slope.org/assets/images/uploads/Kanayurak_2016_Masters_thesis_polar_bear_co-management.pdf|title=A Case Study of Polar Bear Co-Management in Alaska|last=Kanayurak|first=Nicole|date=2016|access-date=2021-04-30|archive-date=2021-04-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419141550/http://www.north-slope.org/assets/images/uploads/Kanayurak_2016_Masters_thesis_polar_bear_co-management.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=Forbes|first=Donald|title=State of the Arctic coast 2010: scientific review and outlook|journal=AGU Fall Meeting Abstracts|url=https://library.arcticportal.org/1277/1/state_of_the_arctic_coast_2010.pdf|volume=2010|pages=GC54A–07|date=2011|publisher=Institute of Coastal Research|bibcode=2010AGUFMGC54A..07R}}</ref>

Because of melting ice, global climate change makes Arctic Indigenous lands more accessible for resource extraction.<ref name=WhyteDecolonizing /> Whyte cites a source saying that this increased accessibility brings oil production projects having laborers' camps that "attract violent [[Missing and murdered Indigenous women|sex trafficking]] of Indigenous persons".<ref name=WhyteDecolonizing />

Wildfires impact both urban and rural communities, and Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities.<ref name=":152">{{Cite journal|last1=Trainor|first1=Sarah F.|last2=Calef|first2=Monika|last3=Natcher|first3=David|last4=Stuart Chapin Iii|first4=F.|last5=McGuire|first5=A. David|last6=Huntington|first6=Orville|last7=Duffy|first7=Paul|last8=Scott Rupp|first8=T.|last9=DeWilde|first9=La'Ona|last10=Kwart|first10=Mary|last11=Fresco|first11=Nancy|date=January 2009|title=Vulnerability and adaptation to climate-related fire impacts in rural and urban interior Alaska|journal=Polar Research|volume=28|issue=1|pages=100–118|bibcode=2009PolRe..28..100T|doi=10.1111/j.1751-8369.2009.00101.x|issn=1751-8369|doi-access=free|s2cid=15594292}}</ref> However, [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous communities]] do not have the same economic resources to deal with these fires, and their lifestyles and cultures are more dependent on the land.<ref name=":152"/> Rural communities rely more on surrounding land for wild food harvest and nutritional intake, and thus are at risk for food insecurity.<ref name=":152"/>

Warming temperatures in the Arctic allow [[beaver]]s to extend their habitat further north, where their [[Beaver dam#Effects|dams impair]] boat travel, impact access to food, affect water quality, and endanger downstream fish populations.<ref name=Guardian_20220104/> Pools formed by the dams store heat, thus changing local [[hydrology]] and causing localized [[Permafrost#Thaw|thawing of permafrost]] that [[Climate change feedback|in turn]] contributes to global warming.<ref name=Guardian_20220104>{{cite news |last1=Milman |first1=Oliver |title=Dam it: beavers head north to the Arctic as tundra continues to heat up |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/jan/04/beavers-arctic-north-climate-crisis |newspaper=The Guardian |date=January 4, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220104220623/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/jan/04/beavers-arctic-north-climate-crisis |archive-date=January 4, 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{anchor|IceCellar}}For generations, people in Alaska's [[Arctic Alaska|far-north]] whaling villages have relied on ice cellars (food caches) dug deep into the [[permafrost]] to store and age their subsistence food, and keep it cold throughout the year.<ref name=IceCellars/> However, global warming—along with changes in sediment chemistry, local hydrology, and urbanization—are causing ice cellars to fail through flooding and collapse.<ref name=IceCellars>{{cite journal |last1=Nyland |first1=Kelsey E. |last2=Klene |first2=Anna E. |last3=Brown |first3=Jerry |last4=Shiklomanov |first4=Nikolay I. |last5=Nelson |first5=Frederick E. |last6=Streletskiy |first6=Dmitry A. |last7=Yoshikawa |first7=Kenji |display-authors=4 |title=Traditional Iñupiat Ice Cellars (SIĠḷUAQ) in Barrow, Alaska: Characteristics, Temperature Monitoring, and Distribution |journal=Geographical Review |date=2017 |volume=107 |issue=1 |pages=143–158 |doi=10.1111/j.1931-0846.2016.12204.x |bibcode=2017GeoRv.107..143N |s2cid=163572393 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/am-pdf/10.1111/j.1931-0846.2016.12204.x}} ([https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/am-pdf/10.1111/j.1931-0846.2016.12204.x full text] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220213215229/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/am-pdf/10.1111/j.1931-0846.2016.12204.x |date=2022-02-13 }}) ● Explained by {{cite news |last1=D'Oro |first1=Rachel |title=Failing permafrost cellars signal change in Alaska whaling towns |url=https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/rural-alaska/2019/11/25/failing-permafrost-cellars-signal-change-in-alaska-whaling-towns/ |work=Anchorage Daily News |date=November 25, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526145554/https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/rural-alaska/2019/11/25/failing-permafrost-cellars-signal-change-in-alaska-whaling-towns/ |archive-date=May 26, 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Security===
{{further|Climate change and national security}}
Climate change is a threat to the national security of the United States, according to the Department of Defense.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Macias |first1=Amanda |title=Climate crisis threatens U.S. national security, Defense secretary says |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/04/22/climate-crisis-poses-existential-threat-to-us-security-defense-chief-austin.html |access-date=2 July 2021 |agency=CNBC |date=22 April 2021}}</ref> The President Joe Biden claims that top military officials described climate change as the biggest threat to the security of the country. Army Gen. [[Mark Milley]], the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in reaction that from a strictly military point of view Russia and China are the biggest threats but national security is a much broader issue.<ref>{{cite news |title=Top Military Officer Clarifies Biden's Threat Assessment: Climate Change – But Also China and Russia |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/national-news/articles/2021-06-10/top-military-officer-clarifies-bidens-threat-assessment-climate-change-but-also-china-and-russia |access-date=2 July 2021 |agency=U.S. news |date=10 June 2021}}</ref> Studies have also found that some dimensions of climate change increase rates of violent crime.<ref>{{cite news | title= Weird Winter Weather in the Anthropocene: How Volatile Temperatures Shape Violent Crime  |author=Thomas, C. and Wolff, K.|journal=Journal of Criminal Justice   |year=2023    |volume=87   |issue=4      |url=https://academicworks.cuny.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1546&context=jj_pubs   }}</ref> Overall, the IPCC reports with medium confidence that climate change is related to both violent and property crime in the US.<ref>{{cite news |title=Chapter 14: North America |url=https://report.ipcc.ch/ar6wg2/pdf/IPCC_AR6_WGII_FinalDraft_Chapter14.pdf |access-date=2022-02-28 |archive-date=2022-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220228140214/https://report.ipcc.ch/ar6wg2/pdf/IPCC_AR6_WGII_FinalDraft_Chapter14.pdf }}</ref>

Calculations in 2021 showed that, for giving the world a 50% chance of avoiding a temperature rise of 2 degrees or more USA should increase its climate commitments by 38%.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal|last1=R. Liu|first1=Peiran|last2=E. Raftery|first2=Adrian|date=9 February 2021|title=Country-based rate of emissions reductions should increase by 80% beyond nationally determined contributions to meet the 2 °C target|journal=Communications Earth & Environment|volume=2|issue=1|page=29|doi=10.1038/s43247-021-00097-8|doi-access=free|pmid=33899003|pmc=8064561|bibcode=2021ComEE...2...29L}}</ref>{{rp|Table 1}} For a 95% chance it should increase the commitments by 125%. For giving a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 degrees USA should increase its commitments by 203%.<ref name=":3" />

Increasing use of [[public transport]] and related [[transit-oriented development]] can reduce transportation emissions in human settlements by 78% and overall US emissions by 15%.<ref>{{cite book |title=Public Transportation's Role in Responding to Climate Change |date=2010 |publisher=U.S. Department of Transportation Federal Transit Administration |page=5 |url=https://www.transit.dot.gov/sites/fta.dot.gov/files/docs/PublicTransportationsRoleInRespondingToClimateChange2010.pdf |access-date=1 April 2022}}</ref>

In April, 2022, wind and solar energy sources provided more electricity than nuclear power plants, overtaking nuclear for the first time in U.S. history.<ref name=Newsweek_20220708/> Clean energy (also including geothermal, hydroelectric and biomass) comprised nearly 30% of the total electricity in the U.S., compared to about 20% in 2021.<ref name=Newsweek_20220708>{{cite news |last1=Thomson |first1=Jessica |title=U.S. Produces More Power from Wind and Solar than Nuclear for First Time |url=https://www.newsweek.com/wind-solar-power-more-electricity-nuclear-usa-1722856 |magazine=Newsweek |date=July 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220712130843/https://www.newsweek.com/wind-solar-power-more-electricity-nuclear-usa-1722856 |archive-date=July 12, 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Efforts to reduce [[greenhouse gas emissions by the United States]] include [[Energy policy of the United States|energy policies]] which encourage efficiency through programs like [[Energy Star]], [[Commercial Building Integration]], and the [[Industrial Technologies Program]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Industrial Technologies Program: BestPractices |url=http://www.eere.energy.gov/industry/bestpractices/index.html |access-date=26 August 2010 |publisher=Eere.energy.gov}}</ref>

In the absence of substantial federal action, state governments have adopted emissions-control laws such as the [[Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative]] in the Northeast and the [[Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006]] in California.<ref>{{cite news |last=Barringer |first=Felicity |date=13 October 2012 |title=In California, a Grand Experiment to Rein in Climate Change |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/14/science/earth/in-california-a-grand-experiment-to-rein-in-climate-change.html}}</ref> In 2019 a new climate change bill was introduced in Minnesota. One of the targets, is making all the energy of the state carbon free, by 2030.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kahn |first1=Brian |date=13 April 2019 |title=Minnesota Introduces Bold New Climate Change Bill Crafted by Teens |agency=Gizmodo |url=https://www.gizmodo.com.au/2019/04/minnesota-introduces-bold-new-climate-change-bill-crafted-by-teens/ |access-date=15 April 2019}}</ref>

Several pieces of legislation introduced in the 116th and 117th Congresses, including the ''Climate Stewardship Act of 2019,''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Haaland |first=Debra A. |date=2019-09-16 |title=Text – H.R.4269 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Climate Stewardship Act of 2019 |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/4269/text |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428055905/https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/4269/text |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> the ''Ocean Based Climate Solutions Act of 2020'',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grijalva |first=Raul M. |date=2020-11-17 |title=H.R.8632 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Ocean-Based Climate Solutions Act of 2020 |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/8632 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210524204037/https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/8632 |archive-date=May 24, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> the ''Healthy Soil, Resilient Farmers Act of 2020'',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spanberger |first=Abigail Davis |date=2020-10-01 |title=Text – H.R.8057 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Healthy Soil, Resilient Farmers Act of 2020 |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/8057/text |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428055902/https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/8057/text |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> and the ''Healthy Soils Healthy Climate Act of 2020'',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wyden |first=Ron |date=2020-10-23 |title=Text – S.4850 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Healthy Soils Healthy Climate Act of 2020 |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/4850/text |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428055858/https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/4850/text |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> have sought to increase [[carbon sequestration]] on private and public lands through financial incentivization.

Several state governments, including [[California]], [[Hawaii]], [[Maryland]], and [[New York (state)|New York]], have passed versions of a [[carbon farming]] tax credit, which seek to improve soil health and increase carbon sequestration by offering financial assistance and incentives for farmers who practice [[regenerative agriculture]], carbon farming, and other climate change mitigation practices.<ref>{{Cite web |title=6 States Tapping into the Benefits of Carbon Farming – Soil Solutions |url=https://soilsolution.org/2017/07/6-states-tapping-into-the-benefits-of-carbon-farming/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421203051/https://soilsolution.org/2017/07/6-states-tapping-into-the-benefits-of-carbon-farming/ |archive-date=April 21, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |language=en-NZ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Greenhouse Gas Sequestration Task Force |url=https://planning.hawaii.gov/ghgstf/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424071357/https://planning.hawaii.gov/ghgstf/ |archive-date=April 24, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=planning.hawaii.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Maryland HB1063 {{!}} 2017 {{!}} Regular Session |url=https://legiscan.com/MD/bill/HB1063/2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421203053/https://legiscan.com/MD/bill/HB1063/2017 |archive-date=April 21, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=LegiScan |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=CDFA – OEFI – Healthy Soils Program |url=https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/oefi/healthysoils/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210410141520/https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/oefi/healthysoils/ |archive-date=April 10, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=www.cdfa.ca.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-02-09 |title=NY State Senate Bill S4707 |url=https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2021/s4707 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421203101/https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2021/s4707 |archive-date=April 21, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=NY State Senate |language=en}}</ref> The California Healthy Soils Program is estimated to have resulted in 109,809 metric tons of CO<sub>2</sub> being sequestered annually on average.<ref name=":6" />

A 2011 survey of 568 members of the American Economic Association (AEA) found that 80 percent of professional economists generally agreed with the statement: "The long run benefits of higher [[Carbon tax|taxes on fossil fuels]] outweigh the short run economic costs."<ref name="Fuller & Geide-Stevenson 2011">{{cite journal|last1=Fuller|first1=Dan|last2=Geide-Stevenson|first2=Doris|title=Consensus Among Economists – An Update|year=2014|journal=[[Journal of Economic Education|The Journal of Economic Education]]|publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]]|volume=45|issue=2|page=138|doi=10.1080/00220485.2014.889963|s2cid=143794347|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261884738}}</ref> A 2021 survey of 1,422 AEA members found that 88 percent of professional economists generally agreed with the same statement.<ref name="2021 AEA survey" /> Relatedly, surveys of AEA members since the 1970s have shown that professional economists generally agree with the statement: "[[Environmental tax|Pollution taxes]] and [[Emissions trading|marketable pollution permits]] represent a better approach to pollution control than emission standards."{{refn|group=list|name=EconomistsConsensus|<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kearl|first1=J. R.|last2=Pope|first2=Clayne L.|last3=Whiting|first3=Gordon C.|last4=Wimmer|first4=Larry T.|year=1979|title=A Confusion of Economists?|journal=American Economic Review|publisher=American Economic Association|volume=69|issue=2|pages=28–37|jstor=1801612}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alston |first1=Richard M. |last2=Kearl |first2=J.R. |author-link2=James R. Kearl |last3=Vaughan |first3=Michael B. |title=Is There a Consensus Among Economists in the 1990's? |date=May 1992 |journal=[[The American Economic Review]] |volume=82 |issue=2 |pages=203–209 |jstor=2117401 |url=http://www.weber.edu/wsuimages/AcademicAffairs/ProvostItems/global.pdf |archive-date=2017-04-08 |access-date=2023-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170408191354/http://www.weber.edu/wsuimages/AcademicAffairs/ProvostItems/global.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fuller |first1=Dan |last2=Geide-Stevenson |first2=Doris |title=Consensus Among Economists: Revisited |date=Fall 2003 |journal=[[Journal of Economic Education|The Journal of Economic Education]] |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=369–387 |jstor=30042564 |doi=10.1080/00220480309595230|s2cid=143617926 }}</ref><ref name="Fuller & Geide-Stevenson 2011" /><ref name="2021 AEA survey" />}} Likewise, in its September 2020 report, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission subcommittee concluded that financial markets will only be able to efficiently channel resources to activities that reduce greenhouse gas emissions if a [[carbon price]] that reflects the true [[social cost of carbon]] is in place across the economy.<ref name="CFTC 2020" />

The White House and USDA are reportedly developing plans to use $30 billion in funds from the [[Commodity Credit Corporation]] (CCC) for the creation of a carbon bank program, which would involve giving carbon credits to farmers and landowners in return for adopting carbon sequestration practices, which they could then sell in a [[Carbon price|cap and trade market.]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=Plume |first=Karl |date=2021-02-02 |title=USDA can steer farm aid money to fight climate change, Biden ag secretary nominee says |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-biden-usda-vilsack-idUSKBN2A22O8 |url-status=live |access-date=2021-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428155106/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-biden-usda-vilsack-idUSKBN2A22O8 |archive-date=April 28, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A 'carbon bank' could mean extra cash for Midwest farmers |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2021/02/07/a-carbon-bank-could-mean-extra-cash-for-midwest-farmers |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428155107/https://www.mprnews.org/story/2021/02/07/a-carbon-bank-could-mean-extra-cash-for-midwest-farmers |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |access-date=2021-04-28 |website=MPR News|date=7 February 2021 }}</ref>

In November 2023, the first commercial [[direct air capture]] (DAC) plant in the U.S. began operation.<ref name=NYTimes_20231109/> DAC technology captures carbon dioxide—a greenhouse gas contributing to global warming—and seals it permanently in a solid such as concrete.<ref name=NYTimes_20231109/> That plant removes only 1,000 tons of carbon dioxide per year, equal to the exhaust from about 200 cars.<ref name=NYTimes_20231109/> However, a $1.2 billion Biden administration award for DAC aims to expand the technology and reduce cost per ton.<ref name=NYTimes_20231109>{{cite news |last1=Plumer |first1=Brad |title=In a U.S. First, a Commercial Plant Starts Pulling Carbon From the Air |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/09/climate/direct-air-capture-carbon.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=9 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231109180826/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/09/climate/direct-air-capture-carbon.html |archive-date=9 November 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Carbon emissions trading schemes by state and regional programs ====
{{See also|Carbon emissions trading}}
In 2003, [[New York State]] proposed and attained commitments from nine [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] states to form a cap-and-trade [[carbon dioxide]] emissions program for power generators, called the [[Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative]] (RGGI). This program launched on January 1, 2009, with the aim to reduce the carbon "budget" of each state's electricity generation sector to 10% below their 2009 allowances by 2018.<ref>[http://www.rggi.org/docs/mou_12_20_05.pdf Memorandum of Understanding] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511191906/http://www.rggi.org/docs/mou_12_20_05.pdf|date=2011-05-11}} – Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative</ref>

Also in 2003, U.S. corporations were able to trade CO<sub>2</sub> emission allowances on the [[Chicago Climate Exchange]] under a voluntary scheme. In August 2007, the Exchange announced a mechanism to create [[Carbon offset|emission offsets]] for projects within the United States that cleanly destroy [[ozone]]-depleting substances.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brüning |first1=Kristian |last2=Cohen |first2=Jeff |date=2008-03-07 |title=Beyond the Kyoto six |url=http://www.carbon-financeonline.com/index.cfm?section=features&id=11092&action=view&return=home |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727011403/https://www.carbon-financeonline.com/index.cfm?section=features&id=11092&action=view&return=home |archive-date=2011-07-27 |access-date=2011-07-26 |work=Carbon Finance |publisher=Fulton Publishing}}</ref>

In 2006, the [[California Legislature]] passed the California Global Warming Solutions Act, [[AB-32]]. Thus far, flexible mechanisms in the form of project based offsets have been suggested for three main project types. The project types include: [[manure management]], forestry, and destruction of ozone-depleted substances. However, a ruling from Judge Ernest H. Goldsmith of San Francisco's Superior Court stated that the rules governing California's cap-and-trade system were adopted without a proper analysis of alternative methods to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite news |last=Barringer |first=Felicity |date=4 February 2011 |title=California Law to Curb Greenhouse Gases Faces a Legal Hurdle |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/05/science/earth/05emit.html |url-status=live |access-date=9 February 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308201548/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/05/science/earth/05emit.html |archive-date=March 8, 2021}}</ref>  The tentative ruling, issued on January 24, 2011, argued that the [[California Air Resources Board]] violated state environmental law by failing to consider such alternatives. If the decision is made final, the state would not be allowed to implement its proposed cap-and-trade system until the California Air Resources Board fully complies with the [[California Environmental Quality Act]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Buchanan |first=Wyatt |date=4 February 2011 |title=Calif. cap-trade plan dealt blow by S.F. judge |newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle |url=https://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/2011-02-04/news/27100791_1_air-board-ab32-emissions-plan |url-status=dead |access-date=9 February 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110208141038/http://articles.sfgate.com/2011-02-04/news/27100791_1_air-board-ab32-emissions-plan |archive-date=8 February 2011}}</ref> However, on June 24, 2011, the Superior Court's ruling was overturned by the Court of Appeals.<ref name="cap-and-trade">{{cite web |date=December 21, 2011 |title=Cap and Trade Regulations Approved and Transmitted; Preliminary List of Covered Entities Now Available |url=http://blog.aklandlaw.com/2011/12/articles/climate-change/cap-and-trade-regulations-approved-and-transmitted-preliminary-list-of-covered-entities-now-available/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630064821/http://blog.aklandlaw.com/2011/12/articles/climate-change/cap-and-trade-regulations-approved-and-transmitted-preliminary-list-of-covered-entities-now-available/ |archive-date=June 30, 2012 |access-date=2021-06-23}}</ref> By 2012, some of the emitters obtained allowances for free, which is for the electric utilities, industrial facilities and natural gas distributors, whereas some of the others have to go to the auction.<ref>[http://www.c2es.org/us-states-regions/action/california/cap-trade-regulation Summary of California's Cap and Trade Program] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110105934/http://www.c2es.org/us-states-regions/action/california/cap-trade-regulation|date=2016-11-10}}, Center for Climate and Energy Solutions.</ref> The California cap-and-trade program came into effect in 2013.

In 2014, the [[Texas Legislature|Texas legislature]] approved a 10% reduction for the Highly Reactive Volatile Organic Compound (HRVOC) emission limit.<ref name="tceq.texas.gov">{{Cite web |title=Highly Reactive Volatile Organic Compound Emissions Cap and Trade Program |url=https://www.tceq.texas.gov/airquality/banking/hrvoc_ept_prog.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210527111025/https://www.tceq.texas.gov/airquality/banking/hrvoc_ept_prog.html |archive-date=May 27, 2021 |access-date=2017-11-30 |website=TCEQ}}</ref> This was followed by a 5% reduction for each subsequent year until a total of 25% percent reduction was achieved in 2017.<ref name="tceq.texas.gov" />

In February 2007, five U.S. states and four Canadian provinces joined to create the [[Western Climate Initiative]] (WCI), a regional greenhouse gas emissions trading system.<ref>[http://www.westernclimateinitiative.org/ Western Climate Initiative] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080423080828/http://www.westernclimateinitiative.org/|date=2008-04-23}}.</ref> In July 2010, a meeting took place to further outline the cap-and-trade system.<ref>[https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-jul-28-la-me-climate-pact-20100728-story.html "California, New Mexico and 3 Canadian provinces outline regional cap-and-trade program"], ''Los Angeles Times'', 28 July 2010.</ref> In November 2011, Arizona, Montana, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah and Washington withdrew from the WCI.<ref>"[http://www.platts.com/RSSFeedDetailedNews/RSSFeed/ElectricPower/6695863 Six US states leave the Western Climate Initiative] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230729235316/https://www.spglobal.com/commodityinsights/en/market-insights/latest-news|date=July 29, 2023}}" (18 November 2011). S&P Global Platts. Retrieved 2016-11-26.</ref><ref>"[http://www.sustainablebusiness.com/index.cfm/go/news.display/id/23178 6 States Pull Out of Western Climate Initiative] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161127085752/http://www.sustainablebusiness.com/index.cfm/go/news.display/id/23178|date=November 27, 2016}}" (22 November 2011). ''SustainableBusiness.com News''. Retrieved 2016-11-26.</ref> As of 2021, only the U.S. state of [[California]] and the [[Canada|Canadian]] province of [[Quebec]] participate in the WCI.<ref>The Canadian province of [[Nova Scotia]] is a member of the WCI, but its carbon market is not linked to that of California and Quebec.</ref>

In 1997, the State of [[Illinois]] adopted a trading program for [[volatile organic compound]]s in most of the Chicago area, called the Emissions Reduction Market System.<ref>{{cite web |year=2007 |title=Emissions Reduction Market System What Is ERMS? |url=http://www.epa.state.il.us/air/erms/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141128104812/http://www.epa.state.il.us/air/erms/ |archive-date=2014-11-28 |access-date=2005-09-22 |publisher=Illinois EPA}}</ref> Beginning in 2000, over 100 major sources of pollution in eight Illinois counties began trading pollution credits.

===Adaptation===
{{See also|Climate change adaptation}}
The state of [[California]] enacted the first comprehensive state-level climate action plan with its 2009 "California Climate Adaptation Strategy."<ref>{{cite web |title=California Climate Adaptation Strategy |url=http://www.climatechange.ca.gov/adaptation/index.html |access-date=7 August 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090806134038/http://climatechange.ca.gov/adaptation/index.html| archive-date= 6 August 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> California's electrical grid has been impacted by the increased fire risks associated with climate change. In the 2019 "red flag" warning about the possibility of wildfires declared in some areas of California, the electricity company Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) was required to shut down power to prevent inflammation of trees that touch the electricity lines. Millions were impacted.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosane |first1=Olivia |title=Power Outage Intended to Prevent Wildfires Will Affect Millions of Californians Who Use PG&E |url=https://www.ecowatch.com/power-outage-california-wildfires-2640897787.html |access-date=10 October 2019 |agency=Ecowatch |date=9 October 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Blaauw |first1=Maddie |title=Climate Change Dictates That The PG&E Power Outage Likely Won't Be The Last |url=https://therising.co/2019/10/13/climate-change-dictates-that-the-pge-power-outage-likely-wont-be-the-last/ |access-date=15 October 2019 |agency=The Rising |date=13 October 2019 |archive-date=24 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224193728/https://therising.co/2019/10/13/climate-change-dictates-that-the-pge-power-outage-likely-wont-be-the-last/ }}</ref>

Within the state of [[Florida]] four counties ([[Broward County, Florida|Broward]], [[Miami-Dade]], [[Monroe County, Florida|Monroe]], [[Palm Beach County, Florida|Palm Beach]]) have created the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact in order to coordinate adaptation and mitigation strategies to cope with the impact of climate change on the region.<ref>{{cite web |title=Southeast Florida Climate Change Compact |url=https://www.southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org |access-date=20 January 2014}}</ref> The Commonwealth of [[Massachusetts]] has issued grants to coastal cities and towns for adaptation activities such as fortification against flooding and preventing coastal erosion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/08/21/baker-administration-gives-million-grants-communities-vulnerable-climate-change/Wrn5ZnsZ1deeB0bRsRg5LP/story.html?p1%3DArticle_InThisSection_Bottom |title=Communities vulnerable to climate change get $2m in state grants |website=[[The Boston Globe]] |access-date=29 October 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304085056/http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/08/21/baker-administration-gives-million-grants-communities-vulnerable-climate-change/Wrn5ZnsZ1deeB0bRsRg5LP/story.html?p1=Article_InThisSection_Bottom |archive-date=4 March 2016 }}</ref>

[[New York (state)|New York]] State is requiring climate change be taken into account in certain infrastructure permitting, zoning, and open space programs; and is mapping sea level rise along its coast.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dec.ny.gov/energy/100236.html |title=Adaptation to Climate Change - NYS Dept. Of Environmental Conservation |access-date=29 October 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161025080303/http://www.dec.ny.gov/energy/100236.html |archive-date=25 October 2016 }}</ref>  After [[Hurricane Sandy]], New York and New Jersey accelerated voluntary government buy-back of homes in flood-prone areas. New York City announced in 2013 it planned to spend between $10 and $20 billion on local flood protection, reduction of the heat island effect with reflective and green roofs, flood-hardening of hospitals and public housing, resiliency in food supply, and beach enhancement; rezoned to allow private property owners to move critical features to upper stories; and required electrical utilities to harden infrastructure against flooding.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.climatecentral.org/news/new-york-launches-20-billion-climate-resiliency-plan-16106 |title=New York Launches $19.5 Billion Climate Resiliency Plan |access-date=29 October 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220020320/http://www.climatecentral.org/news/new-york-launches-20-billion-climate-resiliency-plan-16106 |archive-date=20 December 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www1.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/122-15/mayor-de-blasio-releases-npcc-2015-report-providing-climate-projections-2100-the-first |title=Mayor Releases NPCC 2015 Report, Providing Climate Projections Through 2100 for the First Time |date=17 February 2015 |access-date=29 October 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161213035649/http://www1.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/122-15/mayor-de-blasio-releases-npcc-2015-report-providing-climate-projections-2100-the-first |archive-date=13 December 2016 }}</ref>

In 2019, a $19.1 billion "disaster relief bill" was approved by the Senate. The bill should help the victims of extreme weather that was partly fueled by climate change.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rosane|first1=Olivia|date=24 May 2019|title=Senate Approves $19.1 Billion in Disaster Funding After Years of Climate-Fueled Disasters|agency=Ecowatch|url=https://www.ecowatch.com/disaster-relief-funding-congress-2638024503.html|access-date=26 May 2019}}</ref>

In mid February 2014, President [[Barack Obama]] announced his plan to propose a $1 billion "[[Climate resilience|Climate Resilience]] Fund".<ref name="News">{{Cite web |last=Malakoff |first=David |date=2014-02-15 |title=Obama to Propose $1 Billion Climate Resilience Fund |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/obama-propose-1-billion-climate-resilience-fund |access-date=2020-01-25 |website=Science {{!}} AAAS |language=en}}</ref> Obama's fund incorporates facets of both urban resiliency and human resiliency theories, by necessarily improving communal infrastructure and by focusing on societal preparation to decrease the country's vulnerability to the impacts of climate change.

==== Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) ====
{{see also|Traditional ecological knowledge#Differences from science}}
A 2013 USDA Technical Report stated that Indigenous peoples' [[traditional ecological knowledge]] (TEK) has the potential to play a vital role in indigenous climate change assessment and adaptation efforts, and that contributions from both Western science and TEK knowledge systems are imperative.<ref name="USDA_TEK_201305"/> Bridging these two knowledge systems is said to "produce() a better understanding of the issue than either would alone."<ref name="SustSci_2015">{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Jay T. |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11625-015-0349-x.pdf |date=2015 |title=Weaving Indigenous and sustainability sciences to diversify our methods |journal=Sustainability Science |volume=11 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1007/s11625-015-0349-x |s2cid=131199874 }}</ref>

Western climate science and TEK represent complementary and overlapping views of the causes and consequences of change.<ref name="EcologicalProcesses_2018"/> TEK provides information about changes in the natural world useful for adaptation at the community level, information that is not readily available to western science observations.<ref name="EcologicalProcesses_2018">{{cite journal|last1=Hatfield|first1=Samantha Chisholm|last2=Marino|first2=Elizabeth|last3=Whyte|first3=Kyle Powys|last4=Dello|first4=Kathie D.|last5=Mote|first5=Philip W.|date=2018|title=Indian time: time, seasonality, and culture in Traditional Ecological Knowledge of climate change|url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s13717-018-0136-6.pdf|journal=Ecological Processes|volume=7|issue=25|page=25 |doi=10.1186/s13717-018-0136-6|bibcode=2018EcoPr...7...25C |s2cid=51798012 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Specifically, TEK—described as the "accumulation of highly localized, experiential, place-based wisdom over a long period, most often passed down orally from generation to generation"<ref name="USDA_TEK_201305">{{cite web|last1=Vinyeta|first1=Kirsten|last2=Lynn|first2=Kathy|date=May 2013|title=Exploring the Role of Traditional Ecological Knowledge in Climate Change Initiatives|url=https://www.arlis.org/docs/vol1/F/851473873.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211222153803/https://www.arlis.org/docs/vol1/F/851473873.pdf|archive-date=December 22, 2021|website=arlis.org (Alaska Resources Library and Information Services)|publisher=Forest Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture}}</ref>—provides wisdom for community-level adaptation.<ref name="EcologicalProcesses_2018" /> TEK often focuses on [[phenology]] (the study of the dates of recurrent natural events such as the flowering of certain plants or the first or last appearance of migrant birds<ref name="Britannica_Phenology">{{cite web|title=phenology|url=https://www.britannica.com/science/phenology|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211123023847/https://www.britannica.com/science/phenology|archive-date=November 23, 2021|website=Britannica.com}}</ref>) in relation to seasonal climatic changes.<ref name="EcologicalProcesses_2018" /> TEK-based adaptations include traditional food substitutions, and adjusting timing sequences of hunting, gathering, and fishing.<ref name="UnionConcernedScientists_20170118">{{cite news|last1=Hatfield|first1=Samantha Chisholm|date=January 18, 2017|title=The Importance of Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) When Examining Climate Change|publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists|url=https://blog.ucsusa.org/science-blogger/the-importance-of-traditional-ecological-knowledge-tek-when-examining-climate-change/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210913064028/https://blog.ucsusa.org/science-blogger/the-importance-of-traditional-ecological-knowledge-tek-when-examining-climate-change/|archive-date=September 13, 2021}}</ref>

==== Adaptive forestry practices ====
Within the United States, federal agencies have developed two overlapping frameworks for guiding their own actions with regard to forest resources,<ref name="usda-2024">{{cite web |title=Climate Adaptation Frameworks: RAD and RRT |url=https://www.climatehubs.usda.gov/hubs/northwest/topic/climate-adaptation-frameworks-rad-and-rrt |access-date=22 November 2024 |website=Climate Hubs |publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture}}</ref> as well as offering guidance for managers of other forest lands within the nation. The first framework is known as RRT (Resistance, Resilience, Transition), and it was developed by [[U.S. Forest Service]] research scientists. The [[National Park Service]] developed its RAD framework (Resist, Accept, Direct), with assistance from scientists within the [[U.S. Geological Survey]].<ref name="2024-frameworks">{{cite web |last1=Christensen |first1=Janelle |title=Two Frameworks to Help with Climate Adaptation (2024) |url=https://agclimate.net/two-frameworks-to-help-with-climate-adaptation/ |access-date=21 March 2024 |website=AgClimate Network |publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture}}</ref> Both frameworks attribute their origins to a 2007 paper titled "Climate Change and Forests of the Future: Managing in the Face of Uncertainty".<ref name="Millar-2007">{{cite journal |last1=Millar |first1=Constance I |last2=Stephenson |first2=Nathan L |last3=Stephens |first3=Scott L |date=2007 |title=Climate Change and Forests of the Future: Managing in the Face of Uncertainty |url=https://scc.ca.gov/webmaster/ftp/pdf/climate_change/psw_2007_millar029.pdf |journal=Ecological Applications |volume=17 |issue=8 |pages=2145–2151 |bibcode=2007EcoAp..17.2145M |doi=10.1890/06-1715.1 |pmid=18213958}}</ref> The Adaptive Silviculture for Climate Change (ASCC) project is a collaborative effort to establish a series of experimental silvicultural trials across a network of different forest ecosystem types throughout the United States and Canada.<ref name="ASCC-about">{{cite web |title=Adaptive Silviculture for Climate Change |url=https://www.adaptivesilviculture.org/ |access-date=31 March 2024 |website=AdaptiveSilviculture}}</ref> It includes staff from both Canadian and U.S. forestry agencies, state forestry agencies, academic institutions, and forestry interest groups.<ref name="ASCC-people">{{cite web |title=ASCC Network Collaborators |url=https://www.adaptivesilviculture.org/people-partners |access-date=31 March 2024 |website=AdaptiveSilviculture}}</ref>

=== Policies, legislation and legal actions ===
{{Main|Climate change policy of the United States}}

Federal, state, and local governments have all debated climate change policies, but the resulting laws vary considerably. The U.S. Congress has not adopted a comprehensive greenhouse gas emissions reduction scheme, but long-standing environmental laws such as the [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]] have been used by the executive branch and litigants in lawsuits to implement regulations and voluntary agreements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Basseches |first=Joshua A. |last2=Bromley-Trujillo |first2=Rebecca |last3=Boykoff |first3=Maxwell T. |last4=Culhane |first4=Trevor |last5=Hall |first5=Galen |last6=Healy |first6=Noel |last7=Hess |first7=David J. |last8=Hsu |first8=David |last9=Krause |first9=Rachel M. |last10=Prechel |first10=Harland |last11=Roberts |first11=J. Timmons |last12=Stephens |first12=Jennie C. |date=2022-02-16 |title=Climate policy conflict in the U.S. states: a critical review and way forward |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-022-03319-w |journal=Climatic Change |language=en |volume=170 |issue=3 |pages=32 |doi=10.1007/s10584-022-03319-w |issn=1573-1480 |pmc=8853238 |pmid=35194272}}</ref>
The federal government has the exclusive authority to regulate emissions from new motor vehicles under the Clean Air Act, but has granted the state of California a waiver allowing it to adopt more stringent emission standards. Other states may choose to adopt either the federal standards or California's standards. States also retain authority to regulate emissions from electricity generation and industrial sources, while building energy codes are primarily developed and enforced at the state and local levels. Governments at all levels may also reduce greenhouse gas emissions through measures such as improving the energy efficiency of public buildings, purchasing alternative-fuel vehicles, and reducing waste.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Engel |first1=Kirsten H. |last2=Orbach |first2=Barak Y. |title=Micro-Motives for State and Local Climate Change Initiatives |journal=Harvard Law & Policy Review |volume=2 |issue=1 |year=2008 |pages=119–137}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Limiting the Magnitude of Future Climate Change |publisher=National Academies Press |year=2010 |doi=10.17226/12785}}</ref>

Political opponents of emissions regulations have argued that such measures reduce economic activity in the fossil fuel industry, a significant [[extractive industry]] in the United States, and increase costs for consumers, including drivers, electricity users, and building owners. Some have also argued that stringent environmental regulations may impose unnecessary constraints on individual economic choices. Supporters of emissions regulations contend that the economic benefits of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, including avoided climate damages and public health improvements, outweigh the associated compliance costs, and that government intervention is necessary because market forces alone have not adequately addressed climate change. Several states have implemented policies to encourage employment in renewable energy industries, while coal-producing regions have experienced economic challenges associated with declining coal demand, increased competition from inexpensive natural gas, and environmental regulations affecting coal-fired electricity generation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Dryzek |first=John S. |last2=Norgaard |first2=Richard B. |last3=Schlosberg |first3=David |title=The Oxford Handbook of Climate Change and Society |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2011 |isbn=9780199566600}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mildenberger |first1=Matto |last2=Leiserowitz |first2=Anthony |title=Public opinion on climate change: Is there an economy–environment tradeoff? |journal=Environmental Politics |volume=26 |issue=5 |year=2017 |pages=801–824 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2017.1322275}}</ref><!-- I cannot find this as an existing book. I think it may have been multiple stuck together as the title refers to https://academic.oup.com/book/32159 <ref>{{cite book |last=Friedman |first=Lisa |title=Short Circuiting Policy: Interest Groups and the Battle over Clean Energy and Climate Policy in the American States |publisher=State University of New York Press |year=2012 |isbn=9781438442346}}</ref> -->

In 2021 phase 4 of the [[Keystone XL]] pipeline, considered a symbol of the battle over [[Attribution of recent climate change|climate change and fossil fuels]], was cancelled, following strong objections from [[Environmental movement|environmentalists]], [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|indigenous peoples]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|The Democratic Party]], and [[Environmental policy of the Joe Biden administration|the Joe Biden administration]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davenport |first1=Coral |title=The Keystone XL pipeline project has been terminated. |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/09/business/keystone-xl-pipeline-canceled.html |access-date=11 June 2021 |agency=The New York Times |date=9 June 2021}}</ref> The current [[U.S. Special Presidential Envoy for Climate]] is [[John Kerry]].

The [[Inflation Reduction Act of 2022]] is the largest investment in climate change mitigation in US history, with $369 billion allocated towards energy and climate initiatives.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dinneen |first=James |title=What does the Inflation Reduction Act mean for US carbon emissions? |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2332499-what-does-the-inflation-reduction-act-mean-for-us-carbon-emissions/ |access-date=2022-08-19 |website=[[New Scientist]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

====State and regional policy====
Across the country, regional organizations, [[U.S. state|states]], and cities are achieving real emissions reductions and gaining valuable policy experience as they take action on climate change. According to the report of [[America's Pledge]], 65% of the American population, 51% of the GHG emissions and 68% of the GDP, are now part of different coalitions that support climate action and want to fulfill the commitments of the US in the Paris Agreement. The coalitions include [[We Are Still In]], [[US Climate Alliance]], [[Climate Mayors]] and more.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.bbhub.io/dotorg/sites/28/2019/12/Accelerating-Americas-Pledge.pdf|title=ACCELERATING AMERICA'S PLEDGE|date=2019|publisher=Bloomberg Philanthropies with University of Maryland Center for Global Sustainability, Rocky Mountain Institute, and World Resources Institute.|location=New York|pages=2, 50|access-date=3 February 2020}}</ref>

These actions include increasing [[renewable energy]] generation, selling agricultural [[carbon sequestration]] credits, and encouraging [[efficient energy use]].<ref name="autogenerated1">{{citation|author=Engel, Kirsten and Barak Orbach|title=Micro-Motives for State and Local Climate Change Initiatives|year=2008|publisher=[[Harvard Law & Policy Review]], Vol. 2, pp. 119-137|ssrn=1014749}}</ref> The [[U.S. Climate Change Science Program]] is a joint program of over twenty U.S. cabinet departments and federal agencies, all working together to investigate climate change. In June 2008, a report issued by the program stated that weather would become more extreme, due to climate change.<ref name="AP 6-19-08">{{cite web|last=Schmid|first=Randolph E.|date=June 19, 2008|title=Extreme weather to increase with climate change|url=https://news.yahoo.com/s/ap/20080619/ap_on_go_ot/sci_weather_extremes;_ylt=ApgxLfjbrNsYCTb0l7Xyx6ZI2ocA|publisher=Associated Press}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=June 19, 2008|title=U.S. experts: Forecast is more extreme weather|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna25268181|work=[[NBC News]]}}</ref>  States and municipalities often function as "policy laboratories", developing initiatives that serve as models for federal action.  This has been especially true with environmental regulation—most federal environmental laws have been based on state models.  In addition, state actions can significantly affect emissions, because many individual states emit high levels of greenhouse gases. Texas, for example, emits more than France, while California's emissions exceed those of Brazil.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pew Center Climate change reports.|url=http://www.pewclimate.org/policy_center/policy_reports_and_analysis/state/index.cfm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051031185246/http://www.pewclimate.org/policy_center/policy_reports_and_analysis/state/index.cfm|archive-date=2005-10-31|access-date=2010-01-11}}</ref>{{Better source needed|date=December 2021|reason=old}} State actions are also important because states have primary jurisdiction over many areas—such as electric generation, agriculture, and [[land use]]—that are critical to [[Climate change mitigation|addressing climate change]].

Many states are participating in [[regional climate change initiatives in the United States|regional climate change initiatives]], such as the [[Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative]] in the northeastern United States, the [[Western Governors' Association]] (WGA) Clean and Diversified Energy Initiative, and the Southwest Climate Change Initiative.

Inside the ten northeastern states implementing the [[Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative]], carbon dioxide emissions per capita decreased by about 25% from 2000 and 2010, as the state economies continued to grow while enacting various energy efficiency programs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.njspotlight.com/stories/13/03/26/report-urges-nj-to-re-join-regional-greenhouse-gas-initiative/|title=Report Urges NJ to Rejoin Regional Greenhouse-Gas Initiative - NJ Spotlight<!-- Bot generated title --> |date=27 March 2013 }}</ref>

In May 2023, Republican lawmakers in Montana passed a law—possibly the nation's most aggressive anti-[[climate action]] law—prohibiting state agencies from considering climate change impacts when considering permits for projects like coal mines and power plants.<ref name=InsideClimateNews_20230516/> Tennessee and Louisiana had already passed laws requiring colleges to teach "both sides" of the debate over whether human-made climate change is real.<ref name=InsideClimateNews_20230516>{{cite news |last1=Tigue |first1=Kristoffer |title=Montana's New Anti-Climate Law May Be the Most Aggressive in the Nation |url=https://insideclimatenews.org/news/16052023/todays-climate-montana-anti-climate-law/ |work=Inside Climate News |date=May 16, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230519003729/https://insideclimatenews.org/news/16052023/todays-climate-montana-anti-climate-law/ |archive-date=May 19, 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Legal actions====
In April 2010, Virginia's Republican Attorney General [[Ken Cuccinelli]] claimed that climate scientist [[Michael E. Mann]] had possibly violated state fraud laws, and without providing evidence of wrongdoing, filed the [[Attorney General of Virginia's climate science investigation]]. The case involved extensive demands for document production, and was seen as an assault on academic freedom.<ref name=Guardian_20120302/> After two years of litigation, the Virginia Supreme Court ruled in March 2012 that Cuccinelli did not have the authority to demand such records, and dismissed the action.<ref name=Guardian_20120302>{{Cite news |last=Goldenberg |first=Suzanne |date=2 March 2012 |title=Virginia court rejects sceptic's bid for climate science emails: Environment |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2012/mar/02/virginia-court-sceptic-access-climate-emails |access-date=2 March 2012}}</ref><ref name="AAAS2010-05-18">{{cite web |date=18 May 2010 |title=Statement of the AAAS Board Of Directors Concerning the Virginia Attorney General's Investigation of Prof. Michael Mann's Work While on the Faculty of University of Virginia |work=AAAS - The World's Largest General Scientific Society |url=http://www.aaas.org/news/releases/2010/media/0518board_statement_cuccinelli.pdf |access-date=30 July 2010 |publisher=[[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]]}}</ref><ref name="PBS_Article2010-08-25">{{cite news |last=Gentile |first=Sal |title=Climate scientist calls Va. attorney general's fraud probe 'harassment' |publisher=PBS |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/need-to-know/environment/climate-scientist-says-va-attorney-generals-fraud-probe-is-harassment/3080/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100827015203/http://www.pbs.org/wnet/need-to-know/environment/climate-scientist-says-va-attorney-generals-fraud-probe-is-harassment/3080/ |archive-date=August 27, 2010 |access-date=7 September 2010}}</ref><ref name="ucsusa.org">{{cite web |title=Judge Dismisses Ken Cuccinelli's Misguided Investigation of Michael Mann Union of Concerned Scientists<!-- Bot generated title --> |url=http://www.ucsusa.org/news/press_release/judge-dismisses-ken-cuccinelli-mann-0437.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100902015145/http://www.ucsusa.org/news/press_release/judge-dismisses-ken-cuccinelli-mann-0437.html |archive-date=2 September 2010}}</ref><ref name="Wapo 020312">{{Cite news |last=Kumar |first=Anita |date=2 March 2012 |title=Va. Supreme Court tosses Cuccinelli's case against former U-Va. climate change researcher – Virginia Politics |publisher=The Washington Post blogs |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/virginia-politics/post/va-supreme-court-tosses-cuccinellis-case-against-u-va/2012/03/02/gIQAeOqjmR_blog.html |access-date=2 March 2012}}</ref>
