In June 2023, [[Multnomah County, Oregon]] filed a lawsuit against seven defendants, including Exxon Mobil, Shell, Chevron and the Western States Petroleum Association, for materially contributing to the [[2021 Western North America heat wave|2021 heat wave]] in the Pacific Northwest, which is thought to have killed hundreds of people.<ref name=NBCnews_20230622/> According to the Center for Climate Integrity, the Multnomah County lawsuit is the 36th action filed against fossil fuel interests for worsening the effects of climate change.<ref name=NBCnews_20230622>{{cite news |last1=Bush |first1=Evan |title=Oregon county sues fossil fuel companies, alleging they caused deadly 2021 heat wave in Northwest |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/oregon-county-sues-fossil-fuel-companies-alleging-caused-deadly-2021-h-rcna90707 |agency=NBC News |date=June 22, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230623013656/https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/oregon-county-sues-fossil-fuel-companies-alleging-caused-deadly-2021-h-rcna90707 |archive-date=June 23, 2023}}</ref>

=== International cooperation ===
{{Further|United States and the Paris Agreement}}[[File:Barack Obama with European leaders at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Copenhagen.jpg|thumb|US president [[Barack Obama]] briefs several European leaders during the [[2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference]].]]
[[File:Secretary Kerry Delivers a Major Address at COP21 Climate Change Conference in Paris (23336043410).jpg|thumb|US [[United States Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[John Kerry]] speaking at the [[2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference]].]]
[[File:Donald Trump, speech with teleprompters, 2017 (cropped).jpg|thumb|President [[Donald Trump]] announcing [[United States withdrawal from the Paris Agreement|U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement]] in 2017.]]
[[File:Joe Biden signs his first executive orders in the Oval Office on Jan 20 2021.ogv|thumb|President [[Joe Biden]] signing his first [[executive order]] re-joining the Paris Agreement in 2021.]]
The United States, although a [[Signature|signatory]] to the 1997 [[Kyoto Protocol]], under [[Bill Clinton|President Clinton]], neither [[ratified]] nor withdrew from the protocol. In 1997, the U.S. Senate voted unanimously under the [[Byrd–Hagel Resolution]] that it was not the sense of the senate that the United States should be a signatory to the Kyoto Protocol, and in March 2001, the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush Administration]] announced that it would not implement the treaty, saying it would create economic setbacks in the U.S. and does not put enough pressure to limit emissions from developing nations.<ref>Alex Kirby, [https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/1247518.stm US blow to Kyoto hopes], 2001-03-28, BBC News (online).</ref>  In February 2002, Bush announced his alternative to the Kyoto Protocol, by bringing forth a plan to reduce the intensity of greenhouse gasses by 18 percent over 10 years. The intensity of greenhouse gasses specifically is the ratio of greenhouse gas emissions and economic output, meaning that under this plan, emissions would still continue to grow, but at a slower pace. Bush stated that this plan would prevent the release of 500 million metric tons of greenhouse gases, which is about the equivalent of 70 million cars from the road. This target would achieve this goal by providing [[tax credits]] to businesses that use renewable energy sources.<ref>[http://archives.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/02/14/bush.global.warming/index.html Bush unveils voluntary plan to reduce global warming] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081212054358/http://archives.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/02/14/bush.global.warming/index.html|date=2008-12-12}}, CNN.com, 2002-02-14.</ref>

In 2007, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the case ''[[Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency]]'' that [[Regulation of greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act|EPA regulation of carbon dioxide]] is required under the [[Clean Air Act (United States)|Clean Air Act]].

President Barack Obama proposed a [[cap-and-trade]] program as part of the [[2010 United States federal budget]], but this was never adopted by Congress.<ref>{{Cite web|title=President's Budget Draws Clean Energy Funds from Climate Measure|url=http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/rea/news/article/2009/03/presidents-budget-draws-clean-energy-funds-from-climate-measure|access-date=2009-04-03|publisher=Renewable Energy World|archive-date=2015-01-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150114203327/http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/rea/news/article/2009/03/presidents-budget-draws-clean-energy-funds-from-climate-measure}}</ref>

President Obama committed in the December 2009 [[Copenhagen Climate Change Summit]] to reduce carbon dioxide emissions in the range of 17% below 2005 levels by 2020, 42% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 83% below 2005 levels by 2050.<ref name="nrdc.org">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nrdc.org/resources/copenhagen-accord-foundations-international-action-climate-change|title=The Copenhagen Accord: Foundations for International Action on Climate Change|website=NRDC|date=23 June 2010 }}</ref> Data from an April 2013 report by the [[Energy Information Administration]] (EIA), showed a 12% reduction in the 2005 to 2012 period. Just over half of this decrease has been attributed to the recession, and the rest to a variety of factors such as replacing coal-based power generation with natural gas and increasing energy efficiency of American vehicles (according to a [[Council of Economic Advisors]] analysis).<ref>{{cite news|last=Lashof|first=Dan|date=April 8, 2013|title=Carbon-Dioxide Emissions Falling, But Is That Enough?|publisher=[[LiveScience]]|url=https://www.livescience.com/28530-carbon-dioxide-falling.html|access-date=May 14, 2013}}</ref>

In an address to the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]] in June 2013, the President detailed a specific action plan to achieve the 17% carbon emissions cut from 2005 by 2020, including measures such as shifting from [[Coal power in the United States|coal-based power generation]] to solar and natural gas production.<ref name="bypass">[https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/jun/25/barack-obama-climate-change-strategy Barack Obama pledges to bypass Congress to tackle climate change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191225162352/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/jun/25/barack-obama-climate-change-strategy |date=2019-12-25 }} 25 June 2013</ref> Some Republican and Democratic lawmakers expressed concern at the idea of imposing new fines and regulations on the coal industry while the U.S. still tries to recover from the [[Great Recession|world economic recession]], with [[Speaker of the United States House of Representatives|Speaker of the House]] [[John Boehner]] saying that the proposed rules "will put thousands and thousands of Americans out of work".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/cb2a6450-de79-11e2-b990-00144feab7de|title=Obama's 'war on coal' carries risks in battleground states|website=www.ft.com}}</ref> [[Christiana Figueres]], executive director of the [[2013 United Nations Climate Change Conference|UN's climate secretariat]], praised the plan as providing a vital benchmark that people concerned with climate change can use as a paragon both at home and abroad.<ref name="verdict">[https://www.theguardian.com/environment/blog/2013/jun/25/obama-climate-speech-expert-verdict Obama's climate speech: 'It is time for Congress to share his ambition' Was it enough? Experts give their verdict on the US president's long-awaited speech addressing climate change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170317235515/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/blog/2013/jun/25/obama-climate-speech-expert-verdict |date=2017-03-17 }} 25 ''[[The Guardian]]'' June 2013</ref>

After not participating in previous climate international treaties, the United States signed the [[Paris Agreement]] on April 22, 2016, during the [[Obama administration]]. Though this agreement does not mandate a specific reduction for any given country, it sets global goals, asks countries to set their own goals, and mandates reporting. United States international leadership was considered crucial in the negotiation during the [[2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference]] and successful adoption of the international treaty.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=Charles F. |last2=Karlsson |first2=Christer |date=2018-05-04 |title=The UN climate change negotiations and the role of the United States: assessing American leadership from Copenhagen to Paris |journal=Environmental Politics |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=519–540 |doi=10.1080/09644016.2018.1442388 |bibcode=2018EnvPo..27..519P |s2cid=158705120 |issn=0964-4016|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The U.S. submitted its action plan in March 2015, ahead of the treaty signing.<ref>{{Cite web|title=UNFCCC|url=http://newsroom.unfccc.int/unfccc-newsroom/united-states-submits-its-climate-action-plan-ahead-of-2015-paris-agreement/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701050900/http://newsroom.unfccc.int/unfccc-newsroom/united-states-submits-its-climate-action-plan-ahead-of-2015-paris-agreement|archive-date=2016-07-01|access-date=2016-07-06}}</ref> Reaffirming the November 2014 announcement it made with China,<ref>{{Cite web|date=2014-11-12|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=U.S.-China Joint Announcement on Climate Change|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2014/11/11/us-china-joint-announcement-climate-change}}</ref> the United States declared it would reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 26–28% below 2005 levels by 2025.  This is to be accomplished by several executive actions:<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-03-31|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=FACT SHEET: U.S. Reports its 2025 Emissions Target to the UNFCCC|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/03/31/fact-sheet-us-reports-its-2025-emissions-target-unfccc}}</ref>
* [[Clean Power Plan]] - regulating sources of electricity (put on hold by the Supreme Court in February, 2016, pending the outcome of a lawsuit){{Update inline|date=December 2021}}
* New emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles, finalized by EPA in March, 2016<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-08-19|title=Transportation, Air Pollution, and Climate Change|url=https://www.epa.gov/air-pollution-transportation}}</ref>
* Department of Energy efficiency standards for commercial buildings, appliances, and equipment{{citation needed|date=July 2016}}
* Various actions to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases other than carbon dioxide, including regulation and voluntary efforts related to methane from landfills, agriculture, coal mines; and [[hydrofluorocarbons]] (HFCs) reduction through domestic regulation and amendment of the [[Montreal Protocol]]

In June 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced [[United States withdrawal from the Paris Agreement]], although the exit process specified by the treaty (which Trump said the U.S. would follow) will last until at least November 4, 2020.<ref>{{Cite news|last=DiChristopher|first=Tom|date=19 September 2017|title=Trump is still pulling out of Paris Agreement, despite chatter of a reversal, experts say|work=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/09/19/trump-is-not-reversing-on-paris-agreement-heres-why.html}}</ref> Trump states that dropping out the agreement will create more job opportunities in the United States, but it may actually have the opposite effect by stifling the renewable energy industries.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Taneja|first=Hemant|date=2 January 2017|title=Why pulling out of Paris Accord damages America's economic future|work=TC News|url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/06/02/why-pulling-out-of-paris-accords-damages-americas-economic-future/}}</ref> At the same time, Trump administration shut down the United States Environmental Protection Agency's climate change web pages and removed mentions of the topic elsewhere on the site.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Heikkinen|first=Niina|date=25 January 2017|title=Trump Administration Orders EPA to Remove Its Climate Change Web Page|work=E&E News|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/trump-administration-orders-epa-to-remove-its-climate-change-web-page1/}}</ref> In April 2018, the Trump administration cancelled NASA's Carbon Monitoring System (CMS) program, which helped with the monitoring of CO<sub>2</sub> emissions and deforestation in the United States and in other countries.<ref>{{cite news|date=2018-05-10|title=Trump White House axes Nasa research into greenhouse gas cuts|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-44067797|access-date=May 13, 2018}}</ref> The Trump administration also moved to increase fossil fuel consumption and roll back environmental policies that are considered to be burdensome to businesses.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Popovich|first1=Nadja|last2=Albeck-Ripka|first2=Livia|date=2017-10-05|title=52 Environmental Rules on the Way Out Under Trump|newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2017/10/05/climate/trump-environment-rules-reversed.html|access-date=December 8, 2017}}</ref>

For offsetting the dismantlement of the [[Clean Power Plan]] approximately 10 billion trees would need to be planted. Activists try to plant this number of trees.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Arrieta-Kenna|first1=Ruairí|date=29 August 2017|title="Trump Forest": why environmentalists are planting trees to thwart the president|agency=Vox}}</ref>

In January 2020 Trump announced that the USA would join the [[Trillion Tree Campaign]]. Climate activists critiqued the plan for ignoring the root causes of climate change.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Davidson|first1=Jordan|date=22 January 2020|title=Trump Says U.S. Will Join 1 Trillion Trees Initiative, While Ignoring the Root of the Problem and Attacking Climate Activists|agency=Ecowatch|url=https://www.ecowatch.com/trump-trillion-trees--2644889576.html|access-date=24 January 2020}}</ref> House Natural Resources Committee Chairman [[Raul Grijalva]] critiqued the plan as "a feel-good participatory gesture" without a broader portfolio of environmental actions surrounding it.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wilner|first1=Michael|last2=Dumain|first2=Emma|date=14 February 2020|title=Courting young conservatives, Republicans speed up their 'evolution' on climate change|url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article240298461.html|access-date=5 May 2020}}</ref>

In 2019, Democrats proposed a plan for climate action in USA aiming to not sell greenhouse gas emitting cars by 2035, reach zero emissions from the energy sector by 2040 and reduce to zero all the greenhouse gas emission of the country by 2050. The plan includes some actions to improve [[environmental justice]]. In 2016, 38% of adults in United States thought that stopping climate change are a top priority which rose to 52% in 2020. Many Republicans share this opinion.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Flavelle|first1=Christopher|date=29 June 2020|title=Democrats Detail a Climate Agenda Tying Environment to Racial Justice|work=The New York Times |agency=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/29/climate/house-democrats-climate-plan.html|access-date=2 July 2020}}</ref>
In November 2020 the [[Federal Reserve]] asked to join the [[Network for Greening the Financial System]] and included Climate Change in the list of risks to the economy.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Dougherty|first1=Sarah|title=The Federal Reserve's new signals on climate change and risk|url=https://www.greenbiz.com/article/federal-reserves-new-signals-climate-change-and-risk|access-date=30 November 2020|website=GreenBiz|date=30 November 2020 |publisher=NRDC}}</ref> On November 2, ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' published an article about Trump administration efforts to distort and suppress information about climate change by firing the acting chief scientist of the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] and distorting the use of climate models at the [[United States Geological Survey]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Federman|first1=Adam|date=November 2, 2020|title=Trump's Attacks on Climate Science Are Coming to Fruition|language=en-us|magazine=Wired|url=https://www.wired.com/story/trumps-attacks-on-climate-science-are-coming-to-fruition/|access-date=December 13, 2020}}</ref>

On his first day as president, January 20, 2021, [[Joe Biden]] signed an [[executive order]] pledging that the US would rejoin the Paris Agreement.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rott|first=Nathan|date=January 20, 2021|title=Inauguration Day: Live Updates: Biden Moves To Have U.S. Rejoin Climate Accord|publisher=National Public Radio|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/inauguration-day-live-updates/2021/01/20/958923821/biden-moves-to-have-u-s-rejoin-climate-accord|access-date=February 21, 2021}}</ref> The US rejoined the agreement on February 19, 2021.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Knickmeyer|first1=Ellen|last2=Borenstein|first2=Seth|date=February 19, 2021|title=Back in Paris pact, US faces tougher climate steps ahead|publisher=Associated Press|url=https://apnews.com/article/us-return-paris-climate-world-leaders-ee8eb8b6744394ad41e33f94843b6586|access-date=February 21, 2021}}</ref> This means that countries responsible for two thirds of global greenhouse gas emissions have pledged to become carbon neutral; without the US, it had been half.<ref>{{cite web|title=Secretary-General welcomes US return to Paris Agreement on Climate Change|url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2021/01/1082602|access-date=22 January 2021|website=UN News|date=20 January 2021|publisher=United Nations}}</ref>

A survey taken by the [[Public Religion Research Institute]] (PRRI) in 2023 found that the majority of respondents (61%) believed that climate change was mostly being caused by human activates while 28% said it was being caused by natural patterns in the Earth's environment and 10% said there "was no solid evidence that climate change is happening".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-04 |title=The Faith Factor in Climate Change: How Religion Impacts American Attitudes on Climate and Environmental Policy |url=https://prri.org/research/the-faith-factor-in-climate-change-how-religion-impacts-american-attitudes-on-climate-and-environmental-policy/ |access-date=2025-10-03 |website=PRRI |language=en-US}}</ref>

In August 2022, ''[[Nature Communications]]'' published a survey with 6,119 [[Sampling (statistics)|representatively sampled]] Americans that found that 66 to 80% of Americans supported major climate change mitigation policies (i.e. [[100% renewable energy]] by 2035, [[Green New Deal]], [[Carbon fee and dividend|carbon tax and dividend]], renewable energy production siting on [[public land]]) and expressed climate concern, but that 80 to 90% of Americans underestimated the prevalence of support for such policies and such concern by their fellow Americans (with the sample estimating that only 37 to 43% on average supported such policies). Americans in every state and every assessed demographic (e.g. [[Political ideologies in the United States|political ideology]], [[Race and ethnicity in the United States|racial group]], [[List of United States urban areas|urban]]/[[suburb]]an/[[Rural areas in the United States|rural]] residence, [[Educational attainment in the United States|educational attainment]]) underestimated support across all policies tested, and every state survey group and every demographic assessed underestimated support for the climate policies by at least 20 percentage points. The researchers attributed the misperception among the general public to [[pluralistic ignorance]]. Conservatives were found to underestimate support for the policies due to a [[false consensus effect]], [[Red states and blue states#Polarization|exposure to more conservative local norms]], and consumption of [[Media bias in the United States#Conservative|conservative news]], while liberals were suggested to underestimate support for the policies due to a [[false-uniqueness effect]].<ref name="NatureComms_20220823">{{cite journal |last1=Sparkman |first1=Gregg |last2=Geiger |first2=Nathan |last3=Weber |first3=Elke U. |title=Americans experience a false social reality by underestimating popular climate policy support by nearly half |journal=Nature Communications |date=23 August 2022 |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=4779 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-32412-y  |doi-access=free|pmid=35999211 |pmc=9399177 |bibcode=2022NatCo..13.4779S |s2cid=251766448 }}(Fig. 3) ● Explained in {{cite web |last1=Yoder |first1=Kate |title=Americans are convinced climate action is unpopular. They're very, very wrong. / Support for climate policies is double what most people think, a new study found. |url=https://grist.org/politics/americans-think-climate-action-unpopular-wrong-study/ |website=Grist |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220829104543/https://grist.org/politics/americans-think-climate-action-unpopular-wrong-study/ |archive-date=29 August 2022 |date=29 August 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Clifford|first=Catherine|date=August 24, 2022|title=Americans don't think other Americans care about climate change as much as they do|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/08/24/americans-underestimate-how-much-their-peers-care-about-climate-change.html|access-date=August 27, 2022}}</ref>

In the [[exit poll]]s for the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], 67 percent of voters surveyed agreed that climate change is a serious problem,<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Results 2020 President exit polls. |language=en |work=[[CNN]] |url=https://www.cnn.com/election/2020/exit-polls/president/national-results |access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref> while 71 percent of voters surveyed in the exit polls for the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|2022 U.S. House of Representatives elections]] agreed that climate change is a "very serious" or "somewhat serious" problem.<ref>{{cite news |date=November 9, 2022 |title=Exit polls for Midterm Election Results 2022 |publisher=CNN |url=https://www.cnn.com/election/2022/exit-polls/national-results/house/0 |access-date=November 17, 2022}}</ref>

In July 2024, [[Resources for the Future]] and the Political Psychology Research Group of [[Stanford University]] released the 2024 edition of a joint survey of 1,000 U.S. adults that found that while 77% believed that global warming would hurt future generations at least a moderate amount, only 55% believed that global warming would hurt them personally–which was lower than the peak response to the question in the survey series in 2010 when 63% of survey respondents believed that global warming would hurt them personally.<ref>{{cite news|last=Iacurci|first=Greg|date=July 16, 2024|title=Many Americans think they're insulated from climate change. Their finances indicate otherwise|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/07/16/how-climate-change-may-impact-americans-wallets.html|access-date=July 16, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite report|last1=Krosnick|first1=Jon A.|author-link1=Jon Krosnick|last2=MacInnis|first2=Bo|date=July 15, 2024|title=Climate Insights 2024: American Understanding of Climate Change|series=24-11|page=7|publisher=Resources For the Future|url=https://media.rff.org/documents/Report_24-11.pdf|access-date=July 16, 2024}}</ref>

One April 2012 ''[[Stanford Social Innovation Review]]'' article said that public opinion in the United States varies intensely enough to be considered a [[culture war]].<ref>[https://www.ssireview.org/articles/entry/climate_science_as_culture_war ''Climate Science as Culture War: The public debate around climate change is no longer about science&nbsp;– it's about values, culture, and ideology''] Fall 2012 [[Stanford Social Innovation Review]]</ref>

In a January 2013 survey, Pew found that 69% of Americans say there is solid evidence that the Earth's average temperature has gotten warmer over the past few decades, up six points since November 2011 and 12 points since 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 May 2013 |title=Climate Change: Key Data Points from Pew Research &#124; Pew Research Center |work=Pew Research Center |url=http://www.pewresearch.org/2013/04/02/climate-change-key-data-points-from-pew-research/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515145510/http://www.pewresearch.org/2013/04/02/climate-change-key-data-points-from-pew-research/ |archive-date=15 May 2013}}</ref>

A Gallup poll in 2014 concluded that 51% of Americans were a little or not at all worried about climate change, 24% a great deal and 25% were worried a fair amount.<ref name="Riffkin">{{cite news |last1=Riffkin |first1=Rebecca |date=12 March 2014 |title=Climate Change Not a Top Worry in U.S. |publisher=Gallup |url=https://www.gallup.com/poll/167843/climate-change-not-top-worry.aspx |access-date=21 July 2014}}</ref>

A 2016 Gallup poll found that 64% of Americans were worried about global warming, that 59% believed that global warming was already happening, and 65% were convinced that global warming was caused by human activities. These numbers show that awareness of global warming was increasing in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news |title=U.S. Concern About Global Warming at Eight-Year High |work=Gallup.com |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/190010/concern-global-warming-eight-year-high.aspx |access-date=25 April 2018}}</ref>

A Gallup poll showed that 62% of Americans believe that the [[effects of global warming]] were happening in 2017.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Global Warming Concern at Three-Decade High in U.S. |work=Gallup.com |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/206030/global-warming-concern-three-decade-high.aspx |access-date=9 December 2017}}</ref>

In 2019, Gallup poll found that one-third of Americans blame unusual winter temperatures on climate change.<ref>{{Cite news |title=One-Third in U.S. Blame Unusual Winter Temps on Climate Change |work=Gallup.com |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/247910/one-third-blame-unusual-winter-temps-climate-change.aspx?g_source=link_NEWSV9&g_medium=TOPIC&g_campaign=item_&g_content=One-Third%2520in%2520U.S.%2520Blame%2520Unusual%2520Winter%2520Temps%2520on%2520Climate%2520Change |access-date=26 March 2019}}</ref>

==== Grouping into six categories ====
The [[Yale Program on Climate Change Communication]] has studied the [[Public opinion on climate change|public opinion about climate change]] in the US, and how it changes with time. Since 2007<ref name="YaleCCC_Leiserowitz_2007">{{citation |last1=Leiserowitz |first1=Anthony |title=Global Warming's Six Americas |date=2007 |location=Bridgeport, CN |last2=Maibach |first2=M. |last3=Roser-Renouf |first3=Connie}}</ref><ref name="YaleCCC_Leiserowitz_2008">{{citation |last1=Leiserowitz |first1=A. |title=Global Warming's Six Americas: An Audience Segmentation |date=2008 |location=[[New Haven, Connecticut]] |publisher=Yale University |last2=Maibach |first2=Edward |last3=Roser-Renouf |first3=Connie}}</ref> and continuing into 2021,<ref name="YaleCCC_20210727">{{Cite web |last1=Goldberg |first1=Matthew |last2=Wang |first2=Xinran |last3=Marlon |first3=Jennifer |last4=Carman |first4=Jennifer |last5=Lacroix |first5=Karine |last6=Kotcher |first6=John |last7=Rosenthal |first7=Seth |last8=Maibach |first8=Edward |last9=Leiserowitz |first9=Anthony |date=July 27, 2021 |title=Segmenting the climate change Alarmed: Active, Willing, and Inactive |url=https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/segmenting-the-climate-change-alarmed-active-willing-and-inactive/ |access-date=October 30, 2021 |work=Yale Program on Climate Change Communication}}</ref> Yale University researchers have been analysing public opinion on climate change using a six-group framework, called the Six Americas, to describe and quantify positions people hold in terms of "levels of engagement and concern and awareness" of an issue. 

They have divided the population of the USA into six categories:<ref name="YaleGMU_20220112">{{cite web |last1=Leiserowitz |first1=Anthony |last2=Maibach |first2=Edward |last3=Rosenthal |first3=Seth |last4=Kotcher |first4=John |last5=Neyens |first5=Liz |last6=Marlon |first6=Jennifer |last7=Carman |first7=Jennifer |last8=Lacroix |first8=Karine |last9=Goldberg |first9=Matthew |display-authors=4 |date=12 January 2022 |title=Global Warming's Six Americas, September 2021 |url=https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/global-warmings-six-americas-september-2021/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220113144538/https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/global-warmings-six-americas-september-2021/ |archive-date=13 January 2022 |website=climatecommunication.yale.edu |publisher=Yale Program on Climate Change Communication}}</ref>
* ''Alarmed'': people who think that climate change happens, it is man made, and an urgent threat.
* ''Concerned'': people who think climate change exists, it is man made, and it is a serious problem.
* ''Cautious'': people that have heard about climate change but are not sure what causes it and are "not very worried about it".
* ''Disengaged'': people that do not know much about climate change.
* ''Doubtful'': people who think that climate change probably does not exist or it is not man made, but are not sure. They consider climate change as "a low risk".
* ''Dismissive'': people that think that man made climate change does not exist, and who mostly oppose climate measures.
According to the report on the 2017-2021 Climate Change in the American Mind survey, the percentages had changed—the "Alarmed" increasing to 24% of the population, the "Concerned" to 30%, "Cautious" remained the same at 19%, "Disengaged" decreased to 5%, the "Doubtful" increased to 15%, and the "Dismissive" increased to 10%.<ref name="YaleCCC_20210727" />

In 2019, the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication found that 69% of Americans believe that climate change is happening. However, Americans underestimate the number of fellow Americans who believe that global warming is taking place. Americans estimated that only 54% of Americans believed that climate change is happening, when the number was much higher.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ballew |first=Matthew |last2=Gustafson |first2=Abel |last3=Bergquist |first3=Parrish |last4=Goldberg |first4=Matthew |last5=Rosenthal |first5=Seth |last6=Kotcher |first6=John |last7=Maibach |first7=Edward |last8=Leiserowitz |first8=Anthony |date=July 2, 2019 |title=Americans Underestimate How Many Others in the U.S. Think Global Warming is Happening |url=https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/americans-underestimate-how-many-others-in-the-u-s-think-global-warming-is-happening/ |website=Yale Program on Climate Change Communication}}</ref> Researchers have called this misperception a ''false social reality,'' a form of [[pluralistic ignorance]].<ref name=NatureComms_20220823/>

A survey conducted in 2021 by the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and the [[George Mason University]] Center for Climate Change Communication indicated that Americans are "alarmed" (33%), "concerned" (25%), "cautious" (17%), "disengaged" (5%), "doubtful" (10%), and "dismissive" (9%) about climate change.<ref name="YaleGMU_20220112" /> About 6 of 10 Americans are alarmed or concerned about climate change. Overall, the support for climate policy is growing. The "Alarmed" section has almost doubled. The Cautious, Doubtful, and Dismissive groups all shrank compared to the earlier years of the study.<ref name="YaleGMU_20220112" /><ref name=":5" />

Previously, in 2015, the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication had reported that 32% of Americans were worried about global warming as a great deal. Those numbers rose to 37% in 2016, and 45% in 2017. A poll taken in 2016 shows that 52% of Americans believe climate change to be [[Causes of global warming|caused by human activity]], while 34% state it is caused by natural changes.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Yale Climate Opinion Maps - U.S. 2016 - Yale Program on Climate Change Communication |work=Yale Program on Climate Change Communication |url=http://climatecommunication.yale.edu/visualizations-data/ycom-us-2016/?est=happening&type=value&geo=county |access-date=12 February 2018 |archive-date=18 February 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180218155930/http://climatecommunication.yale.edu/visualizations-data/ycom-us-2016/?est=happening&type=value&geo=county }}</ref> 

In 2009, the same study team had reported the following results: People were alarmed (18%), concerned (33%), cautious (19%), disengaged (12%), doubtful (11%) or dismissive (7%). The alarmed and concerned make out the largest percentage and think something should be done about global warming. The cautious, disengaged and doubtful are less likely to take action. The dismissive are convinced global warming is not happening. These audiences can be used to define the best approaches for environmental action.<ref name="YaleCCC_2009" />

===Political ideologies===

[[File:20220831 Climate change is a "major threat" to my country - Pew survey.svg |thumb|The U.S. political divide on the seriousness of climate change is more than about double that of all other countries surveyed, except Australia.<ref name=Pew_20220831/> Right-wing opinion in the U.S. was found to be more dismissive than any other country in this Pew survey.<ref name=Pew_20220831>{{cite web |last1=Poushter |first1=Jacob |last2=Fagan |first2=Moira |last3=Gubbala |first3=Sneha |title=Climate Change Remains Top Global Threat Across 19-Country Survey |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2022/08/31/climate-change-remains-top-global-threat-across-19-country-survey/ |website=pewresearch.org |publisher=Pew Research Center |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220831225832/https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2022/08/31/climate-change-remains-top-global-threat-across-19-country-survey/ |archive-date=31 August 2022 |date=31 August 2022 | quote=Only statistically significant differences shown. |url-status=live }}</ref>]]
Historical support for environmental protection has been relatively [[non-partisan]]. Republican [[Theodore Roosevelt]] established national parks whereas Democrat [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] established the [[Soil Conservation Service]].

A 1977 memo from [[Jimmy Carter|President Carter]]'s chief science adviser [[Frank Press]] warned of the possibility of catastrophic climate change caused by increasing carbon dioxide concentrations introduced into the atmosphere by fossil fuel consumption.<ref name=Guardian_20220614/> However, other issues—such as known harms to health from pollutants, and avoiding energy dependence on other nations—seemed more pressing and immediate.<ref name=Guardian_20220614/> Energy Secretary [[James Schlesinger]] advised that "the policy implications of this issue are still too uncertain to warrant Presidential involvement and policy initiatives", and the fossil fuel industry began sowing doubt about climate science.<ref name=Guardian_20220614>{{cite news |last1=Pattee |first1=Emma |title=The 1977 White House climate memo that should have changed the world |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/14/1977-us-presidential-memo-predicted-climate-change |work=The Guardian |date=14 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220617151837/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/14/1977-us-presidential-memo-predicted-climate-change |archive-date=17 June 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Historical non-partisanship began to change during the 1980s when the [[Reagan administration]] stated that environmental protection was an economic burden. Views over global warming began to seriously diverge among [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] when ratifying the [[Kyoto Protocol]] was being debated in 1998. Gaps in opinions among the general public are often amplified among political figures, such as [[Member of Congress|members of Congress]], who tend to be more polarized.<ref name="Dunlap2008RepublicanDemocraticGap">{{Cite web|last=Dunlap|first=Riley E.|date=29 May 2009|title=Climate-Change Views: Republican-Democratic Gaps Expand|url=https://www.gallup.com/poll/107569/ClimateChange-Views-RepublicanDemocratic-Gaps-Expand.aspx|access-date=22 Dec 2009|publisher=Gallup}}</ref> A 2017 study by the [[Center for American Progress#Center for American Progress Action Fund|Center for American Progress Action Fund]] of [[climate change denial]] in the [[United States Congress]] found 180 members who deny the [[Scientific opinion on climate change|science behind climate change]]; all were Republicans.<ref>{{cite web|date=April 28, 2017|title=RELEASE: CAP Action Releases 2017 Anti-Science Climate Denier Caucus|url=https://www.americanprogressaction.org/press/release/2017/04/28/167312/release-cap-action-releases-2017-anti-science-climate-denier-caucus/|access-date=September 5, 2017|publisher=[[Center for American Progress#Center for American Progress Action Fund|Center for American Progress Action Fund]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Moser|first1=Claire|last2=Koronowski|first2=Ryan|date=April 28, 2017|title=The Climate Denier Caucus in Trump's Washington|url=https://thinkprogress.org/115th-congress-climate-denier-caucus-65fb825b3963/|access-date=September 5, 2017|website=[[ThinkProgress]]}}</ref>

On January 20, 2017, within moments of [[Donald Trump]]'s inauguration as president, all references to climate change were [[Trump administration political interference with science agencies|removed]] from the White House website. The U.S. has been considered the most authoritative researcher of this information, and there was concern amongst the scientific community as to how the Trump administration would prioritize the issue.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Davenport|first=Coral|date=2017-01-20|title=With Trump in Charge, Climate Change References Purged From Website|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/20/us/politics/trump-white-house-website.html|access-date=2019-10-06|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In early indications to news media of the first federal budget process under Donald Trump's administration, there were signs that most efforts under the Obama administration to curb U.S. greenhouse gas emissions would [[Environmental policy of the first Trump administration|effectively be rolled back]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kahn|first=Brian|date=February 27, 2017|title=Here's the Early Context for Trump's Budget|url=https://www.climatecentral.org/news/early-context-trump-budget-21198|access-date=2019-10-06|website=Climate Central|language=en}}</ref> In July 2018, the Trump Administration released its ''[[Fourth National Climate Assessment|Draft Environmental Impact Statement]]'' from the [[NHTSA]]. In it was the prediction that on our current course the planet will warm a disastrous seven degrees Fahrenheit (or about 3.9 degrees Celsius) by the end of this century.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Eilperin|first1=Juliet|last2=Dennis|first2=Brady|last3=Mooney|first3=Chris|date=September 28, 2018|title=Trump administration sees a 7-degree rise in global temperatures by 2100|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/trump-administration-sees-a-7-degree-rise-in-global-temperatures-by-2100/2018/09/27/b9c6fada-bb45-11e8-bdc0-90f81cc58c5d_story.html|access-date=2019-10-06|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> Speaking to the California Secretary for Natural Resources during the [[2020 California wildfires]], Trump said of the changing climate, "It'll start getting cooler, you just watch".<ref name=Politico_20200917/> When the Secretary implied that the science disagreed, Trump responded, "I don't think science knows, actually".<ref name=Politico_20200917>{{cite news |last1=Colman |first1=Zack |last2=Guillén |first2=Alex |title=Trump's climate change rollbacks to drive up U.S. emissions |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/09/17/trump-climate-rollbacks-increase-emissions-417311 |work=Politico |date=17 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210226023146/https://www.politico.com/news/2020/09/17/trump-climate-rollbacks-increase-emissions-417311 |archive-date=26 February 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Many pages were created to examine and compare the views of the candidates in the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 presidential election]] on climate change. The [[League of Conservation Voters]] create a special site, entirely dedicated to the issue called: "Change the Climate 2020".<ref>{{cite web|title=CHANGE THE CLIMATE 2020|url=https://www.changetheclimate2020.com/change-the-climate-2020/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920043437/https://www.changetheclimate2020.com/change-the-climate-2020/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=September 20, 2020|access-date=24 January 2020|website=Change the Climate 2020|publisher=League of Conservation Voters}}</ref> Similar pages were created in the site of [[Natural Resources Defense Ballotpedia,<ref>{{cite web|title=2020 presidential candidates on climate change|url=https://ballotpedia.org/2020_presidential_candidates_on_climate_change|access-date=27 January === Activism ===
{{Further|Environmental movement in the United States}}
[[File:Seattle Climate Rally (48766671928).jpg|thumb|Protesters at the [[September 2019 climate strikes|September 2019 climate strike]] in [[Seattle]].]]
The [[climate movement]] and [[Individual action on climate change|climate change protests]] have taken place in the United States. The [[2014 People's Climate March]] attracted hundreds of thousands of demonstrators to New York.<ref>{{Cite magazine |title=Hundreds of Thousands Converge on New York to Demand Climate-Change Action |url=https://time.com/3415162/peoples-climate-march-new-york-manhattan-demonstration/ |access-date=2022-07-22 |magazine=Time |language=en}}</ref> Some [[Evangelical environmentalism|evangelical Christian groups]] have also partaken in climate change activism.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gerten |first1=Dieter |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EFISBwAAQBAJ&dq=climate+change+activism+in+the+united+states&pg=PA132 |title=Religion in Environmental and Climate Change: Suffering, Values, Lifestyles |last2=Bergmann |first2=Sigurd |date=2011-11-17 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4411-6628-9 |language=en |chapter=Religious Climate Activism in the United States}}</ref>

=== Research and educational institutions ===
[[NASA]] conducts, publishes and communicates research on climate change.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://climate.nasa.gov/ |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=Climate Change: Vital Signs of the Planet}}</ref>

The [[University of Maine#Climate Change Institute|University of Maine Climate Change Institute]] (founded 1973) has mapped the difference between climate during the Ice Age and during modern times, and found that the climate can change abruptly through analysis of Greenland ice cores.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-21 |title=UMaine Climate Change Institute celebrates 50th anniversary - UMaine News - University of Maine |url=https://umaine.edu/news/blog/2022/11/21/umaine-climate-change-institute-celebrates-50th-anniversary/ |access-date=2023-05-30 |website=UMaine News |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2011, the [[University of California, Davis]], incorporated 4.1 MW of [[solar panel]]s in the student housing community of West Village effectively reaching 82% of [[Zero-energy building|net zero energy.]]<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal |last1=Clair |first1=Matthew |last2=Chiang |first2=Lifang |date=2016-12-12 |title=Chapter 2. The University as a Living Laboratory for Climate Solutions |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311633692 |journal=Collabra |volume=2 |page=16 |doi=10.1525/collabra.61|doi-access=free }}</ref> The [[University of California, Irvine]], added [[hydrogen fuel]] cell buses to their [[Microgrid|mircrogrid]], which contain no tailpipe emissions of carbon, better fuel economy than diesel and natural gas buses and have a significant longer range than battery powered buses.<ref name="auto" /> The [[University of California, Merced]], began the UC Solar initiative in which 9 out of the 10 US campuses installed 1-megawatt solar array where researchers are utilizing [[Nonimaging optics|non-imaging optics]] to design thermal and [[Concentrator photovoltaics|photovoltaic solar concentrators]].<ref name="auto" />

===Business community===
{{update|section|date=October 2020}}
{{See also|Business action on climate change}}
In 2015, according to ''The New York Times'' and others, [[Petroleum industry|oil companies]] knew that [[Petroleum|burning oil and gas]] could cause global warming since the 1970s but, nonetheless, funded deniers for years.<ref name="NYT-20151105" /><ref name="TG-20150708" /> Likewise, scientists at General Motors and the Ford Motor Company knew as early as the 1960s that their products caused climate change and the companies did the same.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Frazin |first1=Rachel |title=Ford, GM scientists knew in 1960s that emissions caused climate change: report |url=https://thehill.com/policy/transportation/522762-automakers-knew-1960s-emissions-caused-climate-change-report |access-date=23 April 2021 |work=TheHill |date=26 October 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

A review, published in 2016, of academic literature that explores the potential for greenhouse emissions related liability, calculated that climate change related liability could reach trillions of dollars based on lost revenue from nations that would forced to evacuate because of sea level rise.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Heidari|first1=Negin|last2=Pearce|first2=Joshua M.|year=2016|title=A Review of Greenhouse Gas Emission Liabilities as the Value of Renewable Energy for Mitigating Lawsuits for Climate Change Related Damages|url=https://www.academia.edu/19418589|journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews|volume=55C|pages=899–908|doi=10.1016/j.rser.2015.11.025 |bibcode=2016RSERv..55..899H }}</ref>

==Climate change by state or territory==

The impacts of climate change are different from state to state. Generally, states that emit more [[carbon dioxide]] per person and block climate action, are suffering more.<ref name="nature.com"/><ref name="ecowatch.com"/>{{update inline|date=October 2020}} To learn more about the climate change by state, see the following articles: {{United States topic|prefix=Climate change in|state=uncollapsed}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change policy of the United States
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{About|the policy regarding climate change|other aspects of climate change in this country|Climate change in the United States}}
{{Update|inaccurate=yes|date=July 2025}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2021}}

The [[Climate policy|climate change policy]] of the [[United States]] has major impacts on global [[climate change]] and global [[climate change mitigation]]. This is because the United States is the second largest emitter of [[greenhouse gasses]] in the world after [[greenhouse gas emissions by China|China]], and is among the [[List of countries by greenhouse gas emissions per capita|countries with the highest greenhouse gas emissions per person]] in the world. Cumulatively, the United States has emitted over a trillion metric tons of greenhouse gases, more than any country in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Fig. 4 {{!}} Scientific Data |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02041-1/figures/4 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |language=en}}</ref>

Climate change policy is developed at the [[U.S. state|state]] and [[US Federal government|federal]] levels of government.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-10-21|title=Federal Action on Climate|url=https://www.c2es.org/content/federal-action-on-climate/|access-date=2020-02-26|website=Center for Climate and Energy Solutions}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) defines climate change as "any significant change in the measures of climate lasting for an extended period of time." Essentially, climate change includes major changes in temperature, precipitation, or wind patterns, as well as other effects, that occur over several decades or longer.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://19january2017snapshot.epa.gov/climatechange/climate-change-basic-information_.html |title=Climate Change: Basic Information |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) |location=Washington, D.C. |date=2017-01-17}}</ref> The policy with the biggest US investment in [[climate change mitigation]] is the [[Inflation Reduction Act of 2022]].

The [[politics of climate change]] have [[Political polarization in the United States|polarized]] certain political parties and other organizations.<ref>{{Cite web  |date=2016-10-04 |title=The Politics of Climate |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2016/10/04/the-politics-of-climate/ |access-date=2022-05-20 |website=Pew Research Center Science & Society |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[U.S. Democratic Party|Democratic Party]] advocates for an expansion of climate change mitigation policies whereas the [[U.S. Republican Party|Republican Party]] tends to advocate for slower change, inaction, or reversal of existing climate change mitigation policies. In 2025, the second Trump administration promoted [[climate change denial]] and misinformation and moved to undo the [[regulation of greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act]].

Most lobbying on climate policy in the United States is done by corporations that are publicly opposed to reducing carbon emissions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cory|first1=Jared|last2=Lerner|first2=Michael|last3=Osgood|first3=Iain|date=2020|title=Supply Chain Linkages and the Extended Carbon Coalition|journal=American Journal of Political Science|volume=65|pages=69–87|language=en|doi=10.1111/ajps.12525|hdl=2027.42/166293 |s2cid=219437282|issn=1540-5907|url=https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/122459/ |hdl-access=free}}</ref>
