======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Economic analysis of climate change
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2016}}

'''Economic analysis of climate change''' uses economic tools and models to calculate the scale and distribution of damages caused by [[climate change]]. It can also give guidance for the best policies for [[Climate change mitigation|mitigation]] and [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation to climate change]] from an economic perspective. There are many economic models and frameworks. For example, in a [[cost–benefit analysis]], the trade offs between climate change impacts, adaptation, and mitigation are made explicit. For this kind of analysis, [[Integrated assessment modelling|integrated assessment models]] (IAMs) are useful. Those models link main features of society and economy with the biosphere and atmosphere into one modelling framework.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wang |first1=Zheng |title=Integrated Assessment Models of Climate Change Economics |last2=Wu |first2=Jing |last3=Liu |first3=Changxin |last4=Gu |first4=Gaoxiang |date=2017 |publisher=Springer Singapore |isbn=978-981-10-3943-0 |location=Singapore |doi=10.1007/978-981-10-3945-4}}</ref>

In general, climate damages increase the more the global surface temperature increases.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |author=IPCC |author-link=IPCC |title={{Harvnb|IPCC AR5 WG2 A|2014}} |year=2014 |page=12 |chapter=Summary for Policymakers |ref={{harvid|IPCC AR5 WG2 Summary for Policymakers|2014}} |access-date=15 February 2020 |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar5/wg2/ar5_wgII_spm_en.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219013825/https://archive.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar5/wg2/ar5_wgII_spm_en.pdf |archive-date=19 December 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> Many [[effects of climate change]] are linked to market transactions and therefore directly affect [[Econometrics|metrics]] like [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] or [[inflation]].<ref name="smith" />{{rp|936–941}} For instance, climate change can drive inflation in food via heat and droughts, but also drives up overall inflation.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Kotz |first1=Maximilian |last2=Kuik |first2=Friderike |last3=Lis |first3=Eliza |last4=Nickel |first4=Christiane |date=2024 |title=Global warming and heat extremes to enhance inflationary pressures |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=116 |doi=10.1038/s43247-023-01173-x  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2024ComEE...5..116K |issn=2662-4435}}</ref> There are also non-market impacts which are harder to translate into economic costs.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Vuong, Q.-H.|date=2021|title=The semiconducting principle of monetary and environmental values exchange |url=https://reunido.uniovi.es/index.php/EBL/article/view/15872|journal=Economics and Business Letters|volume=10|issue=3|pages=284–290|doi=10.17811/ebl.10.3.2021.284-290}}</ref> These include the [[Effects of climate change on human health|impacts of climate change on human health]], [[Effects of climate change on biomes|biomes]] and [[ecosystem service]]s.

Economic analysis also looks at the [[economics of climate change mitigation]] and the [[Climate finance#Adaptation costs and adaptation financing needs|cost of climate adaptation]]. Mitigation costs will vary according to how and when emissions are cut. Early, well-planned action will minimize the costs.<ref name="stern">Stern, N. (2006). ''Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change: Part III: The Economics of Stabilisation.'' HM Treasury, London: http://hm-treasury.gov.uk/sternreview_index.htm</ref> Globally, the benefits and co-benefits of keeping warming under 2&nbsp;°C exceed the costs.<ref name="Sampedro-2020">{{Cite journal |last1=Sampedro |first1=Jon |last2=Smith |first2=Steven J. |last3=Arto |first3=Iñaki |last4=González-Eguino |first4=Mikel |last5=Markandya |first5=Anil |last6=Mulvaney |first6=Kathleen M. |last7=Pizarro-Irizar |first7=Cristina |last8=Van Dingenen |first8=Rita |date=2020 |title=Health co-benefits and mitigation costs as per the Paris Agreement under different technological pathways for energy supply |journal=Environment International |language=en |volume=136 |article-number=105513 |bibcode=2020EnInt.13605513S |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2020.105513 |pmid=32006762 |s2cid=211004787 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=10810/44202}}</ref> Cost estimates for mitigation for specific regions depend on the quantity of emissions allowed for that region in future, as well as the timing of policies.<ref>IPCC, 2007: [https://web.archive.org/web/20181017035910/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg3/ar4_wg3_full_report.pdf Technical Summary] – [http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/publications_ipcc_fourth_assessment_report_wg3_report_mitigation_of_climate_change.htm Climate Change 2007: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091211015940/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/publications_ipcc_fourth_assessment_report_wg3_report_mitigation_of_climate_change.htm|date=11 December 2009}} [B. Metz, O.R. Davidson, P.R. Bosch, R. Dave, L.A. Meyer (eds)], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, United States., XXX pp.</ref>{{rp|90}} Economists estimate the incremental cost of climate change mitigation at less than 1% of [[Gross domestic product|GDP]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=The energy transition will be much cheaper than you think |url=https://www.economist.com/interactive/briefing/2024/11/14/the-energy-transition-will-be-much-cheaper-than-you-think |access-date=27 December 2024 |newspaper=The Economist |issn=0013-0613 |quote=The incremental bill to cut emissions is likely to be less than $1trn a year, which is to say less than one percent of global GDP.}}</ref> Across all developing countries, adaptation costs have been estimated to be about US$215 billion per year up to 2030, and are expected to be higher after.<ref>United Nations Environment Programme (2023). [https://www.unep.org/resources/adaptation-gap-report-2023 Adaptation Gap Report 2023: Underfinanced.Underprepared. Inadequate investment and planning on climate adaptation leaves world exposed]. Nairobi. {{doi|10.59117/20.500.11822/43796}}</ref>{{rp |35–36}}{{TOC limit|3}}

== Purposes ==
Economic analysis of climate change investigates the economic impacts of the [[effects of climate change]], the costs and benefits of preventing climate change, and the cost of adapting to a changing climate. These analyses can focus on:<ref name=":022">O'Neill, B., M. van Aalst, Z. Zaiton Ibrahim, L. Berrang Ford, S. Bhadwal, H. Buhaug, D. Diaz, K. Frieler, M. Garschagen, A. Magnan, G. Midgley, A. Mirzabaev, A. Thomas, and R.Warren, 2022: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Chapter16.pdf Chapter 16: Key Risks Across Sectors and Regions]. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/ Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, M. Tignor, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem, B. Rama (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2411–2538, {{doi|10.1017/9781009325844.025}}</ref>{{rp|2495}}

* Global aggregate economic costs of climate change (i.e. global climate damages)
* Sectoral or regional economic costs of climate change (e.g. costs to agriculture sector or energy services)
* Economic costs and benefits of implementing climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies
* Estimating the projected impacts to society per additional metric tonne of carbon emissions ([[social cost of carbon]])
* informing policy decisions, interntionally or nationally

The economic impacts of climate change also include any mitigation (for example, limiting the global average temperature below 2&nbsp;°C) or adaption (for example, building flood defences) employed by nations or groups of nations, which might infer economic consequences.<ref name=":0a">{{Cite report |title=Global Climate Change Governance: The search for effectiveness and universality |last=Luomi |first=Mari |date=2020 |publisher=International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) |jstor=resrep29269}}</ref><ref name="Eryn2">{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Eryn |date=30 September 2021 |title=Now is the time to prepare for the economic shocks of battling climate change |url=https://knowablemagazine.org/article/food-environment/2021/cost-of-climate-change |journal=Knowable Magazine |doi=10.1146/knowable-093021-1 |access-date=21 January 2022 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Rezai2">{{cite journal |last1=van der Ploeg |first1=Frederick |last2=Rezai |first2=Armon |date=6 October 2020 |title=Stranded Assets in the Transition to a Carbon-Free Economy |journal=Annual Review of Resource Economics |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=281–298 |doi=10.1146/annurev-resource-110519-040938 |issn=1941-1340 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=10419/215027}}</ref> Some regions or sectors may benefit from low levels of warming, for example through lower energy demand or improved crop yields.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2496}}<ref name=":3">IPCC, 2022: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf Summary for Policymakers] [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, M. Tignor, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem (eds.)]. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/sixth-assessment-report-working-group-ii/ Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, M. Tignor, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem, B. Rama (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA, pp. 3–33, {{doi|10.1017/9781009325844.001}}</ref>{{rp|11}}

In some areas, policies designed to [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate climate change]] may contribute towards other [[sustainable development]] objectives, such as abolishing [[fossil fuel subsidies]] which would reduce [[air pollution]] and thus save lives.<ref name="parry sustainability">
{{citation |title=Climate Change 2007: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability |chapter=TS.5.4 Perspectives on climate change and sustainability. In (book chapter) Technical summary |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg2/en/tssts-5-4.html |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Parry |author-first1=M. L.}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG2|2007}}
</ref><ref name="sathaye mitigation and development">
{{citation |title=Climate Change 2007: Mitigation of Climate Change |chapter=12.3 Implications of mitigation choices for sustainable development goals. In (book chapter) 12. Sustainable Development and mitigation |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg3/en/ch12s12-3.html |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Sathaye |author-first1=J.|series=Journal of Environmental Quality |date=2009 |volume=38 |issue=2 |page=837 |doi=10.2134/jeq2008.0024br |bibcode=2009JEnvQ..38..837V |url=https://oceanrep.geomar.de/id/eprint/57739/1/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_FinalDraft_FullReport.pdf }}, in {{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG3|2007}}
</ref><ref name="Shindell_et_al_2018">{{cite journal |author1=Shindell D |author2=Faluvegi G |author3=Seltzer K |author4=Shindell C |year=2018 |title=Quantified, Localized Health Benefits of Accelerated Carbon Dioxide Emissions Reductions. |journal=Nat Clim Change |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=291–295 |bibcode=2018NatCC...8..291S |doi=10.1038/s41558-018-0108-y |pmc=5880221 |pmid=29623109}}</ref> Direct global fossil fuel subsidies reached $319&nbsp;billion in 2017, and $5.2&nbsp;trillion when indirect costs such as air pollution are priced in.<ref name="pmid31733928">{{cite journal |author1=Watts N |author2=Amann M |author3=Arnell N |author4=Ayeb-Karlsson S |author5=Belesova K |author6=Boykoff M |display-authors=etal |year=2019 |title=The 2019 report of The Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: ensuring that the health of a child born today is not defined by a changing climate. |journal=Lancet |volume=394 |issue=10211 |pages=1836–1878 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(19)32596-6 |pmc= 7616843|pmid=31733928 |bibcode=2019Lanc..394.1836W |s2cid=207976337|hdl=10871/40583 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In other areas, the cost of climate change mitigation might divert [[resource]]s away from other socially and environmentally beneficial [[investment]]s (the [[opportunity cost]]s of climate change policy).<ref name="parry sustainability" /><ref name="sathaye mitigation and development" />

== Types of economic models ==
Many economic tools are employed to understand the economic aspects around impacts of climate change, [[Economics of climate change mitigation|climate change mitigation]] and [[Climate change adaptation|adaptation]]. Several approaches exist. [[Econometric model]]s (statistical models) are used to estimate the impacts of weather and climate on economic variables, either globally or for a specific sector. [[Computable general equilibrium|Structural economic models]] look at market and non-market impacts affecting the whole economy through its inputs and outputs. [[Integrated assessment modelling|Process models]] simulate physical, chemical and biological processes under climate change, and the economic effects.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2495}}

==== Aggregate cost-benefit models ====
{{See also|Integrated assessment modelling#Aggregate cost-benefit models}}
[[Integrated assessment modelling|Integrated assessment models]] (IAMs) are also used to make aggregate estimates of the costs of climate change. These (cost-benefit) models balance the economic implications of mitigation and climate damages to identify the pathway of emissions reductions that will maximize total economic welfare.<ref name=":4">Clarke L., K. Jiang, K. Akimoto, M. Babiker, G. Blanford, K. Fisher-Vanden, J.-C. Hourcade, V. Krey, E. Kriegler, A. Löschel, D. McCollum, S. Paltsev, S. Rose, P.R. Shukla, M. Tavoni, B.C.C. van der Zwaan, and D.P. van Vuuren, 2014: [https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ipcc_wg3_ar5_chapter6.pdf Assessing Transformation Pathways.] In: Climate Change 2014: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [Edenhofer, O., R. Pichs-Madruga, Y. Sokona, E. Farahani, S. Kadner, K. Seyboth, A. Adler, I. Baum, S. Brunner, P. Eickemeier, B. Kriemann, J. Savolainen, S. Schlömer, C. von Stechow, T. Zwickel and J.C. Minx (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA.</ref> In other words, the trade-offs between climate change impacts, adaptation, and mitigation are made explicit. The costs of each policy and the outcomes modelled are converted into monetary estimates.

The models incorporate aspects of the natural, social, and economic sciences in a highly aggregated way. Compared to other climate-economy models (including process-based IAMs), they do not have the structural detail necessary to model interactions with energy systems, land-use etc. and their economic implications.<ref name=":4" />

=== Statistical (econometric) methods ===
{{See also|Econometric model}}
A third modelling approach uses empirical, statistical methods to investigate how the economy is affected by weather variation.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2495}}<ref name=":2">Dell, M., Jones, B. F., & Olken, B. A. (2014). [[doi:10.1257/jel.52.3.740|What do we learn from the weather? The new climate-economy literature.]] ''Journal of Economic literature'', ''52''(3), 740–798.</ref>{{rp|755}} This approach can identify effects of temperature, rainfall, drought and storms on agriculture, energy demand, industry and other economic activity. [[Panel analysis|Panel data]] of weather variation over time and space, e.g. from ground station observations or (interpolated) gridded data is aggregated for economic analysis to investigate effects on national economies.<ref name=":2" /> These studies show that for example, hot years are linked to lower income growth in poor countries, and low rainfall is linked to reduced incomes in Africa.<ref name=":2" />{{rp|755}} Other econometric studies show that there are negative impacts of hotter temperatures on agricultural output, on labour productivity and in outdoor industries such as mining and forestry. The analyses are used to estimate the costs of climate change in the future.<ref name=":2" />

== Analytical frameworks ==

=== Cost–benefit analysis ===
{{See also|Integrated assessment modelling#Aggregate cost-benefit models}}
Standard [[cost–benefit analysis]] (CBA) has been applied to the problem of climate change. In a CBA framework, the negative and positive impacts associated with a given action are converted into monetary estimates.<ref name=":72">IPCC, 2022: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Annex-II.pdf Annex II: Glossary] [Möller, V., R. van Diemen, J.B.R. Matthews, C. Méndez, S. Semenov, J.S. Fuglestvedt, A. Reisinger (eds.)]. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/sixth-assessment-report-working-group-ii/ Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, M. Tignor, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem, B. Rama (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2897–2930, {{doi|10.1017/9781009325844.029}}</ref> This is also referred to as a monetized cost–benefit framework. Various types of model can provide information for CBA, including energy-economy-environment models ([[Integrated assessment modelling#Process models|process models]]) that study energy systems and their transitions. Some of these models may include a physical model of the climate. [[Computable general equilibrium|Computable General Equilibrium]] (CGE) structural models investigate effects of policies (including climate policies) on economic growth, trade, employment, and public revenues. However, most CBA analyses are produced using [[Integrated assessment modelling#Aggregate cost-benefit models|aggregate integrated assessment models]]. These aggregate-type IAMs are particularly designed for doing CBA of climate change.<ref name=":4" />{{rp|428}}<ref name=":5">Kolstad C., K. Urama, J. Broome, A. Bruvoll, M. Cariño Olvera, D. Fullerton, C. Gollier, W.M. Hanemann, R. Hassan, F. Jotzo, M.R. Khan, L. Meyer, and L. Mundaca, 2014: [https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ipcc_wg3_ar5_chapter3.pdfhttps://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ipcc_wg3_ar5_chapter3.pdf Social, Economic and Ethical Concepts and Methods]{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar5/wg3/ Climate Change 2014: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Edenhofer, O., R. Pichs-Madruga, Y. Sokona, E. Farahani, S. Kadner, K. Seyboth, A. Adler, I. Baum, S. Brunner, P. Eickemeier, B. Kriemann, J. Savolainen, S. Schlömer, C. von Stechow, T. Zwickel and J.C. Minx (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA</ref>{{rp|238–239}}

The CBA framework requires (1) the valuation of costs and benefits using [[willingness to pay]] (WTP) or willingness to accept (WTA) compensation<ref name="pearce monetized cba">
{{citation |author-last1=Pearce |author-first1=D. W. |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996|pp=184–185}} |chapter=6.1.2 The nature of damage assessment. In (book chapter) 6. The Social Costs of Climate Change: Greenhouse Damage and the Benefits of Control |display-authors=etal}}
</ref><ref name="Markandya" /><ref>
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG2|2001}} |chapter=2.5.3 Nonmarket impacts. In (book chapter) 2. Methods and Tools |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Ahmad |author-first1=Q. K.}}
</ref><ref name="ahmad cost benefit analysis">
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG2|2001}} |chapter=2.7.2.2 Cost-Benefit Analysis. In (book chapter) 2. Methods and Tools |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Ahmad |author-first1=Q. K.}}
</ref> as a measure of value,<ref name="goldemberg standard cba">
{{citation |author-last1=Goldemberg |author-first1=J. |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996|p=24}} |chapter=1.3 Contribution of Economics. In (book chapter) 1. Introduction: scope of the Assessment |display-authors=etal}}
</ref> and (2) a criterion for accepting or rejecting proposals:<ref name="goldemberg standard cba" />

For (1), in CBA where WTP/WTA is used, climate change impacts are aggregated into a monetary value,<ref name="pearce monetized cba" /> with environmental impacts converted into [[consumption (economics)|consumption]] equivalents,<ref name="arrow consumption and certainty equivalents">
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996|pp=130–131}} |chapter=4.1.1 Areas of agreement and disagreement. In (book chapter) 4. Intertemporal Equity, Discounting, and Economic Efficiency |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Arrow |author-first1=K. J.}}
</ref> and risk accounted for using [[certainty equivalent]]s.<ref name="arrow consumption and certainty equivalents" /><ref>
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG2|2001}} |chapter=2.5.4.1. Insurance and the Cost of Uncertainty. In (book chapter) 2. Methods and Tools |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Ahmad |author-first1=Q. K.}}
</ref> Values over time are then discounted to produce their equivalent [[present value]]s.<ref>
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG2|2001}} |chapter=2.5.1.3 Discounting the future. In (book chapter) 2. Methods and Tools |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Ahmad |author-first1=Q. K.}}
</ref> The valuation of costs and benefits of climate change can be controversial<ref name="smith">{{cite book |author-last1=Smith |author-first1=J. B. |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/WGII_TAR_full_report-2.pdf |title=Climate Change 2001: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |editor-last1=McCarthy |editor-first1=J. J. |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, N.Y. |pages=913–970 |chapter=19. Vulnerability to Climate Change and Reasons for Concern: A Synthesis |display-authors=etal |access-date=19 January 2022 |display-editors=etal |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/wg2TARchap19.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|936–938}} because some climate change impacts are difficult to assign a value to, e.g., ecosystems and human health.<ref name="decanio iam limitations">{{cite journal |last1=Ackerman |first1=Frank |last2=DeCanio |first2=Stephen J. |last3=Howarth |first3=Richard B. |last4=Sheeran |first4=Kristen |date=August 2009 |title=Limitations of integrated assessment models of climate change |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10584-009-9570-x.pdf |journal=Climatic Change |volume=95 |issue=3–4 |pages=297–315 |bibcode=2009ClCh...95..297A |doi=10.1007/s10584-009-9570-x |s2cid=14011838 |access-date=21 January 2022}}</ref><ref name="Spash">{{cite journal |year=2008 |title=The economics of avoiding action on climate change |url=https://www.clivespash.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/2008_Spash_Adbusters_finalcopy.pdf |journal=Adbusters #75 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=4–5 |access-date=21 January 2022 |author-last1=Spash |author-first1=C. L.}}</ref>

For (2), the standard criterion is the [[Kaldor–Hicks efficiency|Kaldor–Hicks]]<ref name="de canio 2007 climate change">{{citation |author=DeCanio, S. J. |title=Reflections on Climate Change, Economic Development, and Global Equity: Presented at the 2007 Leontief Prize Ceremony Tufts University Global Development and Environment Institute October 17, 2007 |date=17 October 2007 |website=www.academia.edu |url=https://www.academia.edu/19420793}}</ref>{{Rp|3}} [[compensation principle]].<ref name="goldemberg standard cba" /> According to the compensation principle, so long as those benefiting from a particular project compensate the losers, and there is still something left over, then the result is an unambiguous gain in welfare.<ref name="goldemberg standard cba" /> If there are no mechanisms allowing compensation to be paid, then it is necessary to assign weights to particular individuals.<ref name="goldemberg standard cba" /> One of the mechanisms for compensation is impossible for this problem: mitigation might benefit future generations at the expense of current generations, but there is no way that future generations can compensate current generations for the costs of mitigation.<ref name="de canio 2007 climate change" />{{Rp|4}} On the other hand, should future generations bear most of the costs of climate change, compensation to them would not be possible.<ref name="goldemberg general issues">
{{citation |author-last1=Goldemberg |author-first1=J. |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996|pp=31–32}} |chapter=1.4.1 General issues. In (book chapter) 1. Introduction: scope of the Assessment |display-authors=etal}}
</ref>

CBA has several strengths: it offers an internally consistent and global comprehensive analysis of impacts.<ref name="smith" />{{rp|955}} Furthermore, sensitivity analysis allows critical assumptions in CBA analysis to be changed. This can identify areas where the value of information is highest and where additional research might have the highest payoffs.<ref>{{cite book |author-last1=Downing |author-first1=T. E. |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/WGII_TAR_full_report-2.pdf |title=Climate Change 2001: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |editor-last1=McCarthy |editor-first1=J. J. |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, N.Y. |pages=105–144 |chapter=2. Methods and Tools |display-authors=etal |access-date=19 January 2022 |display-editors=etal |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/wg2TARchap2.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|119}} However, there are many uncertainties that affect cost–benefit analysis, for example, sector- and country-specific damage functions.<ref name="toth">{{cite book |author-last1=Toth |author-first1=F. L. |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/WGIII_TAR_full_report.pdf |title=Climate Change 2001: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |editor-last1=Metz |editor-first1=B. |location=Cambridge |chapter=10. Decision-making Frameworks |display-authors=etal |access-date=20 January 2022 |editor-last2=Davidson |editor-first2=O |editor-last3=Swart |editor-first3=R. |editor-last4=Pan |editor-first4=J. |display-editors=etal}}</ref>{{rp|654}}

==== Damage functions ====
[[File:Estimates of the Economic Damage of Climate Change.png|thumb|right|200px|This graph shows estimation confidence intervals from a meta-analysis of researchers as well as by the [[Stern Review]] in 2006 (damage costs measured as percent [[Gross domestic product|GDP]]).{{Update inline|date=January 2025}}]]Damage functions play an important role in estimating the costs associated with potential damages caused by climate-related hazards. They quantify the relationship between the intensity of the hazard, other factors such as the vulnerability of the system, and the resulting damages. For example, damage functions have been developed for sea level rise, agricultural productivity, or heat effects on labour productivity.<ref>Roson, R. and M. Sartori, 2016: [[doi:10.21642/JGEA.010202AF|Estimation of climate change damage functions for 140 regions in the GTAP 9 data base]]. J. Glob. Econ. Anal., 1(2), doi:10.21642/JGEA.010202AF</ref>

===Cost-effectiveness analysis===

{{See also|Economics of climate change mitigation#Decision analysis}}

[[Cost-effectiveness analysis|Cost-Effectiveness Analysis]] (CEA) is preferable to CBA when the benefits of impacts, adaptation and mitigation are difficult to estimate in monetary terms. A CEA can be used to compare different policy options for achieving a well-defined goal.<ref name=":5" />{{rp|238}} This goal (i.e. the benefit) is usually expressed as the amount of GHG emissions reduction in the analysis of mitigation measures. For adaptation measures, there is no common goal or metric for the economic benefits. Adaptation involves responding to different types of risks in different sectors and local contexts. For example, the goal might be the reduction of land area in hectares at risk to sea level rise.<ref name=":6">Watkiss, P. and Hunt, A. (2012). [https://weadapt.org/knowledge-base/adaptation-decision-making/mediation-cost-effectiveness-analysis/ Cost-effectiveness analysis:: Decision Support Methods for Adaptation], MEDIATION Project, Briefing Note 2. Funded by the EC's 7FWP</ref>{{rp|2}}

CEA involves the costing of each option, providing a cost per unit of effectiveness. For example, cost per tonne of GHG reduced ($/tCO2). This allows the ranking of policy options. This ranking can help decision-maker to understand which are the most cost-effective options, i.e. those that deliver high benefits for low costs. CEA can be used for minimising net costs for achieving pre-defined policy targets, such as meeting an emissions reduction target for a given sector.<ref name=":5" />{{rp|238}}<ref name=":6" />{{rp|2–3}}

CEA, like CBA, is a type of [[decision analysis]] method. Many of these methods work well when different stakeholders work together on a problem to understand and manage risks.<ref name=":112" />{{rp|2543}} For example, by discussing how well certain options might work in the real world. Or by helping in measuring the costs and benefits as part of a CEA.<ref name=":112">New, M., D. Reckien, D. Viner, C. Adler, S.-M. Cheong, C. Conde, A. Constable, E. Coughlan de Perez, A. Lammel, R. Mechler, B. Orlove, and W. Solecki, 2022: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Chapter17.pdf Chapter 17: Decision-Making Options for Managing Risk]. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/ Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, M. Tignor, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem, B. Rama (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2539–2654, {{doi|10.1017/9781009325844.026}}</ref>{{rp|2566,2576}}

Some authors have focused on a ''disaggregated analysis'' of climate change impacts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stern |first1=Nicholas |date=May 2008 |title=The Economics of Climate Change |journal=American Economic Review |volume=98 |issue=2 |pages=1–37 |doi=10.1257/aer.98.2.1 |issn=0002-8282 |s2cid=59019533 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|23}}<ref>
{{citation |title=Climate Change 2007: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability |chapter=19.1.1 Purpose, scope and structure of the chapter. In (book chapter) 19: Assessing Key Vulnerabilities and the Risk from Climate Change |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg2/en/ch19s19-1.html |display-authors=etal |author-last=Schneider |author-first=S.H.}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG2|2007|p=782}}
</ref> "Disaggregated" refers to the choice to assess impacts in a variety of indicators or units, e.g., changes in agricultural yields and loss of biodiversity. By contrast, monetized CBA converts all impacts into a common unit (money), which is used to assess changes in [[welfare economics|social welfare]].
[[File:2021 Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions per person versus GDP per person - scatter plot.svg|thumb|Scaling the effect of wealth to the national level: richer [[Developed country|(developed)]] countries emit more {{CO2}} per person than poorer [[Developing country|(developing)]] countries.<ref name="WashPost_20230301">{{cite news |last1=Stevens |first1=Harry |date=1 March 2023 |title=The United States has caused the most global warming. When will China pass it? |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/interactive/2023/global-warming-carbon-emissions-china-us/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230301130719/https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/interactive/2023/global-warming-carbon-emissions-china-us/ |archive-date=1 March 2023}}</ref> Emissions are roughly proportional to [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] per person, though the rate of increase diminishes with an average GDP/pp of about $10,000.]]

=== Scenario-based assessments ===
{{Main|Climate change scenario|}}

The long time scales and [[uncertainty|uncertainty when it comes]] to global warming have led analysts to develop "[[climate change scenario|scenarios]]" of future [[environment (biophysical)|environmental]], [[social change|social]] and [[economic development|economic]] changes.<ref name="webster 2002 types of emissions projections">{{citation |title=Report 95: Uncertainty Analysis of Climate Change and Policy Response |date=December 2002 |url=http://web.mit.edu/globalchange/www/MITJPSPGC_Rpt95.pdf |pages=3–4 |access-date=20 January 2022 |location=Cambridge MA, USA |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Joint Program on the Science and Policy of Global Change, Joint Program Report Series |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Webster |author-first1=M.}}</ref> These scenarios can help governments understand the potential consequences of their decisions.

The projected temperature in climate change scenarios is subject to scientific uncertainty (e.g., the relationship between concentrations of GHGs and global mean temperature, which is called the [[climate sensitivity]]). Projections of future atmospheric concentrations based on emission pathways are also affected by scientific uncertainties, e.g., over how carbon sinks, such as forests, will be affected by future climate change.

One of the economic aspects of climate change is producing scenarios of future [[economic development]]. Future economic developments can, for example, affect how [[climate change, industry and society#Vulnerability|vulnerable]] society is to future climate change,<ref>
{{citation |title=Climate Change 2007: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability |chapter=7.4 Key future impacts and vulnerabilities. In (book chapter) 7. Industry, Settlement and Society |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg2/en/ch7s7-4.html |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Wilbanks |author-first1=T. J.}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG2|2007}}
</ref> what the future [[effects of global warming|impacts of climate change]] might be, as well as the level of future GHG emissions.<ref>
{{cite book |author-last1=Fisher |author-first1=B. S. |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/ar4_wg3_full_report-1.pdf |title=Climate Change 2007: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-521-88011-4 |editor-last1=Metz |editor-first1=B. |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, N.Y. |chapter=3.1.4 Economic growth and convergence. In (book chapter) 3. Issues related to mitigation in the long term context |display-authors=etal |access-date=19 January 2022 |display-editors=etal |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg3/en/ch3s3-1-4.html}}</ref>

Scenarios are neither "predictions" nor "forecasts" but are stories of possible futures that provide alternate outcomes relevant to a decision-maker or other user.<ref name=":112"/>{{rp|2576}} These alternatives usually also include a "baseline" or reference scenario for comparison. "Business-as-usual" scenarios have been developed in which there are no additional policies beyond those currently in place, and socio-economic development is consistent with recent trends. This term is now used less frequently than in the past.<ref name=":72"/>

In scenario analysis, scenarios are developed that are based on differing assumptions of future development patterns.<ref name="webster 2002 types of emissions projections" /> An example of this are the [[shared socioeconomic pathways]] produced by the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC). These project a wide range of possible future emissions levels.

Scenarios often support sector-specific analysis of the physical effects and economic costs of climate change. Scenarios are used with [[cost–benefit analysis]] or [[cost-effectiveness analysis]] of climate policies.

=== Risk management ===
{{Main|Climate risk}}

Risk management can be used to evaluate policy decisions based a range of criteria or viewpoints.<ref>{{cite book |author=National Research Council |url=https://www.nap.edu/read/12781/ |title=America's climate choices |date=2011 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-14585-5 |location=Washington, D.C. |chapter=Chapter Four: A Framework for Making America's Climate Choices |chapter-url=http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12781&page=42}}</ref>{{rp|42}} Another approach is that of [[uncertainty analysis]],<ref name="webster 2002 types of emissions projections" /> where analysts attempt to estimate the probability of future changes in emission levels. Considerations in a risk-based approach might include, for example, the potential for low-probability, worst-case climate change impacts.<ref>
{{cite book |author-last1=Barker |author-first1=T. |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/ar4_wg3_full_report-1.pdf |title=Climate Change 2007: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=10 September 2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-88011-4 |editor-last1=Metz |editor-first1=B. |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, N.Y. |pages=619–690 |chapter=Article 2 of the Convention and mitigation. In (book chapter) Technical Summary |display-authors=etal |access-date=19 January 2022 |display-editors=etal |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg3/en/tssts-ts-1-3-article-2.html}}</ref>

In a cost-benefit analysis, an acceptable [[risk]] means that the benefits of a climate policy outweigh the costs of the policy.<ref name="halsnaes measuring costs and benefits">
{{citation |author-last1=Halsnæs |author-first1=K. |title={{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG3|2007}} |chapter=2.3.3 Costs, benefits and uncertainties. In (book chapter) 2. Framing issues |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg3/en/ch2s2-3-3.html |display-authors=etal}}
</ref> The rule used by many decision makers is that a risk is acceptable if the anticipated [[net (economics)|net]] [[present value]] is positive.<ref name="halsnaes measuring costs and benefits" /> The expected value is the mean of the distribution of expected outcomes.<ref name="goldemberg">
{{citation |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996}} |chapter=1. Introduction: scope of the Assessment |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Goldemberg |author-first1=J.}}
</ref>{{Rp|25}} In other words, it is the average expected outcome for a particular decision. This criterion has been justified under the conditions that:
* a policy's benefits and costs have known [[probability|probabilities]]<ref name="halsnaes measuring costs and benefits" />
* [[economic agent]]s (people and organizations) can reduce their risk through [[insurance]] and other markets.<ref name="halsnaes measuring costs and benefits" />

These assumptions are not often met, as it is challenging to estimate the costs of climate change, and that many benefits (like improved health) are not easily converted into monetary terms. Insurance is also not always an option, as climate disasters usually hit many people at once, making mutual aid difficult to implement.<ref name="halsnaes measuring costs and benefits" />

Policymakers and investors are beginning to recognize the implications of climate change for the financial sector, from both physical risks (damage to property, infrastructure, and land) and transition risk due to changes in policy, technology, and consumer and market behavior. Financial institutions are becoming increasingly aware of the need to incorporate the economics of low carbon emissions into business models.<ref name="Grippa">{{cite journal |last1=Grippa |first1=Pierpaolo |last2=Schmittmann |first2=Jochen |last3=Suntheim |first3=Felix |date=2019 |title=Climate Change and Financial Risk Central banks and financial regulators are starting to factor in climate change |url=https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2019/12/climate-change-central-banks-and-financial-risk-grippa.htm |journal=Finance & Development |volume=56 |issue=4 |access-date=21 January 2022}}</ref>

In the scientific literature, there is sometimes a focus on "best estimate" or "likely" values of [[climate sensitivity]].<ref>
{{Citation |author=IPCC |title=Climate Change 2007: Synthesis Report |url=http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/syr/en/contents.html |page=8 |year=2007 |editor=Core Writing Team |access-date=20 January 2022 |series=Contribution of Working Groups I, II and III to the [[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report|Fourth Assessment Report]] of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |chapter=Table SPM.1. In (book chapter) Summary for Policymakers |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ar4_syr_spm.pdf |location=Geneva, Switzerland |publisher=IPCC |isbn=978-92-9169-122-7 |editor2=Pachauri, R.K |editor3=Reisinger, A.}}</ref>  However, from a [[risk management]] perspective, values outside of "likely" ranges are relevant, because, though these values are less probable, they could be associated with more severe climate impacts<ref name="schneider climate sensitivity">
{{citation |title=Climate Change 2007: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability |chapter=19.4.2.2 Scenario analysis and analysis of stabilisation targets. In (book chapter) 19. Assessing Key Vulnerabilities and the Risk from Climate Change |chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg2/en/ch19s19-4-2-2.html |display-authors=etal |author-last1=Schneider |author-first1=S. H.}}, in {{harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG2|2007|p=801}}
</ref> (the statistical definition of [[risk]] = probability of an impact × magnitude of the impact).<ref name="Yohe">{{cite book |author-last=Yohe |author-first=G.W. |url=https://www.c2es.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/05/workshop-proceedings-assessing-benefits-avoided-climate-change.pdf |title=Assessing the Benefits of Avoided Climate Change: Cost-Benefit Analysis and Beyond. Proceedings of Workshop on Assessing the Benefits of Avoided Climate Change, March 16–17, 2009 |date=May 2010 |publisher=Pew Center on Global Climate Change |editor-last1=Gulledge |editor-first1=J. |location=Arlington, Virginia, USA |chapter=Addressing Climate Change through a Risk Management Lens |access-date=18 January 2022 |editor-last2=Richardson |editor-first2=L. J. |editor-last3=Adkins |editor-first3=L. |editor-last4=Seidel |editor-first4=S.}}</ref>{{rp|208}}

Analysts have also looked at how uncertainty over climate sensitivity affects economic estimates of climate change impacts.<ref name="Nordhaus2018">{{cite journal |last1=Nordhaus |first1=William |date=August 2018 |title=Projections and Uncertainties about Climate Change in an Era of Minimal Climate Policies |journal=American Economic Journal: Economic Policy |language=en |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=333–360 |doi=10.1257/pol.20170046 |issn=1945-7731 |s2cid=158112579 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  Policy guidance from [[cost-benefit analysis]] (CBA) can be extremely divergent depending on the assumptions employed.<ref name="Ekholm">{{cite journal |last1=Ekholm |first1=Tommi |date=December 2018 |title=Climatic Cost-benefit Analysis Under Uncertainty and Learning on Climate Sensitivity and Damages |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/327701655 |journal=Ecological Economics |volume=154 |pages=99–106 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolecon.2018.07.024 |bibcode=2018EcoEc.154...99E |s2cid=158212518 |access-date=21 January 2022}}</ref>  Hassler ''et al'' use [[integrated assessment modeling]] to examine a range of estimates and what happens at  extremes.<ref name="Hassler">{{cite book |last1=Hassler |first1=John |url=http://hdl.handle.net/10419/215447 |title=The consequences of uncertainty: Climate sensitivity and economic sensitivity to the climate |last2=Krusell |first2=Per |last3=Olovsson |first3=Conny |date=2019 |publisher=Sveriges Riksbank |series=Sveriges Riksbank Working Paper Series, No. 369 |hdl=10419/215447 |access-date=21 January 2022}}</ref>

==== Iterative risk management ====
Two related ways of thinking about the problem of climate change decision-making in the presence of uncertainty are iterative risk management<ref>
{{citation
|author-last1=Fisher |author-first1= B. S. |display-authors=etal |chapter=3.5.1.1 An iterative risk-management framework to articulate options. In (book chapter) 3: Issues related to mitigation in the long-term context
|chapter-url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg3/en/ch3s3-5-1-1.html
| title=Climate Change 2007: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change  
|date= 10 September 2007 | editor-last1=Metz |editor-first1=B. |display-editors=etal
| publisher=Cambridge University Press  |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, N.Y.  | isbn=978-0-521-88011-4 
|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/ar4_wg3_full_report-1.pdf  | access-date=19 January 2022
}}</ref><ref name="Yohe" /> and [[sequential decision making]].<ref name="toth decision uncertainty">
{{citation
 | author-last1=Toth |author-first1= F. L .|display-authors=etal
 | chapter= 10.1.4.1 Decision Making under Uncertainty. In (book chapter) 10. Decision-making Frameworks
|title=Climate Change 2001: Mitigation}}. In {{harvnb|IPCC TAR WG3|2001}}</ref>{{rp|612–614}} One of the responses to the uncertainties of global warming is to adopt a strategy of sequential decision making.<ref name="goldemberg sequential decision making">
{{citation |author-last1=Goldemberg |author-first1=J. |title={{harvnb|IPCC SAR WG3|1996|p=26}} (32 of PDF) |chapter=1.3.2 Sequential decision making. In (book chapter) 1. Introduction: Scope of the assessment |display-authors=etal}}
</ref> This involves making a series of observations before making a final decision.<ref>{{Citation |last=Diederich |first=A. |title=Sequential Decision Making |date=1 January 2001 |pages=13917–13922 |editor-last=Smelser |editor-first=Neil J. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B0080430767006367 |access-date=27 April 2023 |place=Oxford |publisher=Pergamon |language=en |isbn=978-0-08-043076-8 |editor2-last=Baltes |editor2-first=Paul B. |encyclopedia=International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences}}</ref>

An approach based on sequential decision making recognizes that, over time, decisions related to climate change can be revised in the light of improved [[information economics|information]].<ref name="goldemberg sequential decision making" /> This is particularly important with respect to climate change, due to the long-term nature of the problem. A near-term [[Hedge (finance)|hedging]] strategy concerned with reducing future climate impacts might favor stringent, near-term emissions reductions.<ref name="toth decision uncertainty" /> As stated earlier, carbon dioxide accumulates in the atmosphere, and to stabilize the atmospheric concentration of {{co2}}, emissions would need to be drastically reduced from their present level. Stringent near-term emissions reductions allow for greater future flexibility with regard to a low stabilization target, e.g., 450 [[parts-per notation|parts per million]] (ppm) {{CO2}}. This option may be lost if near-term emissions abatement is less stringent.<ref>{{citation |author=United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) |title=The Emissions Gap Report 2012: A UNEP Synthesis Report |date=November 2012 |pages=28–29 |access-date=21 January 2022 |archive-url=http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20160513232928/http://www.unep.org/pdf/2012gapreport.pdf |archive-date=13 May 2016 |chapter=3.7 Results of later action scenarios. In (book chapter) Chapter 3: The emissions gap – an update |chapter-url=http://www.unep.org/pdf/2012gapreport.pdf |location=Nairobi, Kenya |publisher=UNEP}}. Report [http://www.unep.org/publications/ebooks/emissionsgap2012/ website] {{webarchive|url=http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20160513232948/http://www.unep.org/publications/ebooks/emissionsgap2012/|date=13 May 2016}}, which includes the Appendix, and the Executive Summary in other languages.</ref>

Another way of viewing the problem is to look at the potential irreversibility of future climate change impacts (e.g., damages to [[effects of climate change on biomes|biomes and ecosystems]]) against the irreversibility of making investments in efforts to reduce emissions.<ref name="goldemberg sequential decision making" />

==== Portfolio analysis ====
One risk management framework is portfolio analysis. This approach is based on [[modern portfolio theory|portfolio theory]], originally applied in the areas of finance and investment.<ref name=":8">Hunt, A, and Watkiss, P (2013). [https://weadapt.org/knowledge-base/adaptation-decision-making/mediation-portfolio-analysis/ Portfolio Analysis: Decision Support Methods for Adaptation, MEDIATION Project, Briefing Note 5.] Funded by the EC's 7FWP</ref><ref name=":10">Hunt, A., & Fraschini, F. (2020). [https://www.euskadi.eus/web01-a2reveko/es/k86aEkonomiazWar/ekonomiaz/abrirArticulo?idpubl=93&registro=7 Portfolio analysis as a means of managing uncertainties in climate change adaptation: Some initial reflections]. ''Ekonomiaz'', ''97''(1), 63–81.</ref> The idea is that a reasonable response to uncertainty is to invest in a wide portfolio of options to spread risk.<ref name=":8" /> It is important to compare alternative portfolios of options across different future [[climate change scenario]]s in order to take into account uncertainty in climate impacts, GHG emission trends etc. The options should ideally be diversified to be effective in different scenarios: i.e. some options suited for a no/low climate change scenario, with other options being suited for scenarios with severe climate changes.<ref name=":10" />

== Costs of climate impacts ==

=== At the global level ===
[[File:2020- Climate change's projected damage to GDP growth.svg |thumb|upright=1.35 |Estimates of damage to [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] vary widely, and even this approach to predicting damage does not consider impacts of climate tipping points, climate-driven extreme events, human health impacts, resource or migration-driven conflict, geopolitical tension, nature-driven risks, or sea level rise.<ref name=Actuaries_CCandGDP>{{cite web |last1=Trust |first1=Sandy |last2=Saye |first2=Lucy |last3=Bettis |first3=Oliver |last4=Bedenham |first4=Georgina |last5=Hampshire |first5=Oliver |last6=Lenton |first6=Timothy M. |last7=Abrams |first7=Jesse F |title=Planetary Solvency–finding our balance with nature Global risk management for human prosperity |url=https://actuaries.org.uk/document-library/thought-leadership/thought-leadership-campaigns/climate-papers/planetary-solvency-finding-our-balance-with-nature/ |publisher=Institute and Faculty of Actuaries |pages=12–13 (Figure 2) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250117012930/https://actuaries.org.uk/document-library/thought-leadership/thought-leadership-campaigns/climate-papers/planetary-solvency-finding-our-balance-with-nature/ |archive-date=17 January 2025 |date=January 2025 |url-status=live}} ● Trust ''et al.'' cite {{cite journal |last1=Kotz |first1=Maximilian |last2=Levermann |first2=Anders |last3=Wenz |first3=Leonie |title=The economic commitment of climate change |journal=Nature |date=17 April 2024 |volume=628 |issue=8020 |pages=551–557 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-07732-2|pmid=38914865 |pmc=11236700 }}</ref>]]
[[File:1960- Damages caused by countries' emissions of greenhouse gases.svg |thumb |upright=1.35 |Non-linear growth in the global warming effect of accumulating long-lived greenhouse gases contributed to economic damages over a 60-year period estimated to be over five times as large as that of a 30-year period (shown in chart). A ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' article estimated future damages from past emissions to be at least an order of magnitude larger than historical damages from the same emissions.<ref name=Nature_20260325enhanced>
* Data source for '''''1990'''''-2020 panel: Fig. 4 of {{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B }}
* Data source for '''''1960'''''-2020 panel: Fig. S5 of {{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Nature portfolio / Supplementary information / Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |url=https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-026-10272-6/MediaObjects/41586_2026_10272_MOESM1_ESM.pdf |journal=Nature |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260406031318/https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-026-10272-6/MediaObjects/41586_2026_10272_MOESM1_ESM.pdf |archive-date=6 April 2026 |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B |quote=Same as Figure 4 except valuing damages from emissions starting in 1960 rather than 1990. |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
[[File:20201211 Billion dollar events related to climate change - U.S. -en.svg|thumb|upright=1.35| There is a growing number of weather-related disasters in the United States costing above one billion dollars<ref name="BillionDollarDisastersNOAA_2023">Annual data: {{cite web |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters / United States Billion-Dollar Disaster Events 1980– (CPI-Adjusted) |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/time-series/US |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240113044752/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/time-series/US |archive-date=13 January 2024 |publisher=National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)}} Click "Access data".</ref><ref name="NCEI_thru202009">{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=Adam B. |author2=NOAA National Centers For Environmental Information |date=December 2020 |title=Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: Overview / 2020 in Progress |url=https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/billions/ |url-status=live |publisher=National Centers for Environmental Information (NCDC, part of NOAA) |doi=10.25921/stkw-7w73 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210044128/https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/billions/ |archive-date=10 December 2020 |access-date=11 December 2020 |website=NCDC.NOAA}} and {{cite web |date=January 2021 |title=Contiguous U.S. ranked fifth warmest during 2020; Alaska experienced its coldest year since 2012 / 2020 Billion Dollar Disasters and Other Notable Extremes |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108185719/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202012 |archive-date=8 January 2021 |website=NCEI.NOAA.gov |publisher=NOAA}} For 2021 data: {{cite web |date=6 October 2017 |title=Calculating the Cost of Weather and Climate Disasters / Seven things to know about NCEI's U.S. billion-dollar disasters data |url=https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/calculating-cost-weather-and-climate-disasters |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111143455/https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/calculating-cost-weather-and-climate-disasters |archive-date=11 January 2022 |website=ncei.noaa.gov}}</ref>]]Global aggregate costs are all the predicted impacts of climate change across all market sectors (e.g. including costs to agriculture, energy services and tourism) and also includes non-market impacts (e.g. on ecosystems and human health).<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2495}}

Estimates are found to increase non-linearly with global average temperature change. The 2022 IPCC report finds that with high warming (~4&nbsp;°C) and low adaptation, annual global GDP might be reduced by 10–23% by 2100 because of climate change. The same assessment finds smaller GDP changes with reductions of 1–8%, assuming low warming, more adaptation, and using different models. These estimates do not take into account climate tipping points well.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2459}} In addition, these global economic cost estimates do not take into account impacts on social well-being or welfare or distributional effects.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2495}}

Climate damages estimated statistically usually only look only how national weather variations impact GDP. A 2025 study explored adding global weather changes into the statistical analysis, given the trade between countries and how strongly one economy depends on another. This raised the estimates of climate damages from 11% to 40% in 2100 under a [[RCP8.5|very high emission scenario]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Neal |first1=Timothy |last2=Newell |first2=Ben R |last3=Pitman |first3=Andy |date=2025-04-01 |title=Reconsidering the macroeconomic damage of severe warming |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/adbd58 |journal=Environmental Research Letters |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=044029 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/adbd58 |bibcode=2025ERL....20d4029N |issn=1748-9326}}</ref>

Another study, which checked the data from the last 120 years, found that climate change has already reduced welfare by 29% and further temperature rise will bring this number to 47%. The temperature rise between 1960 and 2019 cut current GDP per person by 18%. A rise by 1 degree in global temperature reduces global GDP by 12%. An increase of 3 degrees by 2100, will reduce capital by 50%. The effects are like experiencing the [[Great Depression|1929 Great Depression]] permanently. The associated social cost of carbon is 1065 dollars per tonne of CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bilal |first1=Adrien |last2=R. Känzig |first2=Diego |title=THE MACROECONOMIC IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE: GLOBAL VS. LOCAL TEMPERATURE |date=August 2024 |publisher=NATIONAL BUREAU OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH |location=1050 Massachusetts Avenue Cambridge, MA 02138 |pages=1, 4, 5, 38, 39 |url=https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32450/w32450.pdf |access-date=8 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=1°C global temperature rise could slash GDP by 12%, warns environmentalists |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/information/story/1degc-global-temperature-rise-could-slash-gdp-by-12-warns-environmentalists-2617153-2024-10-15 |access-date=8 November 2024 |agency=India Today |date=15 October 2024}}</ref>

Global economic losses due to extreme weather, climate and water events are increasing. Costs have increased sevenfold from the 1970s to the 2010s.<ref>World Meteorological Society (WMO) (2021). [https://library.wmo.int/idurl/4/57564 WMO Atlas of Mortality and Economic Losses from Weather, Climate and Water Extremes (1970–2019)]. https://library.wmo.int/idurl/4/57564</ref>{{rp|16}} Direct losses from disasters have averaged above US$330 billion annually between 2015 and 2021.<ref name=":132">UNDRR (2023). [https://sendaiframework-mtr.undrr.org/publication/report-midterm-review-implementation-sendai-framework-disaster-risk-reduction-2015-2030 The Report of the Midterm Review of the Implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030]. UNDRR: Geneva, Switzerland.</ref>{{rp|21}} Climate change has contributed to the increased probability and magnitude of extreme events. When a vulnerable community is exposed to extreme climate or weather events, disasters can occur. [[Socioeconomics|Socio-economic]] factors have contributed to the observed trend of global disaster losses, such as population growth and increased wealth.<ref>{{Citation |last=Bouwer |first=Laurens M. |chapter=Observed and Projected Impacts from Extreme Weather Events: Implications for Loss and Damage |date=2019 |title=Loss and Damage from Climate Change: Concepts, Methods and Policy Options |pages=63–82 |editor-last=Mechler |editor-first=Reinhard |series=Climate Risk Management, Policy and Governance |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-72026-5_3 |isbn=978-3-319-72026-5 |editor2-last=Bouwer |editor2-first=Laurens M. |editor3-last=Schinko |editor3-first=Thomas |editor4-last=Surminski |editor4-first=Swenja |doi-access=free}}</ref> This shows that increased exposure is the most important driver of losses. However, part of these are also due to human-induced climate change. [[Extreme event attribution]] quantifies how climate change is altering the probability and magnitude of extreme events. On a case-by-case basis, it is feasible to estimate how the magnitude and/or probability of the extreme event has shifted due to climate change. These attributable changes have been identified for many individual extreme heat events and rainfall events.<ref>Seneviratne, S.I., X. Zhang, M. Adnan, W. Badi, C. Dereczynski, A. Di Luca, S. Ghosh, I. Iskandar, J. Kossin, S. Lewis, F. Otto, I. Pinto, M. Satoh, S.M. Vicente-Serrano, M. Wehner, and B. Zhou, 2021: [[doi:10.1017/9781009157896.013|Weather and Climate Extreme Events in a Changing Climate. In Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp. 1513–1766, {{doi|10.1017/9781009157896.013}}</ref>{{rp|1611}}<ref name=":1">Newman, R., Noy, I. [[doi:10.1038/s41467-023-41888-1|The global costs of extreme weather that are attributable to climate change]]. ''Nat Commun'' 14, 6103 (2023). {{doi|10.1038/s41467-023-41888-1|doi-access=free}}</ref> Using all available data on attributable changes, one study estimated the global losses to average US$143 billion per year between 2000 and 2019. This includes a statistical loss of life value of 90 billion and economic damages of 53 billion per year.<ref name=":1" />

One 2020 study estimated economic losses due to climate change could be between 127 and 616&nbsp;trillion dollars extra until 2100 with current commitments, compared to 1.5&nbsp;°C or well below 2&nbsp;°C compatible action. Failure to implement current commitments raises economic losses to 150–792&nbsp;trillion dollars until 2100.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Yi-Ming |last2=Han |first2=Rong |last3=Wang |first3=Ce |last4=Yu |first4=Biying |last5=Liang |first5=Qiao-Mei |last6=Yuan |first6=Xiao-Chen |last7=Chang |first7=Junjie |last8=Zhao |first8=Qingyu |last9=Liao |first9=Hua |last10=Tang |first10=Baojun |last11=Yan |first11=Jinyue |last12=Cheng |first12=Lijing |last13=Yang |first13=Zili |display-authors=etal |year=2020 |title=Self-preservation strategy for approaching global warming targets in the post-Paris Agreement era. |journal=Nat Commun |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=1624 |bibcode=2020NatCo..11.1624W |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-15453-z  |doi-access=free|pmc=7156390 |pmid=32286257}}</ref> A 2026 study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' estimated that, from 1990 through 2020, [[greenhouse gas emissions|carbon dioxide emissions]] in the US caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020, with about 30% occurring within the US itself.<ref name=Nature_20260325/> Damages from China were estimated at $8.7 trillion, and from the EU, $6.42 trillion.<ref name=Nature_20260325/> The researchers said that future damages from past emissions are at least an order of magnitude larger than historical damages from the same emissions.<ref name=Nature_20260325>{{cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=Marshall |last2=Zahid |first2=Mustafa |last3=Diffenbaugh |first3=Noah S. |last4=Hsiang |first4=Solomon |title=Quantifying climate loss and damage consistent with a social cost of carbon |journal=Nature |date=25 March 2026 |volume=651 |issue=8107 |pages=959–966 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10272-6 |pmid=41882127 |pmc=13017537 |bibcode=2026Natur.651..959B }}</ref>

Economic impacts also include [[inflation]] from rising [[Climate change and insurance in the United States|insurance premiums]],<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |last=Becker |first=William S. |date=22 July 2024 |title=Opinion: Climate inflation is eating your paycheck — and it's only going to get worse |url=https://thehill.com/opinion/energy-environment/4782252-climate-inflation-economic-impact/ |access-date=24 July 2024 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{Cite news |date=23 July 2024 |title=Home insurance rates are rising due to climate change. What could break that cycle? |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/07/18/1198912918/home-insurance-rates-are-rising-due-to-climate-change-what-could-break-that-cycl |work=NPR}}</ref> [[Carbon price|energy costs]] and [[food prices]].<ref name=":22"/><ref>{{Cite web |date=11 July 2024 |title=How is climate change affecting food prices and inflation? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/program/inside-story/2024/7/11/how-is-climate-change-affecting-food-prices-and-inflation |access-date=24 July 2024 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":02" /> Overall impacts of inflation range from 0.32 to 1.18 percentage points per year, depending on the socio-economic future and future emissions. That is, if a country's inflation without climate change would be 2.0%, it could raise to 2.3% to 3.2% per year with climate change. For food inflation, the estimate ranges between 0.92 and 3.23 percentage points.<ref name=":13" />

==== High emissions scenarios ====
The total economic impacts from climate change increase for higher temperature changes.<ref name=":0" /> For instance, total damages are estimated to be 90% less if global warming is limited to 1.5&nbsp;°C compared to 3.66&nbsp;°C, a warming level chosen to represent no mitigation.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last1=Hoegh-Guldberg |first1=O. |title={{Harvnb|IPCC SR15|2018}} |last2=Jacob |first2=D. |last3=Taylor |first3=M. |last4=Bindi |first4=M. |last5=Brown |first5=S. |last6=Camilloni |first6=I. |last7=Diedhiou |first7=A. |last8=Djalante |first8=R. |last9=Ebi |first9=K. |year=2018 |page=256 |chapter=Chapter 3: Impacts of 1.5 °C Global Warming on Natural and Human Systems |ref={{harvid|IPCC SR15 Ch3|2018}} |display-authors=4 |access-date=15 December 2019 |chapter-url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/sites/2/2019/05/SR15_Chapter3_Low_Res.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191115022743/https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/sites/2/2019/05/SR15_Chapter3_Low_Res.pdf |archive-date=15 November 2019 |url-status=live |first14=A. |last10=Engelbrecht |last12=Hijioka |first13=S. |last13=Mehrotra |first10=F. |last11=Guiot |first17=R. |first11=J. |last14=Payne |last18=Zhou |first18=G. |first16=A. |first12=Y. |last16=Thomas |last15=Seneviratne |first15=S. I. |last17=Warren}}</ref> In an Oxford Economics study high emission scenario, a temperature rise of 2 degrees by the year 2050 would reduce global GDP by 2.5–7.5%. By the year 2100 in this case, the temperature would rise by 4 degrees, which could reduce the global GDP by 30% in the worst case.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Koning Beals |first1=Rachel |title=Global GDP will suffer at least a 3% hit by 2050 from unchecked climate change, say economists |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/global-gdp-will-suffer-at-least-a-3-hit-by-2050-from-unchecked-climate-change-say-economists-2019-11-20 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329094156/https://www.marketwatch.com/story/global-gdp-will-suffer-at-least-a-3-hit-by-2050-from-unchecked-climate-change-say-economists-2019-11-20 |archive-date=29 March 2020 |access-date=29 March 2020 |website=MarketWatch |date=20 November 2019 }}</ref>

One 2018 study found that potential global economic gains if countries implement mitigation strategies to comply with the 2&nbsp;°C target set at the [[Paris Agreement]] are in the vicinity of US$17&nbsp;trillion per year up to 2100, compared to a very high emission scenario.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kompas |first1=Tom |last2=Pham |first2=Van Ha |last3=Che |first3=Tuong Nhu |date=2018 |title=The Effects of Climate Change on GDP by Country and the Global Economic Gains From Complying With the Paris Climate Accord |journal=Earth's Future |volume=6 |issue=8 |pages=1153–1173 |bibcode=2018EaFut...6.1153K |doi=10.1029/2018EF000922 |issn=2328-4277 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=1885/265534}}</ref>

===Underestimation of economic impacts===
{{ multiple image | total_width=450
| image1= 2010-2070-2100 Climate change threatens venues of Olympic Winter Games.svg |caption1= The amount by which greenhouse gas emissions are reduced is forecast to substantially affect the number of Winter Olympic Game venues that will have reliably snowy conditions.<ref name="Forbes_20220204">{{cite news |last1=Buchholz |first1=Katharina |date=4 February 2022 |title=Will Climate Change End The Winter Olympics? |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/katharinabuchholz/2022/02/04/will-climate-change-end-the-winter-olympics-infographic/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230112112106/https://www.forbes.com/sites/katharinabuchholz/2022/02/04/will-climate-change-end-the-winter-olympics-infographic/ |archive-date=12 January 2023 |work=Forbes}} —  Bucholz cites {{cite journal |last1=Scott |first1=Daniel |last2=Knowles |first2=Natalie L. B. |last3=Ma |first3=Siyao |last4=Rutty |first4=Michelle |last5=Steiger |first5=Robert |date=10 January 2022 |title=Climate change and the future of the Olympic Winter Games: athlete and coach perspectives |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13683500.2021.2023480 |journal=Current Issues in Tourism |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=480–495 |doi=10.1080/13683500.2021.2023480 |s2cid=245865532}}</ref>
| image2= 20260201 Reliability of venues for snow - Winter Olympics.svg |caption2=Though Europe and North America have the most potential venues for Olympic Winter Games, a higher portion of those venues are projected to be climatically unreliable because of global warming.<ref name=CurrentIssuesTourism_20240913>Fig. 3 of {{cite journal |last1=Steiger |first1=Robert |last2=Scott |first2=Daniel |title=Climate change and the climate reliability of hosts in the second century of the Winter Olympic Games |journal=Current Issues in Tourism |date=13 September 2024 |volume=28 |issue=22 |pages=3661–3674 |doi=10.1080/13683500.2024.2403133}}</ref>
}}
Studies in 2019 suggested that economic damages due to climate change have been underestimated, and may be severe, with the probability of disastrous [[Black swan theory|tail-risk events]].<ref name="DeFries_etal_2019">{{cite report |url=https://www.lse.ac.uk/granthaminstitute/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/The-missing-economic-risks-in-assessments-of-climate-change-impacts-2.pdf |title=The missing economic risks in assessments of climate change impacts |last1=DeFries |first1=Ruth |last2=Edenhofer |first2=Ottmar |date=September 2019 |publisher=Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, London School of Economics and Political Science |last3=Halliday |first3=Alex |last4=Heal |first4=Geoffrey |author-link1=Ruth DeFries |display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref name="Krogstrup_Oman_2019">{{cite report |url=https://www.elibrary.imf.org/doc/IMF001/28337-9781513511955/28337-9781513511955/Other_formats/Source_PDF/28337-9781513512938.pdf |title=Macroeconomic and Financial Policies for Climate Change Mitigation: A Review of the Literature |last1=Krogstrup |first1=Signe |last2=Oman |first2=William |date=4 September 2019 |doi=10.5089/9781513511955.001 |isbn=978-1-5135-1195-5 |issn=1018-5941 |doi-access=free |series=IMF working papers |issue=185 |page=1 |s2cid=203245445}}</ref>

[[Tipping points in the climate system|Tipping points]] are critical thresholds that, when crossed, lead to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the [[climate system]]. The science of tipping points is complex and there is great uncertainty as to how they might unfold.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Carrington |first=Damian |date=27 November 2019 |title=Climate emergency: world "may have crossed tipping points" |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/nov/27/climate-emergency-world-may-have-crossed-tipping-points |newspaper=[[the Guardian]]}}</ref> Economic analyses often exclude the potential effect of tipping points. A 2018 study noted that the global economic impact is underestimated by a factor of two to eight, when tipping points are excluded from consideration.<ref name=":9" />

The [[Stern Review]] from 2006 for the British Government predicted that world GDP would be reduced by several percent due to climate related costs. However, their calculations may omit ecological effects that are difficult to quantify economically (such as human deaths or [[loss of biodiversity]]) or whose economic consequences will manifest slowly.<ref>{{Cite web |author-last1=Harris |author-first1=Jonathan M. |date=2015 |title=The Economics of Global Climate Change |url=https://www.sciencetheearth.com/uploads/2/4/6/5/24658156/2015_harris_the_economics_of_global_climate_change.pdf |website=Global Development and Environment Institute, Tufts University |author-last2=Roach |author-first2=Brian |author-last3=Codur |author-first3=Anne-Marie}}</ref> Therefore, their calculations may be an underestimate. The study has received both criticism and support from other economists.

=== By region ===
Other studies investigate economic losses by GDP change per country or by per country per capita. Findings show large differences among countries and within countries. The estimated GDP changes in some [[Developing country|developing countries]] are similar to some of the worst country-level losses during historical economic recessions.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2459}} Economic losses are risks to living standards, which are more likely to be severe in developing countries. Climate change can push more people into extreme poverty or keep people poor, especially through particularly climate-sensitive sectors such as agriculture and fisheries. Climate change may also increase income inequality within countries as well as between them, particularly affecting low-income groups.<ref name=":022" />{{rp|2461}}

According to a study by [[reinsurance]] company [[Swiss Re]] in 2021 the economies of wealthy countries like the US would likely shrink by approximately 7%, while some developing nations would be devastated, losing around 20% or in some cases 40% of their economic output.<ref name="Swiss Re 2021">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/22/climate/climate-change-economy.html|title="Climate Change Could Cut World Economy by $23 Trillion in 2050, Insurance Giant Warns: Poor Nations Would Be Particularly Hard Hit, But Few Would Escape, Swiss Re Said"|website=[[The New York Times]] |date=22 April 2021 |access-date=16 September 2025}}</ref>

A [[United States]] government report in November 2018 raised the possibility of US GDP going down 10% as a result of the warming climate, including huge shifts in geography, demographics and technology.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Irwin |first=Neil |date=17 January 2019 |title=Climate Change's Giant Impact on the Economy: 4 Key Issues |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/17/upshot/how-to-think-about-the-costs-of-climate-change.html |access-date=22 January 2019 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

===By sector===
