}}
A 1968 study by the [[Stanford Research Institute]] for the [[American Petroleum Institute]] noted:<ref>{{cite web|title=Smoke & Fumes, Sources, Abundance & Fate of Atmospheric Pollutants|url=https://www.smokeandfumes.org/documents/16|year=1968|publisher=Stanford Research Institute|author1=E. Robinson |author2=R.C. Robbins}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|If the earth's temperature increases significantly, a number of events might be expected to occur, including the melting of the [[Antarctic ice cap]], a rise in sea levels, warming of the oceans, and an increase in photosynthesis.{{nbsp}}... Revelle makes the point that man is now engaged in a vast geophysical experiment with his environment, the earth. Significant temperature changes are almost certain to occur by the year 2000 and these could bring about climatic changes.}}

In 1969, [[NATO]] was the first candidate to deal with climate change on an international level. It was planned then to establish a hub of research and initiatives of the organization in the civil area, dealing with environmental topics<ref name= "Hüne"/> as [[acid rain]] and the [[greenhouse effect]]. The suggestion of US President [[Richard Nixon]] was not very successful with [[Kiesinger cabinet|the administration]] of German Chancellor [[Kurt Georg Kiesinger|Kiesinger]]. But the topics and the preparation work done on the NATO proposal by German authorities gained international momentum, (see e.g. the Stockholm [[United Nations Conference on the Human Environment]] 1970) as [[First Brandt cabinet|the government]] of [[Willy Brandt]] started to apply them on the civil sphere instead.<ref name="Hüne">Die Frühgeschichte der globalen Umweltkrise und die Formierung der deutschen Umweltpolitik(1950–1973) (Early history of the environmental crisis and the setup of German environmental policy 1950–1973), [[Kai F. Hünemörder]], Franz Steiner Verlag, 2004 {{ISBN|3-515-08188-7}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=very unclear English, not sure what is being said after some effort to understand.|date=December 2014}}

Also in 1969, [[Mikhail Budyko]] published a theory on the [[ice–albedo feedback]], a foundational element of what is today known as [[Arctic amplification]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2016/06/ice-in-action-sea-ice-at-the-north-pole-has-something-to-say-about-climate-change|title=Ice in Action: Sea ice at the North Pole has something to say about climate change|year=2016|work=YaleScientific}}</ref>  The same year a similar model was published by [[William D. Sellers]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=A Global Climatic Model Based on the Energy Balance of the Earth-Atmosphere System|year=1969|doi=10.1175/1520-0450(1969)008<0392:AGCMBO>2.0.CO;2|author=William D. Sellers|journal=Journal of Applied Meteorology|volume = 8|issue=3|pages=392–400|bibcode=1969JApMe...8..392S|doi-access=free}}</ref> Both studies attracted significant attention, since they hinted at the possibility for a runaway positive feedback within the global climate system.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Mikhail Budyko's (1920–2001) contributions to Global Climate Science: from heat balances to climate change and global ecology|year=2016|author=Jonathan D. Oldfield|doi=10.1002/wcc.412|journal= WIREs Climate Change|volume = 7|issue=5|pages=682–692|doi-access=free|bibcode=2016WIRCC...7..682O }}</ref>

A 1969 memo from White House Urban Affairs Director [[Daniel Patrick Moynihan]] tried to impress the office of U.S. President Nixon with the projected severity of the greenhouse effect.<ref name=NixonLibrary_19690917/> However, action was not taken, even after a 20 December 1971 initiative from the [[Office of Science and Technology]], "Determine the Climate Change Caused by Man and Nature".<ref name=OST_19711220>{{cite web |title=Office of Science and Technology Sub-Initiative, "Determine the Climate Change Caused by Man and Nature", December 20, 1971, folder 1.2.3 Climate Change [1971], Box 82, New Technology Opportunities Series, Edward E. David's Files |url=https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/Document%204_0.pdf |publisher=National Security Archive of the George Washington University |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429050837/https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/Document%204_0.pdf |archive-date=29 April 2024 |date=20 December 1971 |url-status=live}}</ref> 
In the initiative, Nixon's science advisors recommended an international network for [[Environmental monitoring|monitoring]] climate trends and human impact on it.<ref name=ArsTechnica_20240426>{{cite magazine |last1=Lavelle |first1=Marianne (''Inside Climate News'') |title=Lost opportunity: We could've started fighting climate change in 1971 |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2024/04/nixon-administration-couldve-started-monitoring-co2-levels-but-didnt/ |magazine=Ars Technica |date=26 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240426142812/https://arstechnica.com/science/2024/04/nixon-administration-couldve-started-monitoring-co2-levels-but-didnt/ |archive-date=26 April 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Scientists increasingly predict warming, 1970s ===
[[File:Global Cooling Map.png|thumb|Mean temperature anomalies during the period 1965 to 1975 with respect to the average temperatures from 1937 to 1946. This dataset was not available at the time.]]
[[File:1965-1979 Survey of scientific papers re global warming vs cooling.svg |thumb |Anthropogenic global ''warming''—not [[Global cooling|global ''cooling'']] or "imminent ice ages"—dominated [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] literature in the 1970s, contrary to false claims that [[Climatology|climate science]] subsequently reversed its consensus.<ref name=AMS_20080901>{{cite journal |last1=Peterson |first1=Thomas C. |last2=Connolley |first2=William M. |last3=Fleck |first3=John |title=The Myth of the 1970s Global Cooling Scientific Consensus |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society |date=1 September 2008 |volume=89 |issue=9 |pages=1235–1328 |doi=10.1175/2008BAMS2370.1}}</ref>]]
In the early 1970s, evidence that aerosols were increasing worldwide and that the global temperature series showed cooling encouraged [[Reid Bryson]] and some others to warn of the possibility of severe cooling. The questions and concerns put forth by Bryson and others launched a new wave of research into the factors of such global cooling.<ref name=":1" /> Meanwhile, the new evidence that the timing of ice ages was set by predictable orbital cycles suggested that the climate would gradually cool, over thousands of years. Several scientific panels from this time period concluded that more research was needed to determine whether warming or cooling was likely, indicating that the trend in the scientific literature had not yet become a consensus.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/sciencechallenge00nati|title=Science and the Challenges Ahead. Report of the National Science Board|year=1974 |orig-date=i.e. 1975|publisher=Washington, D.C. : National Science Board, National Science Foundation : For sale by Supt. of Docs., U.S. G.P.O.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=W M Connolley|title=The 1975 US National Academy of Sciences/National Research Council Report|url=http://www.wmconnolley.org.uk/sci/iceage/nas-1975.html|access-date=28 June 2009}}</ref><ref>Reid A. Bryson:''A Reconciliation of several Theories of Climate Change'', in: John P. Holdren (Ed.): ''Global Ecology. Readings toward a Rational Strategy for Man'', New York etc. 1971, S. 78–84</ref> For the century ahead, however, a survey of the scientific literature from 1965 to 1979 found 7 articles predicting cooling and 44 predicting warming (many other articles on climate made no prediction); the warming articles were cited much more often in subsequent scientific literature.<ref name=":1" /> Research into warming and greenhouse gases held the greater emphasis, with nearly six times more studies predicting warming than predicting cooling, suggesting concern among scientists was largely over warming as they turned their attention toward the greenhouse effect.<ref name=":1" />

[[John Sawyer (meteorologist)|John Sawyer]] published the study ''Man-made Carbon Dioxide and the "Greenhouse" Effect'' in 1972.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Man-made Carbon Dioxide and the "Greenhouse" Effect|date=1 September 1972|journal=Nature|volume=239|issue=5366|pages=23–26|doi=10.1038/239023a0|author=J. S. Sawyer|bibcode=1972Natur.239...23S|s2cid=4180899}}</ref> He summarized the knowledge of the science at the time, the anthropogenic attribution of the carbon dioxide greenhouse gas, distribution and exponential rise, findings which still hold today. Additionally he accurately predicted the rate of global warming for the period between 1972 and 2000.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Climate: Sawyer predicted rate of warming in 1972|date=30 August 2007|journal=Nature|volume=448|issue=7157|doi=10.1038/448992c|author=Neville Nicholls|page=992|pmid=17728736|bibcode=2007Natur.448..992N|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Climatology versus Pseudoscience: Exposing the Failed Predictions of Global Warming Skeptics|date=3 March 2015|pages=22–25|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mKigBgAAQBAJ&q=John%20Sawyer%20fellow%20royal%20society&pg=PA22|author=Dana Andrew Nuccitelli|publisher=Nature|isbn=978-1-4408-3202-4}}</ref>
{{blockquote|text=''The increase of 25% {{CO2}} expected by the end of the century therefore corresponds to an increase of 0.6&nbsp;°C in the world temperature – an amount somewhat greater than the climatic variation of recent centuries''. – John Sawyer, 1972}}

The first satellite records compiled in the early 1970s showed snow and ice cover over the Northern Hemisphere to be increasing, prompting further scrutiny into the possibility of global cooling.<ref name=":1" /> J. Murray Mitchell updated his global temperature reconstruction in 1972, which continued to show cooling.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mitchell|first=J. Murray|date=November 1972|title=The Natural Breakdown of the Present Interglacial and its Possible Intervention by Human Activities|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/quaternary-research/article/abs/natural-breakdown-of-the-present-interglacial-and-its-possible-intervention-by-human-activities/DE2D651E56017AD5EA6647BCD5F90510|journal=Quaternary Research|language=en|volume=2|issue=3|pages=436–445|doi=10.1016/0033-5894(72)90069-5|bibcode=1972QuRes...2..436M|s2cid=129438640 |issn=0033-5894|url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, scientists determined that the cooling observed by Mitchell was not a global phenomenon. Global averages were changing, largely in part due to unusually severe winters experienced by Asia and some parts of North America in 1972 and 1973, but these changes were mostly constrained to the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern Hemisphere, the opposite trend was observed. The severe winters, however, pushed the issue of global cooling into the public eye.<ref name=":1" />

The mainstream news media at the time exaggerated the warnings of the minority who expected imminent cooling. For example, in 1975, ''[[Newsweek]]'' magazine published a story titled "The Cooling World" that warned of "ominous signs that the Earth's weather patterns have begun to change".<ref name="newsweek-1975">{{cite web |url=http://www.denisdutton.com/newsweek_coolingworld.pdf |title=The Cooling World |author=Peter Gwynne |year=1975 |access-date=5 July 2009 |archive-date=20 April 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420134626/http://denisdutton.com/newsweek_coolingworld.pdf }}</ref> The article drew on studies documenting the increasing snow and ice in regions of the Northern Hemisphere and concerns and claims by Reid Bryson that global cooling by aerosols would dominate carbon dioxide warming.<ref name=":1" /> The article continued by stating that evidence of global cooling was so strong that meteorologists were having "a hard time keeping up with it".<ref name="newsweek-1975" /> On 23 October 2006, ''Newsweek'' issued an update stating that it had been "spectacularly wrong about the near-term future".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newsweek.com/id/72481 |title=Climate Change: Prediction Perils |work=Newsweek |author=Jerry Adler |date=23 October 2006}}</ref> Nevertheless, this article and others like it had long-lasting effects on public perception of climate science.<ref name=":1" />

{{quote box
| title = 1977 Memorandum to the President:<br />Release of Fossil {{CO2}} and the<br />Possibility of a Catastrophic Climate Change
| quote = <br />{{nbsp|3}}  {{gray|(within 60 years:)}} Because of the "greenhouse effect" of atmospheric {{CO2}} the increased concentration will induce a global climatic warming of anywhere from 0.5 to 5 °C.<br />
{{nbsp|3}} ... The potential effect on the environment of a climatic fluctuation of such rapidity could be catastrophic and calls for an impact assessment of unprecedented importance and difficulty. A rapid climatic change may result in large scale crop failures at a time when an increased world population taxes agriculture to the limits of productivity.<br />
{{nbsp|3}} ... The urgency of the problem derives from our inability to shift rapidly to non-fossil fuel sources once the climatic effects become evident not long after the year 2000;&nbsp;...
| source = —[[Frank Press]], 7 July 1977<ref name=Guardian_20220614>{{cite news |last1=Pattee |first1=Emma |title=The 1977 White House climate memo that should have changed the world |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/14/1977-us-presidential-memo-predicted-climate-change |work=The Guardian |date=14 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220617151837/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/14/1977-us-presidential-memo-predicted-climate-change |archive-date=17 June 2022 |url-status=live }}</ref><br />Chief science adviser to U.S. President Carter
| align = right | width = 40% | border = 1px | fontsize = 100% | bgcolor = #fafafa | title_bg = #fafafa | title_fnt = #202060 | qalign = left | salign = right
}}
Such media coverage heralding the coming of a new ice age resulted in beliefs that this was the consensus among scientists, despite this not being reflected by the scientific literature. As it became apparent that scientific opinion was in favor of global warming, the public began to express doubt over how trustworthy the science was.<ref name=":1" /> The argument that scientists were wrong about global cooling, so therefore may be wrong about global warming has been called "the Ice Age Fallacy" by ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' author Bryan Walsh.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=Sorry, a Time Magazine Cover Did Not Predict a Coming Ice Age|url=https://time.com/5670942/time-magazine-ice-age-cover-hoax/|access-date=19 April 2021|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]}}</ref>

In the first two "Reports for the Club of Rome" in 1972<ref>Meadows, D., et al., ''The Limits to Growth''. New York 1972.</ref> and 1974,<ref>Mesarovic, M., Pestel, E., ''Mankind at the Turning Point''. New York 1974.</ref> the anthropogenic climate changes by {{CO2}} increase as well as by [[waste heat]] were mentioned. About the latter [[John Holdren]] wrote in a study<ref>John P. Holdren: "Global Thermal Pollution", in: John P. Holdren (Ed.): ''Global Ecology. Readings toward a Rational Strategy for Man'', New York etc. 1971, S. 85–88. The author became Director of the White House [[Office of Science and Technology Policy]] in 2009.</ref> cited in the 1st report, "that global thermal pollution is hardly our most immediate environmental threat. It could prove to be the most inexorable, however, if we are fortunate enough to evade all the rest". Simple global-scale estimates<ref>[[Robert Döpel|R. Döpel]], "Über die geophysikalische Schranke der industriellen Energieerzeugung". Wissenschaftl. Zeitschrift der Technischen Hochschule Ilmenau, ISSN 0043-6917, Bd. 19 (1973, H.2), 37–52. [http://www.db-thueringen.de/servlets/DocumentServlet?id=12380 online].</ref> that recently have been actualized<ref>H. Arnold, "[[Robert Döpel]] and his Model of Global Warming. An Early Warning – and its Update". Universitätsverlag Ilmenau (Germany) 2013. {{ISBN|978-3-86360 063-1}} [http://www.db-thueringen.de/servlets/DocumentServlet?id=22287 online]</ref> and confirmed by more refined model calculations<ref>{{cite journal | author = Chaisson E. J. | year = 2008 | title = Long-Term Global Heating from Energy Usage | url = http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:15217701| journal = Eos | volume = 89 | issue = 28| pages = 253–260 | doi=10.1029/2008eo280001 | bibcode=2008EOSTr..89..253C| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=flanner>{{cite journal| author=Flanner, M. G. |year=2009 |title=Integrating anthropogenic heat flux with global climate models |journal=Geophys. Res. Lett. |volume=36| issue=2 |pages=L02801 |article-number=2008GL036465 |doi=10.1029/2008GL036465|bibcode = 2009GeoRL..36.2801F |doi-access=free }}</ref> show noticeable contributions from waste heat to global warming after the year 2100, if its growth rates are not strongly reduced (below the averaged 2% p.a. which occurred since 1973).

Evidence for warming accumulated. By 1975, Manabe and Wetherald had developed a three-dimensional [[global climate model]] that gave a roughly accurate representation of the current climate. Doubling CO<sub>2</sub> in the model's atmosphere gave a roughly 2&nbsp;°C rise in global temperature.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Manabe S. |author2=Wetherald R. T. | year = 1975 | title = The Effects of Doubling the CO<sub>2</sub> Concentration on the Climate of a General Circulation Model | journal = Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences | volume = 32 | issue = 3| pages = 3–15 | doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1975)032<0003:teodtc>2.0.co;2| bibcode=1975JAtS...32....3M| doi-access = free }}</ref> Several other kinds of computer models gave similar results: it was impossible to make a model that gave something resembling the actual climate and not have the temperature rise when the CO<sub>2</sub> concentration was increased.

In a separate development, an analysis of deep-sea cores published in 1976 by [[Nicholas Shackleton]] and colleagues showed that the dominating influence on ice age timing came from a 100,000-year Milankovitch orbital change. This was unexpected, since the change in sunlight in that cycle was slight. The result emphasized that the climate system is driven by feedbacks, and thus is strongly susceptible to small changes in conditions.<ref name="Imbrie" />

A 1977 memo (see quote box) from President Carter's chief science adviser [[Frank Press]] warned of the possibility of catastrophic climate change.<ref name=Guardian_20220614/> However, other issues—such as known harms to health from pollutants, and avoiding energy dependence on other nations—seemed more pressing and immediate.<ref name=Guardian_20220614/> Energy Secretary [[James Schlesinger]] advised that "the policy implications of this issue are still too uncertain to warrant Presidential involvement and policy initiatives", and the fossil fuel industry began sowing doubt about climate science.<ref name=Guardian_20220614/>

The 1979 [[World Climate Conference]] (12 to 23 February) of the [[World Meteorological Organization]] concluded "it appears plausible that an increased amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can contribute to a gradual warming of the lower atmosphere, especially at higher latitudes.&nbsp;... It is possible that some effects on a regional and global scale may be detectable before the end of this century and become significant before the middle of the next century."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dgvn.de/fileadmin/user_upload/DOKUMENTE/WCC-3/Declaration_WCC1.pdf |title=Declaration of the World Climate Conference |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |access-date=28 June 2009 }}</ref>

In July 1979 the [[United States National Research Council]] published a report,<ref>{{cite book 
| author=Ad Hoc Study Group on Carbon Dioxide and Climate 
| author2=Climate Research Board 
| author3=Assembly of Mathematical and Physical Sciences 
| author4=National Research Council 
| title=Carbon Dioxide and Climate: A Scientific Assessment 
| publisher=National Academies Press 
| publication-place=Washington, D.C. 
| date=13 March 1979 
| isbn=978-0-309-11910-8 
| doi=10.17226/12181 
| url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/12181 |
 access-date=8 May 2025 
}}</ref>
concluding (in part):
{{blockquote|When it is assumed that the {{CO2}} content of the atmosphere is doubled and statistical thermal equilibrium is achieved, the more realistic of the modeling efforts predict a global surface warming of between 2&nbsp;°C and 3.5&nbsp;°C, with greater increases at high latitudes.

...&nbsp;we have tried but have been unable to find any overlooked or underestimated physical effects that could reduce the currently estimated global warmings due to a doubling of atmospheric {{CO2}} to negligible proportions or reverse them altogether.}}

One week before President Carter left office, the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) issued reports including a suggestion to limit global average temperature to 2&nbsp;°C above preindustrial levels, one goal agreed to in the 2015 [[Paris Agreement|Paris climate accord]].<ref name=InsideClimateNews_20230303>{{cite news |last1=Alter |first1=Jonathan |title=Jimmy Carter Signed 14 Major Environmental Bills and Foresaw the Threat of Climate Change |url=https://insideclimatenews.org/news/03032023/jimmy-carter-climate-change/ |work=Inside Climate News |date=3 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230304215651/https://insideclimatenews.org/news/03032023/jimmy-carter-climate-change/ |archive-date=4 March 2023}}</ref>

=== Consensus begins to form, 1980–1988 ===
{{See also|Climate change denial|Scientific consensus on climate change}}
[[File:James Hansen Crop1.png|thumb|[[James Hansen]] during his 1988 testimony to Congress, which alerted the public to the dangers of global warming]]
By the early 1980s, the slight cooling trend from 1945 to 1975 had stopped.  Aerosol pollution had decreased in many areas due to environmental legislation and changes in fuel use, and it became clear that the cooling effect from aerosols was not going to increase substantially while carbon dioxide levels were progressively increasing.

Hansen and others published the 1981 study ''Climate impact of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide'', and noted: {{blockquote|It is shown that the anthropogenic carbon dioxide warming should emerge from the noise level of natural climate variability by the end of the century, and there is a high probability of warming in the 1980s. Potential effects on climate in the 21st century include the creation of drought-prone regions in North America and central Asia as part of a shifting of [[Climate classification|climatic zones]], erosion of the [[West Antarctic ice sheet]] with a consequent worldwide rise in sea level, and opening of the fabled [[Northwest Passage]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Hansen, J.|year=1981|title=Climate impact of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide|url=https://pubs.giss.nasa.gov/abs/ha04600x.html|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=231|issue=4511|pages=957–966|doi=10.1126/science.213.4511.957|pmid=17789014|display-authors=etal|bibcode=1981Sci...213..957H|s2cid=20971423|url-access=subscription}}</ref>}}

In 1982, [[Greenland]] [[ice core]]s drilled by [[Hans Oeschger]], [[Willi Dansgaard]], and collaborators revealed dramatic temperature oscillations in the space of a century in the distant past.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Dansgaard W. | year = 1982 | title = A New Greenland Deep Ice Core | journal = Science | volume = 218 | issue = 4579| pages = 1273–77 | doi=10.1126/science.218.4579.1273 | pmid=17770148|display-authors=etal| bibcode=1982Sci...218.1273D| s2cid = 35224174 }}</ref> The most prominent of the changes in their record corresponded to the violent [[Younger Dryas]] climate oscillation seen in shifts in types of pollen in lake beds all over Europe. Evidently drastic climate changes were possible within a human lifetime.

In 1973 [[James Lovelock]] speculated that [[chlorofluorocarbon]]s (CFCs) could have a global warming effect.  In 1975 [[Veerabhadran Ramanathan|V. Ramanathan]] found that a CFC molecule could be 10,000 times more effective in absorbing infrared radiation than a carbon dioxide molecule, making CFCs potentially important despite their very low concentrations in the atmosphere.  While most early work on CFCs focused on their role in [[ozone depletion]], by 1985 Ramanathan and others showed that CFCs together with [[methane]] and other [[trace gases]] could have nearly as important a climate effect as increases in {{CO2}}. In other words, global warming would arrive twice as fast as had been expected.<ref name=aiphistoryother>{{cite web |url=http://history.aip.org/climate/othergas.htm |title=Other Greenhouse Gases |work=The Discovery of Global Warming | year=2003 |author=Spencer Weart}}</ref>

[[File:20211115 Progression of global warming - decadal analysis - bar chart.svg|thumb|upright=1.5| Since the 1980s, global average surface temperatures during a given decade have almost always been higher than the average temperature in the preceding decade.]]
In 1985 a joint [[UNEP]]/WMO/[[ICSU]] Conference on the "Assessment of the Role of Carbon Dioxide and Other Greenhouse Gases in Climate Variations and Associated Impacts" concluded that greenhouse gases "are expected" to cause significant warming in the next century and that some warming is inevitable.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.scopenvironment.org/downloadpubs/scope29/statement.html|author = World Meteorological Organisation (WMO)|year = 1986|title = Report of the International Conference on the assessment of the role of carbon dioxide and of other greenhouse gases in climate variations and associated impacts|location = Villach, Austria|access-date = 28 June 2009|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131121040937/http://www.scopenvironment.org/downloadpubs/scope29/statement.html|archive-date = 21 November 2013}}</ref>

Meanwhile, [[ice core]]s drilled by a Franco-Soviet team at the [[Vostok Station]] in [[Antarctica]] showed that {{CO2}} and temperature had gone up and down together in wide swings through past ice ages. This confirmed the {{CO2}}-temperature relationship in a manner entirely independent of computer [[climate model]]s, strongly reinforcing the emerging scientific consensus. The findings also pointed to powerful biological and geochemical feedbacks.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Lorius Claude | year = 1985 | title = A 150,000-Year Climatic Record from Antarctic Ice | journal = Nature | volume = 316 | issue = 6029| pages = 591–596 | doi=10.1038/316591a0|display-authors=etal| bibcode = 1985Natur.316..591L| s2cid = 4368173 | url = https://hal.science/hal-03482744 }}</ref>

In January 1986,<ref>[https://www.dpg-physik.de/veroeffentlichungen/publikationen/stellungnahmen-der-dpg/klima-energie/pm-1986.pdf Erläterungen] von Prof. [[:de:Klaus Heinloth]]</ref> the [[German Physical Society]] published ''warning of an impending climate catastrophe''<ref>[https://www.dpg-physik.de/veroeffentlichungen/publikationen/stellungnahmen-der-dpg/klima-energie/warnung.pdf WARNUNG VOR EINER DROHENDEN KLIMAKATASTROPHE] (pdf)</ref>

In June 1988, [[James E. Hansen]] made one of the first assessments that human-caused warming had already measurably affected global climate.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://image.guardian.co.uk/sys-files/Environment/documents/2008/06/23/ClimateChangeHearing1988.pdf |title=Statement of Dr. James Hansen, Director, NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies |access-date=28 June 2009 | location=London |newspaper=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> Shortly after, a "[[Toronto Conference on the Changing Atmosphere|World Conference on the Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security]]" gathered hundreds of scientists and others in [[Toronto]]. They concluded that the changes in the atmosphere due to human pollution "represent a major threat to international security and are already having harmful consequences over many parts of the globe", and declared that by 2005 the world would be well-advised to push its emissions some 20% below the 1988 level.<ref>{{cite book|last=WMO (World Meteorological Organization) |year=1989 |title=The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security, Toronto, Canada, 27–30 June 1988: Conference Proceedings |place=Geneva |publisher=Secretariat of the World Meteorological Organization |url=http://www.cmos.ca/changingatmosphere1988e.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120629204735/http://www.cmos.ca/changingatmosphere1988e.pdf |archive-date=29 June 2012 }}</ref>

The 1980s saw important breakthroughs with regard to global environmental challenges. [[Ozone depletion]] was mitigated by the [[Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer|Vienna Convention]] (1985) and the [[Montreal Protocol]] (1987). [[Acid rain]] was mainly regulated on national and regional levels.

=== Increased consensus amongst scientists: 1988 to present ===
{{Main |Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change| Scientific consensus on climate change}}
[[File:20211103 Academic studies of scientific consensus - global warming, climate change - vertical bar chart - en.svg|thumb|right |upright=1.5 |''Scientific consensus on causation:'' [[Surveys of scientists' views on climate change|Academic studies of scientific agreement on human-caused global warming]] among climate experts (2010–2015) reflect that the level of consensus correlates with expertise in climate science.<ref name=Cook_2016>{{cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=John |last2=Oreskes |first2=Naomi |author2-link=Naomi Oreskes |last3=Doran |first3=Peter T. |author4-link=William Anderegg |last4=Anderegg |first4=William R. L. |last5=Verheggen |first5=Bart |display-authors=4 |date=2016 |title=Consensus on consensus: a synthesis of consensus estimates on human-caused global warming |journal=Environmental Research Letters |volume=11 |issue=4 |article-number=048002 |bibcode=2016ERL....11d8002C |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/11/4/048002 |doi-access=free |hdl=1983/34949783-dac1-4ce7-ad95-5dc0798930a6 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 

A 2019 study found scientific consensus to be at 100%,<ref name="Powell2019">{{cite journal |last1=Powell |first1=James Lawrence |author-link=James L. Powell |date=20 November 2019 |title=Scientists Reach 100% Consensus on Anthropogenic Global Warming  |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0270467619886266 |journal=Bulletin of Science, Technology & Society |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=183–184 |doi=10.1177/0270467619886266 |s2cid=213454806 |access-date=15 November 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and a 2021 study concluded that consensus exceeded 99%.<ref name=EnvRschLtrs_20211019>{{cite journal |last1=Lynas |first1=Mark |last2=Houlton |first2=Benjamin Z. |author2-link=Benjamin Z. Houlton |last3=Perry |first3=Simon |title=Greater than 99% consensus on human caused climate change in the peer-reviewed scientific literature |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=19 October 2021 |volume=16 |issue=11 |page=114005 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/ac2966 |bibcode=2021ERL....16k4005L |s2cid=239032360 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Another 2021 study found that 98.7% of climate experts indicated that the Earth is getting warmer mostly because of human activity.<ref name=Myers_2021>{{cite journal |last1=Myers |first1=Krista F. |last2=Doran |first2=Peter T. |last3=Cook |first3=John |last4=Kotcher |first4=John E. |last5=Myers |first5=Teresa A. |title=Consensus revisited: quantifying scientific agreement on climate change and climate expertise among Earth scientists 10 years later |journal=[[Environmental Research Letters]] |date=20 October 2021 |volume=16 |issue=10 |page=104030 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/ac2774 |bibcode=2021ERL....16j4030M |s2cid=239047650 |doi-access=free }}</ref>]]

In 1988 the WMO established the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] with the support of the UNEP. The IPCC continues its work through the present day, and issues a series of Assessment Reports and supplemental reports that describe the state of scientific understanding at the time each report is prepared. Scientific developments during this period are summarized about once every five to six years in the IPCC Assessment Reports which were published in 1990 ([[IPCC First Assessment Report|First Assessment Report]]), 1995 ([[IPCC Second Assessment Report|Second Assessment Report]]), 2001 ([[IPCC Third Assessment Report|Third Assessment Report]]), 2007 ([[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report|Fourth Assessment Report]]), 2013/2014 ([[IPCC Fifth Assessment Report|Fifth Assessment Report]]). and 2021 [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report|Sixth Assessment Report]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/publications_and_data_reports.shtml#1|title=IPCC – Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|website=ipcc.ch}}</ref> 
The 2001 report was the first to state positively that the observed global temperature increase was "likely" to be due to human activities. The conclusion was influenced especially by the so-called [[hockey stick graph (global temperature)|hockey stick graph]] showing an abrupt historical temperature rise simultaneous with the rise of greenhouse gas emissions, and by observations of changes in [[ocean heat content]] that had a "signature" matching the pattern that computer models calculated for the effect of greenhouse warming. By the time of the 2021 report, scientists had much additional evidence. Above all, measurements of [[Paleothermometer|paleotemperatures]] from several eras in the distant past, and the record of temperature change since the mid 19th century, could be matched against measurements of {{CO2}} levels to provide independent confirmation of [[supercomputer]] model calculations.

These developments depended crucially on [[Weather satellite]]s, [[Landsat program|other satellites]] and huge globe-spanning observation programs. Since the 1990s research into historical and modern climate change expanded rapidly. International coordination was provided by the [[World Climate Research Programme]] (established in 1980) and was increasingly oriented around providing input to the IPCC reports. Measurement networks such as the [[Global Ocean Observing System]], [[Integrated Carbon Observation System]], and NASA's [[Earth Observing System]] enabled monitoring of the causes and effects of ongoing change.  Research also broadened, linking many fields such as [[Earth science]]s, [[behavioral sciences]], economics, and [[Climate security|security]].

=== Relative importance of human activity versus natural causes ===
A historically important question in climate change research has regarded the relative importance of human activity and natural causes during the period of [[Instrumental temperature record|instrumental record]]. In the 1995 [[IPCC Second Assessment Report|Second Assessment Report]] (SAR), the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] made the widely quoted statement that "The balance of evidence suggests a discernible human influence on global climate". The phrase "balance of evidence" suggested the (English) common-law standard of proof required in civil as opposed to criminal courts: not as high as "beyond reasonable doubt". In 2001 the [[IPCC Third Assessment Report|Third Assessment Report]] (TAR) refined this, saying "There is new and stronger evidence that most of the warming observed over the last 50 years is attributable to human activities".<ref name="WG1-2001-SPM">IPCC, [http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar/wg1/007.htm Summary for Policymakers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617020742/http://www.grida.no/climate/ipcc_tar/wg1/007.htm|date=17 June 2016}}.{{page needed|date=September 2011}} in {{Harvnb|IPCC TAR WG1|2001}}.</ref> The 2007 [[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report|Fourth Assessment Report]] (AR4) strengthened this finding:

* "Anthropogenic warming of the climate system is widespread and can be detected in temperature observations taken at the surface, in the free atmosphere and in the oceans. Evidence of the effect of external influences, both anthropogenic and natural, on the climate system has continued to accumulate since the TAR."<ref>Solomon ''et al.'', [http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ts.html Technical Summary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181128003303/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ts.html|date=28 November 2018}}, [http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-ts.pdf p. ?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100806115645/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-ts.pdf|date=6 August 2010}}.{{page needed|date=September 2011}} in {{Harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG1|2007}}.</ref>

Other findings of the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report include:

* "It is ''extremely unlikely'' (<5%)<ref name="ar4 uncertainty">In the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report, the following scale is used to quantify uncertainty: "virtually certain" >99%; "extremely likely" >95%; "very likely" >90%; "likely" >66%; "more likely than not" >50%; "about as likely as not" 33 to 66%; "unlikely" <33%; "very unlikely" <10%; "extremely unlikely" <5%; "exceptionally unlikely" <1%. {{citation |author=Solomon, S. |title=Technical Summary |access-date=18 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120612142856/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/tssts-2.html |url-status=live |chapter=Box TS.1: Treatment of Uncertainties in the Working Group I Assessment |chapter-url=http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/tssts-2.html |display-authors=etal |archive-date=12 June 2012}}, in {{Harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG1|2007}}.</ref> that the global pattern of warming during the past half century can be explained without external forcing (i.e., it is inconsistent with being the result of internal variability), and ''very unlikely''<ref name="ar4 uncertainty" /> that it is due to known natural external causes alone. The warming occurred in both the ocean and the atmosphere and took place at a time when natural external forcing factors would likely have produced cooling."<ref name="hegerl 2007 executive summary">Hegerl ''et al.'', [http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch9.html Chapter 9: Understanding and Attributing Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128182203/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch9.html|date=28 November 2011}}, [http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch9s9-es.html Executive Summary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181118201756/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/ch9s9-es.html|date=18 November 2018}}, in {{Harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG1|2007}}.</ref>
* "From new estimates of the combined anthropogenic [[Radiative forcing|forcing]] due to greenhouse gases, [[aerosol]]s, and [[Land use|land surface changes]], it is ''extremely likely'' (>95%)<ref name="ar4 uncertainty" /> that human activities have exerted a substantial net warming influence on climate since 1750."<ref name="solomon 2007 drivers of climate change">{{citation |author=Solomon, S. |title=Technical Summary |access-date=18 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120605174243/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/tssts-6.html |chapter=TS.6.1 Changes in Human and Natural Drivers of Climate |chapter-url=http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/tssts-6.html |display-authors=etal |archive-date=5 June 2012}}, in {{Harvnb|IPCC AR4 WG1|2007}}.</ref>
* "It is ''virtually certain''<ref name="ar4 uncertainty" /> that anthropogenic aerosols produce a net negative [[radiative forcing]] (cooling influence) with a greater magnitude in the [[Northern Hemisphere]] than in the [[Southern Hemisphere]]."<ref name="solomon 2007 drivers of climate change" />
Some results from scientific studies on this issue are listed below:

* In 1996, in a paper in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' titled "A search for human influences on the thermal structure of the atmosphere", [[Benjamin D. Santer]] et al. wrote: "The observed spatial patterns of temperature change in the free atmosphere from 1963 to 1987 are similar to those predicted by state-of-the-art climate models incorporating various combinations of changes in carbon dioxide, anthropogenic sulphate aerosol and stratospheric ozone concentrations. The degree of pattern similarity between models and observations increases through this period. It is likely that this trend is partially due to human activities, although many uncertainties remain, particularly relating to estimates of natural variability."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Santer |first1=B. D. |last2=Taylor |first2=K. E. |last3=Wigley |first3=T. M. L. |last4=Johns |first4=T. C. |last5=Jones |first5=P. D. |last6=Karoly |first6=D. J. |last7=Mitchell |first7=J. F. B. |last8=Oort |first8=A. H. |last9=Penner |first9=J. E. |last10=Ramaswamy |first10=V. |last11=Schwarzkopf |first11=M. D. |date=1996 |title=A search for human influences on the thermal structure of the atmosphere |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc624360/m2/1/high_res_d/116649.pdf |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=382 |issue=6586 |pages=39–46 |bibcode=1996Natur.382...39S |doi=10.1038/382039a0 |issn=1476-4687 |access-date=4 October 2021}}</ref>
* A 2002 paper in the ''[[Journal of Geophysical Research]]'' says "Our analysis suggests that the early twentieth century warming can best be explained by a combination of warming due to increases in greenhouse gases and natural forcing, some cooling due to other anthropogenic forcings, and a substantial, but not implausible, contribution from internal variability. In the second half of the century we find that the warming is largely caused by changes in greenhouse gases, with changes in sulphates and, perhaps, volcanic aerosol offsetting approximately one third of the warming."<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Tett SFB |author-link1=Simon Tett |display-authors=etal |year=2002 |title=Estimation of natural and anthropogenic contributions to twentieth century temperature change |url=http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2002/2000JD000028.shtml |url-status=live |journal=J. Geophys. Res. |volume=107 |issue=D16 |page=4306 |bibcode=2002JGRD..107.4306T |doi=10.1029/2000JD000028 |s2cid=29368273 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100404174304/http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/2002/2000JD000028.shtml |archive-date=4 April 2010 |access-date=27 July 2009 |hdl-access=free |hdl=20.500.11820/ab4c4ebd-df4e-4487-bcb7-71647f928873}}</ref><ref>{{cite newsgroup |title=Estimation of natural and anthropogenic contributions to twentieth century temperature change |author=[[William Connolley]] |date=27 May 2003 |newsgroup=sci.environment |message-id=3ed342eb@news.nwl.ac.uk |url=https://groups.google.com/forum/#!original/sci.environment/v-EOwyTtcus/rBbSfLYhhaoJ |access-date=13 June 2012 |archive-date=31 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190531115852/https://groups.google.com/forum/#!original/sci.environment/v-EOwyTtcus/rBbSfLYhhaoJ |url-status=live}}</ref>
* A 2005 review of detection and attribution studies by the International Ad hoc Detection and Attribution Group<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barnett |first=T. |date=May 2005 |title=Detecting and Attributing External Influences on the Climate System: A Review of Recent Advances |url=http://www.llnl.gov/tid/lof/documents/pdf/315840.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Journal of Climate |volume=18 |issue=9 |pages=1291–1314 |bibcode=2005JCli...18.1291. |doi=10.1175/JCLI3329.1 |s2cid=7580329 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071128074638/http://www.llnl.gov/tid/lof/documents/pdf/315840.pdf |archive-date=28 November 2007 |access-date=22 November 2007 |hdl-access=free |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0011-FF92-2}}</ref> found that "natural drivers such as solar variability and volcanic activity are at most partially responsible for the large-scale temperature changes observed over the past century, and that a large fraction of the warming over the last 50 yr can be attributed to greenhouse gas increases. Thus, the recent research supports and strengthens the IPCC Third Assessment Report conclusion that 'most of the global warming over the past 50 years is likely due to the increase in greenhouse gases.'"
* Barnett and colleagues (2005) say that the observed warming of the oceans "cannot be explained by natural internal climate variability or solar and volcanic forcing, but is well simulated by two [[Human impact on the environment|anthropogenically]] forced climate models," concluding that "it is of human origin, a conclusion robust to observational sampling and model differences".<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=etal |vauthors=Barnett TP, Pierce DW, Achutarao KM |date=July 2005 |title=Penetration of human-induced warming into the world's oceans |journal=Science |volume=309 |issue=5732 |pages=284–7 |bibcode=2005Sci...309..284B |doi=10.1126/science.1112418 |pmid=15933161 |s2cid=5641405 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Two papers in the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' in August 2005<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schmidt |first=Gavin A. |author-link=Gavin Schmidt |date=11 August 2007 |title=Et Tu LT? |url=http://www.realclimate.org/index.php?p=170 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051018132052/http://www.realclimate.org/index.php?p=170 |archive-date=18 October 2005 |access-date=15 September 2005 |publisher=RealClimate.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Schmidt |first=Gavin A. |author-link=Gavin Schmidt |date=11 August 2007 |title=The tropical lapse rate quandary |url=http://www.realclimate.org/index.php?p=179 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051018132359/http://www.realclimate.org/index.php?p=179 |archive-date=18 October 2005 |access-date=15 September 2005 |publisher=RealClimate.org}}</ref> resolve the problem, evident at the time of the TAR, of [[Troposphere|tropospheric]] temperature trends. The UAH version of the record contained errors, and there is evidence of spurious cooling trends in the radiosonde record, particularly in the tropics. See [[satellite temperature measurements]] for details; and the 2006 US CCSP report.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wigley |first=Tom M. L. |date=2 May 2006 |title=Temperature Trends in the Lower Atmosphere&nbsp;— Understanding and Reconciling Differences (Executive Summary) |url=http://www.climatescience.gov/Library/sap/sap1-1/finalreport/sap1-1-final-execsum.pdf |journal=The US Climate Change Science Program |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070423150153/http://www.climatescience.gov/Library/sap/sap1-1/finalreport/sap1-1-final-execsum.pdf |archive-date=23 April 2007}}</ref>

===Extreme event attribution===
[[File:20250630 Extreme event attribution - flowchart.svg |thumb|upright=1.2 |Extreme event attribution methods generally involve applying climate change models to scenarios in both the "real" world that is experiencing global warming, and a simulated world that does not suffer the drivers of global warming. Differences between the results of the two processes—especially the frequency, intensity and impacts of extreme weather events—are then analyzed to arrive at the attribution result.<ref name=Conversation_20210825>{{cite web |last1=Zeng |first1=Zubin |title=Is climate change to blame for extreme weather events? Attribution science says yes, for some – here's how it works |url=https://theconversation.com/is-climate-change-to-blame-for-extreme-weather-events-attribution-science-says-yes-for-some-heres-how-it-works-164941 |website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250609064207/https://theconversation.com/is-climate-change-to-blame-for-extreme-weather-events-attribution-science-says-yes-for-some-heres-how-it-works-164941 |archive-date=9 June 2025 |date=25 August 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=ScientificAmerican_20170102>{{cite news |last1=Sneed |first1=Annie |title=Yes, Some Extreme Weather Can Be Blamed on Climate Change |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/yes-some-extreme-weather-can-be-blamed-on-climate-change/ |work=[[Scientific American]] |date=2 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103135143/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/yes-some-extreme-weather-can-be-blamed-on-climate-change/ |archive-date=3 January 2017 }}</ref><ref name=SciAmerican_20180102>{{cite news |last1=Harvey |first1=Chelsea |date=2 January 2018 |title=Scientists Can Now Blame Individual Natural Disasters on Climate Change |work=[[Scientific American]] |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientists-can-now-blame-individual-natural-disasters-on-climate-change/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180102163151/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientists-can-now-blame-individual-natural-disasters-on-climate-change/ |archive-date=2 January 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

[[Extreme event attribution]] (EEA), also known as attribution science, was developed in the early decades of the 21st century.<ref name=AMS_20161201>{{cite web |last1=Herring |first1=Stephanie C. |last2=Hoell |first2=Andrew |last3=Hoerling |first3=Martin P. |last4=Kossin |first4=James P. |last5=Schreck III |first5=Carl J. |last6=Stott |first6=Peter A. |title=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society / Introduction to Explaining Extreme Events of 2015 from a Climate Perspective |url=https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/97/12/bams-d-16-0313.1.xml?tab_body=pdf |publisher=American Meteorological Society |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250628053021/https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/97/12/bams-d-16-0313.1.xml?tab_body=pdf |archive-date=28 June 2025 |date=1 December 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> EEA uses [[climate model]]s to identify and quantify the role that human-caused climate change plays in the frequency, intensity, duration, and impacts of specific individual [[Extreme weather|extreme weather events]].<ref name=NASEMbook>{{cite book |title=Attribution of Extreme Weather Events in the Context of Climate Change |date=2016 |publisher=The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) |location=Washington, D.C. |doi=10.17226/21852 |bibcode=2016nap..book21852N |isbn=978-0-309-38094-2 |url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21852/attribution-of-extreme-weather-events-in-the-context-of-climate-change }}</ref><ref name=ClimateCentral_20241118>{{cite web |last1=McSweeney |first1=Robert |last2=Tandon |first2=Ayesha |title=Mapped: How climate change affects extreme weather around the world |url=https://interactive.carbonbrief.org/attribution-studies/index.html |publisher=Climate Central |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250610154758/https://interactive.carbonbrief.org/attribution-studies/index.html |archive-date=10 June 2025 |date=18 November 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Results of attribution studies allow scientists and journalists to make statements such as, "this weather event was made at least ''n'' times more likely by human-caused climate change" or "this heatwave was made ''m'' degrees hotter than it would have been in a world without global warming" or "this event was effectively impossible without climate change".<ref name=WWA_2021>{{cite web |last1=Clarke |first1=Ben |last2=Otto |first2=Friederike |title=Reporting extreme weather and climate change A guide for journalists |url=https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/wp-content/uploads/ENG_WWA-Reporting-extreme-weather-and-climate-change.pdf |publisher=World Weather Attribution |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250601160944/https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/wp-content/uploads/ENG_WWA-Reporting-extreme-weather-and-climate-change.pdf |archive-date=1 June 2025 |date=2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

A common EEA approach uses [[climate model|model simulations]] to compare events in two worlds—a first world with human-caused greenhouse gas emissions and a second world without such emissions—and attributing differences to human influence.<ref name=NOAA_20161215>{{cite web |last1=Lindsey |first1=Rebecca |last2=Herring |first2=Stephanie |last3=Kapnick |first3=Sarah |last4=van der Wahl |first4=Karin |title=Extreme event attribution: the climate versus weather blame game |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/extreme-event-attribution-climate-versus-weather-blame-game |website=Climate.gov |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250618004431/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/extreme-event-attribution-climate-versus-weather-blame-game |archive-date=18 June 2025 |date=15 December 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> Greater computing power of the 2000s allowed weather to be simulated over and over again, and conceptual breakthroughs in the early to mid 2010s<ref name=ScientificAmerican_20170102/>  enabled attribution science to detect the effects of climate change on some events with high confidence.<ref name=AMS_20161201/> Scientists use methods that have already been [[peer review]]ed, allowing "rapid attribution" studies to be published within a "[[24-hour news cycle|news cycle]]" time frame.<ref name=ScientificAmerican_20170102/>

{{clear right}}

==Discredited theories and reconciled apparent discrepancies==
{{See also|Climate change denial}}

===Analogy of the greenhouse effect to the atmosphere===
The early work of [[Joseph Fourier]] found that a greenhouse heats up mainly due to radiation trapping.  This is analogous to radiation trapping in the atmosphere, leading to the term "[[greenhouse effect]]".<ref>{{cite web |title=IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Chapter 1: Framing, Context and Methods |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-1/ |publisher=Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |page=178}}</ref>

An experiment performed by Prof. [[Robert W. Wood|R. W. Wood]] in 1909 led him to reject radiation trapping, claiming that a greenhouse is heated merely due to [[convection]] blocking.<ref name="RWWood">{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=R. W. |title=Note on the Theory of the Greenhouse |journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |date=1909 |volume=17 |issue=98 |pages=319–320 |doi=10.1080/14786440208636602 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786440208636602 |access-date=18 April 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  This [[Scientific theory|theory]] became a widespread view in the scientific community.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sagan |first1=Carl |title=Global warming testimony before Congress |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wp-WiNXH6hI |website=YouTube.com |access-date=18 April 2024 |date=1985 |quote=It is a misnomer because that is not how a florist's greenhouse works, but that's a very minor point.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Contribution of Working Group I |journal=Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2007 |issue=1 |page=115 |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar4/wg1/ |access-date=18 April 2024 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA |quote=The glass walls in a greenhouse reduce airflow and increase the temperature of the air inside. Analogously, but through a different physical process, the Earth's greenhouse effect warms the surface of the planet.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Simple Models of Climate |url=https://history.aip.org/climate/simple.htm |publisher=American Institute of Physics |access-date=18 April 2024 |quote="The key publication explaining that greenhouses are kept warm less by the radiation properties of glass than because the heated air cannot rise and blow away; see Wood (1909); for the science..."}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Basics of the Carbon Cycle and the Greenhouse Effect |url=https://gml.noaa.gov/outreach/carbon_toolkit/basics.html |publisher=NOAA |access-date=18 April 2024 |quote=Note: This atmospheric process is referred to as the Greenhouse Effect, since both the atmosphere and a greenhouse act in a manner which retains energy as heat. However, this is an imperfect analogy....}}</ref>

Moreover, Wood's theory has been used to reject the analogy, and to doubt the existence of a greenhouse effect in the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nahle |first1=Nasif |title=Wood is correct: There is no Greenhouse Effect |url=https://www.justproveco2.com/papers/Nahle2011GreenhouseEffect.pdf |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sullivan |first1=John |title=Greenhouse Gas Theory Trashed in Groundbreaking Lab Experiment |url=https://johnosullivan.livejournal.com/38420.html |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Postma |first1=Joseph |title=R.W. Wood Had it Right: Sun Heats Earth! |date=7 April 2016 |url=https://climateofsophistry.com/2016/04/07/r-w-wood-had-it-right-sun-heats-earth/ |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Casey |first1=Timothy |title=The Shattered Greenhouse: How Simple Physics Demolishes the "Greenhouse Effect |url=http://greenhouse.geologist-1011.net/ |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref> 
<br/>Experiments have discredited Wood's theory. They have confirmed that radiation trapping is indeed the dominant cause of heating in a greenhouse.  Hence the analogy is valid.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pratt |first1=V. R. |title=Wood's 1909 greenhouse experiment, performed more carefully |url=http://clim.stanford.edu/WoodExpt/ |website=stanford.edu |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Spencer |first1=Roy |title=Revisiting Wood's 1909 greenhouse box experiment, Part II |url=https://www.drroyspencer.com/2013/08/revisiting-woods-1909-greenhouse-box-experiment-part-ii-first-results/ |access-date=18 April 2024 |date=2013}}</ref><ref name="Arveson">{{cite journal |last1=Arveson |first1=Paul |title=Is a Greenhouse Heated by Radiation Trapping or Convection Blocking? |journal=Washington Academy of Sciences |date=2023 |volume=109 |issue=1 |pages=41–62 |url=https://washacadsci.org/Journal/Journalarticles/V.109.1--Is_a_Greenhouse_Heated_by_Convection_Blocking_or_Radiation_Trapping.pdf |access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref>

=== Discussions around locations of temperature measurement stations ===
{{Further|Instrumental temperature record#Siting of temperature measurement stations}}
[[File:Stevenson_screen_exterior.JPG|thumb|Exterior of a [[Stevenson screen]] used for temperature measurements on land stations.]]
There have been attempts to raise public controversy over the accuracy of the [[instrumental temperature record]] on the basis of the [[urban heat island]] effect, the quality of the surface station network, and assertions that there have been unwarranted adjustments to the temperature record.<ref>{{Cite web |author=EPA |date=12 August 2013 |title=Endangerment and Cause or Contribute Findings for Greenhouse Gases under the Clean Air Act – EPA's Denial of Petitions for Reconsideration, Volume 1: Climate Science and Data Issues Raised by Petitioners |url=https://www.epa.gov/climatechange/endangerment-and-cause-or-contribute-findings-greenhouse-gases-under-clean-air-act-1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170203204617/https://www.epa.gov/climatechange/endangerment-and-cause-or-contribute-findings-greenhouse-gases-under-clean-air-act-1 |archive-date=3 February 2017 |access-date=2 February 2017 |website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=13 August 2010 |title=EPA's Denial of the Petitions To Reconsider the Endangerment and Cause or Contribute Findings for Greenhouse Gases Under Section 202(a) of the Clean Air Act |newspaper=Federal Register |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2010/08/13/2010-19153/epas-denial-of-the-petitions-to-reconsider-the-endangerment-and-cause-or-contribute-findings-for |access-date=2 February 2017}}</ref>

Weather stations that are used to compute global temperature records are not evenly distributed over the planet, and their distribution has changed over time. There were a small number of weather stations in the 1850s, and the number did not reach the current 3000+ until the 1951 to 1990 period<ref>{{Cite web |title=Temperature data (HadCRUT, CRUTEM,, HadCRUT5, CRUTEM5) Climatic Research Unit global temperature |url=http://www.cru.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/temperature/#faq}}</ref>

The 2001 IPCC Third Assessment Report (TAR) acknowledged that the urban heat island is an important ''local'' effect, but cited analyses of historical data indicating that the effect of the urban heat island on the ''global'' temperature trend is no more than 0.05&nbsp;°C (0.09&nbsp;°F) degrees through 1990.<ref>J.R. Christy, R.A. Clarke, G.V. Gruza, J. Jouzel, M.E. Mann, J. Oerlemans, M.J. Salinger, S.-W. Wang (2001) [https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/03/TAR-02.pdf Chapter 2: Observed Climate Variability and Change], [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar3/wg1/ Working Group 1 Contribution to TAR Climate Change 2001: The Scientific Basis] of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.</ref> Peterson (2003) found no difference between the warming observed in urban and rural areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peterson |first1=Thomas C. |year=2003 |title=Assessment of urban versus rural in situ surface temperatures in the contiguous United States: no difference found |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1234675 |journal=Journal of Climate |type=Submitted manuscript |volume=16 |issue=18 |pages=2941–59 |bibcode=2003JCli...16.2941P |doi=10.1175/1520-0442(2003)016<2941:AOUVRI>2.0.CO;2 |issn=1520-0442 |s2cid=32302840 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Parker (2006) found that there was no difference in warming between calm and windy nights. Since the urban heat island effect is strongest for calm nights and is weak or absent on windy nights, this was taken as evidence that global temperature trends are not significantly contaminated by urban effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=David |first=Parker |year=2006 |title=A demonstration that large-scale warming is not urban |journal=Journal of Climate |volume=19 |issue=12 |pages=2882–95 |bibcode=2006JCli...19.2882P |citeseerx=10.1.1.543.2675 |doi=10.1175/JCLI3730.1}}</ref> Pielke and Matsui published a paper disagreeing with Parker's conclusions.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Pielke Sr., R.A. |author2=T. Matsui |year=2005 |title=Should light wind and windy nights have the same temperature trends at individual levels even if the boundary layer averaged heat content change is the same? |url=http://climatesci.org/publications/pdf/R-302.pdf |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=32 |issue=21 |pages=L21813 |bibcode=2005GeoRL..3221813P |doi=10.1029/2005GL024407 |s2cid=3773490 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080910213821/http://climatesci.org/publications/pdf/R-302.pdf |archive-date=10 September 2008}}</ref>

In 2005, [[Roger A. Pielke]] and [[Stephen McIntyre]] criticized the US instrumental temperature record and adjustments to it, and Pielke and others criticized the poor quality siting of a number of weather stations in the United States.<ref name="MicroclimateExposures">{{cite journal | last1=Davey | first1=Christopher A. | last2=Pielke | first2=Roger A. | title=Microclimate Exposures of Surface-Based Weather Stations: Implications For The Assessment of Long-Term Temperature Trends | journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society | volume=86 | issue=4 | year=2005 | issn=0003-0007 | jstor=26221293 | pages=497–504 | doi=10.1175/BAMS-86-4-504 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mahmood |first=Rezaul |author2=Stuart A. Foster |author3=David Logan |year=2006 |title=The GeoProfile metadata, exposure of instruments, and measurement bias in climatic record revisited |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/natrespapers/1273 |journal=International Journal of Climatology |volume=26 |issue=8 |pages=1091–1124 |bibcode=2006IJCli..26.1091M |doi=10.1002/joc.1298 |s2cid=128889147|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A study in 2010 examined the siting of temperature stations and found that those measurement stations that were poorly showed a slight cool bias rather than the warm bias which deniers had postulated.<ref name="Menne">{{cite journal |last=Menne |first=Matthew J. |author2=Claude N. Williams Jr. |author3=Michael A. Palecki |year=2010 |title=On the reliability of the U.S. surface temperature record |url=http://www1.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/ushcn/v2/monthly/menne-etal2010.pdf |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |volume=115 |issue=D11 |page=D11108 |bibcode=2010JGRD..11511108M |doi=10.1029/2009JD013094 |quote=In summary, we find no evidence that the CONUS average temperature trends are inflated due to poor station siting...The reason why station exposure does not play an obvious role in temperature trends probably warrants further investigation.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Cook |first=John |date=27 January 2010 |title=Climate sceptics distract us from the scientific realities of global warming |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/blog/2010/jan/27/climate-sceptics-global-warming |access-date=5 February 2010}}</ref>

The [[Berkeley Earth Surface Temperature]] group carried out an independent assessment of land temperature records, which examined issues raised by deniers, such as the urban heat island effect, poor station quality, and the risk of data selection bias. The preliminary results, made public in October 2011, found that these factors had not biased the results obtained by NOAA, the [[Hadley Centre]] together with the [[Climatic Research Unit]] ([[HadCRUT]]) and NASA's GISS in earlier studies. The group also confirmed that over the past 50 years the land surface warmed by 0.911&nbsp;°C, and their results closely matched those obtained from these earlier studies.<ref name="Nature1011">{{cite news |author=Jeff Tollefson |date=20 October 2011 |title=Different method, same result: global warming is real |work=[[Nature News]] |url=http://www.nature.com/news/2011/111020/full/news.2011.607.html |access-date=22 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114232522/http://www.nature.com/news/2011/111020/full/news.2011.607.html |archive-date=14 January 2012 |doi=10.1038/news.2011.607}}</ref><ref name="SciDaily1011">{{cite web |date=21 October 2011 |title=Cooling the Warming Debate: Major New Analysis Confirms That Global Warming Is Real |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/10/111021144716.htm |access-date=22 October 2011 |work=[[Science Daily]]}}</ref><ref name="Guardian1011">{{cite news |author=Ian Sample |date=20 October 2011 |title=Global warming study finds no grounds for climate sceptics' concerns |work=[[The Guardian]] |location=London |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2011/oct/20/global-warming-study-climate-sceptics |access-date=22 October 2011}}</ref><ref name="Econ1011">{{cite news |date=22 October 2011 |title=Climate change: The heat is on |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2011/10/22/the-heat-is-on |access-date=22 October 2011}}</ref>

=== Apparent discrepancy for tropospheric temperature increases in the tropics ===
General circulation models and basic physical considerations predict that in the tropics the temperature of the [[troposphere]] should increase more rapidly than the temperature of the surface. A 2006 report to the [[U.S. Climate Change Science Program]] noted that models and observations agreed on this amplification for monthly and interannual time scales but not for decadal time scales in most observed data sets. Improved measurement and analysis techniques have reconciled this discrepancy: corrected buoy and [[List of climate research satellites|satellite]] surface temperatures are slightly cooler and corrected satellite and [[radiosonde]] measurements of the tropical troposphere are slightly warmer.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Santer |first1=B. D. |last2=Thorne |first2=P. W. |last3=Haimberger |first3=L. |author4=K. E. Taylor |author5=T. M. L. Wigley |author6=J. R. Lanzante |author7=S. Solomon |author8=M. Free |author9=P. J. Gleckler |author10=P. D. Jones |author11=T. R. Karl |author12=S. A. Klein |author13=C. Mears |author14=D. Nychka |author15=G. A. Schmidt |year=2008 |title=Consistency of modelled and observed temperature trends in the tropical troposphere |url=https://www.gfdl.noaa.gov/bibliography/related_files/bds0801.pdf |journal=International Journal of Climatology |volume=28 |issue=13 |pages=1703–22 |bibcode=2008IJCli..28.1703S |doi=10.1002/joc.1756 |s2cid=14941858 |author16=S. C. Sherwood |author17=F. J. Wentz}}</ref> [[Satellite temperature measurements]] show that tropospheric temperatures are increasing with "rates similar to those of the surface temperature", leading the IPCC to conclude in 2007 that this discrepancy is reconciled.<ref>IPCC, 2007: [https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ar4-wg1-spm-1.pdf Summary for Policymakers]. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar4/wg1/ Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Solomon, S., D. Qin, M. Manning, Z. Chen, M. Marquis, K.B. Averyt, M.Tignor and H.L. Miller (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA.</ref>
