{{Short description|Energy stored by oceans}}
[[File:1955- Ocean heat content - NOAA.svg |thumb|upright=1.35 | The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the [[Earth's energy budget|excess heat]] resulting from [[greenhouse gas emissions]] from human activities.<ref name=NOAA_NASA_OHC_1957_>''Top 700 meters:'' {{cite web |last1=Lindsey |first1=Rebecca |last2=Dahlman |first2=Luann |title=Climate Change: Ocean Heat Content |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content |website=climate.gov |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231029171303/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content |archive-date=29 October 2023 |date=6 September 2023 }} ● ''Top 2000 meters:'' {{cite web |title=Ocean Warming / Latest Measurement: December 2022 / 345 (± 2) zettajoules since 1955 |url=https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/ocean-warming/ |website=NASA.gov |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020033606/https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/ocean-warming/ |archive-date=20 October 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters. ]]

'''Ocean heat content''' (OHC) or '''ocean heat uptake''' (OHU) is the energy absorbed and stored by [[ocean]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |date=2016-06-27 |title=Climate Change Indicators: Ocean Heat |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-heat |access-date=2025-06-22 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250624025756/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-heat |archive-date=2025-06-24 }}</ref> It is an important indicator of [[Climate change|global warming]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=Lijing |last2=Foster |first2=Grant |last3=Hausfather |first3=Zeke |last4=Trenberth |first4=Kevin E. |last5=Abraham |first5=John |date=2022 |title=Improved Quantification of the Rate of Ocean Warming |journal=Journal of Climate |volume=35 |issue=14 |pages=4827–4840 |bibcode=2022JCli...35.4827C |doi=10.1175/JCLI-D-21-0895.1 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Ocean heat content is calculated by measuring [[ocean temperature]] at many different locations and depths, and [[Integral|integrating the areal density]] of a change in [[enthalpy|enthalpic energy]] over an ocean basin or entire ocean.<ref name=":1" /> 

Between 1971 and 2018, a steady upward trend<ref name="ncei">NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Assessing the Global Climate in 2024, published online January 2025, Retrieved on March 2, 2025 from https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/global-climate-202413.</ref> in ocean heat content accounted for over 90% of Earth's [[Earth's Energy Imbalance|excess energy]] from global warming.<ref name="EarthSysSciData_20200907" /><ref name="Chen-2021"/> Scientists estimate a 1961–2022 warming trend of 0.43{{nbsp}}±{{nbsp}}0.08{{nbsp}}W/m², accelerating at about 0.15{{nbsp}}±{{nbsp}}0.04{{nbsp}}W/m² per{{nbsp}}decade.<ref name="Storto-2024"/> By 2020, about one third of the added energy had propagated to depths below 700 meters.<ref name="OHC2020">{{cite web |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807080046/http://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content |archive-date=August 7, 2013 |title=Climate Change: Ocean Heat Content |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] |date=2020-08-17 |author=LuAnn Dahlman and Rebecca Lindsey }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.climatecentral.org/news/ocean-depths-are-trapping-heat-19922 |title=Study: Deep Ocean Waters Trapping Vast Store of Heat |year=2016 |work=[[Climate Central]]}}</ref>  The five highest ocean heat observations to a depth of 2000&nbsp;meters all occurred in the period 2020–2024.<ref name="ncei"/> The main driver of this increase has been human-caused [[greenhouse gas emissions]].<ref name="AR6_WG1_Chapter92" />{{rp|1228}}

Ocean heat content measurements are critical for models of climate.  Since before 1960, research vessels and stations have sampled [[sea surface temperature]]s and [[Ocean temperature|temperatures at greater depth]] all over the world. Since 2000, an expanding network of nearly 4000 [[Argo (oceanography)|Argo robotic floats]] has measured temperature anomalies, or the change in ocean heat content.  The upper 2000&nbsp;meters of the global ocean has experienced warming on average since the 1970s, while the rate of warming varies regionally with the subpolar [[North Atlantic]] warming more slowly and the [[Southern Ocean]] taking up a disproportionately large amount of heat.<ref name="AR6_WG1_Chapter92" />{{rp|1230}}  Deep-ocean warming below 2000&nbsp;meters has also been largest in the Southern Ocean compared to other ocean basins.<ref name="AR6_WG1_Chapter92" />{{rp|1230}}

Changes in ocean temperature greatly affect [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]] in oceans and on land. For example, there are multiple impacts on [[coastal ecosystem]]s and communities relying on their [[Ecosystem service|ecosystem services]]. Direct effects include variations in [[sea level]] and [[sea ice]], changes to the [[Effects of climate change on the water cycle|intensity of the water cycle]], and the [[migration (ecology)|migration]] of marine life.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/2016-046-Summ.pdf |title=Ocean warming: causes, scale, effects and consequences. And why it should matter to everyone. Executive summary |publisher=[[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] |year=2016 }}</ref>

== Role in climate stability ==
The Earth's oceans play a critical role in climate stability. The oceans have high [[heat capacity]] so they can store vast amounts of energy with little change in temperature. Oceans also cover 70% of the Earth's surface. Measuring ocean heat content and monitoring changes over time is essential for understanding and modeling climate.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 26, 2025 |title=Climate Change: Ocean Heat Content {{!}} NOAA Climate.gov |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content |access-date=2025-10-12 |website=www.climate.gov |language=en |archive-date=2019-02-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212110601/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-ocean-heat-content }}</ref>

== Definition ==
[[File:1997 Thermoclines.svg|thumb|right|250px|Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus [[ocean temperature]]) based on seasons and latitude<ref name=KnaussBook_2005>{{cite book |last1=Knauss |first1=John A. |title=Introduction to Physical Oceanography |date=18 October 2005 |isbn=978-1-57766-429-1 |page=2 (Overview) |publisher=Waveland Press |url=https://depts.washington.edu/fish437/resources/Week%201/Knauss-%20Intro%20to%20Physical%20Oceanography.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240428151810/https://depts.washington.edu/fish437/resources/Week%201/Knauss-%20Intro%20to%20Physical%20Oceanography.pdf |archive-date=28 April 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

Ocean heat content is a term used in [[physical oceanography]] to describe a type of [[thermodynamic potential|thermodynamic potential energy]] that is stored in the ocean. It is defined in coordination with the [[equation of state]] of seawater. [[TEOS-10]] is an [[international standard]] approved in 2010 by the [[Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.teos-10.org/ |title=TEOS-10: Thermodynamic Equation of Seawater - 2010 |publisher=Joint Committee on the Properties of Seawater |access-date=12 February 2024}}</ref>

== Calculations ==

Calculation of ocean heat content follows that of [[enthalpy]] referenced to the ocean surface, also called [[conservative temperature#potential enthalpy|potential enthalpy]]. OHC changes are thus made more readily comparable to seawater heat exchanges with ice, freshwater, and humid air.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McDougall |first1= Trevor J. |date= 2003|title=Potential Enthalpy: A Conservative Oceanic Variable for Evaluating Heat Content and Heat Fluxes |journal= Journal of Physical Oceanography|volume=33 |issue= 5 |pages=945–963 |doi= 10.1175/1520-0485(2003)033<0945:PEACOV>2.0.CO;2|bibcode= 2003JPO....33..945M |doi-access= free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Graham|first1=Felicity S.|last2=McDougall|first2=Trevor J.|date=2013-05-01|title=Quantifying the Nonconservative Production of Conservative Temperature, Potential Temperature, and Entropy|journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography|language=en|volume=43|issue=5|pages=838–862|doi=10.1175/jpo-d-11-0188.1|bibcode=2013JPO....43..838G |issn=0022-3670|doi-access=free}}</ref>  OHC is always reported as a change or as an "anomaly" relative to a baseline.  Positive values then also quantify ocean heat uptake (OHU) and are useful to diagnose where most of planetary energy gains from global heating are going.

To calculate the ocean heat content, measurements of [[ocean temperature]] from sample [[fluid parcel|parcels]] of seawater gathered at many different locations and depths are required.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2016-06-27 |title=Climate Change Indicators: Ocean Heat |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-heat |access-date=2023-02-28 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230228234725/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-heat |archive-date=2023-02-28 }}</ref> [[Integral|Integrating the areal density]] of ocean heat over an ocean basin, or entire ocean, gives the total ocean heat content. Thus, total ocean heat content is a [[volume integral]] of the product of temperature, density, and heat capacity over the three-dimensional region of the ocean for which data is available.<ref name=":2" /> The bulk of measurements have been performed at depths shallower than about 2000&nbsp;m (1.25&nbsp;miles).<ref name="Abraham-2013" />

The areal density of ocean heat content between two depths is computed as a definite integral:<ref name=":1">{{cite book|last=Dijkstra|first=Henk A.|title=Dynamical oceanography|year=2008|publisher=Springer Verlag|location=Berlin|isbn=978-3-540-76375-8|page=276|edition=[Corr. 2nd print.]}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=McDougall|first1=Trevor J.|last2=Barker|first2=Paul M.|last3=Holmes|first3=Ryan M.|last4=Pawlowicz|first4=Rich|last5=Griffies|first5=Stephen M.|last6=Durack|first6=Paul J.|date=2021-01-19|title=The interpretation of temperature and salinity variables in numerical ocean model output, and the calculation of heat fluxes and heat content|url=https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/14/6445/2021/gmd-14-6445-2021.html|journal=Geoscientific Model Development Discussions|volume=14 |issue=10 |language=English|pages=6445–6466|doi=10.5194/gmd-2020-426|s2cid=234212726 |issn=1991-959X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

<math>H= c_p \int_{h2}^{h1} \rho(z) \Theta(z) dz</math>

where  <math>c_p </math> is the [[specific heat capacity]] of [[sea water]], <math>h_2</math> is the lower depth, <math>h_1</math> is the upper depth, <math>\rho(z)</math> is the in-situ [[properties of water#Density of saltwater and ice|seawater density]] profile, and <math>\Theta(z)</math> is the [[conservative temperature]] profile. <math>c_p </math> is defined at a single depth h0 usually chosen as the ocean surface. In [[SI units]], <math>H</math> has units of [[Joules]] per square metre (J·m<sup>−2</sup>).

In practice, the integral can be approximated by [[summation]] using a smooth and otherwise well-behaved sequence of in-situ data; including temperature (t), pressure (p), [[salinity]] (s) and their corresponding density (ρ). [[Conservative temperature]] <math>\Theta(z)</math> are translated values relative to the reference pressure (p0) at h0. A substitute known as [[potential temperature]] has been used in earlier calculations.<ref>{{citation |url=https://www.teos-10.org/pubs/gsw/pdf/Getting_Started.pdf |title=Getting started with TEOS-10 and the Gibbs Seawater (GSW) Oceanographic Toolbox |version=VERSION 3.06.12 |date=10 July 2020 |website=teos-10.org}}</ref>

Measurements of temperature versus ocean depth generally show an [[mixed layer|upper mixed layer]] (0–200&nbsp;m), a [[thermocline]] (200–1500&nbsp;m), and a [[deep ocean]] layer (>1500&nbsp;m). These boundary depths are only rough approximations. Sunlight penetrates to a maximum depth of about 200&nbsp;m; the top 80&nbsp;m of which is the [[photic zone|habitable zone]] for photosynthetic marine life covering over 70% of Earth's surface.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/457662/photic-zone |title=photic zone (oceanography) |publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Online |access-date=2021-12-15}}</ref> Wave action and other surface [[turbulence]] help to equalize temperatures throughout the upper layer.

Unlike [[Sea surface temperature|surface temperatures]] which decrease with latitude, deep-ocean temperatures are relatively cold and uniform in most regions of the world.<ref>{{Cite web|last=MarineBio|date=2018-06-17|title=The Deep Sea|url=https://marinebio.org/oceans/deep-sea/|access-date=2020-08-07|website=MarineBio Conservation Society|language=en-US}}</ref> About 50% of all ocean volume is at depths below 3000&nbsp;m (1.85&nbsp;miles), with the [[Pacific Ocean]] being the largest and deepest of five oceanic divisions. The thermocline is the transition between upper and deep layers in terms of temperature, nutrient flows, abundance of life, and other properties. It is semi-permanent in the tropics, variable in [[temperate region]]s (often deepest during the summer), and shallow to nonexistent in polar regions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is a thermocline? |url=https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/thermocline.html  |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |access-date=2021-12-23 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Measurements ===
[[File: Argo_floats_in_Feb._2018_colour_coded_by_country.png|thumbnail|320px|The global distribution of active floats in the Argo array<ref name="argosd">{{cite web |title=About Argo |url=https://argo.ucsd.edu/about/ |access-date=27 January 2023 |publisher=Scripps Institute of Oceanography, UC San Diego}}</ref>]]
{{See also|Argo (oceanography)|Ocean temperature}}

Ocean heat content is derived from ocean temperature measurements. Ocean temperature measurements come with difficulties, especially before the deployment of the [[Argo (oceanography)|Argo]] profiling floats.<ref name="Abraham-2013" /> Due to poor spatial coverage and poor quality of data, it has not always been easy to distinguish between long term [[Climate change|global warming]] trends and [[Climate variability and change|climate variability]]. Examples of these complicating factors are the variations caused by [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation]] or changes in ocean heat content caused by major [[Types of volcanic eruptions|volcanic eruptions]].<ref name=":0" />

Argo is an international program of robotic [[profiling floats]] deployed globally since the start of the 21st century.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Toni Feder |year=2000 |title=Argo Begins Systematic Global Probing of the Upper Oceans |journal=Physics Today |volume=53 |issue=7 |page=50 |bibcode=2000PhT....53g..50F |doi=10.1063/1.1292477}}</ref> The program's initial 3000 units had expanded to nearly 4000 units by year 2020. At the start of each 10-day measurement cycle, a float descends to a depth of 1000&nbsp;meters and drifts with the current there for nine days. It then descends to 2000&nbsp;meters and measures temperature, salinity (conductivity), and depth (pressure)  over a final day of ascent to the surface. At the surface the float transmits the depth profile and horizontal position data through [[Argos (satellite system)|satellite relays]] before repeating the cycle.<ref>{{cite web |author=Dale C.S. Destin |date=5 December 2014 |title=The Argo revolution |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/features/argo-revolution |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150126044914/http://www.climate.gov/news-features/features/argo-revolution |archive-date=January 26, 2015 |website=climate.gov}}</ref>

Starting 1992, the [[TOPEX/Poseidon]] and subsequent [[Jason satellite series]] [[satellite altimetry|altimeters]] have observed vertically integrated OHC, which is a major component of sea level rise. Since 2002, [[GRACE and GRACE-FO]] have remotely monitored ocean changes using [[gravimetry]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marti |first1=Florence |last2=Blazquez |first2=Alejandro |last3=Meyssignac |first3=Benoit |last4=Ablain |first4=Michaël |last5=Barnoud |first5=Anne |last6=Fraudeau |first6=Robin |last7=Jugier |first7=Rémi |last8=Chenal |first8=Jonathan |last9=Larnicol |first9=Gilles |last10=Pfeffer |first10=Julia |last11=Restano |first11=Marco |last12=Benveniste |first12=Jérôme |display-authors=5 |title=Monitoring the ocean heat content change and the Earth energy imbalance from space altimetry and space gravimetry |journal=Earth System Science Data |year=2021 |doi=10.5194/essd-2021-220 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The partnership between Argo and satellite measurements has yielded ongoing improvements to estimates of OHC and other global ocean properties.<ref name="argosd" />

==Causes for heat uptake==
[[File:Oceans of Climate Change.ogv |upright=1.25 |thumb |Oceanographer [[Josh Willis]] discusses the [[Properties of water|heat capacity of water]], performs an experiment to demonstrate [[heat capacity]] using a [[water balloon]] and describes how water's ability to store heat affects Earth's climate.]]
{{See also|Causes of climate change}}
Human-caused increases in greenhouse gases have reduced the outgoing infrared radiation from Earth's atmosphere creating an increase in planet-wide heat.<ref name="Trenberth2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Trenberth |first1=Kevin E |last2=Cheng |first2=Lijing |date=2022-09-01 |title=A perspective on climate change from Earth's energy imbalance |journal=Environmental Research: Climate |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=013001 |doi=10.1088/2752-5295/ac6f74 |issn=2752-5295 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
Over 90% of this planetary heat uptake is manifest in ocean heat content. This high percentage is a result of the oceans high [[heat capacity]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=Yuying |last2=Minière |first2=Audrey |last3=von Schuckmann |first3=Karina |last4=Li |first4=Zhi |last5=Li |first5=Yuanlong |last6=Cheng |first6=Lijing |last7=Zhu |first7=Jiang |date=April 11, 2025 |title=Ocean heat content in 2024 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-025-00655-0 |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |language=en |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=249–251 |doi=10.1038/s43017-025-00655-0 |issn=2662-138X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Most extra energy that enters the planet via the atmosphere is taken up and retained by the ocean.<ref name="Scott06">{{cite web |author=Michon Scott |date=24 April 2006 |title=Earth's Big Heat Bucket |url=https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/features/HeatBucket/heatbucket.php |publisher=NASA Earth Observatory}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/earth-system/climate-system/transfer-and-storage-heat-oceans |title=Transfer and Storage of Heat in the Oceans |publisher=UCAR Center for Science Education |access-date=17 November 2023}}</ref><ref name="JEH1985">{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=J. |last2=Russell |first2=G. |last3=Lacis |first3=A. |last4=Fung |first4=I. |last5=Rind |first5=D. |last6=Stone |first6=P. |url=https://pubs.giss.nasa.gov/docs/1985/1985_Hansen_ha09600g.pdf |title=Climate response times: Dependence on climate sensitivity and ocean mixing |journal=Science |volume=229 |pages=857–850 |year=1985 |issue=4716 |doi=10.1126/science.229.4716.857 |pmid=17777925 |bibcode=1985Sci...229..857H}}</ref>

[[File:Earth's Heat Accumulation.png|thumb|upright=1.25|Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.<ref name="EarthSysSciData_20200907" />]]
Planetary heat uptake or heat content accounts for the entire energy added to or removed from the climate system.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ceres.larc.nasa.gov/science/ |title=CERES Science |publisher=NASA |access-date=17 November 2023}}</ref>  It can be computed as an accumulation over time of the observed differences (or [[Earth's Energy Imbalance|imbalances]]) between total incoming and outgoing radiation.
Changes to the imbalance have been estimated from Earth orbit by [[Clouds and the Earth's Radiant Energy System|CERES]] and other [[remote sensing|remote]] instruments,  and compared against [[in-situ]] surveys of heat inventory changes in oceans, land, ice and the atmosphere.<ref name="EarthSysSciData_20200907" /><ref name="Loeb2021">{{cite journal |last1=Loeb |first1=Norman G. |last2=Johnson |first2=Gregory C. |last3=Thorsen |first3=Tyler J. |last4=Lyman |first4=John M. |last5=Rose |first5=Fred G. |last6=Kato |first6=Seiji |display-authors=4 |title=Satellite and Ocean Data Reveal Marked Increase in Earth's Heating Rate |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=15 June 2021 |volume=48 |issue=13 |article-number=e2021GL093047 |doi=10.1029/2021GL093047 |bibcode=2021GeoRL..4893047L |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hakuba |first1=M.Z. |last2=Frederikse |first2=T. |last3=Landerer |first3=F.W. |title=Earth's Energy Imbalance From the Ocean Perspective (2005–2019) |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=48 |issue=16 |date=28 August 2021 |article-number=e2021GL093624 |doi=10.1029/2021GL093624 |doi-access=|bibcode=2021GeoRL..4893624H }}</ref>  Achieving complete and accurate results from either accounting method is challenging, but in different ways that are viewed by researchers as being mostly independent of each other.<ref name="Loeb2021" />   Increases in planetary heat content for the well-observed 2005–2019 period are thought to exceed measurement uncertainties.<ref name="Trenberth2022" />

From the ocean perspective, the more abundant equatorial [[solar irradiance]] is [[electromagnetic absorption by water|directly absorbed]] by Earth's tropical surface waters and drives the overall poleward propagation of heat. The surface also exchanges energy that has been absorbed by the lower [[troposphere]] through wind and wave action. Over time, a sustained imbalance in [[Earth's energy budget]] enables a net flow of heat either into or out of greater ocean depth via [[thermal conduction]], [[downwelling]], and [[upwelling]].<ref>{{cite web |year=2012 |title=Air-Sea interaction: Teacher's guide |url=https://www.ametsoc.org/ams/index.cfm/education-careers/education-program/k-12-teachers/project-atmosphere/training-opportunities/project-atmosphere-peer-led-training/project-atmosphere-peer-training-resources/air-sea/ |access-date=2022-02-22 |publisher=[[American Meteorological Society]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ocean Motion : Definition: Wind Driven Surface Currents - Upwelling and Downwelling |url=http://oceanmotion.org/html/background/upwelling-and-downwelling.htm |access-date=2022-02-22}}</ref>  Releases of OHC to the atmosphere occur primarily via [[evaporation]] and enable the planetary [[water cycle]].<ref>{{cite web |title=NASA Earth Science: Water Cycle |url=https://gpm.nasa.gov/education/articles/nasa-earth-science-water-cycle |access-date=2021-10-27 |publisher=NASA}}</ref> High [[sea-surface temperature|sea surface temperature]]s help drive [[tropical cyclones]], [[atmospheric river]]s, [[heat wave|atmospheric heat waves]] and other [[extreme weather event]]s that can penetrate far inland.<ref>{{cite web |author=Laura Snider |date=2021-01-13 |title=2020 was a record-breaking year for ocean heat - Warmer ocean waters contribute to sea level rise and strengthen storms |url=https://news.ucar.edu/132773/2020-was-record-breaking-year-ocean-heat |publisher=[[National Center for Atmospheric Research]]}}</ref>  Altogether these processes enable the ocean to be Earth's largest [[thermal reservoir]] which functions to regulate the planet's climate; acting as both a [[heat sink|sink]] and a source of energy.<ref name="Scott06" />

{{ multiple image | total_width=450
| image1= 20230706 Excess heat absorbed through ocean's surface - global warming.svg |caption1= Surface air temperatures over land masses have been increasing faster than the [[sea surface temperature]], as most heat from global warming is absorbed by the oceans.<ref name=NASAlandoceanTemps>{{cite web |title=GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (v4) / Analysis Graphs and Plots / Temperature Anomalies over Land and over Ocean |url=https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/graphs_v4/ |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260809020719/https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/graphs_v4/ |archive-date=9 August 2026 |date=2026 |url-status=live}} Under " Temperature Anomalies over Land and over Ocean", download through the "plain text" or "CSV" links.</ref>
| image2= 1960- Warming stripes global temperature graphic - atmospheric heights and ocean depths.png |caption2= The [[greenhouse effect]] traps heat in the lower atmosphere and oceans, so that the upper atmosphere, receiving less reflected energy, cools.<ref name=AMS_20250501>{{cite journal |last1=Hawkins |first1=Ed |last2=Williams |first2=Richard G. |last3=Young |first3=Paul J. |last4=Berardelli |first4=Jeff |last5=Burgess |first5=Samantha N. |last6=Highwood |first6=Ellie |last7=Randel |first7=William |last8=Roussenov |first8=Vassil |last9=Smith |first9=Doug |last10=Placky |first10=Bernadette Woods |title=Warming Stripes Spark Climate Conversations: From the Ocean to the Stratosphere |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society |volume=6 |issue=5 |date=1 May 2025 |pages=E964–E970 |doi=10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0212.1|doi-access=free |bibcode=2025BAMS..106E.964H }}</ref>
}}
From  the perspective of land and ice covered regions,  their portion of heat uptake is reduced and [[climate inertia|delayed]] by the dominant thermal inertia of the ocean. Although the average rise in land surface temperature has exceeded the ocean surface due to the lower inertia (smaller heat-transfer coefficient) of solid land and ice, temperatures would rise more rapidly and by a greater amount without the full ocean.<ref name="Scott06" />  Measurements of how rapidly the heat mixes into the deep ocean have also been underway to better close the ocean and planetary energy budgets.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://argo.ucsd.edu/expansion/deep-argo-mission/ |title=Deep Argo Mission |publisher=Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego |access-date=17 November 2023}}</ref>

== Recent observations and changes ==
Global upper-2000 m ocean heat content reached a new record in 2024, exceeding the 2023 value by 16 ± 8 ZJ, continuing a run of annual records over the past eight years.<ref name="WMO2024" /> In 2025, global upper-2000 m ocean heat content rose by about 23 ± 8 ZJ relative to 2024, setting another record.<ref name="Pan2026">{{cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=Yuying |last2=Cheng |first2=Lijing |last3=Abraham |first3=John |last4=Trenberth |first4=Kevin E. |last5=Reagan |first5=James |last6=Du |first6=Juan |last7=Wang |first7=Zhankun |last8=Storto |first8=Andrea |last9=von Schuckmann |first9=Karina |last10=Zhu |first10=Yujing |display-authors=3 |date=9 January 2026 |title=Ocean Heat Content Sets Another Record in 2025 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0 |journal=Advances in Atmospheric Sciences |doi=10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0}}</ref> Numerous independent studies in recent years have found a multi-decadal rise in OHC of upper ocean regions that has begun to penetrate to deeper regions.<ref name=EarthSysSciData_20200907 /><ref name="Abraham-2013" />
Numerous independent studies in recent years have found a multi-decadal rise in OHC of upper ocean regions that has begun to penetrate to deeper regions.<ref name=EarthSysSciData_20200907 /><ref name="Abraham-2013" /> The upper ocean (0–700&nbsp;m) has warmed since 1971, while it is very likely that warming has occurred at intermediate depths (700–2000&nbsp;m) and likely that deep ocean (below 2000&nbsp;m) temperatures have increased.<ref name="AR6_WG1_Chapter92" />{{rp|1228}} The heat uptake results from a persistent warming imbalance in [[Earth's energy budget]] that is most fundamentally caused by the anthropogenic increase in atmospheric [[greenhouse gases]].<ref name="AR6_WG1_TS" />{{rp|41}} There is very high confidence that increased ocean heat content in response to anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions is essentially irreversible on human time scales.<ref name="AR6_WG1_Chapter92" />{{rp|1233}}

[[File:Ocean heat anomaly map 2020.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|Map of the ocean heat anomaly in the upper 700&nbsp;meters for year 2020 versus the 1993–2020 average.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/reporting-state-climate-2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210825200645/https://climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/reporting-state-climate-2020 |archive-date=August 25, 2021 |title=Reporting on the State of the Climate in 2020 |author=Jessica Blunden |date=25 August 2021 |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |website=Climate.gov}}</ref>  Some regions accumulated more energy than others due to transport drivers such as winds and currents.]]
Studies based on Argo measurements indicate that ocean surface [[wind]]s, especially the [[subtropical ridge|subtropical trade winds]] in the [[Pacific Ocean]], change ocean heat vertical distribution.<ref>{{cite journal |title = Distinctive climate signals in reanalysis of global ocean heat content |year = 2013 |author = Balmaseda, Trenberth & Källén |doi=  10.1002/grl.50382 |volume=40 |issue = 9 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |pages=1754–1759|bibcode = 2013GeoRL..40.1754B |doi-access = free }} [http://www.rmets.org/weather-and-climate/climate/has-global-warming-stalled Essay] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150213035703/http://www.rmets.org/weather-and-climate/climate/has-global-warming-stalled |date=2015-02-13 }}</ref> This results in changes among [[ocean current]]s, and an increase of the [[thermohaline circulation#Movement of thermohaline circulation|subtropical overturning]], which is also related to the [[El Niño]] and [[La Niña]] phenomenon. Depending on stochastic natural variability fluctuations, during La Niña years around 30% more heat from the upper ocean layer is transported into the deeper ocean. Furthermore, studies have shown that approximately one-third of the observed warming in the ocean is taking place in the 700–2000 meter ocean layer.<ref name="LevitusUR">{{cite journal |last1=Levitus |first1=Sydney |title=World ocean heat content and thermosteric sea level change (0–2000 m), 1955–2010 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=17 May 2012 |volume=39 |issue=10 |pages=1–3 |article-number=2012GL051106 |doi=10.1029/2012GL051106 |bibcode=2012GeoRL..3910603L |s2cid=55809622 |issn=0094-8276|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Model studies indicate that [[ocean currents]] transport more heat into deeper layers during La Niña years, following changes in wind circulation.<ref>{{cite journal |title = Model-based evidence of deep-ocean heat uptake during surface-temperature hiatus periods |year = 2011 | author = Meehl|doi= 10.1038/nclimate1229 |display-authors=etal |volume=1 |issue = 7 |journal=Nature Climate Change |pages=360–364|bibcode = 2011NatCC...1..360M }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.skepticalscience.com/The-Deep-Ocean-Warms-When-Global-Surface-Temperatures-Stall--.html |title= The Deep Ocean Warms When Global Surface Temperatures Stall |website=[[SkepticalScience.com]] |author=Rob Painting |date=2 October 2011 |access-date=15 July 2016}}</ref> Years with increased ocean heat uptake have been associated with negative phases of the [[Pacific decadal oscillation|interdecadal Pacific oscillation]] (IPO).<ref>{{cite journal |title = A Looming Climate Shift: Will Ocean Heat Come Back to Haunt us? |date =24 June 2013 |url= http://www.skepticalscience.com/A-Looming-Climate-Shift-Will-Ocean-Heat-Come-Back-to-Haunt-us.html| website=SkepticalScience.com | author = Rob Painting |access-date=15 July 2016 }}</ref> This is of particular interest to climate scientists who use the data to estimate the ''ocean heat uptake''.

The upper ocean heat content in most [[North Atlantic]] regions is dominated by heat transport convergence (a location where ocean currents meet), without large changes to temperature and salinity relation.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Heat content variability in the North Atlantic Ocean in ocean reanalyses|doi=10.1002/2015GL063299|author1=Sirpa Häkkinen |author2=Peter B Rhines |author3=Denise L Worthen |year=2015|pmc=4681455|pmid=26709321|volume=42|issue=8|journal=Geophys Res Lett|pages=2901–2909|bibcode=2015GeoRL..42.2901H}}</ref> Additionally, a study from 2022 on anthropogenic warming in the ocean indicates that 62% of the warming from the years between 1850 and 2018 in the North Atlantic along 25°N is kept in the water below 700 m, where a major percentage of the ocean's surplus heat is stored.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Messias |first1=Marie-José |last2=Mercier |first2=Herlé |title=The redistribution of anthropogenic excess heat is a key driver of warming in the North Atlantic |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=17 May 2022 |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=118 |doi=10.1038/s43247-022-00443-4 |bibcode=2022ComEE...3..118M |s2cid=248816280 |language=en |issn=2662-4435|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A study in 2015 concluded that ocean heat content increases by the Pacific Ocean were compensated by an abrupt distribution of OHC into the Indian Ocean.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Sang-Ki |last2=Park |first2=Wonsun |last3=Baringer |first3=Molly O. |last4=Gordon |first4=Arnold L. |last5=Huber |first5=Bruce |last6=Liu |first6=Yanyun |date=June 2015 |title=Pacific origin of the abrupt increase in Indian Ocean heat content during the warming hiatus |journal=Nature Geoscience |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=445–449 |bibcode=2015NatGe...8..445L |doi=10.1038/ngeo2438 |hdl-access=free |hdl=1834/9681|url=http://oceanrep.geomar.de/28807/3/pm_2015_23_indo-pacific_en.pdf }}</ref>

A large-ensemble reanalysis of ocean warming published in 2024 estimated a 1961–2022 warming trend of 0.43{{nbsp}}±{{nbsp}}0.08{{nbsp}}W/m², along with a statistically significant acceleration rate of 0.15{{nbsp}}±{{nbsp}}0.04{{nbsp}}W/m² per{{nbsp}}decade<ref name="Storto-2024"/> which is consistent with similar independent analysis.<ref name="Li-2023" /><ref name="Miniere-2023" /> The net rate of change in the top 2000&nbsp;meters from 2003 to 2018 was {{val|+0.58|0.08|u=W/m2}} (or annual mean energy gain of 9.3&nbsp;[[zettajoules]]).<ref name=":0" />

=== Southern Ocean Heat Uptake ===
{{excerpt|Southern Ocean overturning circulation#Climate change impacts|paragraphs=1|files=no}}

== Impacts ==
{{Further|Ocean temperature|Effects of climate change on oceans}}
Warming oceans are one reason for [[coral bleaching]]<ref name="theguardian.com">{{Cite news |date=6 June 2016 |title=The Great Barrier Reef: a catastrophe laid bare |newspaper=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2016/jun/07/the-great-barrier-reef-a-catastrophe-laid-bare}}</ref> and contribute to the [[Migration of marine species in the Northern Atlantic Ocean|migration of marine species]].<ref name="Polo-2013" /> [[Marine heat wave]]s are regions of life-threatening and persistently elevated water temperatures.<ref>{{cite web |date=2019-10-08 |title=So what are marine heat waves? - A NOAA scientist explains |url=https://research.noaa.gov/article/ArtMID/587/ArticleID/2559/So-what-are-marine-heat-waves |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |access-date=2021-10-12 |archive-date=2022-01-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124041431/https://research.noaa.gov/article/ArtMID/587/ArticleID/2559/So-what-are-marine-heat-waves }}</ref> Redistribution of the planet's internal energy by [[atmospheric circulation]] and [[ocean currents]] produces internal [[climate variability]], often in the form of irregular [[climate oscillation|oscillations]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=El Niño & Other Oscillations |url=https://www.whoi.edu/main/topic/el-nino-other-oscillations |access-date=2021-10-08 |website=Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution}}</ref> and helps to sustain the global [[thermohaline circulation]].<ref name="Rahm-2003" /><ref name="Rahm-2015" />

The increase in OHC accounts for 30–40% of global [[sea-level rise]] from 1900 to 2020 because of [[thermal expansion]].<ref name="Fred-2020" /><ref>{{cite web |date=2020-08-21 |title=NASA-led study reveals the causes of sea level rise since 1900 |url=https://sealevel.nasa.gov/news/191/nasa-led-study-reveals-the-causes-of-sea-level-rise-since-1900 |publisher=NASA}}</ref>
It is also an accelerator of [[sea ice]], [[iceberg]], and [[tidewater glacier]] melting. The ice loss reduces polar [[albedo]], [[polar amplification|amplifying]] both the regional and global energy imbalances.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Garcia-Soto, Carlos |date=2022-10-20 |title=An Overview of Ocean Climate Change Indicators: Sea Surface Temperature, Ocean Heat Content, Ocean pH, Dissolved Oxygen Concentration, Arctic Sea Ice Extent, Thickness and Volume, Sea Level and Strength of the AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=8 |article-number=642372 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2021.642372 |doi-access=free|hdl=10508/11963 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 
The resulting ice retreat has been rapid and widespread for [[Arctic sea ice]],<ref>{{cite web |author=Rebecca Lindsey |author2=Michon Scott |date=2021-09-21 |title=Climate Change: Arctic sea ice |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-minimum-arctic-sea-ice-extent |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130715074107/http://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-minimum-arctic-sea-ice-extent |archive-date=July 15, 2013 |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration}}</ref> and within northern [[fjords]] such as those of [[List of fjords of Greenland|Greenland]] and [[List of fjords in Canada|Canada]].<ref>{{cite web |author=Maria-Jose Viñas and Carol Rasmussen |date=2015-08-05 |title=Warming seas and melting ice sheets |url=https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2328/warming-seas-and-melting-ice-sheets/ |publisher=NASA}}</ref>
Impacts to [[Antarctic sea ice]] and the vast [[Antarctic ice shelves]] which terminate into the [[Southern Ocean]] have varied by region and are also increasing due to warming waters.<ref name="Slat-2021" /><ref>{{cite web |author=Michon Scott |date=2021-03-26 |title=Understanding climate: Antarctic sea ice extent |url=https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604165512/https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent |archive-date=June 4, 2019 |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration}}</ref>  Breakup of the [[Thwaites Ice Shelf]] and its [[West Antarctica]] neighbors contributed about 10% of sea-level rise in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |author=Carly Cassella |date=2021-04-11 |title=Warm Water Under The 'Doomsday Glacier' Threatens to Melt It Faster Than We Predicted |url=https://www.sciencealert.com/warm-water-underneath-the-doomsday-glacier-threatens-to-its-main-support-point |website=sciencealert.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=British Antarctic Survey |date=2021-12-15 |title=The threat from Thwaites: The retreat of Antarctica's riskiest glacier |url=https://phys.org/news/2021-12-threat-thwaites-retreat-antarctica-riskiest.html |website=phys.org}}</ref>

The ocean also functions as a sink and source of carbon, with a role comparable to that of land regions in Earth's [[carbon cycle]].<ref name="Fried-2020" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Riebeek |first1=Holli |date=16 June 2011 |title=The Carbon Cycle |url=http://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/Features/CarbonCycle/?src=eoa-features |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305010126/http://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/Features/CarbonCycle/?src=eoa-features |archive-date=5 March 2016 |access-date=26 February 2022 |website=Earth Observatory |publisher=NASA |df=dmy-all}}</ref>  In accordance with the temperature dependence of [[Henry's law]], warming surface waters are less able to absorb atmospheric gases including oxygen and the growing emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from human activity.<ref name="Woolf-2016" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Riebeek |first1=Holli |date=1 July 2008 |title=The Ocean's Carbon Cycle |url=https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/features/OceanCarbon/page1.php |access-date=26 February 2022 |website=Earth Observatory |publisher=NASA}}</ref> Nevertheless the rate in which the ocean absorbs anthropogenic carbon dioxide has approximately tripled from the early 1960s to the late 2010s; a scaling proportional to the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide.<ref name="Trends and variability in the ocean carbon sink">{{cite journal |last1=Gruber |first1=Nicolas |last2=Bakker |first2=Dorothee |last3=DeVries |first3=Tim |last4=Gregor |first4=Luke |last5=Hauck |first5=Judith |last6=Landschützer |first6=Peter |last7=McKinley |first7=Galen |last8=Müller |first8=Jens |title=Trends and variability in the ocean carbon sink |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |date=24 January 2023 |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=119–134 |doi=10.1038/s43017-022-00381-x |bibcode=2023NRvEE...4..119G |s2cid=256264357 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-022-00381-x|hdl=20.500.11850/595538 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The increase in CO<sub>2</sub> levels causes ocean acidification, which is where the pH of the ocean decreases due to the uptake of CO<sub>2</sub>. This impacts the various species including reducing growth and calcification rates for calcifiers, lowering the capacity of acid base regulation in bivalves, and being harmful to the metabolic pathways of organisms which can lower the amount of energy these organisms are able to produce.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bock |first1=C. |last2=Götze |first2=S. |last3=Pörtner |first3=H. O. |last4=Lannig |first4=G. |title=Exploring the mechanisms behind swimming performance limits to ocean warming and acidification in the Atlantic king scallop, Pecten maximus |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |date=8 April 2024 |volume=12 |article-number=1347160 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2024.1347160 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024FrEEv..1247160B }}</ref>

Warming of the deep ocean has the further potential to melt and release some of the vast store of frozen [[methane hydrate]] deposits that have naturally accumulated there.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Adam Voiland and Joshua Stevens |date=8 March 2016 |title=Methane Matters |url=https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/features/MethaneMatters |access-date=26 February 2022 |publisher=NASA Earth Observatory}}</ref>
