======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Black carbon
======================================================================

{{short description|Component of fine particulate matter}}
{{hatnote|Not to be confused with [[Carbon black]]. For the cell phone model, see [[Samsung SGH-D900]]}}
{{Pollution sidebar|Air}}
[[Image:The Dark Side of Carbon.jpg|thumb|Black carbon is found worldwide, but its presence and impact are particularly strong in Asia.]]
[[File:Accumulation of Black Carbon Toward The Base Of The Himalayas.ogv|thumb|Black carbon is in the air and circulates the globe.]]
[[File:Aerosol Accumulation Over The Tibetan Plateau And Himalayan Foothills.OGG|thumb|Black carbon travels along [[wind]] currents from [[Asia]]n cities and accumulates over the [[Tibetan Plateau]] and [[Himalayas|Himalayan]] foothills.]]

'''Black carbon''' ('''BC''') is the light-absorbing [[refractory]] form of [[Chemical_element|elemental]] [[carbon]] remaining after [[pyrolysis]] (e.g., [[charcoal]]) or produced by incomplete [[combustion]] (e.g. [[soot]]). 

[[Tihomir Novakov]] originated the term black carbon in the 1970s, after identifying black carbon as fine [[Particulates|particulate matter]] (PM ≤ 2.5&nbsp;[[μm]] [[aerodynamic diameter]]) in aerosols. Aerosol black carbon occurs in several linked forms. Formed through the incomplete combustion of [[fossil fuel]]s, [[biofuel]], and [[biomass]], black carbon is one of the main types of soot particle<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-13|title=Black Carbon: A Deadly Air Pollutant|url=https://nomoreplanet.com/black-carbon/|access-date=2020-11-01|website=NoMorePlanet.com|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304185122/https://nomoreplanet.com/black-carbon/}}</ref> in both [[human impact on the environment|anthropogenic]] and naturally occurring [[soot]].<ref name="Anenberg, ''et al.'', 2012">{{cite journal | last1 = Anenberg | first1 = Susan C. | last2 = Schwartz | first2 = Joel | last3 = Shindell | first3 = Drew | last4 = Amann | first4 = Markus | last5 = Faluvegi | first5 = Greg | last6 = Klimont | first6 = Zbigniew | last7 = Janssens-Maenhout | first7 = Greet | last8 = Pozzoli | first8 = Luca | last9 = Van Dingenen | first9 = Rita | last10 = Vignati | first10 = Elisabetta | last11 = Emberson | first11 = Lisa | last12 = Muller | first12 = Nicholas Z. | last13 = West | first13 = J. Jason | last14 = Williams | first14 = Martin | last15 = Demkine | first15 = Volodymyr | last16 = Hicks | first16 = W. Kevin | last17 = Kuylenstierna | first17 = Johan | last18 = Raes | first18 = Frank | last19 = Ramanathan | first19 = Veerabhadran | title = Global Air Quality and Health Co-benefits of Mitigating Near-Term Climate Change through Methane and Black Carbon Emission Controls | journal = Environmental Health Perspectives | date = June 2012 | volume = 120 | issue = 6 | pages = 831–839 | issn = 0091-6765 | eissn = 1552-9924 | doi = 10.1289/ehp.1104301 | pmid = 22418651 | pmc = 3385429| bibcode = 2012EnvHP.120..831A }}</ref>{{Request quote|date=September 2024|reason=Are soot and black carbon the same?}} As soot, black carbon causes disease and premature death.<ref name="Anenberg, ''et al.'', 2012" /> Because of these human health impacts, many countries have worked to reduce their emissions.<ref name="ReferenceB" />

In [[climatology]], aerosol black carbon is a [[climate forcing]] agent contributing to [[Climate change|global warming]]. Black carbon warms the Earth by absorbing sunlight and heating the atmosphere and by reducing [[albedo]] when deposited on snow and ice (direct effects) and indirectly by interaction with clouds, with the total forcing of 1.1 W/m<sup>2</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Bounding the role of black carbon in the climate system: A scientific assessment|last = Bond|date = 2013|journal = J. Geophys. Res. Atmos. |doi = 10.1002/jgrd.50171|display-authors=etal|bibcode=2013JGRD..118.5380B|volume=118|issue = 11|pages=5380–5552|doi-access = free}}</ref> Black carbon stays in the atmosphere for only several days to weeks. In contrast, potent greenhouse gases have longer lifecycles. For example, [[carbon dioxide]] ({{CO2}}) has an [[atmospheric lifetime]] of more than 100 years.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Ramanathan |first1=V. |last2=Carmichael |first2=G. |title=Global and regional climate changes due to black carbon |journal=Nature Geoscience |date=April 2008 |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=221–227 |doi=10.1038/ngeo156 |bibcode=2008NatGe...1..221R }}</ref> The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] and other climate researchers have posited that reducing black carbon is one of the easiest ways to slow down short term global warming.<ref name="nytimes.com" /><ref name=":0" />

The term ''black carbon'' is also used in [[soil science]] and [[geology]], referring to deposited atmospheric black carbon or directly incorporated black carbon from vegetation fires.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Masiello |first1=C. A.|author1-link=Caroline A. Masiello |year=2004 |title=New directions in black carbon organic geochemistry |journal=Marine Chemistry |volume=92 |issue=1–4 |pages=201–213 |bibcode=2004MarCh..92..201M |doi=10.1016/j.marchem.2004.06.043}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schmidt |first1=M. W. I. |last2=Noack |first2=A. G. |year=2000 |title=Black carbon in soils and sediments: Analysis, distribution, implications and current challenges |journal=Global Biogeochemical Cycles |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=777–793 |bibcode=2000GBioC..14..777S |doi=10.1029/1999gb001208 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Especially in the tropics, black carbon in soils significantly contributes to fertility as it can absorb important plant nutrients.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Glaser |first1=Bruno |title=Prehistorically modified soils of central Amazonia: a model for sustainable agriculture in the twenty-first century |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |date=28 February 2007 |volume=362 |issue=1478 |pages=187–196 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2006.1978 |pmid=17255028 |pmc=2311424 }}</ref>

In climatology, [[biochar carbon removal]] sequesters atmospheric carbon as black carbon to slow global warming.

==Overview==
{{carbon cycle|Forms}}

[[Michael Faraday]] recognized that soot was composed of carbon and that it was produced by the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels.<ref>Faraday, M., Chemical History of a Candle, Harper, New York, 1861</ref> The term black carbon was coined by Serbian physicist [[Tihomir Novakov]], referred to as "the godfather of black carbon studies" by [[James Hansen]], in the 1970s.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Chen|first1=Allan|title=Carbonaceous Aerosols and Climate Change: How Researchers Proved Black Carbon is a Significant Force in the Atmosphere|url=http://eetd.lbl.gov/newsletter/nl17/eetd-nl17-4-blackcarbon.html|publisher=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|access-date=2015-01-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150106075754/http://eetd.lbl.gov/newsletter/nl17/eetd-nl17-4-blackcarbon.html|archive-date=2015-01-06}}</ref> Smoke or soot was the first pollutant to be recognized as having significant [[environmental impact]] yet one of the last to be studied by the contemporary atmospheric research community.

Soot is composed of a complex mixture of organic compounds which are weakly absorbing in the visible spectral region and a highly absorbing black component which is variously called "elemental", "graphitic" or "black carbon". The term elemental carbon has been used in conjunction with thermal and wet chemical determinations and the term graphitic carbon suggests the presence of [[graphite]]-like micro-crystalline structures in soot as evidenced by [[Raman spectroscopy]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rosen | first1 = H. | last2 = Novakov | first2 = T. | s2cid = 4284746 | title = Raman scattering and the characterization of atmospheric aerosol particles | journal = Nature | volume = 266 | issue = 708–710| page = 1977 | doi=10.1038/266708a0| bibcode = 1977Natur.266..708R| year = 1977 }}</ref> The term black carbon is used to imply that this soot component is primarily responsible for the absorption of visible light.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yasa |first1=Z. |last2=Amer |first2=N. M. |last3=Rosen |first3=H. |last4=Hansen |first4=A. D. A. |last5=Novakov |first5=T. |year=1979 |title=Photoacoustic investigations of urban aerosol particles |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9wm382t0 |url-status=live |journal=Appl. Opt. |volume=18 |issue=15 |pages=2528–2530 |bibcode=1979ApOpt..18.2528Y |doi=10.1364/ao.18.002528 |pmid=20212697 |s2cid=207276640 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628225301/https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9wm382t0 |archive-date=2020-06-28 |access-date=2019-02-01}}</ref><ref name="ReferenceC">{{cite journal |last1=Rosen |first1=H. |last2=Hansen |first2=A. D. A. |last3=Dod |first3=R. L. |last4=Novakov |first4=T. |title=Soot in Urban Atmospheres: Determination by an Optical Absorption Technique |journal=Science |date=16 May 1980 |volume=208 |issue=4445 |pages=741–744 |doi=10.1126/science.208.4445.741 |pmid=17771130 |bibcode=1980Sci...208..741R |s2cid=2201964 }}</ref> The term black carbon is sometimes used as a synonym for both the elemental and graphitic component of soot.<ref>Novakov, T., 2nd International Conference on Carbonaceous Particles in the Atmosphere, The Science of Total Environment, Vol. 36, 1984</ref> It can be measured using different types of devices based on absorption or dispersion of a light beam or derived from noise measurements.<ref name="Dekoninck">{{cite journal |last1=Dekoninck |first1=Luc |last2=Botteldooren |first2=Dick |last3=Panis |first3=Luc Int |last4=Hankey |first4=Steve |last5=Jain |first5=Grishma |last6=S |first6=Karthik |last7=Marshall |first7=Julian |title=Applicability of a noise-based model to estimate in-traffic exposure to black carbon and particle number concentrations in different cultures |journal=Environment International |date=January 2015 |volume=74 |pages=89–98 |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2014.10.002 |pmid=25454224 |bibcode=2015EnInt..74...89D |hdl=1854/LU-5915838 |s2cid=34315586 |url=https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/5915838 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

===Early mitigation attempts===
The disastrous effects of coal pollution on human health and mortality in the early 1950s in London led to the UK [[Clean Air Act 1956]]. This act led to dramatic reductions of soot concentrations in the United Kingdom which were followed by similar reductions in US cities like Pittsburgh and St. Louis. These reductions were largely achieved by the decreased use of soft coal for domestic heating by switching either to "smokeless" coals or other forms of fuel, such as fuel oil and natural gas. The steady reduction of smoke pollution in the industrial cities of Europe and United States caused a shift in research emphasis away from soot emissions and the almost complete neglect of black carbon as a significant aerosol constituent, at least in the United States.

In the 1970s, however, a series of studies substantially changed this picture and demonstrated that black carbon as well as the organic soot components continued to be a large component in urban aerosols across the United States and Europe<ref name="ReferenceC"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Novakov |first1=T. |last2=Chang |first2=S. G. |last3=Harker |first3=A. B. |year=1974 |title=Sulfates as pollution particulates:Catalytic formationon carbon(soot) particles |journal=Science |volume=186 |issue=4160 |pages=259–261 |bibcode=1974Sci...186..259N |doi=10.1126/science.186.4160.259 |pmid=17782021 |s2cid=28918312}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=S. G. |last2=Novakov |first2=T. |year=1975 |title=Formation of pollution particulate nitrogen compounds by NO-soot and NH3-soot gas particle surface reactions |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/1vj9z9zw |url-status=live |journal=Atmos. Environ. |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=495–504 |bibcode=1975AtmEn...9..495C |doi=10.1016/0004-6981(75)90109-2 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200619074525/https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vj9z9zw |archive-date=2020-06-19 |access-date=2019-02-01}}</ref> which led to improved controls of these emissions. In the less-developed regions of the world where there were limited or no controls on soot emissions the air quality continued to degrade as the population increased. It was not generally realized until many years later that from the perspective of global effects the emissions from these regions were extremely important.

===Influence on Earth's atmosphere===
Most of the developments mentioned above relate to air quality in urban atmospheres. The first indications of the role of black carbon in a larger, global context came from studies of the Arctic Haze phenomena.<ref>Mitchell. J. M., Visual Range in the polar regions with particular reference to the Alaskan Arctic, ''J. Almos. Terr. Phys.'', suppl., pp. 195–211, 1956.</ref> Black carbon was identified in the Arctic haze aerosols<ref name=Rosen>{{cite journal | last1 = Rosen | first1 = H. | last2 = Novakov | first2 = T. | last3 = Bodhaine | first3 = B. | year = 1981 | title = Soot in the Arctic | journal = Atmos. Environ. | volume = 15 | issue = 8 | pages = 1371–1374 | doi = 10.1016/0004-6981(81)90343-7 | bibcode = 1981AtmEn..15.1371R | osti = 1082154 | url = https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1082154 | access-date = 2020-03-16 | archive-date = 2021-11-22 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211122221543/https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1082154 | url-status = live }}</ref> and in the Arctic snow.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=A. D. |last2=Noone |first2=K. J. |year=1985 |title=Soot in Arctic snowpack: A cause for perturbation in radiative transfer |journal=Atmos. Environ. |volume=19 |issue=12 |pages=2045–2053 |bibcode=1985AtmEn..19.2045C |doi=10.1016/0004-6981(85)90113-1}}</ref>

In general, aerosol particles can affect the radiation balance leading to a cooling or heating effect with the magnitude and sign of the temperature change largely dependent on aerosol optical properties, aerosol concentrations, and the albedo of the underlying surface. A purely scattering aerosol will reflect energy that would normally be absorbed by the earth-atmosphere system back to space and leads to a cooling effect. As one adds an absorbing component to the aerosol, it can lead to a heating of the earth-atmosphere system if the reflectivity of the underlying surface is sufficiently high.

Early studies of the effects of aerosols on atmospheric radiative transfer on a global scale assumed a dominantly scattering aerosol with only a small absorbing component, since this appears to be a good representation of naturally occurring aerosols. However, as discussed above, urban aerosols have a large black carbon component and if these particles can be transported on a global scale then one would expect a heating effect over surfaces with a high surface albedo like snow or ice. Furthermore, if these particles are deposited in the snow an additional heating effect would occur due to reductions in the surface albedo.

===Measuring and modeling spatial distribution===
Levels of black carbon are most often determined based on the modification of the optical properties of a fiber filter by deposited particles. Either filter transmittance, filter reflectance or a combination of transmittance and reflectance is measured. [[Aethalometer]]s are frequently used devices that optically detect the changing absorption of light transmitted through a filter ticket. The USEPA Environmental Technology Verification program evaluated both the aethalometer<ref>{{Cite web |last=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |date=February 2014 |title=ETV Joint Verification Statement |url=https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPDF.cgi/P100MH5J.PDF?Dockey=P100MH5J.PDF |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009172028/https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPDF.cgi/P100MH5J.PDF?Dockey=P100MH5J.PDF |archive-date=2018-10-09 |access-date=2018-10-09}}</ref> and also the Sunset Laboratory thermal-optical analyzer.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://archive.epa.gov/nrmrl/archive-etv/web/html/vt-ams.html#bcm | title=Advanced Monitoring Systems Center Verified Technologies {{pipe}} ETV {{pipe}} US EPA | access-date=2017-10-08 | archive-date=2017-05-08 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170508153956/https://archive.epa.gov/nrmrl/archive-etv/web/html/vt-ams.html#bcm | url-status=live }}</ref> A multiangle absorption photometer takes into account both transmitted and reflected light. Alternative methods rely on satellite based measurements of optical depth for large areas or more recently on spectral noise analysis for very local concentrations.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dekoninck | first1 = L. | display-authors = et al | year = 2013 | title = An instantaneous spatiotemporal model to predict a bicyclist's Black Carbon exposure based on mobile noise measurements | url = https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/4297514 | journal = Atmospheric Environment | volume = 79 | pages = 623–631 | doi = 10.1016/j.atmosenv.2013.06.054 | bibcode = 2013AtmEn..79..623D | hdl = 1854/LU-4297514 | access-date = 2019-06-28 | archive-date = 2020-12-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201210012639/https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/4297514 | url-status = live }}</ref>

In the late 1970s and early 1980s surprisingly large ground level concentrations of black carbon were observed throughout the western Arctic.<ref name=Rosen/> Modeling studies indicated that they could lead to heating over polar ice. One of the major uncertainties in modeling the effects of the Arctic haze on the solar radiation balance was limited knowledge of the vertical distributions of black carbon.

During 1983 and 1984 as part of the [[NOAA]] AGASP program, the first measurements of such distributions in the Arctic atmosphere were obtained with an aethalometer which had the capability of measuring black carbon on a real-time basis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=A. D. A. |last2=Rosen |first2=H. |last3=Novakov |first3=T. |year=1984 |title=The Aethalometer: an instrument for real-time measurement of optical absorption by aerosol particles |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1093206/ |url-status=live |journal=The Science of the Total Environment |volume=36 |pages=191–196 |bibcode=1984ScTEn..36..191H |doi=10.1016/0048-9697(84)90265-1 |s2cid=95269222 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201215011615/https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1093206/ |archive-date=2020-12-15 |access-date=2019-02-01}}</ref> These measurements showed substantial concentrations of black carbon found throughout the western Arctic troposphere including the North Pole. The vertical profiles showed either a strongly layered structure or an almost uniform distribution up to eight kilometers with concentrations within layers as large as those found at ground level in typical mid-latitude urban areas in the United States.<ref name="Rosen2">{{cite journal |last1=Rosen |first1=H. |last2=Hansen |first2=A. D. A. |last3=Novakov |first3=T. |year=1984 |title=Role of graphitic carbon particles in radiative transfer in the Arctic haze |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/1329m0xx |url-status=live |journal=The Science of the Total Environment |volume=36 |pages=103–110 |bibcode=1984ScTEn..36..103R |doi=10.1016/0048-9697(84)90253-5 |s2cid=56218357 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200612044421/https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1329m0xx |archive-date=2020-06-12 |access-date=2019-02-01}}</ref> The absorption [[optical depth]]s associated with these vertical profiles were large as evidenced by a vertical profile over the Norwegian arctic where absorption optical depths of 0.023 to 0.052 were calculated respectively for external and internal mixtures of black carbon with the other aerosol components.<ref name=Rosen2/>

Optical depths of these magnitudes lead to a substantial change in the solar radiation balance over the highly reflecting Arctic snow surface during the March–April time frame of these measurements modeled the Arctic aerosol for an absorption optical depth of 0.021 (which is close to the average of an internal and external mixtures for the AGASP flights), under cloud-free conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Porch |first1=W. M. |last2=McCracken |first2=M. C. |year=1982 |title=Parametric study of the effects of arctic soot on solar radiation |journal=Atmos. Environ. |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=1365–1371 |bibcode=1982AtmEn..16.1365P |doi=10.1016/0004-6981(82)90057-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cess |first1=R. D. |year=1983 |title=Arctic Aerosol Model estimates of interactive influences upon the surface-atmosphere clear sky radiation budget |journal=Atmos. Environ. |volume=17 |issue=12 |pages=2555–2564 |bibcode=1983AtmEn..17.2555C |doi=10.1016/0004-6981(83)90083-5}}</ref> These heating effects were viewed at the time as potentially one of the major causes of Arctic warming trends as described in Archives of Dept. of Energy, Basic Energy Sciences Accomplishments.<ref>Archives of U.S. Department of Energy, Basic Energy Sciences Accomplishments, 1985.</ref>

===Presence in soils===
Typically, black carbon accounts for 1 to 6%, and up to 60% of the [[total organic carbon]] stored in soils is contributed by black carbon.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.fsl.orst.edu/ltep/Biscuit/Biscuit_files/Refs/Gonzales-Perez%20EI2004%20fire.pdf |title=The effect of fire on soil organic matter-a review |last1=Gonzalez-Perez |first1=Jose A. |last2=Gonzalez-Vila |first2=Francisco J. |last3=Almendros |first3=Gonzalo |last4=Knicker |first4=Heike |year=2004 |journal=Environment International |volume=30 |issue=6 |pages=855–870 |access-date=2019-01-04 |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2004.02.003 |pmid=15120204 |bibcode=2004EnInt..30..855G |quote=As a whole, BC represents between 1 and 6% of the total soil organic carbon. It can reach 35% like in Terra Preta Oxisols (Brazilian Amazonia) (Glaser et al., 1998, 2000) up to 45 % in some chernozemic soils from Germany (Schmidt et al., 1999) and up to 60% in a black Chernozem from Canada (Saskatchewan) (Ponomarenko and Anderson, 1999) |hdl=10261/49123 |archive-date=2019-01-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190105043157/http://www.fsl.orst.edu/ltep/Biscuit/Biscuit_files/Refs/Gonzales-Perez%20EI2004%20fire.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Especially for tropical soils black carbon serves as a reservoir for nutrients. Experiments showed that soils without high amounts of black carbon are significantly less fertile than soils that contain black carbon. An example of this increased soil fertility is the ''[[Terra preta]]'' soils of central Amazonia, presumably human-made by pre-Columbian native populations. ''Terra preta'' soils have, on average, three times higher soil organic matter (SOM) content, higher nutrient levels, and a better nutrient retention capacity than surrounding infertile soils.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Glaser | first1 = B. | last2 = Haumaier | first2 = L. | last3 = Guggenberger | first3 = G. | last4 = Zech | first4 = W. | s2cid = 26608101 | year = 2001 | title = The 'Terra preta' phenomenon: a model for sustainable agriculture in the humid tropics | journal = Naturwissenschaften | volume = 88 | issue = 1| pages = 37–41 | doi=10.1007/s001140000193| pmid = 11302125 |bibcode = 2001NW.....88...37G }}</ref> In this context, the [[slash and burn]] agricultural practice used in tropical regions does not only enhance productivity by releasing nutrients from the burned vegetation but also by adding black carbon to the soil. Nonetheless, for sustainable management, a [[slash-and-char]] practice would be better to prevent high emissions of {{CO2}} and volatile black carbon. Furthermore, the positive effects of this type of agriculture are counteracted if used for large patches so that the vegetation does not prevent soil erosion.

===Presence in waters===
Soluble and colloidal black carbon retained on the landscape from wildfires can make its way to groundwater. On a global scale, the flow of black carbon into fresh and salt water bodies approximates the rate of wildfire black carbon production.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=127577 |title=Where Does Charcoal, or Black Carbon, in Soils Go? |series=News Release 13-069 |date=2013-04-13 |publisher=National Science Foundation |access-date=2019-01-09 |quote=...findings show that the amount of dissolved charcoal transported to the oceans is keeping pace with the total charcoal generated by fires annually on a global scale. ... the environmental consequences of the accumulation of black carbon in surface and ocean waters are currently unknown |archive-date=2019-01-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190110073853/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=127577 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Emission sources==

===By region===
[[File:Gas flare, PetroChina Jabung field, Jambi, Indonesia.jpg|thumb|Inefficient [[gas flare]] that creates black carbon at a site in Indonesia]]
Developed countries were once the primary source of black carbon emissions, but this began to change in the 1950s with the adoption of pollution control technologies in those countries.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Whereas the United States emits about 21% of the world's CO<sub>2</sub>, it emits 6.1% of the world's soot.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9, at 4.</ref> The European Union and United States might further reduce their black carbon emissions by accelerating implementation of black carbon regulations that currently take effect in 2015 or 2020<ref>Clean Air Fine Particle Implementation Rule, 72 Fed. Reg. 20586, 20587 (April 25, 2007) (to be codified as 40 C.F.R. pt. 51), ''available at'' http://www.epa.gov/fedrgstr/EPA-AIR/2007/April/Day-25/a6347.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081019102032/http://www.epa.gov/fedrgstr/EPA-AIR/2007/April/Day-25/a6347.pdf |date=2008-10-19 }}; Press Release, European Union, Environment: Commission welcomes final adoption of the air quality directive, (April 14, 2008), ''available at'' http://europa.eu/rapid/pressReleasesAction.do?reference=IP/08/570&type {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122221546/https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_08_570 |date=2021-11-22 }} = HTML&aged=0&language=EN&guiLanguage=en.</ref> and by supporting the adoption of pending International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations.<ref>International Maritime Organization, Press Release, IMO Environment meeting Approves Revised Regulations on Ship Emissions, International Maritime Organization (4 April 2008),'' available at''http://www.imo.org/About/mainframe.asp?topic_id=1709&doc_id=9123(The{{Dead link|date=October 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} IMO has approved amendments to MARPOL Annex VI Regulations for the Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships which are now subject to adoption at an October 2008 meeting.).</ref> Existing regulations also could be expanded to increase the use of clean diesel and [[clean coal technology|clean coal technologies]] and to develop second-generation technologies.

Today, the majority of black carbon emissions are from developing countries<ref>Tami Bond, Testimony for the Hearing on Black Carbon and Climate Change, U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform 2-3 (October 18, 2007), ''available at'' http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110647.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205054556/http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110647.pdf |date=2010-02-05 }} [hereinafter Bond Testimony]</ref> and this trend is expected to increase.<ref name="Reference Jacobson">Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9, at 5.</ref> The largest sources of black carbon are Asia, Latin America, and Africa.<ref>Tami Bond, ''Summary: Aerosols'', Air Pollution as a Climate Forcing: A Workshop, Honolulu, Hawaii, April 29–May 3, 2002, ''available at'' http://www.giss.nasa.gov/meetings/pollution2002/, {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080518033507/http://www.giss.nasa.gov/meetings/pollution2002/|date=2008-05-18}}.</ref> China and India together account for 25–35% of global black carbon emissions.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Black carbon emissions from China doubled from 2000 to 2006.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Existing and well-tested technologies used by developed countries, such as clean diesel and clean coal, could be transferred to developing countries to reduce their emissions.<ref>Ramanathan Testimony,'' supra'' note 4, at 4.</ref>

Black carbon emissions are highest in and around major source regions. This results in regional hotspots of atmospheric solar heating due to black carbon.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Hotspot areas include:<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/>
* the Indo-Gangetic plains of India
* eastern China 
* most of Southeast Asia and Indonesia 
* equatorial regions of Africa 
* Mexico and Central America 
* most of Brazil and Peru in South America.

Approximately three billion people live in these hotspots.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/>

===By source===
[[File:Tahmand alumiiniumpott.JPG|thumb|Black carbon on a cooking pot. Result of a biofuel cooking.]]
Approximately 20% of black carbon is emitted from burning biofuels, 40% from [[fossil fuels]], and 40% from open biomass burning.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Similar estimates of the sources of black carbon emissions are as follows:<ref>See Bond Testimony, ''supra'' note 42, at 2 (figure 1).</ref>

*42% Open biomass burning. (forest and savanna burning)
*18%	Residential biomass burned with traditional technologies.
*14%	[[Diesel exhaust|Diesel engines]] for transportation.
*10%	Diesel engines for industrial use.
*10% 	Industrial processes and power generation, usually from smaller boilers.
*6%	Residential [[coal]] burned with traditional technologies.<ref>Bond Testimony,'' id.'' at 1–2.</ref>

Black carbon sources vary by region. For example, the majority of soot emissions in South Asia are due to biomass cooking,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Venkataraman | first1 = C. | last2 = Habib | first2 = G. | display-authors = etal | year = 2005 | title = Residential Biofuels in South Asia: Carbonaceous Aerosol Emissions and Climate Impacts | journal = Science | volume = 307 | issue = 5714| pages = 1454–1456 | doi=10.1126/science.1104359|bibcode = 2005Sci...307.1454V | pmid=15746423| s2cid = 44767331 }}</ref> whereas in East Asia, coal combustion for residential and industrial uses plays a larger role. In Western Europe, traffic seems to be the most important source since high concentrations coincide with proximity to major roads or participation to (motorized) traffic.<ref name="Dons et al.">{{cite journal
  | last1 = Dons
  | first1 = E
  | title = Impact of time-activity patterns on personal exposure to black carbon
  | journal = Atmospheric Environment
  | volume = 45
  | issue = 21
  | pages = 3594–3602
  | year = 2011
  | doi = 10.1016/j.atmosenv.2011.03.064
  | last2 = Int Panis

Fossil fuel and biomass soot have significantly greater amounts of black carbon than climate-cooling aerosols and particulate matter, making reductions of these sources particularly powerful mitigation strategies. For example, emissions from the diesel engines and marine vessels contain higher levels of black carbon compared to other sources.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 13, at 5-6 (showing that shipping emissions produce more than 3 times as much black carbon as POC, while off-road vehicles produce 40% more black carbon than POC, and on-road vehicles produce 25-60% more black carbon than POC).</ref> Regulating black carbon emissions from diesel engines and marine vessels therefore presents a significant opportunity to reduce black carbon's global warming impact.<ref name="Lack et al 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Lack |first1=Daniel |last2=Lerner |first2=Brian |last3=Granier |first3=Claire |last4=Baynard |first4=Tahllee |last5=Lovejoy |first5=Edward |last6=Massoli |first6=Paola |last7=Ravishankara |first7=A. R. |last8=Williams |first8=Eric |title=Light absorbing carbon emissions from commercial shipping |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=11 July 2008 |volume=35 |issue=13 |pages=L13815 |doi=10.1029/2008GL033906 |bibcode=2008GeoRL..3513815L |s2cid=67823097 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00366464/file/Lack_et_al-2008-Geophysical_Research_Letters.pdf }}</ref>

Biomass burning emits greater amounts of climate-cooling [[aerosol]]s and particulate matter than black carbon, resulting in short-term cooling.<ref name="Hansen et al 2005">{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=J. |last2=Sato |first2=M. |last3=Ruedy |first3=R. |last4=Nazarenko |first4=L. |last5=Lacis |first5=A. |last6=Schmidt |first6=G. |first14=M. |last15=Cheng |first15=Y. |last16=Del Genio |first16=A. |last17=Faluvegi |first17=G. |last18=Fleming |first18=E. |last19=Friend |first19=A. |last20=Hall |first20=T. |last21=Jackman |first21=C. |last22=Kelley |first22=M. |last23=Kiang |first23=N. |last24=Koch |first24=D. |last25=Lean |first25=J. |author25-link=Judith Lean |last26=Lerner |first26=J. |last27=Lo |first27=K. |last35=Rind |first35=D. |last36=Romanou |first36=A. |last37=Shindell |first37=D. |last38=Stone |first38=P. |last39=Sun |first39=S. |last40=Tausnev |first40=N. |last41=Thresher |first41=D. |date=1 September 2005 |volume=110 |issue=D18 |pages=D18104 |doi=10.1029/2005JD005776 |bibcode=2005JGRD..11018104H }}</ref> However, over the long-term, biomass burning may cause a net warming when CO<sub>2</sub> emissions and deforestation are considered.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jacobson |first1=Mark Z. |title=The Short-Term Cooling but Long-Term Global Warming Due to Biomass Burning biomass emissions would therefore reduce global warming in the long-term and provide co-benefits of reduced air pollution, CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, and deforestation. It has been estimated that by switching to [[slash-and-char]] from [[slash-and-burn]] agriculture, which turns biomass into ash using open fires that release black carbon<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Menon |first1=Surabi |last2=Hansen |first2=James |last3=Nazarenko |first3=Larissa |last4=Luo |first4=Yunfeng |title=Climate Effects of Black Carbon Aerosols in China and India |journal=Science |date=27 September 2002 |volume=297 |issue=5590 |pages=2250–2253 |doi=10.1126/science.1075159 |pmid=12351786 |bibcode=2002Sci...297.2250M |s2cid=38570609 }}</ref> and GHGs,<ref name="Lehmann et al 2006">{{cite journal |last1=Lehmann |first1=Johannes |last2=Gaunt |first2=John |last3=Rondon |first3=Marco |title=Bio-char Sequestration in Terrestrial Ecosystems – A Review |journal=Mitigation and carbon emissions caused by land use change could be reduced annually,<ref name="Lehmann et al 2006"/> which is approximately 0.66 Gt CO<sub>2</sub>-eq. per year, or 2% of all annual global CO<sub>2</sub>-eq emissions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Raupach |first1=Michael R. |last2=Marland |first2=Gregg |last3=Ciais |first3=Philippe |last4=Le Quéré |first4=Corinne |last5=Canadell CO<sub>2</sub> eq. of 31.9 Gt CO<sub>2</sub> eq. of global emissions—17.25% of total. A reduction of 12% of land use emissions equals 0.66 Gt CO<sub>2</sub> eq., approximately 2% of annual global CO<sub>2</sub> eq. emissions. Lehmann's original estimates were based on a 0.2 GtC offset of the 1.7 GtC emissions from land use change estimated in 2001 by the IPCC''). See also'' Lehmann, ''et al.'', ''supra'' note 49, at 407-08. Thus, despite an increase in overall CO<sub>2</sub> eq. emissions, using Lehmann's original 0.2 GtC reduction still results in an approximate 2% reduction in global CO<sub>2</sub> eq. emissions). In a research study published in June 2022,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maloney |first1=Christopher M |last2=Portmann |first2=Robert W |last3=Ross |first3=Martin N |last4=Rosenlof |first4=Karen H |date=2022-06-27 |title=The Climate and Ozone Impacts of Black Carbon Emissions From Global Rocket Launches |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021JD036373 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres |language=en |volume=127 |issue=12 |article-number=e2021JD036373 |doi=10.1029/2021JD036373 |bibcode=2022JGRD..12736373M |s2cid=249296442 |issn=2169-897X}}</ref> atmospheric scientist Christopher Maloney and his colleagues noted that rocket launches release tiny particles called aerosols in the stratosphere and increase ozone layer loss.<ref name="space">{{Cite magazine |last=Skibba |first=Ramin |title=The Black Carbon Cost of Rocket Launches |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/story/the-black-carbon-cost-of-rocket-launches/ |access-date=2022-07-18 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> They used a climate model to determine the impact of the black carbon coming out of the rocket's engine nozzle. Using various scenarios of growing number of rocket launches, they found that each year, rocket launches could expel 1–10 gigagrams of black carbon at the lower end to 30–100 gigagrams at the extreme end in next few decades.<ref name="space"/> In another study published in June 2022, researchers used a 3D model to study the impact of rocket launches and reentry. They determined that the black carbon particles emitted by the rockets results in an enhanced warming effect of almost 500 times more than other sources.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Piesing |first=Mark |title=The pollution caused by rocket launches |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20220713-how-to-make-rocket-launches-less-polluting |access-date=2022-07-19 |website=www.bbc.com |date=15 July 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

==Impacts==
Black carbon is a form of ultrafine [[particulate matter]], which when released in the air causes premature human mortality and disability. In addition, atmospheric black carbon changes the radiative energy balance of the climate system in a way that raises air and surface temperatures, causing a variety of detrimental environmental impacts on humans, on agriculture, and on plant and animal ecosystems.

===Public health impacts===
Particulate matter is the most harmful to public health of all air pollutants in Europe. Black carbon particulate matter contains very fine [[carcinogen]]s and is therefore particularly harmful.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eea.europa.eu/highlights/black-carbon-better-monitoring-needed|title=Black carbon: Better monitoring needed to assess health and climate change impacts|website=European Environment Agency|access-date=2014-05-06|archive-date=2014-05-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506213534/http://www.eea.europa.eu/highlights/black-carbon-better-monitoring-needed|url-status=live}}</ref>

It is estimated that from 640,000 to 4,900,000 premature human deaths could be prevented every year by using available mitigation measures to reduce black carbon in the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weinhold |first1=Bob |title=Global Bang for the Buck: Cutting Black Carbon and Methane Benefits Both Health and Climate |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |date=June 2012 |volume=120 |issue=6 |pages=b |doi=10.1289/ehp.120-a245b |pmid=22659132 |pmc=3385456 }}</ref>

Humans are exposed to black carbon by inhalation of air in the immediate vicinity of local sources. Important indoor sources include candles and biomass burning whereas traffic and occasionally forest fires are the major outdoor sources of black carbon exposure. Concentrations of black carbon decrease sharply with increasing distance from (traffic) sources which makes it an atypical component of [[particulate matter]]. This makes it difficult to estimate exposure of populations. For particulate matter, epidemiological studies have traditionally relied on single fixed site measurements or inferred residential concentrations.<ref name="Dons et al. 2013 hourly">{{cite journal |last1=Dons |first1=Evi |last2=Van Poppel |first2=Martine |last3=Kochan |first3=Bruno |last4=Wets |first4=Geert |last5=Int Panis |first5=Luc |title=Modeling temporal and spatial variability of traffic-related air pollution: Hourly land use regression models for black carbon |journal=Atmospheric Environment |date=August 2013 |volume=74 |pages=237–246 |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2013.03.050 |bibcode=2013AtmEn..74..237D }}</ref> Recent studies have shown that as much black carbon is inhaled in traffic and at other locations as at the home address.<ref name="Dons et al. 2011">{{cite journal |last1=Dons |first1=Evi |last2=Int Panis |first2=Luc |last3=Van Poppel |first3=Martine |last4=Theunis |first4=Jan |last5=Willems |first5=Hanny |last6=Torfs |first6=Rudi |last7=Wets |first7=Geert |title=Impact of time–activity patterns on personal exposure to black carbon |journal=Atmospheric Environment |date=July 2011 |volume=45 |issue=21 |pages=3594–3602 |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2011.03.064 |bibcode=2011AtmEn..45.3594D }}</ref><ref name="Dons et al. 2012">{{cite journal |last1=Dons |first1=Evi |last2=Int Panis |first2=Luc |last3=Van Poppel |first3=Martine |last4=Theunis |first4=Jan |last5=Wets |first5=Geert |title=Personal exposure to Black Carbon in transport microenvironments |journal=Atmospheric Environment |date=August 2012 |volume=55 |pages=392–398 |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2012.03.020 |bibcode=2012AtmEn..55..392D }}</ref>

Despite the fact that a large portion of the exposure occurs as short peaks of high concentrations, it is unclear how to define peaks and determine their frequency and health impact.<ref name="Dons et al. 2019">{{cite journal |last=Dons |first=E. |year=2019 |title=Transport most likely to cause air pollution peak exposures in everyday life: Evidence from over 2000 days of personal monitoring |journal=Atmospheric Environment |volume=213 |pages=424–432 |bibcode=2019AtmEn.213..424D |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2019.06.035 |s2cid=197131423 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10044/1/80194}}</ref> High peak concentrations are encountered during car driving. High in-vehicle concentrations of black carbon have been associated with driving during rush hours, on highways and in dense traffic.<ref name="Dons et al. 2013">{{cite journal |last1=Dons |first1=E. |last2=Temmerman |first2=P. |last3=Van Poppel |first3=M. |last4=Bellemans |first4=T. |last5=Wets |first5=G. |last6=Int Panis |first6=L. |year=2013 |title=Street characteristics and traffic factors determining road users' exposure to black carbon |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=447 |pages=72–79 |bibcode=2013ScTEn.447...72D |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2012.12.076 |pmid=23376518}}</ref>

Even relatively low exposure concentrations of black carbon have a direct effect on the lung function of adults and an inflammatory effect on the respiratory system of children.<ref name="Laeremans et al. 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Laeremans |first1=Michelle |last2=Dons |first2=Evi |last3=Avila-Palencia |first3=Ione |last4=Carrasco-Turigas |first4=Glòria |last5=Orjuela-Mendoza |first5=Juan Pablo |last6=Anaya-Boig |first6=Esther |last7=Cole-Hunter |first7=Tom |last8=De Nazelle |first8=Audrey |last9=Nieuwenhuijsen |first9=Mark |last10=Standaert |first10=Arnout |last11=Van Poppel |first11=Martine |last12=De Boever |first12=Patrick |last13=Int Panis |first13=Luc |title=Black Carbon Reduces the Beneficial Effect of Physical Activity on Lung Function |journal=Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise |date=September 2018 |volume=50 |issue=9 |pages=1875–1881 |doi=10.1249/MSS.0000000000001632 |pmid=29634643 |hdl=1942/27574 |s2cid=207183760 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="De Prins et al. 2014">{{cite journal |last1=De Prins |first1=Sofie |last2=Dons |first2=Evi |last3=Van Poppel |first3=Martine |last4=Int Panis |first4=Luc |last5=Van de Mieroop |first5=Els |last6=Nelen The public health benefits of reduction in the amount of soot and other particulate matter has been recognized for years. However, high concentrations persist in industrializing areas in Asia and in urban areas in the West such as [[Chicago]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|last=Lydersen|first=Kari|title=Black Carbon Testing Finds High Levels|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/22/us/22cnccarbon.html|access-date=April 22, 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=April 21, 2011|quote=Major American cities generally have background levels of one to three micrograms of black carbon per cubic meter.|archive-date=April 26, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110426052735/http://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/22/us/22cnccarbon.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[World Health Organization|WHO]] estimates that air pollution causes nearly two million premature deaths per year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs313/en/index.html|title=Ambient (outdoor) air quality and health|website=World Health Organization|access-date=2020-10-04|archive-date=2014-02-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140214011748/http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs313/en/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By reducing black carbon, a primary component of fine particulate matter, the health risks from air pollution will decline. In fact, public health concerns have given rise to leading to many efforts to reduce such emissions, for example, from diesel vehicles and cooking stoves.

===Climate impacts===
'''Direct effect''' Black carbon particles directly absorb sunlight and reduce the planetary albedo when suspended in the atmosphere.

'''Semi-direct effect''' Black carbon absorb incoming solar radiation, perturb the temperature structure of the atmosphere, and influence cloud cover. They may either increase or decrease cloud cover under different conditions.<ref name="Koch and Del Genio, 2010">{{cite journal |last1=Koch |first1=D. |last2=Del Genio |first2=A. D. |date=2010 |title=Black carbon semi-direct effects on cloud cover: review and synthesis |journal=Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics |volume=10 |issue=16 |pages=7685–7696 |bibcode=2010ACP....10.7685K |doi=10.5194/acp-10-7685-2010 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

'''Snow/ice albedo effect''' When deposited on high albedo surfaces like ice and snow, black carbon particles reduce the total surface albedo available to reflect solar energy back into space. Small initial snow albedo reduction may have a large forcing because of a positive feedback: Reduced snow albedo would increase surface temperature. The increased surface temperature would decrease the snow cover and further decrease surface albedo.<ref name=JGR032612>{{cite journal |last1=Bond |first1=T. C. |last2=Doherty |first2=S. J. |last3=Fahey |first3=D. W. |last4=Forster |first4=P. M. |last5=Berntsen |first5=T. |last6=DeAngelo |first6=B. J. |last7=Flanner |first7=M. G. |last8=Ghan |first8=S. |last9=Kärcher |first9=B. |last10=Koch |first10=D. |last11=Kinne |first11=S. |last12=Kondo |first12=Y. |last13=Quinn |first13=P. K. |last14=Sarofim |first14=M. C. |last15=Schultz |first15=M. G. |last16=Schulz |first16=M. |last17=Venkataraman |first17=C. |last18=Zhang |first18=H. |last19=Zhang |first19=S. |last20=Bellouin |first20=N. |last21=Guttikunda |first21=S. K. |last22=Hopke |first22=P. K. |last23=Jacobson |first23=M. Z. |last24=Kaiser |first24=J. W. |last25=Klimont |first25=Z. |last26=Lohmann |first26=U. |last27=Schwarz |first27=J. P. |last28=Shindell |first28=D. |last29=Storelvmo |first29=T. |last30=Warren |first30=S. G. |last31=Zender |first31=C. S. |title=Bounding the role of black carbon in the climate system: A scientific assessment: BLACK CARBON IN THE CLIMATE SYSTEM |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres |date=16 June 2013 |volume=118 |issue=11 |pages=5380–5552 |doi=10.1002/jgrd.50171 |bibcode=2013JGRD..118.5380B |s2cid=140626771 }}</ref>

'''Indirect effect''' Black carbon may also indirectly cause changes in the absorption or reflection of solar radiation through changes in the properties and behavior of clouds. Research scheduled for publication in 2013 shows black carbon plays a role second only to carbon dioxide in climate change. Effects are complex, resulting from a variety of factors, but due to the short life of black carbon in the atmosphere, about a week as compared to carbon dioxide which last centuries, control of black carbon offers possible opportunities for slowing, or even reversing, climate warming.<ref name=JGR032612/><ref name="NYT011513">{{cite news |author=Rosenthal |first=Elizabeth |date=January 15, 2013 |title=Burning Fuel Particles Do More Damage to Climate Than Thought, Study Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/16/science/earth/burning-fuel-particles-do-more-damage-to-climate-than-thought-study-says.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130116135942/http://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/16/science/earth/burning-fuel-particles-do-more-damage-to-climate-than-thought-study-says.html |archive-date=January 16, 2013 |access-date=January 17, 2013 |newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name="SA011713">{{cite news |author=Bloudoff-Indelicato |first=Mollie |date=January 17, 2013 |title=A Smut Above: Unhealthy Soot in the Air Could Also Promote Global Warming: Atmospheric black carbon is not only bad for the lungs, but can also act as greenhouse particles under certain circumstances |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=unhealthy-soot-could-promote-global-warming |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130213211929/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=unhealthy-soot-could-promote-global-warming |archive-date=February 13, 2013 |access-date=January 22, 2013 |newspaper=Scientific American}}</ref>

====Radiative forcing====
Estimates of black carbon's globally averaged direct radiative forcing vary from the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]]'s estimate of + 0.34 watts per square meter (W/m<sup>2</sup>) ± 0.25,<ref>IPCC, ''Changes in Atmospheric Constituents and in Radiative Forcing'', in CLIMATE CHANGE 2007: THE PHYSICAL SCIENCE BASIS. CONTRIBUTION OF WORKING GROUP I TO THE FOURTH ASSESSMENT REPORT OF THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL PANEL ON CLIMATE CHANGE 129, 132 (2007), available at https://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/ar4-wg1.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005012229/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-chapter9.pdf |date=2018-10-05 }}. (Magnitudes and uncertainties added together, as per standard uncertainty rules)</ref> to a more recent estimate by V. Ramanathan and G. Carmichael of 0.9 W/m<sup>2</sup>.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/>

The IPCC also estimated the globally averaged snow albedo effect of black carbon at +0.1 ± 0.1 W/m<sup>2</sup>.

Based on the IPCC estimate, it would be reasonable to conclude that the combined direct and indirect snow albedo effects for black carbon rank it as the third largest contributor to globally averaged positive radiative forcing since the pre-industrial period. In comparison, the more recent direct radiative forcing estimate by Ramanathan and Carmichael<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> would lead one to conclude that black carbon has contributed the second largest globally averaged radiative forcing after carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), and that the radiative forcing of black carbon is "as much as 55% of the CO<sub>2</sub> forcing and is larger than the forcing due to the other greenhouse gasses (GHGs) such as CH<sub>4</sub>, CFCs, N<sub>2</sub>O, or tropospheric ozone."

'''Table 1: Estimates of Black Carbon Radiative Forcing, by Effect'''
{| class="wikitable"
