====Effects on Arctic ice and Himalayan glaciers====
According to the {{abbr|IPCC|Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change}}, "the presence of black carbon over highly reflective surfaces, such as snow and ice, or clouds, may cause a significant positive radiative forcing".<ref>IPCC, ''supra'' note 13, at 397. ("While the radiative forcing is generally negative, positive forcing occurs in areas with a very high surface reflectance such as desert regions in North Africa, and the snow fields of the Himalayas.")</ref><ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004"/> The IPCC also notes that emissions from [[biomass]] burning, which usually have a negative forcing,<ref name="Hansen et al 2005"/> have a positive forcing over snow fields in areas such as the Himalayas.<ref>IPCC, ''supra'' note 13, at 397.</ref> A 2013 study quantified that [[gas flare]]s contributed over 40% of the black carbon deposited in the Arctic.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stohl |first1=A. |last2=Klimont |first2=Z. |last3=Eckhardt |first3=S. |last4=Kupiainen |first4=K. |last5=Shevchenko |first5=V. P. |last6=Kopeikin |first6=V. M. |last7=Novigatsky |first7=A. N. |title=Black carbon in the Arctic: the underestimated role of gas flaring and residential combustion emissions |journal=Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics |date=5 September 2013 |volume=13 |issue=17 |pages=8833–8855 |doi=10.5194/acp-13-8833-2013 |bibcode=2013ACP....13.8833S |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://arctic-council.org/images/PDF_attachments/COP24_2018/2018-11-10-COP24-Stanley-flaring-World-Bank-BC.pdf |title=Gas flaring: An industry practice faces increasing global attention |author=Michael Stanley |publisher=World Bank |date=2018-12-10 |access-date=2020-01-20 |archive-date=2019-02-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215231453/https://www.arctic-council.org/images/PDF_attachments/COP24_2018/2018-11-10-COP24-Stanley-flaring-World-Bank-BC.pdf }}</ref>

According to Charles Zender, black carbon is a significant contributor to Arctic ice-melt, and reducing such emissions may be "the most efficient way to mitigate Arctic warming that we know of".<ref>Zender Testimony, ''supra''note 3, at 6.</ref> The "climate forcing due to snow/ice albedo change is of the order of 1.0&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup> at middle- and high-latitude land areas in the Northern Hemisphere and over the Arctic Ocean."<ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004"/> The "soot effect on snow albedo may be responsible for a quarter of observed global warming".<ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004"/> "Soot deposition increases surface melt on ice masses, and the meltwater spurs multiple radiative and dynamical feedback processes that accelerate ice disintegration," according to [[NASA]] scientists James Hansen and Larissa Nazarenko.<ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004"/> As a result of this feedback process, "BC on snow warms the planet about three times more than an equal forcing of CO<sub>2</sub>."<ref>See ''supra'' note 18</ref> When black carbon concentrations in the Arctic increase during the winter and spring due to [[Arctic Haze]], surface temperatures increase by 0.5&nbsp;°C.<ref name="Quinn et al 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Quinn |first1=P. K. |last2=Bates |first2=T. S. |last3=Baum |first3=E. |last4=Doubleday |first4=N. |last5=Fiore |first5=A. M. |last6=Flanner |first6=M. |last7=Fridlind |first7=A. |last8=Garrett |first8=T. J. |last9=Koch |first9=D. |last10=Menon |first10=S. |last11=Shindell |first11=D. |last12=Stohl |first12=A. |last13=Warren |first13=S. G. |title=Short-lived pollutants in the Arctic: their climate impact and possible mitigation strategies |journal=Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics |date=25 March 2008 |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=1723–1735 |doi=10.5194/acp-8-1723-2008 |bibcode=2008ACP.....8.1723Q |s2cid=15048988 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Shukman |first1=David |title=Vast cracks appear in Arctic ice |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/7417123.stm |work=BBC News |date=23 May 2008 |access-date=8 July 2008 |archive-date=26 May 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080526021959/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/7417123.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Black carbon emissions also significantly contribute to Arctic ice-melt, which is critical because "nothing in climate is more aptly described as a 'tipping point' than the 0&nbsp;°C boundary that separates frozen from liquid water—the bright, reflective snow and ice from the dark, heat-absorbing ocean."<ref>Charles Zender, Written Testimony for the Hearing on Black Carbon and Climate Change, U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform 1 (18 October 2007),''available at'' http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110919.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205054543/http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110919.pdf |date=2010-02-05 }} [hereinafter Zender Testimony].</ref>

Black carbon emissions from northern Eurasia, North America, and Asia have the greatest absolute impact on Arctic warming.<ref name="Quinn et al 2008"/> However, black carbon emissions actually occurring within the Arctic have a disproportionately larger impact per particle on Arctic warming than emissions originating elsewhere.<ref name="Quinn et al 2008"/> As Arctic ice melts and shipping activity increases, emissions originating within the Arctic are expected to rise.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=J. |last2=Sato |first2=M. |last3=Ruedy |first3=R. |last4=Kharecha |first4=P. |last5=Lacis |first5=A. |last6=Miller |first6=R. |last7=Nazarenko |first7=L. |last8=Lo |first8=K. |last9=Schmidt |first9=G. A. |last10=Russell |first10=G. |last11=Aleinov |first11=I. |last12=Bauer |first12=S. |last13=Baum |first13=E. |last14=Cairns |first14=B. |last15=Canuto |first15=V. |last16=Chandler |first16=M. |last17=Cheng |first17=Y. |last18=Cohen |first18=A. |last19=Del Genio |first19=A. |last20=Faluvegi |first20=G. |last21=Fleming |first21=E. |last22=Friend |first22=A. |last23=Hall |first23=T. |last24=Jackman |first24=C. |last25=Jonas |first25=J. |last26=Kelley |first26=M. |last27=Kiang |first27=N. Y. |last28=Koch |first28=D. |last29=Labow |first29=G. |last30=Lerner |first30=J. |last31=Menon |first31=S. |last32=Novakov |first32=T. |last33=Oinas |first33=V. |last34=Perlwitz |first34=Ja. |last35=Perlwitz |first35=Ju. |last36=Rind |first36=D. |last37=Romanou |first37=A. |last38=Schmunk |first38=R. |last39=Shindell |first39=D. |last40=Stone |first40=P. |last41=Sun |first41=S. |last42=Streets |first42=D. |last43=Tausnev |first43=N. |last44=Thresher |first44=D. |last45=Unger |first45=N. |last46=Yao |first46=M. |last47=Zhang |first47=S. |title=Dangerous human-made interference with climate: a GISS modelE study |journal=Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics |date=7 May 2007 |volume=7 |issue=9 |pages=2287–2312 |doi=10.5194/acp-7-2287-2007 |arxiv=physics/0610115 |bibcode=2007ACP.....7.2287H |s2cid=14992639 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In some regions, such as the Himalayas, the impact of black carbon on melting snowpack and glaciers may be equal to that of CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Warmer air resulting from the presence of black carbon in South and East Asia over the Himalayas contributes to a warming of approximately 0.6&nbsp;°C.<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> An "analysis of temperature trends on the Tibetan side of the Himalayas reveals warming in excess of 1 °C."<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> A summer aerosol sampling on a glacier saddle of Mt. Everest (Qomolangma) in 2003 showed industrially induced sulfate from South Asia may cross over the highly elevated Himalaya.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = Jing | last2 = Zhang | first2 = Dongqi | last3 = Kang | first3 = Shichang | display-authors = etal | year = 2007 | title = Aerosol and fresh snow chemistry in the East Rongbuk Glacier on the northern slope of Mt. Qomolangma (Everest) | journal = J. Geophys. Res. | volume = 112 | issue = D15| page = D15307 | doi = 10.1029/2007JD008618 | bibcode = 2007JGRD..11215307M | doi-access = free }}</ref> This indicated BC in South Asia could also have the same transport mode. And such kind of signal might have been detected in at a black carbon monitoring site in the hinterland of Tibet.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = Jing | last2 = Xiao | first2 = Cunde | last3 = Sun | first3 = Junying | display-authors = etal | year = 2010 | title = Carbonaceous particles in the atmosphere and precipitation of the Nam Co region, central Tibet | journal = J. Environ. Sci.-CHINA | volume = 22 | issue = 11| pages = 1748–1756 | doi = 10.1016/s1001-0742(09)60315-6 | pmid = 21235163 | bibcode = 2010JEnvS..22.1748M }}</ref> Snow sampling and measurement suggested black carbon deposited in some Himalayan glaciers may reduce the surface albedo by 0.01–0.02.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = Jing | last2 = Xiao | first2 = Cunde | last3 = Cachier | first3 = Helene | display-authors = etal | year = 2009 | title = Black carbon in the snow of glaciers in west China and its potential effects on albedos | journal = Atmos. Res. | volume = 92 | issue = 1| pages = 114–123 | doi = 10.1016/j.atmosres.2008.09.007 | bibcode = 2009AtmRe..92..114M }}</ref> Black carbon record based on a shallow ice core drilled from the East Rongbuk glacier showed a dramatic increasing trend of black carbon concentrations in the ice stratigraphy since the 1990s, and simulated average radiative forcing caused by black carbon was nearly 2&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup> in 2002.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = Jing | last2 = Cachier | first2 = H. | last3 = Xiao | first3 = C. |display-authors=et al | year = 2008 | title = Black carbon record based on a shallow Himalayan ice core and its climatic implications | journal = Atmos. Chem. Phys. | volume = 8 | issue = 5| pages = 1343–1352 | doi=10.5194/acp-8-1343-2008| bibcode = 2008ACP.....8.1343M | doi-access = free }}</ref> This large warming trend is the proposed causal factor for the accelerating retreat of Himalayan glaciers,<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> which threatens fresh water supplies and food security in China and India.<ref>Lester R. Brown, ''Melting Mountain Glaciers Will Shrink Grain Harvests in China and India'', PLAN B UPDATE, Earth Policy Institute (20 March 2008), ''available at'' http://www.earth-policy.org/Updates/2008/Update71.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080717103222/http://www.earth-policy.org/Updates/2008/Update71.htm |date=2008-07-17 }} (Melting Himalayan glaciers will soon reduce water supply for major Chinese and Indian rivers (Ganges, Yellow River, Yangtze River) that irrigate rice and wheat crops that feed hundreds of millions and "could lead to politically unmanageable food shortages".).</ref> A general darkening trend in the mid-Himalaya glaciers revealed by MODIS data since 2000 could be partially attributed to black carbon and light absorbing impurities like dust in the springtime, which was later extended to the whole Hindu Kush-Kararoram-Himalaya glaciers research finding a widespread darkening trend of -0.001&nbsp;yr<sup>−1</sup> over the period of 2000–2011.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = Jing | last2 = Du | first2 = Zhencai | last3 = Xiao | first3 = Cunde | display-authors = etal | year = 2012 | title = Darkening of the mid-Himalaya glaciers since 2000 and the potential causes | journal = Environ. Res. Lett. | volume = 7 | issue = 1| article-number = 014021 | doi = 10.1088/1748-9326/7/1/014021 | bibcode = 2012ERL.....7a4021M | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Ming, J 2015">{{cite journal | last1 = Ming | first1 = J | last2 = Wang | first2 = Y | last3 = Du | first3 = Z | last4 = Zhang | first4 = T | last5 = Guo | first5 = W | last6 = Xiao | first6 = C | last7 = Xu | first7 = X | last8 = Ding | first8 = M | last9 = Zhang | first9 = D | last10 = Yang | first10 = W | year = 2015 | title = Widespread albedo decreasing and induced melting of Himalayan snow and ice in the early 21st century | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 10 | issue = 6| article-number = e0126235 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0126235 | pmid = 26039088 | pmc = 4454657 | bibcode = 2015PLoSO..1026235M | doi-access = free }}</ref> The most rapid decrease in albedo (more negative than -0.0015&nbsp;yr<sup>−1</sup>) occurred in the altitudes over 5500&nbsp;m above sea level.<ref name="Ming, J 2015"/>

===Global warming===
In its 2007 report, the IPCC estimated for the first time the direct [[radiative forcing]] of black carbon from fossil fuel emissions at +&nbsp;0.2&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup>, and the radiative forcing of black carbon through its effect on the surface albedo of snow and ice at an additional +&nbsp;0.1&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup>.<ref>IPCC, ''Changes in Atmospheric Constituents and in Radiative Forcing'', in CLIMATE CHANGE 2007: THE PHYSICAL SCIENCE BASIS. CONTRIBUTION OF WORKING GROUP I TO THE FOURTH ASSESSMENT REPORT OF THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL PANEL ON CLIMATE CHANGE 129, 136, 163 (2007), ''available at'' https://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/ar4-wg1.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005012229/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-chapter9.pdf |date=2018-10-05 }}</ref> More recent studies and public testimony by many of the same scientists cited in the IPCC's report estimate that emissions from black carbon are the second-largest contributor to global warming after carbon dioxide emissions, and that reducing these emissions may be the fastest strategy for slowing climate change.<ref name="nytimes.com" /><ref name=":0">''See id''. at 164, 170, 174–76, 217–34 (citing studies by Ramanathan, Jacobson, Zender, Hansen, and Bond); ''supra'' notes 3-4 (Zender Testimony and Ramanathan Testimony); ''infra'' notes 9 and 42 (Jacobson Testimony and Bond Testimony).</ref>

Since 1950, many countries have significantly reduced black carbon emissions, especially from fossil fuel sources, primarily to improve public health from improved air quality, and "technology exists for a drastic reduction of fossil fuel related BC" throughout the world.<ref>V. Ramanathan, Testimony for the Hearing on Black Carbon and Climate Change, U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform 4 (18 October 2007), ''available at ''http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110734.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205054547/http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110734.pdf |date=2010-02-05 }} [hereinafter Ramanathan Testimony] (The developed nations have reduced their black carbon emissions from fossil fuel sources by a factor of 5 or more. Thus the technology exists for a drastic reduction of fossil fuel related black carbon); ''but compare'' Bond, T. C., E. Bhardwaj, R. Dong, R. Jogani, S. Jung, C. Roden, D. G. Streets, and N. M. ''Trautmann Historical emissions of black and organic carbon aerosol from energy-related combustion, 1850–2000'', 21 Global Biogeochemical Cycles GB2018 (2007) (Previous work suggests a rapid rise in [global] black carbon emissions between 1950 and 2000; this work supports a more gradual, smooth increase between 1950 and 2000).</ref>

Given black carbon's relatively short lifespan, reducing black carbon emissions would reduce warming within weeks. Because black carbon remains in the atmosphere only for a few weeks, reducing black carbon emissions may be the fastest means of slowing climate change in the near term.<ref name="nytimes.com">[https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/16/science/earth/16degrees.html "Third-World Stove Soot Is Target in Climate Fight"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227094536/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/16/science/earth/16degrees.html |date=2017-02-27 }} article by Elizabeth Rosenthal in ''[[The New York Times]]'' April 15, 2009</ref> Control of black carbon, particularly from fossil-fuel and biofuel sources, is very likely to be the fastest method of slowing global warming in the immediate future,<ref name="ReferenceB">Mark Z. Jacobson, Testimony for the Hearing on Black Carbon and Arctic, U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (18 October 2007), ''available at'' http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110606.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205054610/http://oversight.house.gov/images/stories/documents/20071018110606.pdf |date=2010-02-05 }} [hereinafter Jacobson Testimony]</ref> and major cuts in black carbon emissions could slow the effects of climate change for a decade or two.<ref>Ramanathan Testimony, ''supra'' note 8, at 3 ("Thus a drastic reduction in BC has the potential of offsetting the CO<sub>2</sub> induced warming for a decade or two.").</ref> Reducing black carbon emissions could help keep the climate system from passing the [[Tipping points in the climate system|tipping points]] for [[abrupt climate change]]s, including significant [[sea level rise|sea-level rise]] from the melting of Greenland and/or Antarctic ice sheets.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lenton |first1=Timothy M. |last2=Held |first2=Hermann |last3=Kriegler |first3=Elmar |last4=Hall |first4=Jim W. |last5=Lucht |first5=Wolfgang |last6=Rahmstorf |first6=Stefan |last7=Schellnhuber |first7=Hans Joachim |title=Tipping elements in the Earth's climate system |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=12 February 2008 |volume=105 |issue=6 |pages=1786–1793 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0705414105 |pmid=18258748 |pmc=2538841 |bibcode=2008PNAS..105.1786L |doi-access=free }}</ref>

"Emissions of black carbon are the second strongest contribution to current global warming, after carbon dioxide emissions".<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Calculation of black carbon's combined climate forcing at 1.0–1.2&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup>, which "is as much as 55% of the CO<sub>2</sub> forcing and is larger than the forcing due to the other [GHGs] such as CH<sub>4</sub>, CFCs, N<sub>2</sub>O or tropospheric ozone."<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Other scientists estimate the total magnitude of black carbon's forcing between + 0.2 and 1.1&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup> with varying ranges due to uncertainties. (See Table 1.) This compares with the IPCC's climate forcing estimates of 1.66&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup> for CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.48&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup> for CH<sub>4</sub>. (See Table 2.)<ref>IPCC, "Technical Summary", in ''Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science basis,''. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 21 (2007) ''available at'' https://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/ar4-wg1.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005012229/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-chapter9.pdf |date=2018-10-05 }}.</ref> In addition, black carbon forcing is two to three times as effective in raising temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere and the Arctic than equivalent forcing values of CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004">{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=James |last2=Nazarenko |first2=Larissa |title=Soot climate forcing via snow and ice albedos |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=13 January 2004 |volume=101 |issue=2 |pages=423–428 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2237157100 |pmid=14699053 |pmc=327163 |bibcode=2004PNAS..101..423H |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Flanner |first1=Mark G. |last2=Zender |first2=Charles S. |last3=Randerson |first3=James T. |last4=Rasch |first4=Philip J. |title=Present-day climate forcing and response from black carbon in snow |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |date=5 June 2007 |volume=112 |issue=D11 |pages=D11202 |doi=10.1029/2006JD008003 |bibcode=2007JGRD..11211202F |s2cid=16698758 |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/9k7037cz }}</ref>

Jacobson calculates that reducing fossil fuel and biofuel soot particles would eliminate about 40% of the net observed global warming.<ref>Gross global warming should result in about 2&nbsp;°C (4&nbsp;°F) temperature rise. However, observed global warming is only about 0.8 °C because cooling particles off set much of the warming. Reducing fossil fuel and biofuel soot would reduce about 40% of the observed warming and about 16% of the gross warming. Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 13, at 3. ("The figure also shows that fossil-fuel plus biofuel soot may contribute to about 16% of gross global warming (warming due to all greenhouse gases plus soot plus the heat island effect), but its control in isolation could reduce 40% of net global warming.").</ref> (See Figure 1.) In addition to black carbon, fossil fuel and biofuel soot contain aerosols and particulate matter that cool the planet by reflecting the sun's radiation away from the Earth.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''id.'' at 4.</ref> When the aerosols and particulate matter are accounted for, fossil fuel and biofuel soot are increasing temperatures by about 0.35&nbsp;°C.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''id.''</ref>

Black carbon alone is estimated to have a 20-year [[Global Warming Potential]] (GWP) of 4,470, and a 100-year GWP of 1,055–2,240.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''id.'' As an aerosol, there is not standardized formula for developing global warming potentials (GWP) for black carbon. However, attempts to derive GWP100 range from 190 – 2240 relative to CO<sub>2</sub>.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jacobson |first1=Mark Z. |title=Correction to 'Control of fossil-fuel particulate black carbon and organic matter, possibly the most effective method of slowing global warming' |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres |date=27 July 2005 |volume=110 |issue=D14 |article-number=2005JD005888 |pages=n/a |doi=10.1029/2005JD005888 |bibcode=2005JGRD..11014105J }}</ref><ref name=pmid17513270/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bond |first1=Tami C. |last2=Sun |first2=Haolin |title=Can Reducing Black Carbon Emissions Counteract Global Warming? |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |date=August 2005 |volume=39 |issue=16 |pages=5921–5926 |doi=10.1021/es0480421 |pmid=16173547 |bibcode=2005EnST...39.5921B }}</ref><ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9 at 4 (GWP BC – 2240).</ref> Fossil fuel soot, as a result of mixing with cooling aerosols and particulate matter, has a lower 20-year GWP of 2,530, and a 100-year GWP of 840–1,280.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9, at 4.</ref>

The Integrated Assessment of Black Carbon and Tropospheric Ozone published in 2011 by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Meteorological Organization calculates that cutting black carbon, along with tropospheric ozone and its precursor, methane, can reduce the rate of global warming by half and the rate of warming in the Arctic by two-thirds, in combination with CO<sub>2</sub> cuts. By trimming "peak warming", such cuts can keep current global temperature rise below 1.5&nbsp;˚C for 30 years and below 2&nbsp;˚C for 60 years, in combination with CO<sub>2</sub> cuts. (FN: UNEP-WMO 2011.) See Table 1, on page 9 of the [http://www.unep.org/dewa/Portals/67/pdf/Black_Carbon.pdf UNEP-WMO report] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105162007/http://www.unep.org/dewa/Portals/67/pdf/Black_Carbon.pdf |date=2011-11-05 }}.<ref name="autogenerated1">UNEP and World Meteorological Organization, INTEGRATED ASSESSMENT OF BLACK CARBON AND TROPOSPHERIC OZONE, SUMMARY FOR DECISION MAKERS (June 2011).</ref>

The reduction of CO<sub>2</sub> as well as SLCFs could keep global temperature rise under 1.5&nbsp;˚C through 2030, and below 2&nbsp;˚C through 2070, assuming CO<sub>2</sub> is also cut.<ref name="autogenerated1"/> See the graph on page 12 of the [http://www.unep.org/dewa/Portals/67/pdf/Black_Carbon.pdf UNEP-WMO report] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105162007/http://www.unep.org/dewa/Portals/67/pdf/Black_Carbon.pdf |date=2011-11-05 }}.<ref name="autogenerated1"/>

==Control technologies==
Ramanathan notes that "developed nations have reduced their black carbon emissions from fossil fuel sources by a factor of 5 or more since 1950. Thus, the technology exists for a drastic reduction of fossil fuel related black carbon."<ref>Ramanathan Testimony, ''supra'' note 4, at 4.</ref>

Jacobson believes that "[g]iven proper conditions and incentives, [soot] polluting technologies can be quickly phased out. In some small-scale applications (such as domestic cooking in developing countries), health and convenience will drive such a transition when affordable, reliable alternatives are available. For other sources, such as vehicles or coal boilers, regulatory approaches may be required to nudge either the transition to existing technology or the development of new technology."<ref name="ReferenceB" />

Hansen states that "technology is within reach that could greatly reduce soot, restoring snow albedo to near pristine values, while having multiple other benefits for climate, human health, agricultural productivity, and environmental aesthetics. Already soot emissions from coal are decreasing in many regions with transition from small users to power plants with scrubbers."<ref name="Hansen & Nazarenko 2004"/>

Jacobson suggests converting "[U.S.] vehicles from fossil fuel to electric, plug-in-hybrid, or hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, where the electricity or hydrogen is produced by a renewable energy source, such as wind, solar, geothermal, hydroelectric, wave, or tidal power. Such a conversion would eliminate 160 Gg/yr (24%) of U.S. (or 1.5% of world) fossil-fuel soot and about 26% of U.S. (or 5.5% of world) carbon dioxide."<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9, at 9.</ref> According to Jacobson's estimates, this proposal would reduce soot and CO<sub>2</sub> emissions by 1.63 GtCO<sub>2</sub>–eq. per year.<ref>Jacobson offers an estimate of total U.S. CO<sub>2</sub> emissions in 2005 of 6270 metric tonnes, 26% of which is 1630.'' Id.''</ref> He notes, however, "that the elimination of hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides would also eliminate some cooling particles, reducing the net benefit by at most, half, but improving human health", a substantial reduction for one policy in one country.<ref>Jacobson Testimony, ''supra'' note 9, at 9.</ref>

For diesel vehicles in particular there are several effective technologies available.<ref>Manufacturers of Emission Controls Association (MECA), "Emission Control Technologies for Diesel-Powered Vehicles," 9 (December 2007) ("Diesel oxidation catalysts installed on a vehicle's exhaust system can reduce total PM typically by as much as 25 to over 50 percent by mass, under some conditions depending on the composition of the PM being emitted"), available at:http://www.meca.org/galleries/default-file/MECA%20Diesel%20White%20Paper%2012-07-07%20final.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081203144941/http://www.meca.org/galleries/default-file/MECA%20Diesel%20White%20Paper%2012-07-07%20final.pdf |date=2008-12-03 }}.</ref> Newer, more efficient [[diesel particulate filter]]s (DPFs), or traps, can eliminate over 90% of black carbon emissions,<ref>''Id.'', ("DPFs can achieve up to, and in some cases, greater than a 90 percent reduction in PM. High efficiency filters are extremely effective in controlling the carbon fraction of the particulate, the portion of the particulate that some health experts believe may be the PM component of greatest concern").</ref> but these devices require [[ultra-low sulfur diesel]] fuel (ULSD). To ensure compliance with new particulate rules for new on-road and non-road vehicles in the U.S., the EPA first required a nationwide shift to ULSD, which allowed DPFs to be used in diesel vehicles in order to meet the standards. Because of recent EPA regulations, black carbon emissions from diesel vehicles are expected to decline about 70 percent from 2001 to 2020."<ref>''Id.'', at 5, ("Mobile source black carbon emissions are estimated at 234 Gg in 2001, representing 54 percent of the nationwide black carbon emissions of 436 Gg. Under Scenario F, mobile source emissions are projected to decline to 71 Gg, a reduction of 163 Gg."</ref> Overall, "BC emissions in the United States are projected to decline by 42 percent from 2001 to 2020.<ref>Bahner, Mark A., Weitz, Keith A., Zapata, Alexandra and DeAngelo, Benjamin, Use of Black Carbon and Organic Carbon Inventories for Projections and Mitigation Analysis," 1, (2007) available at: http://www.epa.gov/ttn/chief/conference/ei16/session3/k.weitz.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204085200/http://www.epa.gov/ttn/chief/conference/ei16/session3/k.weitz.pdf |date=2008-12-04 }}.</ref> By the time the full fleet is subject to these rules, EPA estimates that over 239,000 tons of particulate matter will be reduced annually.<ref>EPA, Heavy-Duty Highway Diesel Program, available at: http://www.epa.gov/oms/highway-diesel/index.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080717101651/http://www.epa.gov/oms/highway-diesel/index.htm|date=2008-07-17}} ("Once this action is fully implemented...Soot or particulate matter will be reduced by 110,000 tons a year"); EPA, Clean Air Nonroad Diesel Rule—Facts and Figures, available at: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120730161759/http://www.epa.gov/nonroad-diesel/2004fr/420f04037.htm}}  ("Environmental Benefits When the Fleet of Older Nonroad Engines Has Fully Turned Over by 2030: Annual reductions of Fine PM (PM2.5): 129,000 tons").</ref> Outside of the US diesel oxidation catalysts are often available and DPFs will become available as ULSD is more widely commercialized.

Another technology for reducing black carbon emissions from diesel engines is to shift fuels to compressed natural gas. In [[New Delhi]], India, the [[supreme court]] ordered shift to compressed natural gas for all public transport vehicles, including buses, taxis, and rickshaws, resulted in a climate benefit, "largely because of the dramatic reduction of black carbon emissions from the diesel bus engines".<ref name="Reynolds & Kandlikar 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Reynolds |first1=Conor C. O. |last2=Kandlikar |first2=Milind |title=Climate Impacts of Air Quality Policy: Switching to a Natural Gas-Fueled Public Transportation System in New Delhi |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |date=August 2008 |volume=42 |issue=16 |pages=5860–5865 |doi=10.1021/es702863p |pmid=18767636 |bibcode=2008EnST...42.5860R }}</ref><ref name="Narain et al 2005">{{cite journal |last1=Narain |first1=Urvashi |last2=Bell |first2=Ruth Greenspan |last3=Narain |first3=Urvashi |last4=Bell |first4=Ruth Greenspan |title=Who Changed Delhi's Air? The Roles of the Court and the Executive in Environmental Policymaking |series=Discussion Paper 05-48 |date=2005 |doi=10.22004/ag.econ.10466 }}</ref> Overall, the fuel switch for the vehicles reduced black carbon emissions enough to produce a 10 percent net reduction in CO<sub>2</sub>-eq., and perhaps as much as 30 percent.<ref name="Reynolds & Kandlikar 2008"/> The main gains were from diesel bus engines whose CO<sub>2</sub>-eq. emissions were reduced 20 percent.<ref>''Id.'', at Section 3.1 ("In total there is about a 10% reduction of net CO<sub>2</sub>(e) emissions, and if buses are considered separately, net CO<sub>2</sub>(e) emissions are reduced by about 20%").</ref> According to a study examining these emissions reductions, "there is a significant potential for emissions reductions through the [UNFCCC] Clean Development for such fuel switching projects."<ref name="Reynolds & Kandlikar 2008"/>

Technologies are also in development to reduce some of the 133,000 metric tons of particulate matter emitted each year from ships.<ref name="Lack et al 2008"/> Ocean vessels use diesel engines, and particulate filters similar to those in use for land vehicles are now being tested on them. As with current particulate filters these too would require the ships to use ULSD, but if comparable emissions reductions are attainable, up to 120,000 metric tons of particulate emissions could be eliminated each year from international shipping. That is, if particulate filters could be shown reduce black carbon emissions 90 percent from ships as they do for land vehicles, 120,000 metric tons of today's 133,000 metric tons of emissions would be prevented.<ref>That is, if particulate filters could be shown reduce black carbon emissions 90 percent from ships as they do for land vehicles, 120,000 metric tons of today's 133,000 metric tons of emissions would be prevented.</ref> Other efforts can reduce the amount of black carbon emissions from ships simply by decreasing the amount of fuel the ships use. By traveling at slower speeds or by using shore side electricity when at port instead of running the ship's diesel engines for electric power, ships can save fuel and reduce emissions.

Reynolds and Kandlikar estimate that the shift to [[compressed natural gas]] for public transport in New Delhi ordered by the Supreme Court reduced climate emissions by 10 to 30%.<ref name="Reynolds & Kandlikar 2008"/><ref name="Narain et al 2005"/>

Ramanathan estimates that "providing alternative energy-efficient and smoke-free cookers and introducing transferring technology for reducing soot emissions from coal combustion in small industries could have major impacts on the radiative forcing due to soot".<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/> Specifically, the impact of replacing biofuel cooking with black carbon-free cookers (solar, bio, and natural gas) in South and East Asia is dramatic: over South Asia, a 70 to 80% reduction in black carbon heating; and in East Asia, a 20 to 40% reduction."<ref name="Ramanathan & Carmichael 2008"/>

== Biodegradation ==

Condensed aromatic ring structures indicate black carbon degradation in soil. [[Saprotrophic nutrition|Saprophytic]] [[fungi]] are being researched for their potential role in the degradation of black carbon.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Direct molecular evidence for the degradation and mobility of black carbon in soils from ultrahigh-resolution mass spectral analysis of dissolved organic matter from a fire-impacted forest|journal=Organic Chemistry Soil|year=2006|author1=Hockaday WC|author2=Grannas AM|author3=Kim S|author4=Hatcher PG|volume=37|issue=4|pages=501–510|doi=10.1016/j.orggeochem.2005.11.003}}</ref>

==Policy options==
Many countries have existing national laws to regulate black carbon emissions, including laws that address particulate emissions. Some examples include:

*banning or regulating slash-and-burn clearing of forests and savannas;
*requiring shore-based power/electrification of ships at port, regulating idling at terminals, and mandating fuel standards for ships seeking to dock at port;
*requiring regular vehicle emissions tests, retirement, or retrofitting (e.g., adding particulate traps<ref>O. Boucher and M.S. Reddy, ''Climate trade-off between black carbon and carbon dioxide emissions'', 36 [[Energy Policy (journal)|ENERGY POLICY]] 193, 196-198 (2007) (Particulate traps on diesel engines reduce black carbon emissions and associated climate forcing but are partially offset by an increase in fuel consumption and CO<sub>2</sub> emissions. Where the fuel penalty is 2-3%, black carbon reductions will produce positive benefits for the climate for the first 28-68 years, assuming reduction in black carbon emission is 0.150.30 g/mile, CO<sub>2</sub> emissions are 15002000 g/mile, and a 100-year GWP of 680 is used for black carbon. The net positive benefits for climate will continue for up to centuries in northern regions because of black carbon's effect on snow and ice albedo).</ref>), including penalties for failing to meet air quality emissions standards and heightened penalties for on-the-road "super-emitting" vehicles;
*banning or regulating the sale of certain fuels and/or requiring the use of cleaner fuels for certain uses;
*limiting the use of chimneys and other forms of biomass burning in urban and non-urban areas;
*requiring permits to operate industrial, power generating, and oil refining facilities and periodic permit renewal and/or modification of equipment; and
*requiring filtering technology and high-temperature combustion (e.g. [[Supercritical steam generator|supercritical]] coal) for existing power generation plants and regulating annual emissions from power generation plants.

The International Network for Environmental Compliance & Enforcement issued a Climate Compliance Alert on Black Carbon in 2008, which cited reduction of [[carbon black]]{{Clarify|reason=black carbon not carbon black?|date=September 2024}} as a cost-effective way to reduce a major cause of global warming.<ref>[http://inece.org/climate/INECEClimateComplianceAlert_BlackCarbon.pdf "Jump-Starting Climate Protection: INECE Targets Compliance with Laws Controlling Black Carbon"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008024024/http://inece.org/climate/INECEClimateComplianceAlert_BlackCarbon.pdf |date=2008-10-08 }} analysis by [[International Network for Environmental Compliance and Enforcement]], June 12, 2008, accessed April 22, 2011</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Carbon budget
======================================================================

{{Short description|Limit on carbon dioxide emission for a given climate impact}}
{{About||the assessment of the biogeochemical cycle by which carbon is exchanged at the global level between sources and sinks in the biosphere, pedosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere, also referred to as the Global Carbon Budget|Carbon cycle}}
[[File:Global CO2 Pathways Using Remaining Carbon Budgets.svg|thumb|350px|This figure depicts the rates at which global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions must decline after 2024 to limit the global temperature increase to 1.5, 1.7, or 2.0 degrees Celsius without relying on net-negative emissions.<ref>{{cite web |author=Global Carbon Project |date=2024-11-03 |title=Global CO<sub>2</sub> pathways using Remaining Carbon Budgets |url=https://robbieandrew.github.io/GCB2024/ |website=Figures from the Global Carbon Budget 2024 |location= Exeter, UK |publisher=University of Exeter |access-date=2025-04-03}}</ref>]]

A '''carbon budget''' is a concept used in [[politics of climate change]] to help set [[greenhouse gas emissions]] reduction targets in a fair and effective way. It examines the "maximum amount of cumulative net global anthropogenic carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) emissions that would result in limiting [[Climate change|global warming]] to a given level".<ref name=":17" />{{rp|2220}} It can be expressed relative to the [[Industrialisation|pre-industrial period]] (the year 1750). In this case, it is the ''total carbon budget.'' Or it can be expressed from a recent specified date onwards. In that case it is the ''remaining carbon budget''.<ref name=":17" />{{rp|2220}}

A carbon budget that will keep global warming below a specified temperature limit is also called an '''emissions budget''' or '''quota''', or '''allowable emissions'''.<ref name="pmid19407799">{{cite journal |last1=Meinshausen |first1=Malte |last2=Meinshausen |first2=Nicolai |last3=Hare |first3=William |last4=Raper |first4=Sarah C. B. |last5=Frieler |first5=Katja |last6=Knutti |first6=Reto |last7=Frame |first7=David J. |last8=Allen |first8=Myles R. |title=Greenhouse-gas emission targets for limiting global warming to 2 °C |journal=Nature |date=April 2009 |volume=458 |issue=7242 |pages=1158–1162 |doi=10.1038/nature08017 |pmid=19407799 |bibcode=2009Natur.458.1158M |s2cid=4342402 }}</ref><ref name="matthews">{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=H Damon |last2=Zickfeld |first2=Kirsten |last3=Knutti |first3=Reto |last4=Allen |first4=Myles R |title=Focus on cumulative emissions, global carbon budgets and the implications for climate mitigation targets |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=1 January 2018 |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=010201 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/aa98c9 |bibcode=2018ERL....13a0201D |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last1=Raupach |first1=Michael R. |last2=Davis |first2=Steven J. |last3=Peters |first3=Glen P. |last4=Andrew |first4=Robbie M. |last5=Canadell |first5=Josep G. |last6=Ciais |first6=Philippe |last7=Friedlingstein |first7=Pierre |last8=Jotzo |first8=Frank |last9=van Vuuren |first9=Detlef P. |last10=Le Quéré |first10=Corinne |title=Sharing a quota on cumulative carbon emissions |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=21 September 2014 |volume=4 |issue=10 |pages=873–879 |doi=10.1038/nclimate2384 |bibcode=2014NatCC...4..873R |url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/1kv3p879 |hdl=11250/2484054 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Apart from limiting the [[Instrumental temperature record|global temperature increase]], another objective of such an emissions budget can be to limit [[sea level rise]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clark|first1=Peter U.|last2=Mix|first2=Alan C.|last3=Eby|first3=Michael|last4=Levermann|first4=Anders|author5-link=Joeri Rogelj|last5=Rogelj|first5=Joeri|last6=Nauels|first6=Alexander|last7=Wrathall|first7=David J.|date=2018|title=Sea-level commitment as a gauge for climate policy|url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-018-0226-6|journal=Nature Climate Change|language=en|volume=8|issue=8|pages=653–655|doi=10.1038/s41558-018-0226-6|bibcode=2018NatCC...8..653C |hdl=10044/1/63152 |s2cid=91593244 |issn=1758-678X|hdl-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Scientists combine estimates of various contributing factors to calculate the carbon budget. The estimates take into account the available scientific evidence as well as value judgments or choices.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Rogelj|first1=Joeri|last2=Forster|first2=Piers M.|last3=Kriegler|first3=Elmar|last4=Smith|first4=Christopher J.|last5=Séférian|first5=Roland|date=2019-07-18|title=Estimating and tracking the remaining carbon budget for stringent climate targets|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=571|issue=7765|pages=335–342|doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1368-z|pmid=31316194 |bibcode=2019Natur.571..335R |s2cid=197542084 |issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free|hdl=10044/1/78011|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=H. Damon |last2=Tokarska |first2=Katarzyna B. |last3=Nicholls |first3=Zebedee R. J. |last4=Rogelj |first4=Joeri |last5=Canadell |first5=Josep G. |last6=Friedlingstein |first6=Pierre |last7=Frölicher |first7=Thomas L. |last8=Forster |first8=Piers M. |last9=Gillett |first9=Nathan P. |last10=Ilyina |first10=Tatiana |last11=Jackson |first11=Robert B. |date=2020 |title=Opportunities and challenges in using remaining carbon budgets to guide climate policy |url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-020-00663-3 |journal=Nature Geoscience |language=en |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=769–779 |bibcode=2020NatGe..13..769M |doi=10.1038/s41561-020-00663-3 |issn=1752-0894 |s2cid=227236155|hdl=20.500.11850/454127 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":3">Canadell, J.G., P.M.S. Monteiro, M.H. Costa, L. Cotrim da Cunha, P.M. Cox, A.V. Eliseev, S. Henson, M. Ishii, S. Jaccard, C. Koven, A. Lohila, P.K. Patra, S. Piao, J. Rogelj, S. Syampungani, S. Zaehle, and K. Zickfeld, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_Chapter05.pdf Chapter 5: Global Carbon and other Biogeochemical Cycles and Feedbacks]. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp. 673–816, doi:10.1017/9781009157896.007.</ref>

Global carbon budgets can be further sub-divided into national emissions budgets. This can help countries set their own emission goals. Emissions budgets indicate a finite amount of carbon dioxide that can be emitted over time, before resulting in dangerous levels of global warming. The change in global temperature is independent of the source of these emissions, and is largely independent of the timing of these emissions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zickfeld |first1=K. |last2=Arora |first2=V. K. |last3=Gillett |first3=N. P. |title=Is the climate response to CO emissions path dependent? |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=March 2012 |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=n/a |doi=10.1029/2011gl050205 |bibcode=2012GeoRL..39.5703Z |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="pmid19516338" />

To translate global carbon budgets to the country level, a set of value judgments have to be made on how to distribute the remaining carbon budget over all the different countries. This should take into account aspects of equity and fairness between countries<ref name=":6" /> as well as other methodological choices.<ref name=":5" /> There are many differences between nations, such as population size, level of industrialisation, historic emissions, and mitigation capabilities. For this reason, scientists are attempting to allocate global carbon budgets among countries using various principles of equity.<ref name=":9" />

== Definition ==
The [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report]]s defines ''carbon budget'' as the following two concepts:<ref name=":17">IPCC, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_AnnexVII.pdf Annex VII: Glossary] [Matthews, J.B.R., V. Möller, R. van Diemen, J.S. Fuglestvedt, V. Masson-Delmotte, C.  Méndez, S. Semenov, A. Reisinger (eds.)]. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2215–2256, {{doi|10.1017/9781009157896.022}}</ref>{{rp|2220}}

* "An assessment of carbon cycle sources and sinks on a global level, through the synthesis of evidence for fossil fuel and cement emissions, emissions and removals associated with land use and [[land-use change]], ocean and natural land sources and sinks of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), and the resulting change in atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> concentration. This is referred to as the ''global carbon budget.''"; or
* "The maximum amount of cumulative net global anthropogenic CO<sub>2</sub> emissions that would result in limiting global warming to a given level with a given probability, taking into account the effect of other anthropogenic climate forcers. This is referred to as the ''total carbon budget'' when expressed starting from the pre-industrial period, and as the ''remaining carbon budget'' when expressed from a recent specified date."
Global carbon budgets can be further divided into national emissions budgets, so that countries can set specific climate mitigation goals.

An emissions budget may be distinguished from an [[emissions target]], as an emissions target may be internationally or nationally set in accordance with objectives other than a specific global temperature and are commonly applied to the annual emissions in a single year as well.

== Estimations ==

===Recent and currently remaining carbon budget===
<div class=skin-invert-image>{{multiple image |total_width=500
| image1= 1850- Global carbon budget - Global Carbon Project - offset-stacked bar chart.svg | caption1= Historical (unrestrained) carbon budget: Cumulative contributions to the global carbon budget since 1850 illustrate how source and sink components have been out of balance, causing an approximately 50% rise in atmospheric {{CO2}}.<ref name=GlobalCarbonBudget_2021>{{cite web |title=Global Carbon Budget 2021 |url=https://www.globalcarbonproject.org/carbonbudget/21/files/GCP_CarbonBudget_2021.pdf |website=Global Carbon Project |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211211094754/https://www.globalcarbonproject.org/carbonbudget/21/files/GCP_CarbonBudget_2021.pdf |archive-date=11 December 2021 |page=57 |date=4 November 2021 |url-status=live |quote=The cumulative contributions to the global carbon budget from 1850.  The carbon imbalance represents the gap in our current understanding of sources & sinks. ... Source: Friedlingstein et al 2021; Global Carbon Project 2021 }}</ref>
| image2= Fossil CO2 emissions by source of continued CO2 rise.png |caption2= Fossil {{CO2}} emissions: global; territorial; by fuel type (incl cement); per capita<ref name="10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022"/>
}}</div>
Several organisations provide annual updates to the remaining carbon budget, including the [[Global Carbon Project]], the [[Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change]] (MCC)<ref name="mcc">{{cite web |title=Remaining carbon budget - Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change (MCC) |url=https://www.mcc-berlin.net/en/research/co2-budget.html |website=www.mcc-berlin.net |access-date=27 April 2022}}</ref> and the CONSTRAIN project.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Publications {{!}} Reports Archives |url=https://constrain-eu.org/publications/type/reports/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=Constrain |language=en}}</ref> In March 2022, before formal publication of the "Global Carbon Budget 2021" [[preprint]],<ref name="10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022">{{cite journal |last1=Friedlingstein |first1=Pierre |last2=Jones |first2=Matthew W. |last3=O'Sullivan |first3=Michael |display-authors=et al.  |title=Global Carbon Budget 2021 |journal=Earth System Science Data |date=26 April 2022|volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=1917–2005 |doi=10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022 |bibcode=2022ESSD...14.1917F |language=English |issn=1866-3508 |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/545754 |hdl-access=free }}
* News report: {{cite news |title=Cut emissions "starting now" – Global Carbon Project experts |url=https://www.exeter.ac.uk/news/research/title_909259_en.html |access-date=12 May 2022 |work=[[University of Exeter]] |language=en |archive-date=12 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512104339/https://www.exeter.ac.uk/news/research/title_909259_en.html }}</ref> scientists reported, based on Carbon Monitor<ref>{{cite web |title=Carbon monitor |url=https://carbonmonitor.org/ |website=carbonmonitor.org |access-date=19 April 2022}}</ref> (CM) data, that after [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the environment#Climate change|COVID-19-pandemic-caused]] record-level declines in 2020, global {{CO2}} emissions rebounded sharply by 4.8% in 2021, indicating that at the current trajectory, the carbon budget for a {{frac|2|3}} likelihood for limiting warming to 1.5&nbsp;°C would be used up within 9.5 years.<ref name="10.1038/s43017-022-00285-w">{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zhu |last2=Deng |first2=Zhu |last3=Davis |first3=Steven J. |last4=Giron |first4=Clement |last5=Ciais |first5=Philippe |title=Monitoring global carbon emissions in 2021 |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |date=April 2022 |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=217–219 |doi=10.1038/s43017-022-00285-w |pmid=35340723 |pmc=8935618 |bibcode=2022NRvEE...3..217L |language=en |issn=2662-138X}}</ref>

In April 2022, the now [[peer-review|reviewed]] and officially published [[Global Carbon Project#Global Carbon Budget|The Global Carbon Budget 2021]] concluded that fossil {{CO2}} emissions rebounded<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=R B |last2=Friedlingstein |first2=P |last3=Le Quéré |first3=C |last4=Abernethy |first4=S |last5=Andrew |first5=R M |last6=Canadell |first6=J G |last7=Ciais |first7=P |last8=Davis |first8=S J |last9=Deng |first9=Zhu |last10=Liu |first10=Zhu |last11=Korsbakken |first11=J I |last12=Peters |first12=G P |title=Global fossil carbon emissions rebound near pre-COVID-19 levels |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=1 March 2022 |volume=17 |issue=3 |page=031001 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/ac55b6 |arxiv=2111.02222 |bibcode=2022ERL....17c1001J |s2cid=241035429 |language=en}}</ref> from [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the environment#Climate change|pandemic levels]] by around +4.8% relative to 2020 emissions – returning to 2019 levels.

It identifies three major issues for improving reliable accuracy of monitoring, shows that China and India surpassed 2019 levels (by 5.7% and 3.2%) while the EU and the US stayed beneath 2019 levels (by 5.3% and 4.5%), quantifies various changes and trends, for the first time provides models' estimates that are linked to the official country [[Greenhouse gas inventory|GHG inventories]] reporting, and suggests that the remaining carbon budget at 1. Jan 2022 for a 50% likelihood to [[climate change mitigation|limit global warming]] to 1.5&nbsp;°C (albeit a temporary exceedence is to be expected) is 120&nbsp;GtC (420&nbsp;Gt{{CO2}}) – or 11 years of 2021 emissions levels.<ref name="10.5194/essd-14-1917-2022"/>

This does not mean that likely 11 years remain to cut emissions but that if emissions stayed the same, instead of increasing like in 2021, 11 years of constant GHG emissions would be left in the hypothetical scenario that all emissions suddenly ceased in the 12th year. (The 50% likelihood may be describable as a kind of minimum plausible deniability requirement as lower likelihoods would make the 1.5&nbsp;°C goal "unlikely".) Moreover, other trackers show (or highlight) different amounts of carbon budget left, such as the MCC, which as of May 2022 shows "7 years 1 month left"<ref name="mcc"/> and different likelihoods have different carbon budgets: an 83% likelihood would mean 6.6 ±0.1 years left (ending in 2028) according to CM data.<ref name="10.1038/s43017-022-00285-w"/>

In October 2023 a group of researchers updated the carbon budget including the CO<sub>2</sub> emitted at 2020-2022 and new findings about the role of reduced presence of polluting particles in the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lamboll |first1=Robin D. |last2=Nicholls |first2=Zebedee R. J. |last3=Smith |first3=Christopher J. |last4=Kikstra |first4=Jarmo S. |last5=Byers |first5=Edward |last6=Rogelj |first6=Joeri |title=Assessing the size and uncertainty of remaining carbon budgets |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=December 2023 |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=1360–1367 |doi=10.1038/s41558-023-01848-5|doi-access=free |bibcode=2023NatCC..13.1360L |hdl=11343/338153 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> They found we can emit 250&nbsp;GtCO<sub>2</sub> or 6 years of emissions at current level starting from January 2023, for having a 50% chance to stay below 1.5 degrees. For reaching this target humanity will need to zero CO<sub>2</sub> emissions by the year 2034. To have a 50% chance of staying below 2 degrees humanity can emit 1220&nbsp;Gt{{CO2}} or 30 years of emissions at current level.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McGrath |first1=Matt |title=Carbon emissions threaten 1.5C climate threshold sooner than thought - report |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-67242386 |access-date=1 November 2023 |agency=BBC |publisher=Nature Climate Change |date=31 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=BORENSTEIN |first1=SETH |title=Earth Will Lock in 1.5°C of Warming By 2029 At Current Rate of Burning Fossil Fuels |url=https://time.com/6329852/earth-will-hit-carbon-budget-warming-threshold-in-2029-study/ |access-date=1 November 2023 |agency=Times |date=30 October 2023 }}</ref>

=== Carbon budget in gigatonnes and factors ===
[[File:Figure-2-Scientific-evidence-vs-value-judgement-graphic-v2.jpg|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|Estimating the remaining carbon budget at the global level depends on climate science and value judgments or choices. To translate a global budget to the national level, further value judgments and choices have to be made.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|last1=Nauels|first1=Alex|last2=Rosen|first2=Debbie|last3=Mauritsen|first3=Thorsten|last4=Maycock|first4=Amanda|last5=McKenna|first5=Christine|last6=Roegli|first6=Joeri|last7=Schleussner|first7=Carl-Friedrich|last8=Smith|first8=Ela|last9=Smith|first9=Chris|last10=Forster|first10=Piers|date=2019|title=ZERO IN ON the remaining carbon budget and decadal warming rates. The CONSTRAIN Project Annual Report 2019|publisher=University of Leeds |url=http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/154082/|doi=10.5518/100/20}}</ref>]]
The finding of an almost [[Transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions|linear relationship between global temperature rise and cumulative carbon dioxide emissions]]<ref name=pmid19516338>{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=H. Damon |last2=Gillett |first2=Nathan P. |last3=Stott |first3=Peter A. |last4=Zickfeld |first4=Kirsten |title=The proportionality of global warming to cumulative carbon emissions |journal=Nature |date=June 2009 |volume=459 |issue=7248 |pages=829–832 |doi=10.1038/nature08047 |pmid=19516338 |bibcode=2009Natur.459..829M |s2cid=4423773 }}</ref> has encouraged the estimation of global emissions budgets in order to remain below dangerous levels of warming. Since the pre-industrial period (year 1750) to 2019, approximately 2390 [[Gigatonnes]] of {{CO2}} (Gt {{CO2}}) has already been emitted globally.<ref name=":3" />

Scientific estimations of the remaining global emissions budgets/quotas differ due to varied methodological approaches, and considerations of thresholds.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal|last1=Rogelj|first1=Joeri|last2=Schaeffer|first2=Michiel|last3=Friedlingstein|first3=Pierre|last4=Gillett|first4=Nathan P.|last5=van Vuuren|first5=Detlef P.|last6=Riahi|first6=Keywan|last7=Allen|first7=Myles|last8=Knutti|first8=Reto|date=24 February 2016|title=Differences between carbon budget estimates unravelled|journal=Nature Climate Change|volume=6|issue=3|pages=245–252|bibcode=2016NatCC...6..245R|doi=10.1038/nclimate2868|hdl=1874/330323|s2cid=87929010 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Estimations might not include all amplifying [[climate change feedback]]s,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rogelj |first1=Joeri |last2=Forster |first2=Piers M. |last3=Kriegler |first3=Elmar |last4=Smith |first4=Christopher J. |last5=Séférian |first5=Roland |title=Estimating and tracking the remaining carbon budget for stringent climate targets |journal=Nature |date=17 July 2019 |volume=571 |issue=7765 |pages=335–342 |doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1368-z |pmid=31316194 |bibcode=2019Natur.571..335R |doi-access=free |hdl=10044/1/78011 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/scientists-have-been-underestimating-the-pace-of-climate-change/|title=Scientists Have Been Underestimating the Pace of Climate Change|last=Jamieson|first=[[Naomi Oreskes]], Michael Oppenheimer, Dale|website=Scientific American Blog Network|language=en|access-date=2019-08-21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Comyn-Platt|first=Edward|date=2018|title=Carbon budgets for 1.5 and 2 °C targets lowered by natural wetland and permafrost feedbacks|journal=Nature journal|last1=Lenton|first1=Timothy M.|last2=Rockström|first2=Johan|last3=Gaffney|first3=Owen|last4=Rahmstorf|first4=Stefan|last5=Richardson|first5=Katherine|last6=Steffen|first6=Will|last7=Schellnhuber|first7=Hans Joachim|date=2019-11-27|title=Climate tipping points — too risky to bet against|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=575|issue=7784|pages=592–595|doi=10.1038/d41586-019-03595-0|pmid=31776487|bibcode=2019Natur.575..592L|doi-access=free|hdl=10871/40141|hdl-access=free}}</ref> although the most authoritative carbon budget assessments as summarised by the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] do account explicitly for these.<ref name="IPCC SR15 Ch2">{{cite book |url=http://www.ipcc.ch/report/sr15/ |title=Mitigation pathways compatible with 1.5°C in the context of sustainable development |vauthors=Rogelj J, Shindell D, Jiang K, Fifita S, Forster P, Ginzburg V, Handa C, Kheshgi H, Kobayashi S, Kriegler E, Mundaca L, Séférian R, Vilariño MV |date=2018 |publisher=IPCC/WMO |veditors=Flato G, Fuglestvedt J, Mrabet R, Schaeffer R |pages=93–174 |chapter=Global Warming of 1.5 °C: an IPCC special report on the impacts of global warming of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels and related global greenhouse gas emission pathways, in the context of strengthening the global response to the threat of climate change, sustainable development, and efforts to eradicate poverty}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> Scientists assess the size of remaining carbon budgets using estimates of:

* past warming caused by human activities, 
* the amount of warming per cumulative unit of CO<sub>2</sub> emissions (also known as the [[Transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions|Transient Climate Response to cumulative Emissions of carbon dioxide]], or TCRE), 
* the amount of warming that could still occur once all emissions of CO<sub>2</sub> are halted (known as the Zero Emissions Commitment<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=MacDougall|first1=Andrew H.|last2=Frölicher|first2=Thomas L.|last3=Jones|first3=Chris D.|last4=Rogelj|first4=Joeri|last5=Matthews|first5=H. Damon|last6=Zickfeld|first6=Kirsten|last7=Arora|first7=Vivek K.|last8=Barrett|first8=Noah J.|last9=Brovkin|first9=Victor|last10=Burger|first10=Friedrich A.|last11=Eby|first11=Micheal|date=2020-06-15|title=Is there warming in the pipeline? A multi-model analysis of the Zero Emissions Commitment from {{CO2}}|url=https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/17/2987/2020/|journal=Biogeosciences|language=en|volume=17|issue=11|pages=2987–3016|doi=10.5194/bg-17-2987-2020|bibcode=2020BGeo...17.2987M |issn=1726-4189 |doi-access=free |hdl=10044/1/79876|hdl-access=free}}</ref>), and 
* the impact of Earth system feedbacks that would otherwise not be covered.

The estimates vary according to the global temperature target that is chosen, the probability of staying below that target, and the emission of other non-{{CO2}} [[greenhouse gas]]es (GHGs).<ref name="IPCC SR15 Ch2" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1">{{cite journal|last1=Friedlingstein|first1=P.|last2=Andrew|first2=R. M.|last3=Rogelj|first3=J.|last4=Peters|first4=G. P.|last5=Canadell|first5=J. G.|last6=Knutti|first6=R.|last7=Luderer|first7=G.|last8=Raupach|first8=M. R.|last9=Schaeffer|first9=M.|last10=van Vuuren|first10=D. P.|last11=Le Quéré|first11=C.|date=October 2014|title=Persistent growth of CO 2 emissions and implications for reaching climate targets|journal=Nature Geoscience|volume=7|issue=10|pages=709–715|bibcode=2014NatGe...7..709F|doi=10.1038/ngeo2248|s2cid=129068170 }}</ref> This approach was first applied in the 2018 [[Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C|Special report on Global Warming of 1.5&nbsp;°C]] by the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]],<ref name="IPCC SR15 Ch2" /> and was also used in its 2021 Working Group I Contribution to the [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report|Sixth Assessment Report]].<ref name=":3" />

Carbon budget estimates depend on the likelihood or probability of avoiding a temperature limit, and the assumed warming that is projected to be caused by non-{{CO2}} emissions.<ref name="IPCC SR15 Ch2" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> These estimates assume non-{{CO2}} emissions are also reduced in line with deep [[decarbonisation]] scenarios that reach global [[Net zero emissions|net zero {{CO2}} emissions]].<ref name="IPCC SR15 Ch2" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> Carbon budget estimates thus depend on how successful society is in reducing non-{{CO2}} emissions together with carbon dioxide emissions. Scientists estimated that remaining carbon budgets can be 220&nbsp;Gt {{CO2}} higher or lower depending on how successful non-{{CO2}} emissions are reduced.<ref name=":3" />

==Pathways to stay within carbon budget==
{{excerpt|Climate change mitigation||paragraphs=1|only=paragraphs}}

=== National emissions budgets ===
{{See also|Nationally determined contribution|List of countries by carbon dioxide emissions}}
Carbon budgets are applicable to the global level. To translate these global carbon budgets to the country level, a set of value judgments have to be made on how to distribute the total and remaining carbon budget. In light of the many differences between nations, including but not limited to population, level of industrialisation, national emissions histories, and mitigation capabilities, scientists have made attempts to allocate global carbon budgets among countries using methods that follow various principles of equity.<ref name=":9">{{cite journal | last1 = Ringius | first1 = L. | last2 = Torvanger | first2 = A. | last3 = Underdal | first3 = A. | year = 2002 | title = Burden sharing and fairness principles in international climate policy | url = https://folk.uio.no/stvau1/Journal%20articles/Burdensharing.pdf | journal = International Environmental Agreements | volume = 2 | issue = 1| pages = 1–22 | doi = 10.1023/a:1015041613785 | bibcode = 2002IEAPL...2....1R | s2cid = 73604803 }}</ref> Allocating national emissions budgets is comparable to sharing the effort to reduce global emissions, underlined by some assumptions of state-level responsibility of climate change. Many authors have conducted quantitative analyses which allocate emissions budgets,<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":10" /><ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Nabel |first1=Julia E.M.S. |last2=Rogelj |first2=Joeri |last3=Chen |first3=Claudine M. |last4=Markmann |first4=Kathleen |last5=Gutzmann |first5=David J.H. |last6=Meinshausen |first6=Malte |date=2011 |title=Decision support for international climate policy – The PRIMAP emission module |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1364815211001873 |journal=Environmental Modelling & Software |language=en |volume=26 |issue=12 |pages=1419–1433 |doi=10.1016/j.envsoft.2011.08.004|bibcode=2011EnvMS..26.1419N |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":11" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Kevin |last2=Broderick |first2=John F. |last3=Stoddard |first3=Isak |date=2020-05-28 |title=A factor of two: how the mitigation plans of 'climate progressive' nations fall far short of Paris-compliant pathways |journal=Climate Policy |volume=20 |issue=10 |pages=1290–1304 |doi=10.1080/14693062.2020.1728209 |issn=1469-3062 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2020CliPo..20.1290A }}</ref> often simultaneously addressing disparities in historical GHG emissions between nations.

One guiding principle that is used to allocate global emissions budgets to nations is the principle of "[[Common But Differentiated Responsibilities|common but differentiated responsibilities]] and respective capabilities" that is included in the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC).<ref name=":9" /> This principle is not defined in further detail in the UNFCCC but is broadly understood to recognize nations' different cumulative historical contributions to global emissions as well as their different development stages. From this perspective, those countries with greater emissions during a set time period (for example, since the pre-industrial era to the present) are the most responsible for addressing excess emissions, as are countries that are richer. Thus, their national emissions budgets have to be smaller than those from countries that have polluted less in the past, or are poorer. The concept of national historical responsibility for climate change has prevailed in the literature since the early 1990s<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Grübler | first1 = A. | last2 = Fujii | first2 = Y. | year = 1991 | title = Inter-generational and spatial equity issues of carbon accounts | journal = Energy | volume = 16 | issue = 11–12| pages = 1397–1416 | doi = 10.1016/0360-5442(91)90009-b | bibcode = 1991Ene....16.1397G | url = http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/3489/1/RR-92-06.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = K. R. | year = 1992 | title = Allocating responsibility for global warming: The natural debt index | journal = Ambio. Stockholm | volume = 20 | issue = 2| pages = 95–96 }}</ref> and has been part of the key international agreements on climate change (UNFCCC, the [[Kyoto Protocol]] and the [[Paris Agreement]]). Consequently, those countries with the highest cumulative historical emissions have the most responsibility to take the strongest actions<ref name="botzen">{{cite journal |last1=Botzen |first1=W. J. W. |last2=Gowdy |first2=J. M. |last3=Bergh |first3=J. C. J. M. Van Den |title=Cumulative CO<sub>2</sub> emissions: shifting international responsibilities for climate debt |journal=Climate Policy |date=1 January 2008 |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=569–576 |doi=10.3763/cpol.2008.0539 |bibcode=2008CliPo...8..569B |s2cid=153972794 }}</ref> and help developing countries to mitigate their emissions and adapt to climate change. This principle is recognized in international treaties and has been part of the diplomatic strategies by developing countries, that argue that they need larger emissions budgets<ref name=":13">{{cite journal | last1 = Pan | first1 = J | year = 2003 | title = Emissions rights and their transferability: equity concerns over climate change mitigation | journal = International Environmental Agreements | volume = 3 | issue = 1| pages = 1–16 | doi = 10.1023/A:1021366620577 | bibcode = 2003IEAPL...3....1P | s2cid = 18008551 }}</ref> to reduce inequity and achieve [[sustainable development]].

Another common equity principle for calculating national emissions budgets is the "[[Egalitarianism|egalitarian" principle]]. This principle stipulates individuals should have equal rights, and therefore emissions budgets should be distributed proportionally according to state populations.<ref name=":9" /> Some scientists have thus reasoned the use of national per-capita emissions in national emissions budget calculations.<ref name=":10">{{cite journal | last1 = Baer | first1 = P. | last2 = Athanasiou | first2 = T. | last3 = Kartha | first3 = S. | last4 = Kemp-Benedict | first4 = E. | year = 2009 | title = Greenhouse development rights: A proposal for a fair global climate treaty | journal =  Ethics, Place & Environment| volume = 12 | issue = 3| pages = 267–281 | doi = 10.1080/13668790903195495 | bibcode = 2009EPlaE..12..267B | s2cid = 153611101 }}</ref><ref name=":15" /><ref name=":11">{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=H. Damon |s2cid=87930705 |title=Quantifying historical carbon and climate debts among nations |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=7 September 2015 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=60–64 |doi=10.1038/nclimate2774 |bibcode=2016NatCC...6...60M }}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last=Neumayer|first=Eric|title=In defence of historical accountability for greenhouse gas emissions|journal=Ecological Economics|volume=33|issue=2|pages=185–192|doi=10.1016/s0921-8009(00)00135-x|year=2000|bibcode=2000EcoEc..33..185N |s2cid=154625649|url=https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/18906/}}</ref> This principle may be favoured by nations with larger or rapidly growing populations,<ref name=":13" /> but raises the question whether individuals can have a right to pollute.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last=Caney |first=Simon |date=2009 |title=Justice and the distribution of greenhouse gas emissions1 |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17449620903110300 |journal=[[Journal of Global Ethics]] |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=125–146 |doi=10.1080/17449620903110300 |s2cid=144368369 |issn=1744-9626|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A third equity principle that has been employed in national budget calculations considers national [[Westphalian sovereignty|sovereignty]].<ref name=":9" /> The "sovereignty" principle highlights the equal right of nations to pollute.<ref name=":9" /> The grandfathering method for calculating national emissions budgets uses this principle. Grandfathering allocates these budgets proportionally according to emissions at a particular base year,<ref name=":12" /> and has been used under international regimes such as the Kyoto Protocol<ref>UNFCCC (1998). "Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change".(http://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/kpeng.pdf )</ref> and the early phase of the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS)<ref>{{CELEX|32010D0384|text=2010/384/: Commission Decision of 9 July 2010 on the Community-wide quantity of allowances to be issued under the EU Emission Trading Scheme for 2013 (notified under document C(2010) 4658)}}</ref> This principle is often favoured by developed countries, as it allocates larger emissions budgets to them.<ref name=":13" /> However, recent publications highlight that grandfathering is unsupported as an equity principle as it "creates 'cascading biases' against poorer states,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kartha |first1=Sivan |last2=Athanasiou |first2=Tom |last3=Caney |first3=Simon |last4=Cripps |first4=Elizabeth |last5=Dooley |first5=Kate |last6=Dubash |first6=Navroz K. |last7=Fei |first7=Teng |last8=Harris |first8=Paul G. |last9=Holz |first9=Christian |last10=Lahn |first10=Bård |last11=Moellendorf |first11=Darrel |date=2018 |title=Cascading biases against poorer countries |url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-018-0152-7 |journal=Nature Climate Change |language=en |volume=8 |issue=5 |pages=348–349 |doi=10.1038/s41558-018-0152-7 |bibcode=2018NatCC...8..348K |hdl=20.500.11820/015eb0b4-9942-41f5-afa9-0f0c2a94deff |s2cid=90164339 |issn=1758-678X|hdl-access=free }}</ref> is not a 'standard of equity'<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dooley |first1=Kate |last2=Holz |first2=Christian |last3=Kartha |first3=Sivan |last4=Klinsky |first4=Sonja |last5=Roberts |first5=J. Timmons |last6=Shue |first6=Henry |last7=Winkler |first7=Harald |last8=Athanasiou |first8=Tom |last9=Caney |first9=Simon |last10=Cripps |first10=Elizabeth |last11=Dubash |first11=Navroz K. |date=2021 |title=Ethical choices behind quantifications of fair contributions under the Paris Agreement |url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-021-01015-8 |journal=Nature Climate Change |language=en |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=300–305 |doi=10.1038/s41558-021-01015-8 |bibcode=2021NatCC..11..300D |s2cid=232766664 |issn=1758-678X|hdl=11250/2828413 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rajamani |first1=Lavanya |last2=Jeffery |first2=Louise |last3=Höhne |first3=Niklas |last4=Hans |first4=Frederic |last5=Glass |first5=Alyssa |last6=Ganti |first6=Gaurav |last7=Geiges |first7=Andreas |date=2021-09-14 |title=National 'fair shares' in reducing greenhouse gas emissions within the principled framework of international environmental law |journal=Climate Policy |language=en |volume=21 |issue=8 |pages=983–1004 |doi=10.1080/14693062.2021.1970504 |s2cid=238231789 |issn=1469-3062|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021CliPo..21..983R }}</ref> Other scholars have highlighted that "to treat states as the owners of emission rights has morally problematic consequences".<ref name=":16" />

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Climate change adaptation
======================================================================

{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}}
{{Short description|Process of adjusting to effects of climate change}}
<noinclude>{{multiple image
| perrow = 2
| total_width = 350
| image1 = FrontLines-EGAT 2011 Environment Photo Contest Top Entry (5842818280).jpg
| image2 = Seawallventnor.jpg

| footer = Adapting to climate change involves [[Infrastructure|infrastructural]], institutional, behavioral and [[Nature-based solutions|nature-based]] approaches. Examples shown here from top left are [[mangrove]] planting and [[habitat conservation]], building [[seawall]]s to protect against [[sea level rise]], [[selective breeding]] for [[Xerophyte|drought-resistant crops]], and building [[green roof]]s to reduce [[urban heat island]] effects.
